# Patristic Insights on 2 Corinthians 12

The excerpts focus on the opening of the chapter: Paul's reluctant boasting and his account of being caught up into heaven.

## John Chrysostom: Humility and the Danger of Self-Display

Chrysostom gives the fullest treatment, centering on Paul's words "It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory, [for] I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord."

**1. Paul's true grounds for boasting are his sufferings.** Chrysostom observes that the great grounds of boasting were those which he had recounted, those of his trials. The visions are a different kind of boast, one that to the many (though not to careful examiners) seems to set him off in brighter colors. For Chrysostom, Paul's hardships say more about him than his spiritual experiences do.

**2. Pride comes from publicizing good things, not from having them.** Chrysostom reads "not expedient" as meaning 'lest it lift me up to pride.' He anticipates an objection: Paul knows about these revelations whether he speaks of them or not. His answer is that our knowing of them ourselves does not lift us up so much as our publishing them to others. In his words, it is not the nature of good deeds that uses to lift a man up, but their being witnessed to, and known of, by the many. Paul also wants to avoid giving his hearers an inflated view of him: 'that I may not implant too great an idea of me in those who hear.'

**3. Paul is the opposite of the false apostles.** Chrysostom draws a sharp contrast: the false apostles, said even what was not true about themselves; but this man hides even what is true, and that too although so great necessity lies upon him. In this, Paul is teaching one and all even to superfluity to avoid anything of the sort.

**4. A practical principle.** Self-commendation is attended with no advantage, but even with harm, except there be some necessary and useful reason which induces us thereto.

## Irenaeus: The Third Heaven as Evidence of Spiritual Realities

Irenaeus's excerpt is brief and uses the passage for a broader argument rather than explaining it. He cites Paul's experience as evidence that there are spiritual creatures in the heavens, noting that Paul expressly testifies that there are spiritual things when he declares that he was caught up into the third heaven. The excerpt says nothing about the passage's teaching on boasting or humility, so his contribution here is limited to affirming that the heavenly realm is real.

## Gregory of Nazianzus: Reverent Silence Before the Ineffable

Gregory reflects on the limits of what Paul could communicate. He suggests that had Paul been able to express the experiences gained from the third heaven and his progress, ascent or assumption to it, we should perhaps have known more about God. His response to what remains unknown is reverence rather than speculation: since they were ineffable, let them have the tribute of our silence.

Gregory then links this to Paul's statement "We know in part and we prophesy in part." He stresses that this admission comes not from someone ignorant but from one who is no mere layman in knowledge, of one who threatens to give proof of Christ speaking in him, of a great champion and teacher of truth. Even the greatest teacher confesses that his knowledge of God is partial.

## Common Thread

Chrysostom and Gregory reach a similar conclusion by different routes. Paul's reticence about his heavenly experiences is a model for believers. For Chrysostom, it guards against pride. For Gregory, it shows the right posture before divine mysteries that cannot be put into words. Irenaeus adds that the experience itself testifies to the reality of the spiritual realm.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 2: A Summary

The excerpts come from three early Church writers: Augustine, Bede, and John Chrysostom. All three read Pentecost as the fulfillment of Old Testament patterns, though each stresses different aspects.

---

## 1. Augustine of Hippo: Pentecost as the New Sinai

Augustine's short excerpt draws a parallel between the giving of the Law and the giving of the Spirit.

- **The fifty-day pattern:** Fifty days are reckoned from the celebration of the Passover (which, as Moses ordered, was accomplished by slaying the lamb, a type to signify the future passion of the Lord) to the day on which Moses received the law on tablets written by the finger of God.
- **Fulfillment in Christ:** Likewise, when fifty days had passed from the slaying and resurrection of him who was led as a lamb to the slaughter, the finger of God, that is, the Holy Spirit filled the believers gathered in one place.

**Key insight:** The "finger of God" that wrote the Law on stone is identified with the Holy Spirit, so Pentecost becomes a new giving of the Law.

---

## 2. Bede: Pentecost and the Lord's Day

Bede builds directly on Augustine and adds a point about worship and the calendar.

- **Counting from the Resurrection:** Bede notes that in the old reckoning Pentecost was computed from [the time of] the killing of the [paschal] lamb. But for Christians, it is not from the Lord's passion but from his resurrection, as the blessed Augustine explains it, that we are to calculate the fiftieth day, on which was sent the Holy Spirit, who, recalling the example of the old sign, most clearly consecrated the Lord's day to himself by his coming.
- **Implications for Easter:** By this specific time [of his coming] he also showed that the Passover was to be celebrated on the Lord's day.
- **Fire as at Sinai:** Here too God appeared in a vision of fire, as he had also in the earlier case, citing Exodus on Sinai.

**Key insight:** The Spirit's arrival on a Sunday sanctifies the Lord's Day and supports celebrating Easter on Sunday.

---

## 3. John Chrysostom: The Harvest, the Signs, and Peter's Transformation

Chrysostom gives by far the longest treatment. (Document 4, from his *Homilies on Acts* 4, is a different translation of the opening of the same passage, so the two are treated together here.)

### a. Pentecost as Harvest
Chrysostom reads the feast as a harvest festival fulfilled in the Church's mission. Pentecost was the time when the sickle was to be put to the harvest and the fruits to be gathered. Now the time has come to ply the sickle of the Word. The Spirit, keen-edged, came down in place of the sickle. Christ himself, taking [our nature] as the first fruits, lifted it up high and he was himself the first to ply the sickle.

### b. Why Visible Signs, and Why "Like As"
- **Why outward signs:** If even when the fact was such, men said, "They are full of new wine," what would they not have said, had it been otherwise?
- **Guarding against crude ideas of the Spirit:** Observe how it is always, "like as;" and rightly: that you may have no gross sensible notions of the Spirit.
- **The meaning of wind and fire:** The wind betokens the exceeding vehemence of the Spirit. He also says this betokened the copiousness, as the fire did the vehemence.
- **Fire rather than a dove:** When the Spirit was to be made known to John, then it came upon the head of Christ as in the form of a dove: but now, when a whole multitude was to be converted, it is "like as of fire.
- **"Cloven" tongues:** It is well said, Cloven, for they were from one root; that you may learn, that it was an operation sent from the Comforter.

### c. The Spirit Rests on All Believers
- The Spirit "sat" on them because the sitting is significant of settledness and continuance.
- The gift was not limited to the apostles. Asked whether it came upon the twelve, he answers: Not so; but upon the hundred and twenty. His evidence is that Peter quoted Joel's prophecy about the Spirit poured out "upon all flesh."
- He notes the conditions: when one is continuing in prayer, when one is in charity, then it is that the Spirit draws near.

### d. Greater Than the Prophets
Chrysostom contrasts Pentecost with how Old Testament figures received the Spirit:
- Elisha receives the grace through the medium of a mantle (2 Kings 13.; another by oil, as David (1 Samuel 16:13); and Moses by fire, as we read of him at the bush. At Pentecost, however, it is not so; for the fire itself sat upon them.
- Moses was the greatest of the Prophets, yet he, when others were to receive the Spirit, himself suffered diminution. At Pentecost, by contrast, each one received a fountain of the Spirit.
- He draws a Trinitarian point: where God's hand touched a prophet's tongue, here it is the Holy Ghost Himself: (Jeremiah 1:9) so equal is He in honor with the Father and the Son.

### e. The Crowd and the Nations
- The pilgrims' presence showed piety: that being of so many nations they should have left country, and home, and relations, and be abiding there.
- The list of nations is prophetic: Here is mention made of nations that were hostile to them, Cretans, Arabians, Egyptians, Persians: and that they would conquer them all was here made manifest.
- He contrasts the sincere with the mockers: they pronounce no hasty judgment, but are perplexed: whereas those reckless ones pronounce at once, saying, "These men are full of new wine."

### f. Peter's Transformation
This is perhaps Chrysostom's most memorable theme:
- He who had not endured the questioning of a poor girl, now in the midst of the people, all breathing murder, discourses with such confidence, that this very thing becomes an unquestionable proof of the Resurrection.
- For wherever the Holy Spirit is present, He makes men of gold out of men of clay.
- On apostolic unity: They expressed themselves through one common voice, and he was the mouth of all. The eleven stood by as witnesses to what he said.

### g. Digression and Moral Application
The second half of the long excerpt moves beyond Acts 2 into a lengthy polemic. Chrysostom contrasts Peter, the Galilean fisherman, with Plato and the Greek philosophers. This section is rhetorical and apologetic rather than direct commentary on the text. It ends in a moral exhortation against vainglory: Contempt of glory; this it is that is sufficient to teach all that is good, and to banish from the soul every pernicious passion.

## Common Threads

- **Typology:** All three read Pentecost through Old Testament patterns. Augustine and Bede focus on Sinai and the Law. Chrysostom focuses on the harvest feast and the burning bush.
- **The Spirit's dignity:** Augustine identifies the Spirit as the "finger of God." Chrysostom stresses the Spirit's equality with the Father and the Son.
- **Universality:** Chrysostom in particular emphasizes that the Spirit fell on all the believers and that the gospel was destined for every nation.

# Bede on 3 John 1: Key Insights

All four excerpts come from one commentator, the Venerable Bede, in his *Commentary on the Catholic Epistles*. His comments follow the opening verses of 3 John (roughly vv. 1–5), and a single theme runs through them: **true faith shows itself in concrete good works, especially generous hospitality.**

## 1. Who Was Gaius? (v. 1)

Bede starts by identifying the letter's recipient. He says Gaius's character becomes clear as the letter goes on: he accumulated good deeds in addition to the faith in Christ which he had received, and although he was not sufficient for preaching the word himself, he rejoiced to sustain those who did preach with his resources.

**Identification with Paul's Gaius.** Bede proposes, as his own belief, that this is the one whom Paul mentions in the Epistle to the Romans, saying: "Gaius, my host and the host of the whole church, greets you". He explains the title "host of the whole church" this way: he was the host of the entire church because he kindly received all who came to him, namely both the preachers and the hearers of the word.

**Location in Corinth.** Bede argues that it seems that Gaius was in Corinth, from the fact that Paul, having stayed in that city, wrote the Epistle to the Romans. He supports this with 1 Corinthians, where Paul mentions Gaius as a citizen of Corinth among those he baptized.

*Note:* Bede presents this identification as a reasoned view ("we believe," "it seems"), not a certainty.

## 2. Love "in the Truth" (v. 1)

Bede draws a spiritual point from John's phrase. John loves him in the truth, that is, he appears to love him only with the view of eternal goods, not for the sake of temporal benefits. Even though Gaius was a generous patron, John's affection for him was not transactional. It rested on their shared eternal hope.

## 3. Prayer for Perseverance and Spiritual Prosperity (v. 2)

Bede reads John's prayer as a prayer for perseverance: I frequent prayers to the Lord, that you may complete well what you do well.

He reads the prosperity of the "soul" in moral and charitable terms. It is the internal intention of your mind, which advances in abundant works of alms, and the liberality of a bountiful mind, and the resources of money which you share with the needy. The prayer's goal is that Gaius may always be able to lead a life full of virtues with the Lord's help. Bede thus keeps both human effort and dependence on divine grace in view.

## 4. The Apostle's Greatest Joy (v. 4)

For Bede, John's joy is pastoral. It is the joy of a spiritual father who sees his children remain faithful: that I recognize those whom I have begotten to God by preaching or baptizing, observing the truth both of right faith and good operation. Bede understands "walking in the truth" as having two parts: sound belief and good practice.

## 5. Faith Shown by Works (v. 5)

Bede's last comment states the theme most plainly. On the phrase "you act faithfully," he paraphrases: Just as you are truly faithful, so you act, showing your faith by your works. Gaius's service to traveling believers is the visible evidence of the faith he holds inwardly.

## Summary

Bede's reading of 3 John 1 brings together:
- **Historical identification:** Gaius as Paul's Corinthian host
- **Pure motives:** love grounded in eternal rather than material goods
- **Unity of belief and action:** "truth" includes both right faith and good works
- **Ministry support:** those who cannot preach still share in the mission by supporting those who do

Bede is the only commentator in the provided excerpts, so this summary reflects one voice from the patristic and early medieval tradition. The excerpts cover only the letter's opening verses and do not address later parts of the chapter, such as the passages on Diotrephes or Demetrius.

Gaius's service to traveling believers is the visible evidence of the faith he holds inwardly.

## Summary

Bede's reading of 3 John 1 brings together:
- **Historical identification:** Gaius as Paul's Corinthian host
- **Pure motives:** love grounded in eternal rather than material goods
- **Unity of belief and action:** "truth" includes both right faith and good works
- **Ministry support:** those who cannot preach still share in the mission by supporting those who do

Bede is the only commentator in the provided excerpts, so this summary reflects one voice from the patristic and early medieval tradition. The excerpts cover only the letter's opening verses and do not address later parts of the chapter, such as the passages on Diotrephes or Demetrius.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Romans 2: A Summary

These excerpts focus mostly on the opening of Romans 2 (vv. 1–5), where Paul warns those who judge others while doing the same things. Aquinas offers by far the most extensive treatment. The Augustine and Chrysostom excerpts are brief.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

**A note on the source:** This excerpt is labeled "Augustine on Romans 7–8," but its content plainly comments on Romans 2:1 ("O man, whoever you are"). The label may be a cataloguing error, so the attribution of this passage should be treated with some caution.

**Key insights:**
- **Past sins are in view.** Augustine notes that Paul is speaking here of sins already committed.
- **No one is exempt.** The phrase "O man, whoever you are" is deliberately broad: he includes not only the Gentile but also the Jew who wanted to judge the Gentiles according to the law.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 5 on Romans)

The two Chrysostom excerpts appear to be different translations of the same passage, so they are combined here.

**Key insights:**
- **A historical audience: Rome's rulers.** Chrysostom reads the verse as aimed at those in power. Paul says this with the rulers of the city in mind, because at that time they ruled the entire world.
- **Judging others condemns oneself.** He gives a concrete example: when you condemn an adulterer, and yourself commit adultery, although no man condemns you, in your judgment upon the guilty person you have also passed sentence against yourself. In short, when they pass sentence on someone they are passing sentence on themselves as well.

---

## Thomas Aquinas (Commentary on Romans)

Aquinas offers a detailed, carefully structured reading of the chapter.

### 1. The argument of the chapter
- Having dealt with the Gentiles in chapter 1, the Apostle now shows that neither were the Jews made just by the things in which they gloried. The conclusion: both of them need the power of the gospel's grace for salvation.
- **Historical setting:** Aquinas suggests that Jews and Gentiles converted to the faith judged each other on their previous life. The Jews objected to the Gentiles that when they lived without God's law, they sacrificed to idols. The Gentiles on their part objected to the Jews that even though they received God's law, they did not keep it.

### 2. Why the judge has no excuse
Paul removes two possible excuses:
- **Ignorance.** Ignorance is excluded by the very act of judging. For whoever judges another an evildoer shows that he knows that the conduct is evil and, therefore, that he is himself worthy of condemnation.
- **Innocence.** The reason why you, the judge of others, condemn yourself is that you are doing the very same things for which you condemn them; consequently, it seems that you are acting against your conscience.

### 3. Not all judgment is wrong
Aquinas is careful to say that this does not mean that every judgment is a cause of condemnation.
- He distinguishes judgment that is just, judgment that is unjust, and rash judgment. The first judgment is not a cause for condemnation, but the second and third are.
- Rash judgment happens in two ways: when a person passes judgment on a matter committed to him without due knowledge of the truth, or when a person presumes to judge about hidden matters, of which God alone has the power to judge.
- Some things belong to God alone to know, namely the thoughts of the heart and the contingent future.

### 4. Correcting others when we share their fault
Aquinas offers a pastoral nuance:
- One who is publicly guilty of the sin concerning which he judges another, he seems to be giving scandal by judging, unless perhaps he humbly reproves himself along with the other and laments his sin.
- He then quotes Augustine's *The Lord's Sermon on the Mount*, which counsels that in correcting someone, our common weakness will prod the memory, so that mercy and not hatred will guide that correction. And if we discover that we are presently guilty of the same vice, we should not scold but lament together and invite the other to join you in grieving.

### 5. God's judgment versus human judgment
- Man's judgment, even though it be formed justly, is not always based on the truth of the affair, but on the words of witnesses, which sometimes clash with the truth. This cannot happen with God, who is both judge and witness.

### 6. Do not presume on God's patience (vv. 3–5)
- **The root error:** since man is not punished at once by God for sin, he supposes that he will not be punished.
- **The right response:** the fact that the sinner does evil a hundred times and is patiently endured should not lead him to presume on God, but to conclude that it is good to fear Him.
- **The purpose of God's patience:** do you not know that God's kindness in postponing punishment is meant to lead you to repentance?
- **The danger of hardness:** By refusing to repent, you are storing up wrath for yourself, i.e., you are multiplying the debt of punishment. On the day of judgment, the justice of God's judgment will be revealed then, whereas now it is not believed or does not seem just.

### 7. Digression: the sin against the Holy Spirit
Because a gloss linked "hardness and impenitent heart" to the unforgivable sin, Aquinas surveys three views:
- **Earlier Fathers** (Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom): the sin against the Holy Spirit was the blasphemy whereby the works of the Holy Spirit are attributed to an unclean spirit.
- **Augustine:** final impenitence is a sin against the Spirit and of its very nature unforgivable.
- **Later teachers:** It is sin committed with deliberate malice, which is opposed to the goodness appropriated to the Holy Spirit. Such sin has no ground for excuse, although God does forgive it sometimes, because He is good, just as He sometimes used His power to cure a naturally incurable disease.

Aquinas also lists six forms of this sin, among them despair, presumption, obstinacy (which he identifies with Paul's "hardness"), and an impenitent heart.

---

## Common Threads

1. **Universal accountability.** All three commentators read "whoever you are" as excluding no one, whether Jew, Gentile, or ruler.
2. **Self-condemnation.** Chrysostom and Aquinas agree that judging others for sins we commit ourselves amounts to passing sentence on ourselves.
3. **Humility over harshness.** Aquinas, drawing on Augustine, insists that correction should come from mercy and a shared sense of weakness, not contempt.
4. **Patience as invitation.** Aquinas stresses that God's delay in punishing is not indifference but a call to repentance, and that despising it brings real danger.

98 Later teachers call a sin against the Holy Spirit one that is committed with deliberate malice, which is opposed to the goodness appropriated to the Holy Spirit, just as a sin against the Son of God is one committed from ignorance, which is opposed to the wisdom appropriated to the Son.

But one committed from deliberate malice has no ground for excuse; hence, it is deemed unforgivable, because it has nothing in it to plead forgiveness; although God does forgive it sometimes, because He is good, just as He sometimes used His power to cure a naturally incurable disease.

# Patristic Commentary on John 5: Key Insights

## Augustine of Hippo

Augustine's commentary is by far the most extensive excerpt. He reads the healing at the pool as a rich spiritual allegory about the soul, the law, and love.

**1. The miracle as a sign for the soul**
Augustine says Christ's incarnation matters more than his miracles: it is more important that He healed the faults of souls, than that He healed the weaknesses of mortal bodies. Bodily healings were temporary: whatever was for a time made whole in mortal limbs came to nought in the end: but the soul that believed passed to eternal life. Christ wrought what the soul was able to see, in order to heal that by which it was not able to see.

**2. Why only one man was healed**
Among the many sick, He chose one for healing, thereby to signify unity. Similarly, at the troubled pool only one was healed, signifying unity: whoever came thereafter was not healed, because whoever shall be outside unity cannot be healed.

**3. The pool, the porches, and the troubled water**
- That pool and that water seem to me to have signified the Jewish people.
- The five porches represent the five books of Moses: those books brought forth the sick, not healed them. For the law convicted, not acquitted sinners.
- The troubling of the water points to Christ, who by doing great things, by teaching profitable things, troubled sinners, troubled the water by His presence, and roused it towards His own death. Therefore, to go down into the troubled water means to believe in the Lord's death.

**4. The meaning of "thirty-eight years"**
Augustine treats forty as a number of perfection. He links it to fasting: Moses fasted forty days, and Elias as many; and our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ did Himself fulfill this number of fasting. Since the law is fulfilled in the two commandments of love, he asks: why do you wonder that he was weak and sick, who was short of forty by two?

**5. "Take up your bed, and walk" as the two commands of love**
Augustine sees the two commands given to the healed man as supplying what was missing: by ordering him to do two things, it is as if He filled up that which was lacking.
- **"Take up your bed"** means loving one's neighbor. In this Take up your bed, He seems to me to have said, Love your neighbor. The image fits because the man was once carried by the bed and now carries it: When you were weak your neighbor bore you: you are made whole, bear your neighbor.
- **"Walk"** means journeying toward God. For we are not yet come to the Lord, but we have our neighbor with us. Bear him, then, when you walk, that you may come to Him with whom you desire to abide.
- He explains the order of the two loves: The love of God comes first in the order of enjoying; but in the order of doing, the love of our neighbor comes first.

**6. Finding Jesus in the temple, not the crowd**
The healed man did not at first know who had healed him. Augustine draws a lesson about contemplation: It is difficult in a crowd to see Christ: a certain solitude is necessary for our mind; it is by a certain solitude of contemplation that God is seen. Because the man kept carrying his bed and walking, Jesus sees him afterwards in the temple.

**7. The Sabbath and "My Father works hitherto"**
Augustine says God's rest on the seventh day was not rest from weariness: How can He have been wearied, who made by a word? He proposes that the Sabbath foreshadowed Christ, who when all His works were completed, on the sixth day of the week, He bowed His head and gave up the ghost, and on the Sabbath day He rested in the tomb from all His works. He paraphrases Christ's point to his opponents: The Sabbath day was ordained for you for a sign of me.

**8. Christ's equality with the Father**
Augustine notes that Jesus' opponents correctly understood that he was claiming equality with God: the Jews understand what the Arians do not understand. The Arians, in fact, say that the Son is not equal with the Father, and hence it is that the heresy was driven from the Church. He insists that He did not make Himself equal, but the Father begot Him equal. Drawing on Philippians, Augustine says that in taking the form of a servant, He emptied Himself not by losing what He was, but by taking to Him what He was not.

## Theodore of Mopsuestia

Theodore's brief excerpt focuses on Jesus' motives and method. He says Jesus timed his visit strategically: He chose the time when everybody gathered to offer his help to everyone. Therefore he went to Jerusalem at that time.

He also explains why Jesus did not heal everywhere: He did not think it was necessary to travel around and go to every place where people were ill, so that it might not appear that he was looking for fame. Instead he healed one only and through him he revealed himself to many.

Both Theodore and Augustine address why only one man was healed. Augustine stresses unity as a symbol, while Theodore stresses Christ's humility and how the miracle served his self-revelation.

## Irenaeus

**Against Heresies 2.22.3**
Irenaeus uses John 5 for chronology rather than spiritual interpretation. He places the healing at Jesus' second Passover visit: Afterwards he went up, the second time, to observe the festival day of the Passover in Jerusalem. On this occasion he cured the paralytic man who had lain beside the pool thirty-eight years.

His main point is that Jesus' ministry lasted more than one year: Now, that these three occasions of the Passover are not included within one year, every person whatever must acknowledge.

**Against Heresies Book II (separate excerpt)**
This excerpt is very fragmentary. Its first line restates the same chronological point: Afterwards He went up, the second time, to observe the festival day of the passover. Its second line quotes an epistle ("Every one that believeth that Jesus is the Christ, has been born of God"). Without more context, it does not clearly comment on John 5, so no further insight can be drawn from it.

## Summary

- **Augustine** offers a deep allegorical and doctrinal reading. In his view, the law exposes sin but cannot heal, Christ heals through faith in his death, and the healed believer must love both neighbor and God. He also defends Christ's full equality with the Father.
- **Theodore** emphasizes Christ's humility and his purpose of revealing himself through a single, well-timed miracle.
- **Irenaeus** uses John 5 mainly as a chronological marker supporting a ministry spanning several Passovers.

# Bede on Luke 7: Summary of Key Insights

All four excerpts come from one commentator, **the Venerable Bede** (*On the Gospel of Luke*). They cover only the opening of Luke 7 (vv. 1–5): Jesus' entry into Capernaum and the healing of the centurion's servant. Later parts of the chapter are not addressed in these excerpts.

---

## 1. The Timing of Jesus' Entry into Capernaum (Luke 7:1)

Bede reads the opening verse carefully. He notes that Jesus did not enter before these words had been finished, but it is not stated after what interval of time, once he had finished these discourses, he entered Capernaum. This gap lets him reconcile the order of events in Luke and Matthew: Within that interval, that leper was cleansed whom Matthew interposes in his own place, but this one anticipates beforehand.

**Insight:** Differences in Gospel sequence need not be contradictions. Each evangelist may place events differently within an unstated span of time.

---

## 2. "About to Die": Faith, Compassion, and Providence (Luke 7:2)

Bede addresses a possible objection: how could Luke call the servant "about to die" if he was healed? He answers that the servant truly was about to die if he had not been restored to life by the faith of his beseeching master and the compassion of Christ.

He supports this with the example of King Hezekiah, who was about to die according to a certain manner of human nature, yet by the hidden judgment of divine providence, which has arranged all things in measure, number, and weight, he was to obtain fifteen more years of life through tears and prayers.

**Insight:** Scripture can speak of what would happen by natural course while God's providence, responding to faith and prayer, brings about a different outcome.

---

## 3. The Jewish Elders as Witnesses (Luke 7:3)

Bede sees God's purpose in the centurion's choice of messengers: By divine dispensation it happened that the elders of the Jews were sent to the Lord, and while they stood by, the one who was ill was healed, so that they would be without excuse if, while a Gentile man believed, they did not believe.

**Insight:** The Gentile's faith, seen firsthand by the elders, serves as a testimony and a challenge to those who should have recognized Christ.

---

## 4. Reconciling Luke and Matthew: Approaching Christ by Faith

This is the theological heart of the excerpts. Bede addresses how it agrees that Luke says the Centurion sent messengers, but Matthew narrates that he himself approached the Lord.

- **Matthew's brevity:** Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that he himself approached, whose desire and will were truly conveyed to the Lord, even though others were carrying it.
- **Faith as true approach:** Because Christ so praised the faith of the Centurion, by which one truly approaches Jesus, Matthew chose to describe the centurion himself as approaching.
- **Luke's fuller account:** Luke revealed the whole event as it happened, so that from this we might be forced to understand how the other, who could not lie, said he had approached.
- **A parallel:** Bede compares this to the woman with the issue of blood, who touched the Lord "more because she believed" than those crowds by whom he was pressed, so also the centurion, the more he believed, the more he approached the Lord.

**Insight:** Nearness to Christ is measured by faith, not physical proximity. The two Gospel accounts complement rather than contradict each other.

---

## 5. "Synagogue" as Both People and Place (Luke 7:5)

On the elders' remark that the centurion built their synagogue, Bede observes that just as we call the Church, so also they were accustomed to call the synagogue, not only the assembly of the faithful, but also the place where they gathered.

**Insight:** This is mainly a linguistic note. "Synagogue," like "Church," can mean both the community of believers and the building where they meet.

---

## Overall Themes in Bede's Commentary

1. **Gospel harmony:** Bede consistently reconciles apparent differences between Luke and Matthew, treating them as complementary witnesses.
2. **The primacy of faith:** The centurion's faith is central. It brings healing and is the true means of "approaching" Christ.
3. **Divine providence:** Events, including who witnesses a miracle and whether death comes, unfold under God's ordering.
4. **Gentile faith as testimony:** The believing Gentile is set against unbelief among those who should have believed.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 15: A Summary

**A note on scope:** These excerpts cover only the opening verses of Genesis 15: God's promise of protection and reward, and Abram's question about an heir. They do not address the later parts of the chapter, such as the counting of the stars, Abram's faith being credited as righteousness, or the covenant ceremony. Bede's second excerpt also breaks off mid-sentence, just before the Lord's response.

---

## Bede

**God confirms Melchizedek's blessing.** Bede links Genesis 15 directly to the previous chapter. He argues that the blessing that Abraham had received from the priest Melchizedek, the Lord himself now confirms. He matches the two passages line by line: the Lord says, "I am your shield," echoing the priest's blessing of the God "who has delivered your enemies into your hand".

**What the "reward" recognizes.** For Bede, the reward honors Abram's whole life of faithfulness, not one act. It covers not only the affection he had shown to his brother in distress but also all the devotion with which he had served the Lord with a whole heart since he left his homeland and relatives.

**Abram's question is not doubt.** Bede defends Abram's response ("what will you give me?") against any charge of unbelief. Abram does not ask as though doubtful of God's promises, but simply inquires what reward he, who has no son in whom to rejoice as heir and participant of the divine promise, will receive from the Lord, and whether his servant will be his heir instead. Bede presents God as responsive to this honest longing: the Lord, favoring Abram's desires, promised him this reward which he sought.

**A historical aside.** Bede passes on a tradition that the servant was called by two names, that is, Damascus, Eliezer, by whom, they say, the city of Damascus was both founded and named.

---

## Ambrose of Milan

**God rewards those who refuse worldly gain.** Ambrose reads the promise as God's answer to Abram's integrity: because Abraham did not seek recompense from man, he received it from God.

**God's promptness and generosity.** Ambrose's distinctive point is pastoral. God does not delay his reward, because he cares for believers who are struggling: The Lord is not slow to reward. He is eager to promise, and he gives in abundance, lest any delay cause weak souls to repent of having despised visible things. He uses a vivid financial image: God pays back, so to speak, at high interest, rewarding with great abundance the one who has not been seduced by the things of this world that were offered to him.

---

## John Chrysostom

**Why "Do not be afraid"?** Chrysostom sees in God's opening words the extraordinary degree of his care. He reads them as reassurance after Abram turned down the king's offer: Since Abraham had scorned so much wealth by giving little importance to the offerings of the king, God said to him, Have no fear for despising gifts of such value.

**The personal touch of a name.** Chrysostom notices that God addresses Abram by name, observing that it proves to be no little help in encouraging a person to invoke the name of the person we are addressing.

**"I am your shield" recalls God's past faithfulness.** Chrysostom finds the phrase rich in meaning and paraphrases it as God reviewing his care for Abram: I summoned you from the Chaldeans. I led you to this point. I rescued you from the perils of Egypt. I promised once and again to give this land to your descendants. The shield means active defense: I will struggle in your place.

**A reward beyond what was refused.** God's reward will far exceed what Abram gave up: I will provide you with a reward, not to the degree that you would have received but wonderfully, exceedingly great.

---

## Common Threads

- **Continuity with Genesis 14:** All three read God's words as a response to Abram's conduct in the previous chapter. Bede links them to Melchizedek's blessing, while Ambrose and Chrysostom link them to Abram's refusal of the king's goods.
- **God's tender care:** Each stresses God's attentiveness. Bede emphasizes God honoring Abram's desires, Ambrose God's eagerness to reward, and Chrysostom God's gentle encouragement.
- **Generous reward for faithfulness:** All agree that God's reward surpasses anything Abram gave up or could have received from human hands.

# Patristic Commentary on John 1: Origen and Augustine

The excerpts come from two early Church writers, **Origen of Alexandria** and **Augustine of Hippo**. Both focus mainly on the opening verses of John 1 (vv. 1–9), especially "In the beginning was the Word."

---

## Origen of Alexandria

### 1. The many meanings of "beginning"
Origen starts with the word "beginning" itself, noting that one will discover many different meanings of the expression [“beginning”] even in the Word of God. He lists several:
- the start of a path ("The beginning of the right path is to do justice.")
- the beginning of creation
- God as source (the Father is the beginning of the Son, and the Creator is the beginning of the things created)
- the pattern by which things are made (Christ, for instance, is the beginning of those made according to the image of God)

### 2. "Beginning" in John 1:1 means Wisdom
Applying this to John's opening, Origen rules out some meanings: we are not to understand it in its meaning related to change or a way and length. His conclusion is that it is as the beginning that Christ is Creator, according to which he is wisdom. Therefore as wisdom he is called the beginning. He connects this to Proverbs, where wisdom says in Solomon, “God created me in the beginning of his ways for his works,” that “the Word might be in the beginning,” in wisdom.

### 3. Wisdom and Word: contemplation and communication
Origen distinguishes the two titles. Wisdom relates to the structure of contemplation and the thoughts of all things, but it is the Word that is received, taken in relation to the communication of the things that have been contemplated to spiritual beings. In short, Wisdom is the divine understanding, and the Word is that understanding expressed. Being "in Wisdom" does not lessen the Word's divinity, because it does not prevent the Word from being “with God,” and himself being God.

### 4. The eternal "was"
Origen stresses the verb "was." The Word does not “come to be” “in the beginning” from not being “in the beginning,” nor does he pass from not being “with God” to coming to be “with God,” for before all time and eternity “the Word was in the beginning,” and “the Word was with God.” He also suggests the order of John's clauses is deliberate: John did not place “the Word was God” before “the Word was with God,” so that we might not be hindered in seeing the individual meaning of each proposition.

### 5. Two "beginnings" of Christian teaching
Origen notes that in nature Christ is the beginning of doctrine insofar as he is “the wisdom” and “power of God.” From the human side, however, the beginning of doctrine is “the Word became flesh,” that he might dwell among us who are able to receive him only in this way at first. The Incarnation is God meeting us where we can begin to understand.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

### 1. Humility before the text
Augustine admits the passage exceeds human grasp, even John's: perhaps not John himself spoke of the matter as it is, but even he only as he was able; for it was man that spoke of God, inspired indeed by God, but still man.

### 2. John as a "mountain": hope rests in God, not the messenger
Using Psalm imagery, Augustine calls John one of the "mountains" who received revelation for others. To reach the truth of John 1:1, John unless he rose above all those things which were created, he would not arrive at Him by whom all things were made. Readers should look to Scripture's human authors but must not place their hope in them, since they did not shine of themselves, but He was the true light.

### 3. The Word that does not pass away
Augustine contrasts human speech with the divine Word. Our words sound and pass away. Yet even in human speech, that which the sound signified, and was in the speaker as he thought of it, and in the hearer as he understood it, that remains while the sounds pass away. He adds an architect analogy, asking his hearers whether they wish to see what a design of God is the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the Word of God? Mark this fabric of the world.

### 4. Against the Arians: the Word "was," not "was made"
Augustine argues from logic: How can it be that the Word of God was made, when God by the Word made all things? If the Word of God was itself also made, by what other Word was it made? He stresses the evangelist's word choice: The evangelist might have said, In the beginning the Word was made: but what does he say? In the beginning was the Word. If He was, He was not made. This also matters for salvation: If, however, your belief about the Word be wrong, you will not be able to be new-made by the Word.

### 5. "Without Him was nothing made": the scope of creation
Augustine warns against treating "nothing" as a thing. Sin, indeed, was not made by Him; and it is plain that sin is nothing, and men become nothing when they sin. Everything that truly exists was made by the Word, from an angel even to a worm.

He illustrates this with a story about a Manichaean (a dualist sect) who persuaded someone annoyed by flies that God did not make them. Step by step, the Manichaean led him to conclude that man was not made by God. Augustine's lesson is to understand that God made all things, and arranged them in their orders. He adds that troublesome creatures serve to humble human pride.

### 6. "That which was made, in Him is life": the carpenter's box
Augustine addresses how to punctuate verses 3–4. He warns against a reading the Manichaeans used to claim that a stone has life, that a wall has a soul. Instead: read thus That which was made; here make a short pause, and then go on, in Him is life.

His analogy is a carpenter's box: The actual box is not life, the box in design is life; because the soul of the artificer, where all these things are before they are brought forth, is living. In the same way, created things externally they are bodies, in design they are life.

### 7. The life is the light of men, seen by the pure in heart
This light belongs to rational creatures: man was made in the image of God, and has a rational mind, by which he can perceive wisdom. When people fail to see it, the problem lies with them, not with the light. Augustine compares this to a blind man placed in the sun, the sun is present to him, but he is absent from the sun. The remedy is moral cleansing: Let him become pure, that he may be able to see God.

---

## Common Threads

Both commentators, in their own ways:
- **Stress the verb "was"** in John 1:1 as evidence of the Word's eternity, not his creation.
- **Link the Word with God's Wisdom.** Origen calls Wisdom the "beginning" in which the Word exists, while Augustine treats the Wisdom of God as containing the design of all creation.
- **Acknowledge that understanding is gradual.** Origen calls the Incarnation the starting point "in relation to us." Augustine urges those not yet ready for "strong meat" to not leave Christ born through the flesh till he arrive at Christ born of the Father alone.

All of the provided excerpts address John 1, though parts of Augustine's sermon, such as the anecdote about the flies, are pastoral applications rather than direct exposition of the text.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 27: Summary of Key Insights

## John Chrysostom (*Homilies on Genesis* 53)

Chrysostom reads Jacob's blessing mainly as a story of **divine providence working through human action**.

**God's purpose behind Rebekah's plan.** Chrysostom contrasts Isaac's intentions with God's: whereas the father gave evidence of natural affection by giving these directions to Esau, the wise and resourceful Lord caused his own prediction to be brought to pass by means of Rebekah, thus teaching us the power of virtue and mildness of manner. He presents Rebekah's role as divinely guided: See a mother's affection, or rather God's designs: He it was who prompted her to make plans and also made sure all turned out well.

**Character determines the outcome.** Chrysostom sees the reversal between the brothers as a moral lesson. Esau considered himself to hold pride of place by birthright and by his father's preference for him, and yet he was suddenly found to be bereft of all this. Jacob, by contrast, being endowed with homely virtues and enjoying the help of favor from above, won his father's blessing against his will. Esau lost everything, forfeiting what was his because of the evil of his ways. The principle he draws is: Nothing is more powerful than the person helped by that mighty right hand.

**Jacob's hesitation as respect for his father.** Chrysostom reads Jacob's worry about being discovered (vv. 11–12) generously, as remarkable the child's dutifulness and his respect for his father, and as evidence of Jacob's circumspection in showing his mildness of manner in his reply.

**Rebekah's self-sacrificing love.** Chrysostom says Rebekah was not concocting this only out of her own thinking but was also implementing the prediction from on high. He points out that instead of promising him that he would be able to deceive his father and elude detection, she offered to take any curse on herself. He concludes: This really is a mother's love, readily accepting everything for her child's sake.

## Jerome (*Hebrew Questions on Genesis*)

Jerome's comment on 27:11 is **linguistic rather than theological**. He notes that where it is written that he was hairy, in Hebrew it is written Seir, and explains that therefore, afterwards the mountains of Seir and the region in which he lived were called Seir. His contribution is a wordplay that links Esau's physical description to the later name of his homeland. The excerpt draws no further spiritual lesson from it.

## Ambrose of Milan (*Jacob and the Happy Life* 2.2.9)

Ambrose offers an **allegorical reading** focused on Esau's garments.

**Jacob's merit.** Ambrose says Jacob received his brother's clothing, because he excelled the elder in wisdom and because he was conspicuous in the merit of his faith.

**The garments as the heritage of the Old Testament.** For Ambrose, Rebekah presented this clothing as a symbol of the church; she gave to the younger son the clothing of the Old Testament, the prophetic and priestly clothing, the royal Davidic clothing. That inheritance passes to the Christian people, who would know how to use the garment they had received, and when they put it on, it shone brightly.

**"The voice is Jacob's voice."** Ambrose interprets Isaac's confusion symbolically: Isaac recognized the clothing of the Old Testament, but the voice of the people of old he did not recognize; therefore he knew that it had been changed.

**Faith and works.** Reflecting on Isaac smelling the garments, Ambrose suggests, tentatively ("perhaps"), that we are not justified by works but by faith, because the weakness of the flesh is a hindrance to works, but the brightness of faith puts the error that is in humanity's deeds in the shadow and merits for us the forgiveness of our sins.

## Comparing the Approaches

- **Chrysostom** stays close to the story. He emphasizes providence, virtue, and family relationships, and he presents Rebekah's plan as carrying out God's prediction.
- **Jerome** supplies a Hebrew word study that connects the narrative to geography. It is not a theological reading.
- **Ambrose** reads the scene as a figure of the Church inheriting the Old Testament, and from it he draws a reflection on faith and works.

Chrysostom and Ambrose both explain why Jacob, not Esau, receives the blessing. Chrysostom attributes it to virtue and divine favor; Ambrose attributes it to wisdom and faith.

# Summary of Commentaries on Romans 8

All four excerpts focus on the opening verses of Romans 8 (roughly vv. 1–6): "no condemnation" for those in Christ, the "law of the Spirit of life," Christ's coming "in the likeness of sinful flesh," and the contrast between walking according to the flesh and according to the Spirit. Aquinas's excerpt is by far the longest. The others are brief, and Chrysostom's breaks off mid-sentence.

---

## Origen of Alexandria: From Struggle to Freedom

Origen reads Romans 8 as a turning point from chapter 7. After having taught what conflict there is in those who are caught in the struggle between a mind which lives according to the law of God and the desires of the flesh which lead them into sin, Paul now goes on to talk not about those who are partly in the flesh and partly in the Spirit but about those who are wholly in Christ. Of these people, he declares that there is nothing in them worthy of condemnation.

**Key insight:** "No condemnation" belongs to those fully given over to Christ, not to those still divided between flesh and Spirit.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: Desire Is Not the Same as Sin

Augustine's excerpt is a single sentence, but it makes an important pastoral distinction: there is no condemnation just because carnal desires exist; it is only if we give in to them and sin that we are condemned.

**Key insight:** Being tempted is not condemnable. Consenting to the temptation is.

---

## Thomas Aquinas: A Systematic Reading

### 1. Freedom from condemnation in two senses
Aquinas sees this passage as completing an argument. After showing that we are freed from sin and the Law through Christ's grace, the Apostle now shows that through the same grace we are freed from damnation. This freedom is complete, because the damnation has been removed both as regards guilt and as regards punishment.

### 2. Two conditions for receiving this benefit
- **Being in Christ Jesus**, which means incorporated in him by faith and love and the sacrament of faith.
- **Not walking according to the flesh**, which means people who do not follow the desires [concupiscentia] of the flesh.

### 3. Are involuntary impulses mortal sins?
Aquinas rejects the view that in unbelievers who are not in Christ Jesus the first movements [of desire] are mortal sins, even though they do not consent to them. His reasoning is that the first movement [of desire] is not a mortal sin is because it does not reach reason, in which the notion of sin is completed. He gives an illustration: if the habit of adultery is present in a person, the stirring of adulterous desire, which is an imperfect act, is not a mortal sin for that person, but only the perfect motion that exists by the consent of reason. This closely parallels Augustine's distinction between desire and consent.

### 4. What is the "law of the Spirit"?
Aquinas offers two readings:
- It may be the Holy Spirit himself. Human law works by merely indicating what ought to be done; but the Holy Spirit dwelling in the mind not only teaches what is to be done by instructing the intellect but also inclines the affection to act aright.
- It may be the proper effect of the Holy Spirit, namely, faith working through love.

Either way, this law of the spirit is called the new law, which is the Holy Spirit himself or something which the Holy Spirit produces in our hearts. He also identifies four "laws" in Paul's argument: the law of Moses, the law of inclination to sin [fomes], the natural law in one sense of the term, and the new law.

The Spirit is given only within union with Christ: just as the natural spirit does not reach a member not connected to the head, so the Holy Spirit does not reach a man not joined to Christ, the head.

### 5. "In the likeness of sinful flesh"
Aquinas guards against two errors:
- Christ's flesh was real. The phrase should not be taken to mean that he did not have true flesh but only the likeness of flesh, as though it were imaginary, as the Manicheans say.
- Christ's flesh was not sinful, because his flesh was conceived by the Holy Spirit who takes away sin.

The "likeness" means he was like sinful flesh in the fact that he was able to suffer.

### 6. How Christ "condemned sin in the flesh"
Aquinas prefers to read this as Christ having weakened the inclination to sin [fomes] in our flesh, of sin, i.e., through the power of his passion and death, which is called sin on account of its likeness to sin or because through it he was made a victim for sin. The Law's failure was not a defect in the Law itself. It happened because of a weakness of the flesh, a weakness which was in man due to the corruption of inclination [fomes], with the result that in spite of the Law man was overcome by sinful desire. For this reason, it was necessary that Christ be incarnated, because the Law could not justify.

### 7. The "prudence" of the flesh versus the Spirit
Aquinas sets out Paul's argument as two parallel syllogisms. The conclusions are that all who walk according to the flesh are brought to death, while all who walk according to the spirit obtain life and peace.

The difference lies in the goal a person pursues:
- **Prudence of the flesh** requires that a person presuppose as his goal a pleasure of the flesh and that he plan and judge and command what leads to this end.
- **Prudence of the Spirit** exists when someone, presupposing a spiritual good as the goal, plans and judges and commands the things which are suitably ordered to that goal.

Drawing on Aristotle, he notes that as a person is, so the end seems to him. In other words, our character shapes what we judge to be good.

---

## John Chrysostom: Responsibility After Baptism

Chrysostom addresses a practical problem: why do believers still sin? Paul anticipated this objection, and says not merely "to them that are in Christ Jesus," but adds, "who walk not after the flesh;" so showing that all afterward comes of our listlessness. The difference grace makes is real: For now we have the power of walking not after the flesh, but then it was a difficult task.

**Key insight:** Grace gives believers real power over the flesh, so sin after baptism comes from spiritual carelessness, not from inability. *(The excerpt ends mid-thought, so his full argument is not available here.)*

---

## Common Threads

- **Union with Christ is the basis of "no condemnation"** (Origen, Aquinas).
- **Desire is distinguished from consent.** Temptation alone does not condemn (Augustine, Aquinas).
- **Walking by the Spirit is a necessary condition, not an optional extra.** Grace empowers holy living, and believers bear responsibility for how they use it (Aquinas, Chrysostom).
- **The Spirit does what the Law could not.** He not only instructs but also moves the heart toward the good (Aquinas).

For if the habit of adultery is present in a person, the stirring of adulterous desire, which is an imperfect act, is not a mortal sin for that person, but only the perfect motion that exists by the consent of reason.

Human law does this by merely indicating what ought to be done; but the Holy Spirit dwelling in the mind not only teaches what is to be done by instructing the intellect but also inclines the affection to act aright: "But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things," as to the first, "and suggest to you all things," as to the second, "all that I have said to you" (Jn 14:26).
In another way the law of the spirit can be the proper effect of the Holy Spirit, namely, faith working through love.

And this law of the spirit is called the new law, which is the Holy Spirit himself or something which the Holy Spirit produces in our hearts: "I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts" (Jer 31:33).

And so, considering what has been said, we find four laws mentioned by the Apostle: first, the law of Moses, about which he says: "I delight in the law of God in my inmost self"; secondly, the law of inclination to sin [fomes]: "I see in my members another law"; thirdly, the natural law in one sense of the term, concerning which he adds, "at war with the law of my mind"; fourthly, the new law, when he says: the law of the spirit.

For just as the natural spirit does not reach a member not connected to the head, so the Holy Spirit does not reach a man not joined to Christ, the head: "By this we know that he abides in us, because he gave us of his own Spirit" (1 Jn 3:24);24 "The Holy Spirit whom God has given those who obey him" (Ac 5:32).

This should not be taken to mean that he did not have true flesh but only the likeness of flesh, as though it were imaginary, as the Manicheans say, since the Lord himself says: "A spirit has not flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Lk 24:40).
For he did not have sinful flesh, i.e., conceived with sin, because his flesh was conceived by the Holy Spirit who takes away sin: "That which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 1:20).
But he had the likeness of sinful flesh, i.e., he was like sinful flesh in the fact that he was able to suffer.

But it is better to say that he condemned sin in the flesh, i.e., weakened the inclination to sin [fomes] in our flesh, of sin, i.e., through the power of his passion and death, which is called sin on account of its likeness to sin or because through it he was made a victim for sin.

Now the reason why the Law could not do this was not due to a shortcoming in the Law, but because it was weakened by the flesh, i.e., because of a weakness of the flesh, a weakness which was in man due to the corruption of inclination [fomes], with the 304 result that in spite of the Law man was overcome by sinful desire [concupiscentia]: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Mt 26:41).
Therefore it was necessary that Christ be incarnated, because the Law could not justify.
Therefore, all who walk according to the flesh are brought to death.
Therefore, all who walk according to the spirit obtain life and peace.
Hence, for prudence of the flesh it is required that a person presuppose as his goal a pleasure of the flesh and that he plan and judge and command what leads to this end.

Now according to what has just been said, there is prudence of the spirit when someone, presupposing a spiritual good as the goal, plans and judges and commands the things which are suitably ordered to that goal.
306 The reason for these facts, as the Philosopher says in Ethics III, is that as a person is, so the end seems to him.

Then as the fact that many fall into sin even after baptism presented a difficulty (ἀ ντέπιπτεν]), he consequently hastened to meet it, and says not merely "to them that are in Christ Jesus," but adds, "who walk not after the flesh;" so showing that all afterward comes of our listlessness.
For now we have the power of walking not after the flesh, but then it was a difficult task.

# Patristic Insights on Acts 9: "Saul, Saul, Why Are You Persecuting Me?"

All four excerpts focus on one moment in Acts 9: the risen Lord's words to Saul on the road to Damascus. Each commentator draws out a different aspect of what it means that Christ says "me" when Saul is attacking Christians.

## Augustine of Hippo: Christ Is Both in Heaven and on Earth

Augustine uses the verse to show that Christ is present both in heaven and among his people. He asks a pointed rhetorical question: Had Paul climbed up to heaven then? Had Paul even thrown a stone at heaven? In fact, it was Christians he was persecuting, them he was tying up, them he was dragging off to be put to death.

His conclusion is drawn from the wording of the verse itself. Asking Where is he crying out from? Heaven. So he's up above. But because Christ says "Why are you persecuting me?" So he's down below. The one voice shows that Christ reigns in heaven and also lives in his suffering people on earth.

## Basil of Caesarea: Christ Takes Our Condition as His Own

Basil's excerpt is not mainly about Acts 9. His main concern is a different passage about the Son being "made subject," which he quotes at the outset. He brings in Acts 9 as one example of a broader principle. He argues that Christ makes your subjection his own, and in the same way he even said at one time that he himself was the one persecuted. This happened when Saul was hastening to Damascus, desiring to put in bonds the disciples of Christ.

Basil sets this alongside other cases where Christ identifies with the needy. He calls himself naked, if anyone of his brothers is naked, and when another was in prison, he said that he himself was the one imprisoned. The theological basis is that he himself took up our infirmities and bore the burden of our ills. Basil sums it up this way: even the adversities that happen to us the Lord makes his own, taking upon himself our sufferings because of his fellowship with us.

## Bede: The Church as Christ's Body

Bede pays close attention to Christ's exact words. He did not say, "Why do you persecute my members?" but "Why do you persecute me?" His explanation is that Christ is still suffering from enemies in his body, which is the church.

Bede also points out that this works in both directions. Christ declared that kindnesses bestowed upon his members are also done to him, citing his words, "So long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me." So how people treat believers, whether through persecution or kindness, is how they treat Christ.

## Ephrem the Syrian: The Humility of the Risen Lord

Ephrem focuses on the tone of Christ's words rather than their content. He notes that the One who conquered persecutors [here] below and reigns over angels [in heaven] above spoke from above in a humble voice. He finds a striking contrast: The One who on earth pronounced ten woes against his crucifiers, above pronounced not a single woe against Saul, his persecutor.

For Ephrem, both responses were meant to teach the church. The woes were given to teach his disciples not to flatter their killers, while our Lord spoke humbly from above so that the leaders of his church would speak humbly. His insight is practical and pastoral, holding up Christ's gentleness toward Saul as a model for church leaders.

## Summary

| Commentator | Key Insight |
|---|---|
| **Augustine** | Christ is present both in heaven and in his people on earth |
| **Basil** | Christ makes our sufferings his own (Acts 9 used as a supporting example) |
| **Bede** | The church is Christ's body, so what is done to believers is done to him |
| **Ephrem** | Christ's humble tone toward his persecutor models humility for church leaders |

Augustine, Basil, and Bede agree that Christ is so closely united with his people that persecuting them is persecuting him. Ephrem adds a distinct focus on the humility with which the exalted Christ spoke to the man who would become Paul.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 13:1–2: Jesus Leaves the House and Teaches by the Sea

All four excerpts focus on the opening of Matthew 13, where Jesus leaves the house, sits by the sea, and teaches the crowds from a boat. None of them reaches the parables themselves, so this summary covers only that opening scene.

---

## 1. Origen of Alexandria: Jesus Goes Out Because He Loves People

**Key insight:** Jesus going out of the house shows his love for humanity.

Origen's short excerpt does not quote a specific verse, but it speaks directly to this scene. He draws a contrast between being "inside" and "outside." When Jesus is with the multitudes, he is not in his house, for the multitudes are outside of the house, and it is an act that springs from his love of humanity to leave the house and to go away to those who are not able to come to him.

**Theological point:** Jesus doesn't wait for people to reach him. He goes out to those who cannot come to him. This is a picture of grace that takes the initiative.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: Correction Balanced with Kindness, and a Teacher's Care

Chrysostom's two excerpts overlap (the homily passage is a modern rendering of the commentary's second half). Together they make two main points.

**a) Jesus both corrects and gives.**
Chrysostom ties Jesus' leaving the house to the episode just before it, which involved a request from his mother. He observes: "Do you see, how He both rebuked them, and did what they desired?" He compares this to the wedding at Cana, where He at once reproved her asking unseasonably, and nevertheless did not gainsay her; by the former correcting her weakness, by the latter showing His kindly feeling toward His mother. In the same way, here He both healed the disease of vainglory, and rendered the due honor to His mother, even though her request was unseasonable.

**b) Miracles followed by teaching.**
Chrysostom imagines Jesus saying, "if you desire, says He, to see and hear, behold I come forth and discourse." Thus having wrought many miracles, He affords again the benefit of His doctrine. He also offers an image: He sits by the sea, fishing and getting into His net them that are on the land.

**c) Why he sat by the sea.**
Chrysostom insists the setting was deliberate. It was not without a purpose that he "sat beside the sea." The Gospel writer has expressed this in a hidden manner. The purpose of Jesus' doing this was to order his listeners in a precise way. He wanted to see them all face to face. He left no one at a disadvantage at his back.

**Theological point:** For Chrysostom, Jesus shows pastoral wisdom. He corrects without rejecting, and he arranges his teaching so that everyone can hear him equally.

---

## 3. Jerome: The Mercy of Teaching Outside, and an Allegory of the Sea

**a) Mercy toward those outside.**
Jerome contrasts the disciples with the crowd: the people couldn't enter Jesus' house or be where the apostles were hearing the mysteries. Therefore, the compassionate and merciful Lord goes out of his house and sits by the sea of this world, so that great crowds gather around him and hear on the beach what they do not deserve to hear inside.

**b) An allegorical reading of the boat and shore.**
Jerome reads the scene symbolically. The sea becomes "the sea of this world." Jesus is in the midst of the waves, tossed to and fro by the sea, and in his majesty he approaches his boat to draw near to the land. Meanwhile, the people, not enduring the danger, nor surrounded by temptations that they could not bear, stand firmly on the shore in order to hear what is said.

**Theological point:** Jerome stresses that the crowd receives undeserved grace. In his allegory, Christ enters the turbulent "sea" of the world, while the listeners are kept on firm ground, spared trials beyond their strength.

---

## Common Threads

- **Jesus takes the initiative.** Origen and Jerome both read his going out of the house as compassion toward people who could not come in on their own.
- **Inside and outside.** Origen and Jerome distinguish the "house" (closeness to Jesus, the mysteries given to the apostles) from the crowds outside, yet Jesus still reaches the outsiders.
- **The details have meaning.** Chrysostom sees a deliberate, practical purpose in the seaside setting. Jerome reads the sea, boat, and shore allegorically.
- **Grace joined with wisdom.** Chrysostom in particular shows Jesus balancing correction and kindness, and following his miracles with teaching.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 10

These excerpts come from two early Church Fathers, John Chrysostom and Jerome. Each appears in two different translations, so the four documents contain two core passages. Both focus on the opening of the chapter, where Jesus commissions the Twelve and gives them authority.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 32 on Matthew)

### 1. The source of the disciples' power
Chrysostom raises a theological puzzle. If the Spirit had not yet been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified, how then did the disciples cast out the unclean spirits? His answer is that they did this by his own command, by the Son's authority. The disciples' early miracles depended directly on Christ's personal authority, before the later gift of the Spirit.

### 2. The careful timing of the mission
Chrysostom stresses that Jesus did not send the disciples out too early. They were not sent out at the beginning of their walk with him. Instead, it was only after they had seen the dead raised, the sea rebuked, devils expelled, the legs of a paralytic brought to life, sins remitted, lepers cleansed, and had received a sufficient proof of his power both by deeds and words—only then did he send them out. The lesson is that ministry grows out of time spent with Christ and witnessing his power.

### 3. Gradual preparation for hardship
Jesus also matched the mission to what the disciples could handle. He did not send them out unprepared to do dangerous deeds, for as yet there was no danger in Palestine. They had only to stand against verbal abuse. Even so, Jesus still warned them of larger perils to come, preparing them for what was future. The other translation adds that he did this making them feel as in conflict by His continual predictions of that sort. In this way he trained them for hardship before it arrived.

---

## Jerome (Commentary on Matthew 1.10.1)

### 1. Christ's generosity in sharing his power
Jerome begins with Christ's character: The kind and merciful Lord and Master does not begrudge his followers and disciples their powers. In fact, even as he had healed every disease and every infirmity, he empowered his apostles to heal every disease and every infirmity.

### 2. A key distinction: Christ's power versus delegated power
Jerome then sets a clear boundary: there is a great gap between having and granting, between giving and receiving. Christ possesses power in himself. The apostles only receive it. So whatever he does, he does in the power of the Lord. By contrast, whatever they do, they display their own weakness and the power of the Lord, saying, "In the name of Jesus, arise and walk." The other translation identifies this phrase as coming from (Acts 3:6). Jerome's point is that the apostles' miracles reveal their dependence on Christ, not their own ability.

### 3. An unclear closing remark
Jerome ends with a brief note that is hard to interpret. One translation reads that the power to work miracles is granted to the apostles even to the twelfth man. The other reads that in the twelfth place, the power of signs is granted to the apostles. The first may mean the power extended to all twelve apostles, including the last one listed. The second may refer to where this event falls in the Gospel's sequence. The excerpt does not settle which meaning Jerome intended.

---

## Common Themes

Both writers agree that the apostles' power came from Christ, not from themselves. They highlight different aspects of this:

- **Chrysostom** focuses on the *process* of preparation: when and how Jesus readied his disciples for ministry and for future suffering.
- **Jerome** focuses on the *nature* of the authority: Christ's generosity in sharing it, and the humility of those who receive it.

Together, they present discipleship as a gift received from Christ, exercised under his authority, and developed through patient formation.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew Chapter 3

## John Chrysostom (Homily 10)

Chrysostom's commentary is the most extensive of the excerpts. (The excerpt labeled "Homily 10.1" is a different translation of the same opening passage, so the two are treated together here.)

**1. The meaning of "in those days" (3:1).** Chrysostom notes that the phrase does not refer to Jesus' childhood. He does not mean the days when Jesus was a child at Nazareth but thirty years later, when John came, as Luke also testifies. He explains that the Scripture is always wont to use this manner of speech, not only when it is mentioning what occurs in the time immediately after, but also of things which are to come to pass many years later.

**2. Why Jesus waited until about age thirty.** Chrysostom connects the timing to Christ's fulfillment of the Law: After this baptism He was thenceforth to do away with the law: wherefore even until this age, which admits of all sins, He continues fulfilling it all; that no one might say, that because He Himself could not fulfill it, He did it away. He reasons that temptations differ by life stage: while in the first age of life there is much thoughtlessness and timidity, in that which comes after it, pleasure is more vehement, and after this again the desire of wealth.

**3. "To fulfill all righteousness" (3:15).** Chrysostom reads Jesus' baptism as the final act of a life of perfect obedience. He paraphrases Jesus' meaning as: We have performed all the duties of the law, we have not transgressed so much as one commandment. Since therefore this only remains, this too must be added, and so shall we fulfill all righteousness. In this verse, He here calls by the name of righteousness the full performance of all the commandments.

**4. John's baptism did not itself grant forgiveness.** Chrysostom draws a careful distinction between John's baptism and Christian baptism. Although John preached "for the remission of sins," it had not remission, but this gift pertained unto the baptism that was given afterwards; for in this we are buried with Him, and our old man was then crucified with Him, and before the cross there does not appear remission anywhere; for everywhere this is imputed to His blood. He asks rhetorically: when the sacrifice was not yet offered, neither had the spirit yet come down, nor sin was put away, nor the enmity removed, nor the curse destroyed; how was remission to take place?

**5. John's baptism prepared people for forgiveness.** For Chrysostom, John's real task was to awaken conscience. He argues that self-justification was the root problem. Since therefore this was the cause of their evils, John comes, doing nothing else but bringing them to a sense of their own sins. Repentance was not meant as punishment. Its purpose was that having become by repentance more humble, and condemning themselves, they might hasten to receive remission. The logic is summed up this way: For had they not condemned themselves, they could not have sought after His grace; and not seeking, they could not have obtained remission.

**6. The baptism as a public revelation of Christ.** John's baptism also served to reveal Jesus publicly. A heavenly testimony before a crowd was far more powerful than private persuasion. For neither would it have been as much for him to have gone about to their houses, and to have led Christ around, taking Him by the hand, and to have said, Believe in This Man; as for that blessed voice to be uttered, and all those other things performed in the presence and sight of all. This was needed because the things concerning Christ had been up to that time veiled, and many thought He was dead, owing to the massacre which took place at Bethlehem.

**7. The newness of "the kingdom of heaven."** Chrysostom stresses how unprecedented John's message was. For the first time he with clear voice proclaims things which the Jews had never heard, neither from prophets, nor from any besides; making mention of Heaven, and of the kingdom there, and no longer saying anything touching the earth. He adds that by the kingdom in this place he means His former and His last advent. Even the message's obscurity had a purpose, in order that being roused by the obscurity of my words, they may proceed to seek Him, whom I preach.

**8. John's credibility and prophetic backing.** Chrysostom highlights the impact of John's person. He asks his readers to consider how great a thing it was to see a man after thirty years coming down from the wilderness, being the son of a chief priest, who had never known the common wants of men, and was on every account venerable, and had Isaiah with him.

## Jerome (Commentary on Matthew)

Jerome's excerpt is very brief and comments directly on 3:2. He observes that John the Baptist proclaims the kingdom of heaven, honoring the Lord as its precursor with this privilege. His point is that John's role as forerunner was itself an honor granted to him.

## Cyril of Alexandria (Fragment 17.4)

Cyril offers a spiritual definition of "the kingdom of heaven": This refers to justification by faith and sanctification by the Spirit. He supports this inward reading by noting that it says elsewhere, "the kingdom [of heaven] is within you." The fragment does not explicitly name Matthew 3. However, it addresses the key phrase of John's preaching in 3:2, which is presumably why it is grouped with this chapter.

## A Note on the Sources

The excerpts are uneven in length. Chrysostom's material is substantial and develops a coherent argument, while Jerome's and Cyril's are only one or two sentences each. Their remarks should be read as brief glosses on the phrase "kingdom of heaven," not as full treatments of the chapter. The excerpts also say nothing directly about some parts of Matthew 3, such as the details of the Spirit's descent and the Father's voice, beyond Chrysostom's general remarks.
