# Patristic Insights on John 21: A Summary

All four excerpts address John 21, mainly the miraculous catch of fish after the resurrection. Each commentator draws out a different theological emphasis.

---

## 1. John Chrysostom: Character, Signs, and Love

**The disciples' distinct personalities.** Chrysostom notes that when the disciples recognized Jesus, Peter and John again exhibited the peculiarities of their several tempers. The one was more fervent, the other more lofty; the one more keen, the other more clear-sighted. So John first recognized Jesus, Peter first came to Him.

**Several signs in one event.** Chrysostom counts multiple miracles: First, that so many fish were caught; then, that the net did not break; then, that before they landed, the coals had been found, and fish laid thereon, and bread. He sees a shift in how Christ works: He no longer made things out of matter already subsisting, as, through a certain dispensation, He did before the Crucifixion.

**Peter's devotion.** Peter's leap into the water shows eager love. They were only two hundred cubits off; but not even so could Peter wait to go to Him in the boat, but reached the shore by swimming. Chrysostom asks the reader: Do you see his respect and love?

---

## 2. Clement of Alexandria: Disciples as Children

This excerpt comes from a work on Christian formation (*Christ the Educator*) rather than a commentary on John 21. It uses only one verse from the chapter. Clement cites the scene where "the Lord, standing on the shore, says to the disciples"—they happened to be fishing—"and called aloud, 'Children, have you no fish?'

His point is that Christ addresses those who were already in the position of disciples as children … setting before us, for our imitation, the simplicity that is in children. For Clement, We are the children, the believers whom Christ teaches and trains.

---

## 3. Augustine of Hippo: Two Catches, Two Ages of the Church

**Comparing the two catches.** Augustine contrasts this catch with the earlier one, when Jesus first called the disciples. He says the comparison has a lot to do, after all, with the consolidation of our faith. The differences he notes:
- **Direction:** Before the resurrection, the nets were let out all over the place. After the resurrection, the right side is chosen.
- **Strain:** In the first catch the boats are overloaded, the nets are breaking. In the second, there is no overloading of the boat or breaking of the seine.
- **Number:** The first time, the number of fish caught is not mentioned. After the resurrection, a definite number of fish is mentioned.

**The first catch is the present Church.** The nets are the nets of the word, the nets of preaching. The Church now is mixed and divided: If they all lived good lives, they would not be overloading the boat. If they were not divided by heretics and schisms, the net would not be breaking.

**The second catch is the Church perfected.** It points to the Church that will be realized in that certain, definite number in which no sinner will be found.… And they will be big fish because they will all be immortal, all destined to live without end. Augustine reads the Evangelist's remark that the nets did not tear as a deliberate echo of the first catch. He concludes: This will be the kingdom of heaven, no heretics will be barking, no schismatics setting themselves apart. All will be inside, all will be at peace.

**Christ as the dawn.** Augustine also notes that Day dawned, and they made a catch because they saw Christ the day.

---

## 4. Cyril of Alexandria: From Law to Gospel

**Purpose of the appearance.** Cyril sees this third appearance as given in order that He might confirm their minds, and render them unchangeably steadfast in faith towards Him. The miracle also confirmed Christ's earlier promise. The Saviour, by the actual performance of a palpable miracle, satisfied the holy disciples that they were destined to be, as He had said, fishers of men.

**Night as spiritual darkness.** The fruitless night of fishing signifies that no one, as we shall find, or very few, would be wholly won over by the teaching of the first instructors of old. The reason was that There was still night and darkness, and a kind of mental mist and devilish deceit brooding over the eyes of the mind, not suffering men to perceive the true light of God. Morning came when the mist of the devil was dispersed, and the true light dawned, that is, Christ.

**The right side means the Gospel's superiority.** Cyril reads the "right side" as a contrast with the Law: the blessed Moses also let down the line of instruction, that is, by the letter of the Law; but this was fishing on the left side, the commandment of Christ unto us being on the right. He is careful to say he speaks not wishing to disparage the first commandment given of old, nor with the intent to accuse the Law.

**Mission by Christ's power.** The disciples' obedience means they did not seize fpr themselves the grace of apostleship, but at His bidding went forth to capture the souls of men. The huge catch shows that the growth of the Church is the working of Christ, Who gathereth by His own power the multitude of the saved into the Church on earth, as into the net of the Apostles.

*A note for careful readers:* in retelling the story, Cyril has the disciples reply, "At Thy word we will cast down the net." That wording appears to echo the earlier catch in Luke's Gospel rather than John 21. Cyril may be blending the two accounts, so his paraphrase should not be read as a direct quotation of John.

---

## Common Threads

- **Christ as dawn:** Augustine and Cyril both link the daybreak to Christ's presence ending fruitless labor.
- **The "right side":** Augustine reads it as the purified, chosen Church. Cyril reads it as the Gospel surpassing the Law.
- **The Church and mission:** Augustine focuses on the Church's final perfection. Cyril focuses on its worldwide growth through Christ's power.
- **Personal discipleship:** Chrysostom (Peter's love, John's insight) and Clement (childlike simplicity) focus on the disciples' character.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 10: Summary

The excerpts come from two early church commentators, John Chrysostom and Theodoret of Cyrus. They are brief, but they show how these early readers understood the setting and tone of Paul's argument.

## John Chrysostom (Homilies on the Epistles of Paul to the Corinthians)

**1. A turning point in the letter.** Chrysostom sees chapter 10 as a major shift in the epistle. Having completed his discourse on almsgiving, Paul now turns to less pleasant matters, concluding his epistle with denunciations of the false apostles. The generous, encouraging tone of the collection chapters (8–9) gives way to confrontation.

**2. Paul's self-defense.** Chrysostom notes that he offers explanations of himself and his ministry. He extends this to the whole letter: it would not be wrong to say that the whole epistle is an apology for Paul, because he makes so much mention of the grace and patience given to him. In his reading, Paul defends his ministry by pointing to God's grace at work in him and the patience he was given, not to his own abilities.

**3. Paul's use of irony.** Chrysostom observes that here Paul is speaking ironically, using the words of his critics to good effect. The excerpt does not say which verse he means. It does suggest that Paul sometimes takes up his opponents' accusations in order to turn them back on them.

## Theodoret of Cyrus (Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians)

**1. The background of the conflict.** Theodoret identifies Paul's opponents more specifically than Chrysostom does. He explains that some Jewish believers were ordering Gentile converts to follow the law of Moses. Their attack on Paul was personal and accused him of hypocrisy: they condemned Paul, calling him base and stupid, and claiming that although he kept the law in secret himself, he was prepared to dispense the Gentiles from it publicly, because he thought they were too ignorant to be able to keep it.

**2. Paul's answer: evidence of God's power.** According to Theodoret, Paul does not answer with argument alone. Paul refutes this charge by reminding the Corinthians of the miracles which he had done among them and of the gifts which they had received because of him. The proof of his apostleship is what God visibly did through him among the Corinthians.

**3. Living in the world without yielding to it.** A second short excerpt reads: Although we are surrounded by the world, we do not give in to it. The excerpt does not say which verse it comments on, so its exact place in the chapter cannot be confirmed from this material. It does express a principle of Christian life: believers live within the world but do not submit to its ways.

## Common Themes

- **Defense of Paul's apostleship.** Both writers read the chapter as Paul answering critics who challenged his authority and character.
- **Divine grace, not human standing.** Chrysostom stresses the grace and patience given to Paul. Theodoret points to miracles and spiritual gifts. Both see God's work, not Paul's personal qualities, as the basis of his defense.
- **Identifying the opponents.** Chrysostom calls them "false apostles." Theodoret describes them as Jewish believers pressing the Mosaic law on Gentile converts.

## A Note on the Sources

These excerpts are short fragments, and two of them do not name the verses they discuss. This summary therefore stays with what the commentators say and does not assign their remarks to particular verses of chapter 10.

# Patristic Commentary on Mark 10: Summary of Key Insights

The excerpts focus on the opening of Mark 10 (Jesus' move into Judea and the Pharisees' question about divorce).

---

## 1. Bede: On the Gospel of Mark

### A Geographical and Narrative Turning Point (Mark 10:1)
Bede sees verse 1 as a structural shift in Mark's Gospel. Up to this point the evangelist Mark narrated those things about the Lord which he did and taught in Galilee. Here he begins to narrate those things which he did, taught, or suffered in Judea. He traces the route: first beyond the Jordan to the east, then also on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, Bethany, and Jerusalem.

He also clarifies the term "Judea." While the whole province of the Jews is generally called Judea to distinguish it from other nations, more specifically its southern region is called Judea, to distinguish it from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and other regions in the same province.

### Two Kinds of Hearers: The Crowds and the Pharisees (Mark 10:1–2)
Bede contrasts the motives of those who came to Jesus. One must note the difference in mindset between the crowds and the Pharisees. The crowds came together to be taught and to have their sick healed, while the Pharisees approached to deceive the Savior and Teacher of truth by testing him. His summary: devotion of piety brought these, the goad of envy brought those.

### The Divorce Question as a Trap
Bede explains why the question was a dilemma. The Pharisees asked so that they might trap him in a sort of cunning argument, and whatever he answers, he will be subject to an accusation.
- If Jesus permitted divorce, the preacher of chastity will seem to be teaching contrary to himself.
- If he forbade it, he will be held as guilty of sacrilege and acting against the teaching of Moses and through Moses of God.

### Creation's Design Over Concession
Bede's most significant theological point is that Jesus resolves the dilemma by appealing to God's original intention. The Lord tempers his response in such a way that he avoids their trap, invoking holy Scripture as testimony and opposing the natural law and the original sentence from God to the secondary one, which was granted not by God's will but by the necessity of sinners. In this reading, the Mosaic allowance for divorce was a concession to human sinfulness, not an expression of God's will.

---

## 2. Origen of Alexandria: Commentary on Matthew 14.16

*Note:* This excerpt comes from Origen's commentary on Matthew, not Mark. It applies to Mark 10 only because it addresses the same theme of testing questions.

Origen observes that of those who came to Jesus and interrogated him, some put questions to him simply to trick him. He then applies this to Christian teachers: If our glorious Savior was tested in this way, should any of his disciples called to teach be annoyed when questioned by some who probe, not from the desire to know, but from the intent to trip up?

**Key insight:** Christ's patience with hostile questioners is a model for teachers in the Church, who should expect the same and not resent it.

---

## 3. Clement of Alexandria: Stromata, Book III

*Note:* This excerpt is in Latin and consists mostly of quoted Scripture, with little interpretation of its own. A rough translation:

> "But have you not read that God said to the first-formed [man]: 'You two shall be in one flesh'? Therefore whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery."

The Latin reads: Vos autem non legistis, quod protoplasto Deus dixit: `Eritis duo in carne una? Quare qui dimittit uxorem, praeterquam fornicationis causa, facit eam moechari.

**Observations:**
- Like Bede, Clement grounds the teaching on marriage in God's word at creation, addressed to the "first-formed" man.
- The phrase "except for the cause of fornication" reflects the wording found in Matthew's Gospel rather than Mark 10, which contains no such exception. The excerpt therefore touches Mark 10's theme but does not engage Mark's text directly.
- Because the excerpt is so brief, Clement's own argument cannot be reliably reconstructed from it.

---

## Common Threads

1. **Motives matter.** Bede and Origen both distinguish sincere seekers from those who question Jesus only to trap him.
2. **Creation sets the standard.** Bede and Clement both treat God's original design for marriage as the basis for Jesus' teaching, ranking it above later concessions.
3. **Christ as model.** Origen draws a practical lesson: those who teach in Christ's name should bear hostile questioning patiently, as he did.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Titus 1: A Summary

**A note on the sources:** Only some of these excerpts discuss Titus 1. Chrysostom's homily directly expounds Titus 1:1–2. Theodoret's comments are general remarks on how Paul opens his letters, though they include the wording of Titus 1:1. The two Aquinas excerpts, although labeled as Titus commentary, are actually from his commentary on **Philemon**. They are summarized separately below and should not be read as interpretations of Titus.

---

## 1. John Chrysostom: The Most Substantive Treatment of Titus 1

Chrysostom comments on Paul's opening words, "Paul, a servant of God, and an Apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect."

**The Father and Son are equal.** Chrysostom notes that Paul alternates his titles, sometimes calling himself the "servant of God," and sometimes the "servant of Christ," thus making no difference between the Father and the Son.

**Apostleship is a gift of grace, not a reward for merit.** Chrysostom reads "according to the faith of God's elect" as meaning Paul was entrusted with God's elect, that is, not for any achievements of mine, nor from my toils and labors, did I receive this dignity. It was wholly the effect of His goodness who entrusted me. In his view, God takes the initiative: First we are apprehended, and afterwards we know: first we are known, and then we apprehend: first we were called, and then we obeyed.

**Paul's ministry exists for the people's sake.** Paul is an apostle not for my worthiness, but "for the elect's sake."

**"Truth which is after godliness."** Chrysostom distinguishes ordinary knowledge from saving truth. He writes that knowledge in matters of agriculture, knowledge of the arts, is true knowledge; but this truth is after godliness. Such acknowledgment is from faith, and not from reasonings.

**Old Covenant as type, New Covenant as fulfillment.** Chrysostom says the old covenant was an "acknowledging" and a "godliness," yet not of the Truth, yet neither was it falsehood, it was godliness, but it was in type and figure. Accordingly, "in hope of eternal life" marks a contrast, for the former was in hope of the present life.

**Remembering God's mercies motivates service.** Chrysostom observes that the introduction is full of the mercies of God, and this whole Epistle is especially of the same character. He adds that nothing profits us so much as constantly to remember the mercies of God, whether public or private.

---

## 2. Theodoret of Cyrus: Paul's Opening Formulas

Theodoret's excerpt does not expound Titus 1 in detail, but it places the letter's opening within Paul's usual pattern. Among Paul's varied self-descriptions he lists "Paul a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ", the wording of Titus 1:1. His theological point concerns the blessing: Paul links the title of the Son with God the Father, saying "grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Like Chrysostom, Theodoret sees in Paul's greetings an implicit testimony to the unity of Father and Son.

---

## 3. Thomas Aquinas: Excerpts on Philemon, Not Titus

These passages are about Philemon. Aquinas states that at Colossae an important Christian had a servant who secretly fled to Rome where he was baptized by the Apostle who now writes on his behalf. He also discusses Philemon, Appia, and Archippus. Because they do not address Titus 1, they are noted here only briefly:

- **Suffering for Christ is honorable.** Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus, to give the reason for his chains. Aquinas comments: For it is highly praiseworthy to be imprisoned for the sake of Christ; for in this he is blessed.
- **Master and servant are brothers.** The servant should be treated like a brother, for he is a brother, both with respect to generation of nature, because they have the same author and with respect to the generation of grace, which is the same for both.

(One of Aquinas's citations as given, "2 Peter 4:15," appears to be an error in the source, since 2 Peter has only three chapters. The quoted text matches 1 Peter 4:15–16.)

---

## Key Takeaways for Titus 1

1. **Paul's titles show the unity of Father and Son** (Chrysostom, Theodoret).
2. **Ministry is entrusted by grace, not earned**, and it exists to serve God's people (Chrysostom).
3. **Saving truth is received by faith and leads to godliness**, unlike merely practical knowledge (Chrysostom).
4. **The "hope of eternal life" fulfills what the old covenant foreshadowed** (Chrysostom).
5. **Remembering God's mercies fuels zeal** for Christian living (Chrysostom).

# Summary of Commentaries on Hebrews 11

## Thomas Aquinas

Aquinas's excerpt is by far the most substantial. It focuses almost entirely on the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1.

**Why Hebrews 11 follows what came before.** Aquinas sees chapter 11 as continuing the letter's argument. The Apostle showed Christ's superiority in many ways by preferring Him to the angels, to Moses and to Aaron, and advised the faithful to be united to Christ. Because this union consists principally in faith and begins with faith, the Apostle now commends faith. He does so by defining it, giving examples, and then exhorting his readers in chapter 12.

**A complete but compressed definition.** Aquinas calls Hebrews 11:1 a definition of faith which is complete but obscure. A virtue is properly defined by its matter and its end. In the case of faith, since faith is a theological virtue, its object and end are the same, namely, God.

**"Of things hoped for": faith's goal.** For Aquinas, faith involves both the mind and the will. The act of faith is to believe, because it is an act of the intellect narrowed to one thing by the command of the will. In this life God is not yet seen, so the first truth, not seen but hoped for, is the end of the will on earth and, consequently, is the object of faith. That hope points toward happiness, which consists in the clear vision of God.

Aquinas also explains several finer details of the wording:
- **Why faith is defined by hope, even though faith comes first.** In the order of knowing, the intellect is prior; but in the order of moving, the will is prior.
- **Why "hoped for" rather than "loved."** Charity is concerned with things that are present or absent. Faith, by contrast, concerns a goal not yet possessed.
- **Why "things" is plural.** Happiness is one thing, the vision of God, but it is the principle and root from which the many good things contained under it are derived: for example, the characteristics of the body, companionship with the saints, and many other good things.

**"Substance": heaven begun now.** Aquinas reads "substance" in more than one way:
- **As a cause, through merit.** From the fact that a person makes his intellect captive and submissive to the things of faith, he deserves some day to see the things he hopes for: for vision is the reward of faith.
- **As a cause, by its own nature.** Faith brings it about that what is believed really to lie in the future, be somehow already possessed.
- **As essence, illustrated by an analogy from learning.** A student must first accept a science's principles, and in those principles the entire science is somehow contained, as conclusions are contained in their principles, and an effect in its cause. In the same way, these principles are the articles of faith, which contain the summary of this knowledge. Faith is therefore a beginning in which the whole is, as it were, virtually contained, as conclusions in principles.

**"Evidence of things not seen": certainty without sight.** Aquinas places faith between two other states of mind:
- **Knowledge and understanding,** where we see clearly and are certain.
- **Doubt and opinion,** where we have neither sight nor certainty.

Faith has no evidence, as there is in understanding and science, nor is there doubt, as in doubt and opinion; but it fixes on one side with certainty and firm adherence by a voluntary choice. Crucially, this choice rests on God's authority, and by it the intellect is fixed, so that it clings firmly to the things of faith and assents to them with the greatest of certainty.

**His restated definition.** Aquinas sums up the verse this way: faith is a habit of the mind by which eternal life is begun in us and makes the intellect assent to things that it does not see.

**Answering two objections.**
- **Thomas the apostle "saw and believed."** Aquinas follows Gregory: he saw one thing and believed something else: for he saw the humanity and believed the divinity.
- **Truths philosophers can prove, such as that God is one.** Nothing prohibits one thing being seen by one person and believed by another, just as an illiterate person believes in an eclipse which an astronomer sees. Still, there are some things which absolutely transcend the state of the present life; and in regard to these there is faith in the strict sense.

## Clement of Alexandria

Both excerpts from Clement are essentially quotations of Hebrews 11 itself, with little commentary of his own.
- The first excerpt quotes verses 2 and 6: "For hereby "pre-eminently, "the elders obtained a good report. But without faith it is impossible to please God." His only visible contribution is the word "pre-eminently," which seems to stress that faith is the chief basis of the elders' good standing.
- The *Stromata* excerpt quotes the passage on Abel and then abbreviates the rest. It runs from "By faith Abel offered to God a fuller sacrifice than Cain" down to "than enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season."

Clement clearly treats this long stretch of the chapter as one connected unit. However, the excerpts do not show his interpretation of it, so no further theological insight can fairly be credited to him from this material.

## Theodoret of Cyrus

Theodoret's excerpt is a single brief note on Abel in verse 4. He takes the statement that the dead Abel still speaks to refer to his lasting reputation: "he is still speaking" means, To this day he is famous and celebrated and enjoys a good name among all religious people. This is a modest but helpful point: Abel's faith continues to "speak" through the honor and example it has among believers.

## Overall Assessment

Aquinas provides nearly all the theological depth in these excerpts. He offers a careful reading of Hebrews 11:1 in which faith is both a firm, God-grounded certainty about unseen things and the present beginning of eternal life. Clement's excerpts mainly reproduce the biblical text. Theodoret contributes a single interpretive note on Abel.

# Patristic Insights on Hebrews 1

These excerpts come from three early Church writers. Most of them focus on the opening phrase of Hebrews, "in many and various ways," and on how God's earlier revelations relate to Christ.

## Theodoret of Cyrus

**A note on scope:** Theodoret's first excerpt is an overview of the **entire Epistle to the Hebrews**, not only chapter 1. It is still useful because it shows where chapter 1 fits in the letter's overall argument.

**1. The opening argument: Christ above prophets and angels**
Theodoret says the author begins by showing that Christ is better than all the prophets. He sees two steps in this opening section:
- **Christ's divine nature:** The author shows Christ to be eternal—coeternal with the Father and the Creator of all.
- **Christ compared with angels:** The author turns to sacred Scripture, which openly teaches that Christ is Son and God, while angels are ministers and creatures.

The rest of Theodoret's outline covers later chapters, such as the comparison with Moses, the priesthood of Melchizedek, and the examples of faith.

**2. "In many and various ways" (the opening verse)**
Theodoret reads the phrase on two levels:
- **Many dispensations and visions:** "In many ways" indicates the manifold dispensations, "various ways," the different kinds of divine visions. God appeared to Abraham in one way, to Moses in another, to Elijah in another, to Micaiah in another.
- **God's nature stays hidden:** The variety was not in God himself. The divine nature is not pluriform, but without either shape or appearance, simple and uncomplicated. So the prophets did not see the incomprehensible nature but rather guises of some kind, which the unseen God revealed as need required.
- **Partial ministries versus complete salvation:** Each of the inspired authors was entrusted with some particular dispensation, whereas their God—I mean Christ the Lord—did not provide for some single need, but by becoming man he set all to rights and secured the salvation of human beings.
- **One God across both covenants:** Theodoret concludes that there is one lawgiver of the old and new.

## Augustine of Hippo

**A note on scope:** This excerpt is from a sermon, not a verse-by-verse commentary. Augustine borrows the phrase from Hebrews 1 and applies it to the Old Testament sacrifices.

**Many sacrifices pointing to one sacrifice**
Augustine argues that those old sacrifices of the people of God also represented in a variety of ways this single one that was to come. He gives an example: Christ was both a sheep, because of his innocence and simplicity of soul, and a goat because of "the likeness of sinful flesh." His main point is that whatever else was foretold "in many and various ways" in the sacrifices of the old covenant refers to this single one which has been revealed in the new covenant.

## Eusebius of Caesarea

**The Word of God as the one seen in the Old Testament**
Eusebius addresses an apparent contradiction. Scripture says Israel saw God, yet also says "No one has ever seen God," which might seem to imply that the invisible is visible. His answer uses the language of Hebrews 1: if these appearances are understood as the Word of God, who was seen by the fathers "in many ways and various ways," no contradiction is involved.

He supports this with Jacob's wrestling. Jacob named the place of the struggle the Sight of God, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved", and Eusebius insists that this was no other than the Word of God.

## Common Threads

- **Unity behind variety:** All three writers treat "in many and various ways" as describing real diversity in God's earlier self-revelation, all of it pointing to one reality: Christ.
- **Continuity of the covenants:** Theodoret stresses one lawgiver for the old and new. Augustine sees the old sacrifices fulfilled in the one new-covenant sacrifice.
- **Revelation without exposure of God's essence:** Theodoret and Eusebius both protect God's invisibility. Theodoret says the prophets saw "guises" rather than the divine nature itself. Eusebius identifies the Word of God as the one who was seen.
- **Christ's supremacy:** Theodoret states most directly the chapter's claim that Christ, as eternal Son and Creator, surpasses both prophets and angels.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 8:1–3: Summary of Key Insights

The excerpts focus on the opening verses of Luke 8: Jesus' preaching journey with the Twelve, and the women who traveled with him and supported him.

## Bede: On Christ's Preaching Journey (Luke 8:1)

**The verse:** Bede begins with the text: "And it happened afterward, that he was traveling through cities and villages, preaching and evangelizing the kingdom of God, and the twelve were with him."

**Continuity between the Testaments:** Bede sees Jesus' formation of his disciples as fulfilling an Old Testament pattern. "We see in Christ's disciples the fulfillment of what we read said about that ancient people of the Hebrews." This should not surprise us, "because the same God of both Testaments will give blessing through the Son, who gave the law through the servant."

**The image of the mother eagle:** Bede draws on Deuteronomy 32, where a (mother) eagle provoking her young to fly, and hovering over them, spreads her wings, takes them up, and bears them on her shoulders (Deut. XXXII). He applies the image to spiritual growth: "just as the young birds, newly born, cannot yet conquer the air by flying until they become feathered: so all the faithful, to be able to fly to heavenly things, must first clothe themselves with the wing of virtues in the nest of faith."

**Gradual formation of the apostles:** For Bede, this verse marks a stage in a deliberate process. The apostles themselves, teachers of the faithful, gradually ascend to the heights, so that they can also preside over the teaching of others. He traces the process step by step:
- **Public ministry first:** The Lord teaches in synagogues, performs miracles, spreads renown everywhere, receives the crowds coming to him, heals, instructs.
- **Nurture and protection:** He makes disciples, refreshes at the wedding of the bridegroom, leads them through fields, and defends them from the bites of serpentine Pharisees, continuing the eagle image.
- **Choosing the Twelve:** From these he chooses twelve, whom he names apostles, but he first teaches them in the presence of the crowd.
- **Private instruction:** Now, on this journey, he retains only those who might hear him more intimately, explaining to them alone the mysteries of the kingdom of God, which he had spoken to others in parables.
- **Being sent out:** Finally, with the manifestation of his virtues, firm as with the protection of wings, he gives them the power to heal, and sends them out to preach the kingdom of God.

**Key insight:** Christ forms his followers patiently, as a mother eagle trains her young. Discipleship is a gradual maturing in virtue that prepares believers for mission.

## Gregory of Nazianzus: The Purpose Behind Christ's Actions

*Note:* This excerpt does not explicitly cite Luke 8. Its opening line, however, fits Jesus' travels "through cities and villages" in 8:1, which is presumably why it appears alongside this chapter.

Gregory's insight is that everything Christ did had a sanctifying purpose:
- "He passes from place to place, that He may not only gain many, but may consecrate many places."
- "He sleeps and labors, that He may sanctify sleep and labor."
- "He weeps, that He may give a value to tears."
- "He preaches heavenly things, that He may exalt His hearers."

**Key insight:** By sharing in ordinary human experience, such as travel, work, rest and grief, Christ makes these things holy. His preaching aims to lift his hearers up.

## Bede: On the Women Who Followed Jesus (Luke 8:2–3)

### Mary Magdalene
Bede comments on the verse naming certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary, who is called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 16: Summary of Key Insights

The excerpts come from two commentators. Bede's comments address the Parable of the Unjust Steward (Luke 16:1–9) directly. Basil's excerpt deals with wealth but does not explicitly reference Luke 16.

---

## Bede — *On the Gospel of Luke*

### 1. The "Wisdom" of the Children of This Age
Bede takes up the puzzling verse where the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. He reads it as an ironic rebuke rather than an endorsement of worldly cleverness. He urges: let the wise of this world hear, that they may abandon foolish wisdom and learn the wisdom of God's foolishness. Christ remembers them not as truly wise, but wise in their generation. Bede links this to Isaiah: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight (Isaiah 5).

He also explains the contrast between "children of light" and "children of this age." By using these titles, Christ reproves those who are wise to do evil but know not how to do good as being children of darkness. The underlying principle is that each one is named a child of that of which he performs the works. In other words, a person's identity is revealed by their deeds.

### 2. The Reduced Debts as a Call to Greater Generosity
Bede reads the steward's reductions of the debts (oil from 100 to 50, wheat from 100 to 80) allegorically. He offers his interpretations tentatively, introducing them with "I think," "or," and "unless perhaps."

- **Primary reading:** The figures signify that whatever a Jew did for priests and Levites should abound in righteousness in the Church of Christ beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that whereas they gave tithes, these should give half, as Zacchaeus did.
- **Alternative reading:** doubling the tithes, so that by giving two tithes, they exceed the expenses of the Jews.
- **Simpler reading:** every person who alleviates the indigence of any poor saint, either by half, or certainly by one-fifth, as twenty or fifty to a hundred, will be granted a sure reward of their mercy.

### 3. "Unrighteous Mammon" and True Riches
On the command to make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous mammon, Bede explains that money becomes "riches," in the full sense, only for those who trust in it. These are riches only for the unjust, who place their hope and abundance of happiness in them. For the righteous, by contrast, it is simply money, but they are not riches for them, except heavenly and spiritual.

Bede then argues from the lesser to the greater. If material almsgiving earns eternal welcome, how much more should those who distribute spiritual feasts, who give their fellow servants food at the appropriate time, be raised with the most certain hope of the highest reward? This extends the parable's lesson to those who share spiritual nourishment, such as teaching and preaching.

---

## Basil of Caesarea

Basil's excerpt does not explicitly mention Luke 16 or the parable. It does address the question of where wealth comes from and who it belongs to, which is a related theme.

- **Wealth is often tainted at its source.** On inherited wealth, Basil observes that in a number of predecessors some one must needs be found who has unjustly usurped the property of others.
- **All wealth ultimately comes from God.** Anyone who claims their money comes from themselves is ignorant of God, not having the knowledge of your Creator.
- **Wealth is held in common trust.** Basil concludes: If then whatever is ours belongs to our common Lord, so will it also belong to our fellow-servant.

Basil's idea of possessions as belonging to God and owed to others fits naturally with a stewardship reading of Luke 16. However, the excerpt itself does not draw that connection, so it should be read as a thematic parallel rather than direct commentary on the chapter.

---

## Common Thread
Both writers treat material wealth as something held in trust rather than truly owned. Bede presents generous use of money as the path to eternal reward. Basil grounds this in God's ultimate ownership of everything and our obligation to our fellow servants.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 4: Summary

These excerpts come from three early Church Fathers. Most of them focus on two themes in the chapter: the honesty of Paul's ministry compared with that of his opponents, and the endurance and light that come from God.

## John Chrysostom

**1. Authentic versus deceptive ministry.** Chrysostom contrasts Paul with certain rivals at Corinth. He describes them this way: Some were "walking in craftiness." They had a reputation for taking nothing, but in fact they took it and kept it secret. Their holiness was only on the surface, since they had the seeming character of saints and apostles but were full of innumerable secret wickednesses.

Paul's ministry, by contrast, can withstand scrutiny: Paul takes nothing and calls the Corinthians as his witnesses. Likewise he does nothing wicked and asks them to testify to the truth of what he is saying. For Chrysostom, a genuine apostle's integrity is open and can be verified by the community he serves. A false teacher depends on concealment.

**2. Perseverance as a gift of God.** Chrysostom gives God, not Paul's own strength, the credit for Paul's endurance: This perseverance is to be attributed to God's loving kindness, for not only do we not sink down under the weight of all our trials, but we even rejoice and speak boldly. His point goes beyond survival. God's kindness lets believers rejoice and speak with confidence even while suffering.

## Gregory of Nyssa

Gregory reads the chapter's imagery of light as a call to holy living. He begins with Christ: Knowing Christ as the "true light," "inaccessible" to falsehood, we learn this, namely, that it is necessary for our lives also to be illuminated by the rays of the true light.

He describes the virtues as that light at work in a believer's life: virtues are the rays of "the Sun of Justice," streaming forth for our illumination, through which we "lay aside the works of darkness," so that we "walk becomingly as in the day," and "we renounce those things which shame conceals."

He then argues that believers do more than receive light. They come to share in it: By doing all things in the light, we become the light itself, so that it "shines" before others, which is the peculiar quality of light. He insists this must show in conduct, not just in what a person professes. He urges believers to be true sharers of his name, coinciding in deed and not in word with the power of his sanctification.

## Theodoret of Cyrus

Theodoret's excerpt is a single sentence: Paul is talking here about circumcision, which the false apostles were covertly forcing on newly converted Gentiles. The excerpt does not say which phrase in chapter 4 he is interpreting. It may relate to Paul's rejection of hidden or underhanded practices, which would match Chrysostom's focus on secret dealings. However, the connection is not stated in the text provided, so this reading should be held tentatively.

## Common Threads

- **Openness versus concealment.** Chrysostom and Gregory both stress that true faith is lived openly. Chrysostom emphasizes the visible honesty of Paul's ministry, and Gregory speaks of renouncing what shame hides. Theodoret's mention of "covert" pressure from false apostles may also fit this theme.
- **God as the source.** For Chrysostom, endurance comes from God's loving kindness. For Gregory, virtue is the light of Christ shining through believers.
- **Faith shown in action.** Both writers hold that genuine Christian witness is proven by conduct: Paul's honest dealings in Chrysostom, and holiness "in deed and not in word" in Gregory.

# Augustine of Hippo on Matthew 25: The Parable of the Ten Virgins

**Note on scope:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 93). They focus only on the parable of the wise and foolish virgins at the start of Matthew 25. They do not address the rest of the chapter, such as the parable of the talents or the judgment of the nations, so those passages are not covered here.

## 1. Why "Five," and Who Counts as a "Virgin" (Sermon 93.2)

Augustine reads the number five symbolically, linking it to human life in the body: every soul that enlivens a body is denoted by the number five, because it makes use of five senses. He explains that there is nothing of which we have perception by the body except through this fivefold gate, either by sight, or hearing, or smelling, or tasting or touching.

He then reinterprets "virginity" as moral purity across all the senses rather than only in the physical sense: whoever abstains from unlawful seeing, unlawful hearing, unlawful smelling, unlawful tasting and unlawful touching, by reason of blamelessness, is here called by the name of virgin.

**Key insight:** The virgins stand for anyone who guards the "gates" of the senses, so the parable applies to every believer, not only to the literally celibate.

## 2. The Parable Addresses the Whole Church (Sermon 93.5)

Augustine insists the parable is universal: this parable relates to us all, that is, to the whole church together, not to the clergy only, of whom we spoke yesterday, nor to the laity only but generally to all. He describes the ten as all Christian souls together.

He then narrows this in a sobering way. The virgins are not souls of every sort but such souls as have the catholic faith and seem to have good works in the church of God. Yet even of them it is said, "Five are wise, and five are foolish."

**Key insight:** The parable is a warning to people inside the church. Orthodox belief and outwardly good works do not by themselves guarantee readiness. Augustine's word "seem" suggests that appearances can mislead.

## 3. What It Means to "Go Out to Meet the Bridegroom" (Sermon 93.5)

Augustine notes that they wished to go to meet the bridegroom and asks what this means. His answer is: to go with all the heart, to eagerly await his coming.

**Key insight:** Going out to meet the bridegroom means wholehearted, eager expectation of Christ's coming, which is an inward disposition and not just outward participation.

## 4. The Oil as the Dividing Line (Sermon 93.4)

Augustine observes that even of these, who were virgins and carrying lamps, some are wise and some foolish. He asks how they can be told apart and answers: Only by whether the oil is present or missing.

**Key insight:** Since all ten share the outward marks of virginity and lamps, the real difference lies in something less visible, the oil. This excerpt does not say what the oil symbolizes. Augustine presumably explains this elsewhere in the sermon, but it would be speculation to supply his answer here.

## Summary

Augustine treats the parable as a searching message to the whole church. The virgins are believers who guard their senses and hold the true faith, yet the community is still divided between wise and foolish. Meeting the bridegroom requires wholehearted, eager waiting, and what ultimately separates the two groups is not outward appearance but whether the oil is present.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Thessalonians 3: Key Insights

All four excerpts center on one verse: Paul's request that the Thessalonians pray for him so that "the word of the Lord may run and be glorified." Each commentator draws a different lesson from it.

## John Chrysostom (Homily 54)

**Paul's request is about the gospel, not his own safety.** Chrysostom points out that Paul's prayers go both ways: he indeed had prayed for them, that they might be established; and now he asks of them, entreating them to pray for him, not that he may not incur danger, for to this he was appointed, but that "the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, even as also it is with you." Paul accepts danger as part of his calling. What he wants prayer for is the spread of the gospel.

**Encouragement is part of Paul's approach.** Chrysostom notes that the request is accompanied with commendation. The phrase "even as also it is with you" quietly praises the Thessalonians for how they received the word.

## Augustine of Hippo (Letter 217)

**The word "runs" when people come to faith.** Augustine asks, how else could the word of God run and be glorified except by the conversion to the faith of those to whom it is preached, when Paul says to present believers, "Even as among you"?

**Prayer shows that God is the one who converts.** Since Paul asks for prayer, Augustine argues, surely he knows that this is accomplished by him to whom he wishes prayer to be made. His conclusion: No one is so unlearned, so carnal, so slow of wit as not to see that God does what he commands us to ask him to do.

**"Not all have faith" points to God's election.** Augustine reads Paul's closing remark predestinarily. He paraphrases it as "The word of God will not be glorified among all, even though you are praying" because those who were likely to believe were the ones "who were ordained to life everlasting," predestined "to the adoption of children through Jesus Christ to himself" and chosen "in him before the foundation of the world." This passage belongs to Augustine's broader teaching on grace.

## Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 13)

This excerpt does not quote 2 Thessalonians 3 directly. It does take up the same theme: apostles asking for prayer.

**Everyone needs prayer, including leaders.** Augustine tells his congregation, do not think that you need my prayers, but that I have no need of yours. Instead, we have mutual need of one another's prayers, for those reciprocal prayers are enkindled by charity and—like a sacrifice offered on the altar of piety—are fragrant and pleasing to the Lord.

**Humility from the apostles' example.** He reasons, if the apostles used to ask for prayers on their own behalf, how much more does it behoove me to do so? He admits I am far from being their equal, although I long to follow their footsteps as closely as possible.

## Ambrose of Milan (Isaac, or the Soul)

This excerpt is not a commentary on 2 Thessalonians 3. It is a reflection on the soul's longing for God. Ambrose only alludes briefly to the image of the running word, writing that the soul hastens to the Word and asks that she be drawn to him, so that she may not, perhaps, be left behind, for "the Word of God runs and is not bound." His wording ("is not bound") differs from the verse as quoted by Augustine and Chrysostom. Ambrose uses the "running" image devotionally: the Word moves swiftly, and the soul must hurry to keep up with Christ.

## Common Threads

- **The gospel's progress depends on God, so prayer matters.** Chrysostom and Augustine both see Paul's request as aimed at the spread of the word rather than his own comfort.
- **Prayer is mutual.** Chrysostom notes that Paul both prays for the Thessalonians and asks for their prayers. Augustine's sermon builds on this example to teach that every believer, whatever their rank, needs the prayers of others.
- **Different emphases:** Chrysostom stresses Paul's pastoral warmth, Augustine draws out divine grace and election, and Ambrose turns the image of the "running" Word into a call for personal devotion.

His wording ("is not bound") differs from the verse as quoted by Augustine and Chrysostom. Ambrose uses the "running" image devotionally: the Word moves swiftly, and the soul must hurry to keep up with Christ.

## Common Threads

- **The gospel's progress depends on God, so prayer matters.** Chrysostom and Augustine both see Paul's request as aimed at the spread of the word rather than his own comfort.
- **Prayer is mutual.** Chrysostom notes that Paul both prays for the Thessalonians and asks for their prayers. Augustine's sermon builds on this example to teach that every believer, whatever their rank, needs the prayers of others.
- **Different emphases:** Chrysostom stresses Paul's pastoral warmth, Augustine draws out divine grace and election, and Ambrose turns the image of the "running" Word into a call for personal devotion.

# Patristic Commentary on Philippians 1: A Summary

## Theodoret of Cyrus: Church Order in the Greeting (Phil. 1:1–2)

Theodoret focuses on whom Paul addresses in the opening verses and what the titles mean.

- **An inclusive greeting:** Paul writes to the whole church. He sends his news to everyone, both those who have been deemed worthy of ordination and those who are shepherded by them.
- **The meaning of "saints":** Holiness is tied to baptism. By "those who are holy" he means those who have worthily received holy baptism.
- **"Bishops" as presbyters:** Theodoret argues that he applies the term bishops to presbyters, for at that time they had both names. He gives two reasons:
  - Paul joins the deacons to the bishops, making no mention of the presbyters.
  - It was not possible for many bishops to be shepherds to one city.
- **Epaphroditus as overseer:** Theodoret notes that in this same letter he calls the blessed Epaphroditus their apostle, … and thus he indicates plainly that he was entrusted with an episcopal function because he had the name of an apostle.

**Key insight:** Theodoret reads the greeting as evidence that church leadership titles were still fluid in the apostolic period, while the role of chief shepherd may have been held under a different name.

## John Chrysostom: Suffering, Consolation, and Unity

Chrysostom's excerpt is a general introduction to the whole epistle, followed by a moral sermon. Several of his points bear directly on Chapter 1.

**1. The church's origins.** He recalls that Philippi is a city in Macedonia, a city that is a colony, as Luke says. He notes that here that seller of purple was converted, a woman of uncommon piety and heedfulness, and that here was Paul scourged with Silas.

**2. Suffering as a gift.** Paul honors the Philippians, calling them his own crown, and saying they had suffered much. Chrysostom cites 1:29: To you, he says, it has been granted of God, not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer in His behalf.

**3. Paul's imprisonment.**
- On 1:13, Chrysostom reads the "praetorium" as Nero's palace: So that my bonds became manifest in Christ in the whole prætorium, calling the palace of Nero the prætorium.
- He argues that Paul was imprisoned more than once: he was loosed from his bonds and again bound after he had been to them.
- He takes Paul's confidence that he will "abide" (1:25) as a sign that he was not about to die at that time.

**4. Consolation for an anxious church.**
- The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus to carry him money, and to know the things concerning him, for they were most lovingly disposed toward him.
- Chrysostom sees Paul answering their concern immediately in 1:12: But I would have you know that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the progress of the Gospel.
- So in the opening of the epistle he offers them much consolation about his bonds, showing that they should not merely not be disturbed, but even rejoice.

**5. Unity matters more than chains.** This is perhaps Chrysostom's most striking pastoral point: it is not being in bonds that is painful to your teachers, but their disciples not being of one mind. For the former brings even furtherance to the Gospel, but the latter distracts.

**6. A letter of encouragement.** Paul never in any place writes any thing of reproof, which is a proof of their virtue. Chrysostom also cites Paul's affection for them: Because I have you in my heart, and in my bonds.

**7. Application: lifelong mercy.** Chrysostom's closing exhortation on almsgiving moves beyond Chapter 1, but it grows from the Philippians' example. He urges hearers to imitate their earnestness in well doing, and not think, if we have given once or twice, that we have fulfilled all. He also teaches that he that gives alms, as he ought to give, learns to despise wealth.

**Key insight:** For Chrysostom, the opening of Philippians reframes suffering. Imprisonment advances the gospel and is a gift to share in, while division among believers is the real danger.

## Irenaeus: An Incomplete Fragment

The Irenaeus excerpt is cut off mid-sentence. It states that the apostle himself also, being one who had been formed in a womb, and had issued thence, wrote to us, and confessed in his Epistle to the Philippians that "to live in the flesh was the fruit of. This seems to point to Philippians 1:22. Because the quotation and the surrounding argument are missing, a reliable theological conclusion can't be drawn from it. At most, Irenaeus links Paul's bodily birth to his words about living "in the flesh."

## Summary

| Commentator | Main Focus | Central Insight |
|---|---|---|
| **Theodoret** | Greeting (1:1–2) | "Saints" are the baptized; "bishops" here means presbyters; leadership titles were still fluid |
| **Chrysostom** | Paul's bonds and the church's response (1:12–13, 1:25, 1:29) | Suffering advances the gospel and is a gift; disunity is more harmful than chains |
| **Irenaeus** | Probably 1:22 | Fragment is incomplete; no firm conclusion possible |

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on Revelation 16

## Bede: The Bowls as Spiritual Judgment Through the Church

Bede reads the bowl judgments mainly as **spiritual realities carried out through the Church's ministry**, rather than as purely physical catastrophes.

**1. The Church's authority to bind and loose**
For Bede, the command to pour out the bowls shows that the Church is given the power to impose judgment on the damned and to mercifully grant absolution to the converted. Judgment and mercy belong to the same ministry.

**2. The meaning of the number seven**
Bede notes that all angels are commanded to pour out on the earth; but these earthly men receive different names due to the variety of their sins, so that just as the fullness of preaching and vengeance, so also the fullness of guilt is reckoned by the number seven. The seven bowls therefore express completeness: complete proclamation, complete judgment, and complete human guilt.

**3. Three ways the bowls are poured out**
On the first bowl, Bede explains that preachers pour out the bowls of God's wrath in two ways: either by spiritually judging and imposing punishments on the impious, as Peter did to Simon, saying: Your money perish with you (Acts VIII); or by manifesting it through preaching to the holy Church. He then adds a third way, in which any sinner, upon hearing the preaching of the truth, is corrupted by a more severe wound of contradiction. He supports this with Christ's words: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin (John XV). The point is sobering. Hearing the gospel increases accountability, and rejecting the truth itself becomes a wound.

**4. The first bowl: the sore**
Bede interprets the "severe wound" as self-inflicted spiritual ruin: those who, having forsaken the Lord, worship the devil, will perish spiritually by the grievous wound of the same impiety. Sin carries its own punishment.

**5. The second bowl: the sea turned to blood**
Bede applies this bowl to persecutors. He says that those who are not only marked with the character of the Antichrist but also attack the stability of Christ's servants with the waves of bitter persecution will be punished with a spiritual vengeance, which he calls blood; and those who boasted of living will be proven to have served the author of death. The image of the sea suits the "waves" of persecution, and the blood reveals that the persecutors' apparent life was service to death.

## Irenaeus: The Plagues as a New Exodus

Irenaeus's excerpt (*Against Heresies* 4.30.4) does not mention Revelation 16 or the bowls by name. It speaks more generally about the plagues in the Apocalypse. Still, it offers a helpful interpretive framework for the chapter.

**1. The Exodus as a type of the Church's deliverance**
Irenaeus teaches that the whole exodus of the people out of Egypt, which took place under divine guidance, was a type and image of the exodus of the church that should take place from among the Gentiles. He adds that God leads [the church] out at last from this world into his own inheritance, which Moses the servant of God did not give but which Jesus the Son of God shall give for an inheritance.

**2. The end-time plagues mirror Egypt's plagues**
Irenaeus observes that anyone who studies the prophets and those that John the disciple of the Lord saw in the Apocalypse, he will find that the nations [are to] receive the same plagues universally, as Egypt once did particularly. The final judgments are Egypt's plagues writ large, now falling on the whole world, while God's people are led toward their inheritance.

## Comparing the Two Approaches

- **Bede** focuses on the *spiritual and moral* meaning of the bowls. They describe the Church's ministry of judgment and mercy and the self-destructive nature of sin and persecution.
- **Irenaeus** focuses on the *redemptive-historical pattern*. The plagues of Revelation echo the Exodus, framing final judgment as part of God's deliverance of his people.

Together they show two complementary emphases in early Christian reading of Revelation: the inward, spiritual reality of judgment, and its place in the larger story of salvation.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 3: Key Insights

The provided excerpts come from two early Christian writers, the Venerable Bede and St. Jerome. They focus only on the opening verses of Acts 3 (verses 1–2), where Peter and John go up to the Temple and meet the lame man at the Beautiful Gate.

---

## The Venerable Bede

Bede reads the passage allegorically, treating each detail as a symbol of larger spiritual realities about Israel, Christ, and the Church.

### 1. The Apostles' Late-Day Mission (Acts 3:1)
Bede reads the timing of the apostles' activity as a picture of salvation history. He notes that laboring continuously until evening, they imbued many thousands of people with the word of faith, because the teachers of the church, coming at the end of the world, also preach first to ailing Israel and afterwards to the Gentile world. He links the apostles to a familiar image: they are the laborers whom the householder brought into the vineyard at the ninth and the eleventh hour.

**Insight:** For Bede, the "lateness" of the hour stands for the Church's mission in the last age of the world, a mission that follows an order: first to Israel, then to the nations.

### 2. The Lame Man as a Figure of Israel (Acts 3:2)
Bede sees the man lame from birth as a symbol of God's people. Because the people of Israel were found rebellious not only after the Lord's incarnation but even from the earliest times when the law was given, they were as if lame from the mother's womb.

He connects this to the patriarch Jacob, suggesting it was well prefigured by Jacob's being blessed, indeed, but lame when he wrestled with the angel, for this same people, when they prevailed over the Lord in his passion, was in some of [its members] blessed through the faith but in others lame through infidelity.

**Insight:** The Jacob parallel lets Bede describe Israel as divided, blessed in those who believed and "lame" in those who did not.

### 3. Christ as the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:2)
Bede's most striking image is his reading of the Temple gate: The beautiful gate of the temple is the Lord. Whoever enters through him will be saved.

He also explains why the lame man was carried there. Enfeebled Israel, being unable to walk to this gate, was brought there by the words of the law and the prophets, so that they might request help from those who were entering into the interior places of the wisdom of the faith. He adds that those who place the prophecies of things to come are, as it were, hearers at the gate.

### 4. Peter as Guide into the Temple
Bede gives Peter a special role: Peter is the guide into the temple. He explains that to him, in virtue of his strong profession of faith, the epithet of "rock" and the keys of heaven were given.

**Insight:** In Bede's reading, the Law and the Prophets bring people to the threshold of Christ, but apostolic preaching leads them inside.

---

## St. Jerome

**A note on this excerpt:** Jerome's passage comes from his *Commentary on Daniel* (on Daniel 6:10), not from a commentary on Acts. He mentions Acts 3:1 only briefly, as an example. It is included here because of that one reference, not because Jerome offers an extended interpretation of Acts 3.

### Fixed Hours of Prayer
While discussing Daniel praying three times a day, Jerome observes that there are three times in the day when we should bow our knees unto God, and the tradition of the Church understands them to be the third hour, the sixth hour, and the ninth hour. He supports this from Acts: it was at the third hour that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles (Acts 2:15); It was at the sixth hour that Peter, purposing to eat, ascended to the upper room for prayer (Acts 10:9). Finally, It was at the ninth hour that Peter and John were on their way to the Temple (Acts 3:1).

**Insight:** Jerome treats Peter and John's trip to the Temple as evidence that the apostles kept regular hours of prayer, a practice the Church inherited.

---

## Summary Comparison

| Commentator | Approach | Main Contribution to Acts 3 |
|---|---|---|
| **Bede** | Allegorical and historical-theological | The lame man stands for Israel, the Beautiful Gate for Christ, and Peter for the apostolic guide into faith; the mission goes first to Israel, then to the Gentiles. |
| **Jerome** | Practical and devotional (in passing) | Acts 3:1 shows the apostles keeping the ninth hour of prayer, part of the Church's three daily prayer times. |

The two approaches complement each other. Bede draws out the symbolic meaning of the healing scene, while Jerome points to the apostles' prayer as a model for Christian devotion. These excerpts cover only the first two verses of the chapter, so they do not address the healing itself or Peter's sermon that follows.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Acts 1: Key Insights

These excerpts focus mainly on the opening verse of Acts, especially Luke's reference to his "former treatise" and to "all that Jesus began both to do and teach," and on the value of the book as a whole.

---

## 1. Augustine of Hippo: Luke's Gospel as a Selective Account

Augustine reads Acts 1:1 as a statement about Luke's earlier work and its scope.

- **Luke's Gospel is authoritative.** The opening verse shows that previous to this, Luke had written one of those four books of the gospel which are held in the loftiest authority in the church.
- **"All" does not mean "everything."** When Luke says he wrote of "all" that Jesus did and taught, we are not to take this to mean that he actually has given us a full account in his Gospel of all that Jesus did and said when he lived with his apostles on earth. Augustine gives two reasons:
  - Such a reading would be contrary to what John affirms when he says that there are also many other things which Jesus did, and if they should all be written down, the world itself could not contain the books.
  - All agree that many things are narrated by the other Evangelists, which Luke himself does not mention in his history.
- **Luke made a purposeful selection.** Augustine concludes that Luke made a selection out of the whole mass of materials for his narrative and introduced those facts which he judged fit and suitable to fulfill the duty laid upon him.

**Insight:** Augustine offers an early model for reading the Gospels together. Each evangelist chose material deliberately, so differences among the Gospels reflect purposeful selection rather than contradiction.

---

## 2. Bede: The Reader as "Theophilus" and Jesus as the Model Teacher

Bede draws pastoral and moral lessons from the opening verse.

- **Every believer is addressed.** Theophilus means lover of God or beloved of God. Therefore, anyone who is a lover of God may believe that this work was written for him, because the physician Luke wrote it in order that the reader might find health for his soul. Bede plays on Luke's profession: the physician writes for the soul's healing.
- **Doing comes before teaching.** Bede notes the word order "do and teach": first "do" and then "teach," because Jesus, establishing the pattern of a good teacher, taught nothing except those things which he did.

**Insight:** For Bede, the order of words in the text carries a lesson. Jesus' integrity, practicing what he taught, is a pattern for anyone who teaches in the church.

---

## 3. Thomas Aquinas: Discipline Before Preaching

Aquinas's excerpt is very brief. It attaches to the phrase "that Jesus began to do and to teach," but its content concerns Christ's life after his baptism rather than the events of Acts 1 itself:

- Immediately after His baptism Christ adopted a strict form of life, in order to teach us the need of taming the flesh before passing on to the office of preaching.

**Insight:** Like Bede, Aquinas sees "doing" as coming before "teaching," applied here to personal discipline as preparation for ministry. Because the excerpt begins with "Consequently," it appears to be part of a longer argument that is not included. Its connection to Acts 1 should therefore be read cautiously and not expanded beyond what is given.

---

## 4. John Chrysostom: Acts as a Neglected Treasure and Fulfilled Prophecy

Chrysostom's excerpt introduces the Book of Acts as a whole rather than commenting on specific verses of chapter 1.

- **A neglected book.** He observes that to many people this book, both its content and its author, is so little known that they are not even aware it exists. He preaches on it both to initiate those who are ignorant and so that such a treasure shall not remain hidden out of sight.
- **Equal in value to the Gospels.** Acts will profit us no less than the Gospels themselves, so replete is it with Christian wisdom and sound doctrine, especially in what is said concerning the Holy Spirit.
- **Christ's predictions fulfilled.** Here we can see the predictions Christ utters in the Gospels actually come to pass. These include the promise that believers would do "even greater things," and the prophecies that the disciples would be brought before rulers, suffer, and preach the gospel worldwide. All these came to pass in this book exactly as predicted.
- **The Spirit transforms the disciples.** Truth shines brightly through the facts themselves, and a great change for the better takes place in the disciples now that the Spirit has come upon them.

**Insight:** Chrysostom presents Acts as the confirmation of the Gospels. The Holy Spirit's work in the apostles shows that Christ's words were true.

---

## Common Threads

- **Continuity between Luke's Gospel and Acts:** Augustine and Chrysostom both treat Acts as building on the Gospel record, as its sequel and as the fulfillment of its predictions.
- **"Do and teach":** Bede and Aquinas both stress that action precedes instruction, offering a model of integrity and discipline for Christian teachers.
- **Pastoral purpose:** Bede (the soul's health) and Chrysostom (a hidden treasure for the church) both emphasize the spiritual benefit Acts offers its readers.

# Patristic Commentary on John 20: A Summary

**Scope:** All of these excerpts focus on the opening verse of John 20, which describes Mary Magdalene coming to the tomb early on the first day of the week. Together they address three questions: why that day matters, why John names only Mary, and how John's timing fits with the other Gospels. The excerpts do not discuss the rest of the chapter, so this summary does not either.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

**1. The theological significance of the day (*Tractates on John* 120.6)**
Augustine connects the resurrection to Christian worship. He notes that the first of the week is what Christian practice now calls the Lord's day, because of the resurrection of the Lord. The Sunday the Church observes rests on the event this chapter records.

**2. Harmonizing the Gospel accounts (*Harmony of the Gospels* 3.24.69)**
Augustine reconstructs a single sequence of events from the four Gospels:
- He begins from shared ground: it was in the early morning of the first day of the week that the women came to the sepulcher, as all the Evangelists are at one in attesting.
- He places Matthew's unique details first. By that time, all that is recorded by Matthew alone had already taken place, that is to say, in regard to the quaking of the earth, and the rolling away of the stone and the terror of the guards.
- Then, as John informs us, Mary Magdalene came.

**3. Why John names only Mary Magdalene**
Augustine explains John's focus on Mary by her devotion. She was unquestionably more ardent in her love than these other women who had ministered to the Lord. So it was not unreasonable in John to only mention her, leaving the other women unnamed who, however, were with her, as we gather from the reports given by other Evangelists. For Augustine, John's narrower focus does not contradict the other Gospels. It highlights Mary's exceptional love.

---

## Theodore of Mopsuestia

**Answering charges of contradiction (*Commentary on John* 7.20.1)**
Theodore acknowledges that it seems to those who dissent that here also the words of the Evangelists do not agree with one another, but he holds that their words are perfectly consistent.

**A distinctive reading of "early"**
Theodore argues that the word early is not referred here to the morning. His evidence is John's wording: he does not say while it was "still" dark, which should have been said with regard to morning. On his reading, "early" designates the whole day following the Sabbath.

**The biblical reckoning of days**
He supports this from Scripture's way of counting days. The holy Scripture usually defines both day and night with the word day, which he finds confirmed by Moses, who says, "And there was evening and there was morning, the first day".

**His conclusion**
John means that when the night began, the women came, in order to perform the proper honor according to customs. Theodore's view is notable because it places the women's visit at nightfall rather than at dawn.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

**Confidence in the agreement of Scripture (*Commentary on John* 12)**
Cyril starts from trust in the inspired writers: No one, I suppose, will imagine that the inspired writers disagree or that they fix the time of the resurrection differently. He believes careful study shows that their accounts add up.

**A meeting point in the middle of the night**
Cyril resolves the timing question differently from Theodore. He argues that early dawn and late night fix the same point of time, that is, the very dead of night, so to say. He explains that the one, taking as his starting point the end of night, and the other the beginning, both reach the middle watch and meet at the same point. In his view, the Evangelists describe one moment from two different starting points.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Shared conviction:** All three writers assume the Gospels are consistent and treat apparent tensions as invitations to read more closely.
- **Different solutions:** Augustine builds a sequence of events, Theodore reinterprets "early" through biblical day-reckoning, and Cyril finds a common midpoint in the night. Theodore and Cyril reach different conclusions about the timing.
- **Theological emphasis:** Augustine adds two devotional insights beyond the timing question: the resurrection is the basis of the Lord's Day, and Mary Magdalene's love explains why John gives her a central place.

# Summary of Commentary on Acts 25

**Note on the sources:** Both excerpts come from one commentator, **John Chrysostom**, and they are brief. This summary covers only what they contain and does not attempt a full account of his reading of the chapter.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. Paul's trials keep repeating
Chrysostom begins by emphasizing how often Paul is put on trial: "Again accusers, again at Cæsarea, again Paul is brought forth." The repeated "again" stresses the persistence of Paul's opponents and how long his legal ordeal has lasted. He also notes how quickly the new governor acts: "And having come, immediately he sat on the judgment-seat".

*Insight:* The repetition invites readers to notice Paul's endurance through a series of trials that seem to have no end.

### 2. The governor's motives in offering Paul a choice
Chrysostom's most developed point concerns the governor's suggestion that Paul might be tried elsewhere. He reads it as a calculated political move rather than real fairness. In his view, the governor's implied message is "I am not giving you up to them— but this was the fact— and he leaves the point to his own choice, that by this mark of respect he might get him to yield".

He explains the reason for this indirect approach: since his was the sentence, and it would have been too barefaced, when he had been convicted of nothing here, to take him back there.

*Insight:* Chrysostom exposes the gap between appearance and reality in human justice. The governor:
- presents his proposal as respect for Paul's wishes,
- while in fact trying to hand Paul over,
- and avoids doing so openly because Paul had been **convicted of nothing**, which would make an open transfer look shameless.

This reading highlights Paul's innocence and the moral compromise of an official who wants to please Paul's accusers while keeping up the appearance of fairness.

### 3. Paul's response
The excerpt ends as Chrysostom moves to Paul's reply: "But Paul said, At Cæsar's tribunal am I standing, etc." The text breaks off here, so we cannot see how Chrysostom interpreted Paul's answer. Placed right after his analysis of the governor's maneuver, though, it shows Paul declining the offered "choice" and holding to the proper Roman court.

---

## Key Takeaways
- **Endurance under repeated trial:** Chrysostom's repeated "again" draws attention to how persistent Paul's opposition was.
- **Discernment of motives:** He reads beneath polite official language and finds political pressure disguised as courtesy.
- **Paul's innocence:** He stresses that Paul had been "convicted of nothing," which makes the attempt to send him back unjust.

**Limitation:** Since there are only two short fragments, this summary cannot represent Chrysostom's full treatment of Acts 25, and no other commentators appear in the material provided.
