# Hebrews 4 in Chrysostom and Aquinas: Summary of the Excerpts

The excerpts come from two commentators: **John Chrysostom** (Homily 6 on Hebrews) and **Thomas Aquinas** (Commentary on Hebrews). Both focus mainly on the theme of God's "rest" in Hebrews 4:1–11.

**A note on scope:** Parts of Chrysostom's homily discuss verses from Hebrews 3 (e.g., 3:9, 3:13–19), which he weaves into his reading of chapter 4. The Aquinas excerpt stops at verse 8. Neither excerpt addresses Hebrews 4:13–16 (Christ as the great high priest), so that passage is not covered here.

---

## John Chrysostom

**1. "Today" means every moment of life, and it offers hope.**
Chrysostom reads the call to hear God's voice "Today" broadly: "Today" is "at every time". He sees this as pastoral encouragement. The word is used that they might never be without hope. In his words, even if a man have sinned, as long as it is "Today," he has hope: let no man then despair so long as he lives. He even calls despair a form of deception: to say, 'What is there left? I have sinned once for all, I have no hope of recovering myself,' is deceit.

**2. Hearing is not enough without faith.**
On verse 2, Chrysostom says: They also heard, as we hear: but no profit came to them. Do not suppose then that by "hearing" what is proclaimed ye will be profited; seeing that they also heard, but derived no benefit because they did not believe. He gives a distinctive reading of "not mixed with faith," pointing to Caleb and Joshua. These two because they agreed not with those who did not believe, escaped the vengeance that was sent forth against them. The phrase means they stood apart, but not factiously when all the others had one and the same mind. He also traces Israel's failure to its root: in all cases the provocation and the angering arises from unbelief.

**3. The remaining rest is neither Canaan nor the seventh day.**
Chrysostom argues by elimination. For of Palestine we have not to speak: for they were already in possession of it. Nor can he be speaking of the seventh [day]; for surely he was not discoursing about that which had taken place long before. It follows therefore that he hints at some other, that which is rest indeed. He notes the significance of the word "Sabbath-keeping" (v. 9): the author was calling the kingdom "Sabbath-keeping," by the appropriate name. Just as on the Sabbath only what serves God and whatsoever profits the soul, and nothing else is done, so also [will it be] then.

**4. The Word of God as a warning of judgment (v. 12).**
Chrysostom reads verse 12 as a warning: lest any think that they will simply be deprived of rest only, he adds also the punishment. The stakes are higher than in the wilderness: Here it is not the falling of carcasses nor, as there, the being deprived of a country, but of a heavenly kingdom.

**5. What the heavenly rest is like.**
Chrysostom describes the rest vividly. It is where there are neither cares, nor labors, nor struggle, nor fear stunning and shaking the soul; but only that fear of God which is full of delight. He admits words fall short: language is too weak (as I said) to set forth the whole. Experience is necessary. His most striking point is that earthly joys fade with familiarity, but yonder it not only does not diminish, but even increases.

---

## Thomas Aquinas

**1. A healthy, "chaste" fear (v. 1).**
Aquinas reads "let us fear" as a chaste fear and with anxiety. He sees it as constructive, not paralyzing: such fear is a useful admonition to give, and it is the companion of three spiritual virtues, namely, of hope, faith, and charity. The danger is losing the promise through one's own fault, which we abandon by deserting faith, hope, and charity, through which we can enter. And this is done by mortal sin.

**2. Old Testament promises have a spiritual meaning (v. 2).**
On "good news came to us as to them," Aquinas notes that the things promised in the Old Testament should be understood spiritually.

**3. "Mixed with faith": the union of heart and faith.**
Aquinas compares faith to knowing something: just as the union of intellect and thing understood make one thing, so the believer's heart and formed faith make one thing. He adds that the words of God are so efficacious that they should be believed as soon as they are heard.

**4. Two kinds of rest.**
He distinguishes them: there is a twofold rest: one in external goods, and a man passes to it from peace of mind; the other is in spiritual good, which is within, and to it a man enters.

**5. What it means that God "rested" (vv. 3–4).**
This is Aquinas's most philosophical contribution. He answers the objection that God is always working by explaining that 'rest' is not taken as the opposite of labor, but as the opposition of motion. God is said to have rested because He ceased producing new species. Following Augustine, he stresses that God rested *from* His works, not *in* them. Unlike a human craftsman who works out of need, God does not act out of need but to communicate His goodness; hence, he does not rest in His work, but from producing a work; and He rests only in His goodness.

**6. Why a rest must still remain (vv. 6–8).**
Aquinas grounds the argument in God's purpose for humanity. If God created man for eternal happiness, for he created him according to His own image and likeness, He prepared a rest for him. Therefore, although someone might be excluded because of his sin, God does not wish that preparation to have been made in vain. He illustrates this with the parable of the wedding feast. On verse 8, he concludes that if Joshua had given final rest, another rest would not remain for us. Therefore that rest was a sign of spiritual rest.

## Shared Themes and Distinct Emphases

Both commentators agree on three points:
- Hearing God's word without faith does not profit.
- Unbelief was the cause of Israel's exclusion.
- The "rest" of Hebrews 4 points beyond Canaan to a spiritual, heavenly rest.

Their emphases differ:
- **Chrysostom** is more pastoral and vivid. He stresses hope ("Today" is never over while we live) and paints an inspiring picture of heaven.
- **Aquinas** is more systematic. He connects fear to the virtues of faith, hope, and charity, explains carefully what God's "rest" means, and grounds the promise in God's purpose in creating humanity.

*A minor textual note:* Aquinas's Scripture references follow older Latin (Vulgate) numbering, so some citations (e.g., Psalms, Sirach) may differ from modern Bibles. # Patristic Insights on Galatians 6

**Scope note:** All four excerpts focus on a single verse, Galatians 6:1, which concerns restoring a fellow believer who has fallen into sin. They do not address the rest of the chapter, so this summary is limited to that verse.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

### 1. What it means to be "overtaken" (*Against Lying* 22)
This excerpt does not quote Galatians directly, but it takes up the word "overtaken" from 6:1. Augustine identifies two ways a person can be overtaken by sin. One is overtaken on those occasions either when one sins without seeing at the time that it is a sin or when one sees this and is still overcome. He traces these to two root causes: One sins either in ignorance of truth or under the limitations of infirmity.

**Insight:** Augustine recognizes that sin often comes from blindness or weakness rather than calculated rebellion. This invites a more understanding response from those who correct others.

### 2. Correction as the test of spiritual maturity (*Epistle to the Galatians* 56)
Augustine makes a striking claim: There is no surer test of the spiritual person than his treatment of another's sin. The truly spiritual person takes care to deliver the sinner rather than triumph over him, to help him rather than punish him and, so far as lies in his capacity, to support him.

**Insight:** For Augustine, spirituality is shown less by personal achievement than by how one handles a brother or sister's failure. The goal is rescue, not victory or punishment.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. The pastoral problem Paul was addressing
Chrysostom reads 6:1 against a specific problem in Galatia. The Galatians were gratifying their private feelings under pretext of rebuke. They appeared to be doing this to correct the sins of others. Paul wanted to put a stop to their love of being first.

**Insight:** "Correction" can become a disguise for pride and ambition. Paul's instructions are meant to expose and remedy that tendency.

### 2. Paul's careful word choices
Chrysostom pays close attention to Paul's wording:

- **"Overtaken," not "commits":** he does not say "if he trespasses" but "if he is overtaken," that is, if he is caught off guard.
- **"Restore," not "punish":** He says not "chastise" nor "judge," but "set right."
- **"In a spirit of meekness":** Paul adds this phrase to show that it behooved them to be very gentle towards those who had lost their footing. The word "spirit" signals that this is acceptable to the Spirit, and that to be able to administer correction with mildness is a spiritual gift.

**Insight:** Gentle correction is not merely good manners. It is a gift of the Holy Spirit.

### 3. Humility for the one who corrects
Paul's warning, "Looking to yourself, lest you also be tempted," is meant to prevent the one being unduly exalted by having to correct the other. Chrysostom offers an analogy: as rich men convey contributions to the indigent, that in case they should be themselves involved in poverty they may receive the same bounty, so ought we also to do.

**Insight:** The one who restores others today may need restoration tomorrow. Mercy shown now is mercy one may later need.

### 4. Paul as advocate for the offender
Chrysostom observes that Paul effectively defends the person who has fallen. He apologizes for the offender, first, by saying "if you be overtaken;" next, by employing a term indicative of great infirmity ; lastly, by the words "lest you also be tempted," thus arraigning the malice of the devil rather than the remissness of the soul.

**Insight:** Paul places much of the blame on the devil's attack rather than on the sinner's carelessness, which encourages compassion rather than contempt.

---

## Common Themes

Augustine and Chrysostom agree on several points:

1. **Sin often overtakes people** through ignorance, weakness, or being caught off guard, not only through deliberate wickedness.
2. **The aim of correction is restoration**, not punishment, judgment, or personal triumph.
3. **Gentleness is a mark of true spirituality**, which Chrysostom calls a gift of the Spirit and Augustine treats as the surest test of a spiritual person.
4. **Those who correct must stay humble**, remembering their own vulnerability to temptation.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 28: A Summary

The excerpts come from three early church writers. Most of the material focuses on Paul's shipwreck on Malta (Acts 28:1–10) and his arrival in Rome (28:11–17).

---

## 1. Eusebius of Caesarea: Paul's voyage as fulfilled prophecy

This excerpt comes from Eusebius's **commentary on Isaiah**, not a commentary on Acts. He uses Acts 28 as an illustration of a prophetic text.

- **Prophecy fulfilled in mission:** He interprets the verse "And they shall be scattered on the merchant ships of foreigners and together plunder the sea" as describing the apostles. He says they made a swift course through the sea so that they might proclaim the gospel to most nations in a short time.
- **"Plundering" the islands:** For Eusebius, to "plunder the sea" means the apostles plundered the sea, that is the islands, through which they passed and made known to their inhabitants the salvific teaching.
- **Malta as the example:** He offers Paul as the case in point: when he was shipwrecked on the island called Malta he worked a miracle of great astonishment to the inhabitants, and by healing the physically ill, he so amazed the onlookers that he plundered many and drew them to the salvific teaching.

**Key insight:** Paul's shipwreck was not an accident. Eusebius reads it as part of God's foretold plan to spread the gospel across the nations.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: Providence, hospitality, and the good hidden in adversity

Two excerpts are attributed to Chrysostom. Document 3 (*Homilies on Acts* 54) appears to be a different translation of the same passage found in the "recapitulation" section of Document 2, so the two are summarized together. Chrysostom gives the fullest treatment.

### a) Paul's miracles were never for show
Chrysostom notes Paul's humble activity in gathering brushwood. He comments: observe how we nowhere find him doing miracles for the sake of doing them, but only upon emergency. Even Paul's prophecy during the storm was given when there was a cause, and not for the sake of prophesying.

### b) The viper miracle was beyond doubt
He sees God's hand in letting the islanders voice their suspicion first: Well also was this permitted, that they should both see the thing and utter the thought, in order that, when the result ensued, there might be no disbelieving the miracle. The slow unfolding added credibility, because the miracle did not take place suddenly, but the men went by the length of time, "after they had looked a great while," so plainly was there no deceit. He also notes that the islanders' later declaration that Paul was a god was another excess on the part of these men, comparing it to Acts 14:11.

### c) The "barbarians" put believers to shame
This is one of his most pointed applications. He contrasts the Jews, who saw so many miracles, persecuted and harassed Paul, with the islanders, who saw none and were kind to him solely because of his misfortune. He then challenges his hearers: Let those be ashamed that say, Do not do good to those in prison: let these barbarians shame us; for they knew not who these men were, but simply because they were in misfortune (they were kind): thus much they perceived, that they were human beings, and therefore they considered them to have a claim upon their humanity.

### d) Natural knowledge of providence
Chrysostom reads the islanders' remark that "justice" would not let Paul live as evidence that they too had an account of providence. In his view, These barbarians were far closer to truth than the philosophers. The philosophers did not allow providence to extend to the sphere below the moon. The islanders, by contrast, believed that God was present everywhere and that, even if one should escape many dangers, he would not escape in the end.

### e) Publius's hospitality rewarded
Publius took them in purely out of compassion for their misfortune, so Paul as a requital for his receiving them, "healed him." Chrysostom insists that the honors Paul's party received afterward were not payment: not that he received wages, God forbid; but as it is written, "The workman is worthy of his meat." He also reasons that the islanders' sustained generosity points to genuine conversions, so that from this we may see a strong proof of the great number there was of those that believed.

### f) The voyage as training in faith
Everything on Malta served a purpose for Paul's companions: See how all this is done for the sake of Paul, to the end that the prisoners should believe, and the soldiers, and the centurion. His fellow voyagers were herein under training for faith.

### g) Paul's humanity
On Paul taking courage when he met the believers from Rome, Chrysostom observes: Although he had worked so many miracles, nevertheless even from sight he received an accession (of confidence). From this we learn, that he was both comforted after the manner of men, and the contrary.

### h) Custody in Rome as protection
Chrysostom sees Paul's guarded house arrest as divine protection. He writes: in fact they were not keeping Paul in custody, but guarding him, so that nothing unpleasant should happen. From this he draws his central theme: this is a marvellous thing, that not by the things which seem to be for our security, but by their very opposites, all comes to be for us.

### A note on the broader reflection
From this point, the excerpt moves **beyond Acts 28** into a general sermon on providence and suffering. It includes examples from Moses, Cain and Abel, Adam, and Judas, and a discussion of the devil's role in human sin. These sections are not commentary on the chapter itself, but they grow directly out of his reading of Paul's circumstances. Two ideas stand out:
- Adversity strengthens the soul: our reverses and our afflictions are as it were a whetstone to sharpen us.
- Moral responsibility rests with us: it is not the devil who puts into us the beginning, it is we that receive and invite him.

---

## 3. Theodoret of Cyrus: The viper and the armor of virtue

This brief excerpt (from a catena on Acts 28:3) gives a moral and allegorical reading of the viper.

- **Sinlessness as protection:** He describes the viper, which since it did not find any entry of sin in him, immediately released him and threw itself into the fire by inflicting on itself a punishment, because it had made an attack against an impenetrable body.
- **Application:** Therefore let us fear the beasts, if we do not possess the full armor of virtue.

**Key insight:** Paul's immunity becomes a picture of the spiritual protection that comes from a virtuous life.

---

## Common Threads

All three writers see **God's providence** at work in Paul's shipwreck and arrival in Rome:
- **Eusebius** treats it as prophecy fulfilled.
- **Chrysostom** sees God turning apparent misfortune into blessing and drawn-out events into proof.
- **Theodoret** treats Paul's deliverance as a moral lesson about virtue.

Chrysostom's material stands out for its practical challenge to show compassion to strangers and prisoners, and for his reflection on how hardship can serve the believer's good.

So that in fact they were not keeping Paul in custody, but guarding him, so that nothing unpleasant should happen: for it was not possible now, in so great a city, and with the Emperor there, and with Paul's appeal, for anything to be done contrary to order.
For this is a marvellous thing, that not by the things which seem to be for our security, but by their very opposites, all comes to be for us.
But as it is, our reverses and our afflictions are as it were a whetstone to sharpen us.
It was he that himself gave the devil a wide room for entering into him: so that it is not the devil who puts into us the beginning, it is we that receive and invite him.

# Bede on Genesis 11: A Summary of Key Theological Insights

**A note on sources:** All four excerpts come from a single commentator, the Venerable Bede, so this summary is organized by theme rather than by commentator. The excerpts cover only the opening verses of Genesis 11 (the one shared language, the migration to Shinar, and the brick-making that leads to the city). The later parts of the Babel story are not addressed here.

---

## 1. Unity Comes from Humility, Division from Pride

Bede's starting point is that the Babel story explains why humanity is divided. He observes that the text shows "that as long as the human race served its Creator with due humility, it also harmonized with itself in peaceful charity." The reverse also held: "once it raised its neck against its Author in pride, it was soon justly punished and could not have peace even with itself."

**Key insight:** For Bede, human disunity is a spiritual problem, not just a linguistic or political one. Peace with one another depends on a right relationship with God.

## 2. Babel and Pentecost: Two Cities, Two Outcomes

Bede's most memorable move is to read Babel alongside Pentecost (Acts 2). He argues that the potential for human happiness, even after the fall, "is testified by the grace of our Lord, the Creator and Redeemer, who gave the knowledge of all languages to His disciples faithfully adhering to Him by sending the Spirit from above".

He draws the contrast sharply:
- **At Babel**, "through the division of languages due to pride, the nations were dispersed throughout the world"
- **At Pentecost**, "due to the merit of humility, the diversity of languages brought together, people collected from every nation under heaven resonated with one unvarying confession and faith"

He supports this with the meaning of the two city names. The city where languages were divided "is called Babylon, that is, Confusion; the other is called Jerusalem, that is, Vision of Peace, in which, through the united languages of all nations in the praise of God, concord was made." In Jerusalem, "with tongues united by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the faithful, even of all foreigners who had come, were able to understand the voice and all together in one bond of charity and faith praise the same God and Lord."

**Key insight:** Pentecost reverses Babel. What pride scattered, the Spirit gathers. Notably, Pentecost does not erase linguistic diversity. Instead, it unites diverse peoples in one confession.

## 3. The East as a Symbol of Christ

Bede reads the detail that the people "journeyed from the east" both literally and spiritually.

**Literally**, he concludes "that even the first humans held the region of the East; thus it should be considered the head of the world, not only because the light of the stars rises from there, but also because the human race first inhabited it."

**Spiritually**, the East "rightly signifies Him who said: I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). Those who remain in Christ "are of one language and the same speech: for there is certainly one confession of faith, the same purity of action, common charity, and hope of eternal things". In his reading, humanity kept one language only "as long as men remained in the East: but when they moved from the East, soon because of the words or deeds of pride, they were separated from each other and were expelled further from their Creator."

## 4. Truth Is One; Error Is Many

Bede adds a striking point about the nature of unbelief: "just as there is one norm of faith, so there is not one and the same norm of infidelity". There is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God, in whom is the salvation of the elect: but there are many lords of the reprobate, various winding paths of perfidy", all of which lead to "one destruction of damnation".

**Key insight:** The confusion of tongues pictures the fragmentation that follows when people turn from God. Faith unifies. Error splinters into countless directions, yet they all end in the same ruin.

## 5. The Plain of Shinar: Settling into Worldliness

Bede treats the "plain" where the people settled as a moral image: "withdrawing from the light of righteousness, the reprobate found for themselves the broad ways of the world in which they might remain with a fickle mind; and this in the stench of carnal vices." He interprets the name Shinar as "their stench" and explains it as "the rotten lust of carnal slothfulness".

He also notes how sin spreads in community. Those who settle comfortably in such vice soon provoke their neighbors to wrongdoing, "For it follows that one said to his neighbor: Come, let us make bricks, and bake them with fire."

## 6. Bricks vs. Living Stones: Two Kinds of Cities

Bede closes with a contrast between two kinds of building:

| The City of Babel/Nimrod | The City of God (Jerusalem/the Church) |
|---|---|
| Built of bricks on a plain | "is not built of bricks, but of stone: not on a plain, but on a mountain" |
| The impious "serves the devil with filthy, sordid, and earthly works, and they build for him not any other city than themselves by living wickedly" | "the Church, indeed, the city of Christ, is built of living stones, that is, souls strong in faith and action" (drawing on 1 Peter 2:4–5) |
| Associated with Nimrod, whose name signifies "the transgressors and tyrants" | Its members "strive not to relax in the weak pleasures of carnal things, but rather to bind and elevate themselves to higher desires" (cf. Phil. 3:20) |

**Key insight:** The wicked do not really build a city out of bricks. They build one *out of themselves* by how they live. In the same way, believers are themselves the "living stones" of Christ's Church, raised on the mountain of the Lord.

---

## Summary

Bede reads Genesis 11 as a story about two opposing ways of life. Pride leads away from Christ (the "East"), downward into worldliness (the "plain of Shinar"), and into confusion and division ("Babylon"). Humility keeps people in the light of Christ, lifts them toward heavenly desires (the "mountain"), and unites them in one faith and praise ("Jerusalem," fulfilled at Pentecost). His approach is typical of patristic interpretation: he takes the literal details seriously and then reads them as figures of spiritual realities.

*A minor textual note:* The excerpt attributes the quotation "Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King" to "Psalm LXVII, 3." In modern Bibles this verse is found at Psalm 48:2 (Psalm 47:3 in the Latin numbering). The reference as given may reflect a transcription error.

# Summary of Commentary on Matthew 2

## A Note on Sources

Only one short excerpt was provided, so this summary is necessarily limited. The document is labeled as Augustine of Hippo's commentary, but the excerpt itself carries different attributions:

- **"Hil."** (probably Hilary) appears at the start, but no text follows it, so no insight can be attributed to him.
- The substantive comment is marked Quaest. N. and N. Test.9. This appears to refer to a work of *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*. Its authorship is uncertain. It has traditionally been associated with Augustine but is often considered the work of another writer. I have therefore attributed the insight to this work rather than definitely to Augustine.

## Key Insight: Why Rachel Mourns

The excerpt explains why Rachel is described as mourning her sons. It offers an alternative reading, introduced with "Or."

**1. Rachel's own descendants were already lost.**
The commentator notes that the sons of Benjamin, who were akin to Rachel, were formerly cut off by the other tribes, and so extinct both then and ever after.

**2. Her grief was awakened by her sister's children.**
On this reading, Rachel's mourning is prompted by another family's honor: Rachel began to mourn her sons, when she saw those of her sister cut off in such a cause, that they should be heirs of eternal life. The "sister" would be Leah. The children "cut off" seem to be the infants killed in Matthew 2. The excerpt does not name them, however, so this identification is inferred from the chapter's context.

**3. A psychological principle.**
The commentator grounds the interpretation in common human experience: he who has experienced any misfortune, is made more sensible of his losses by the good fortune of a neighbour.

## Theological Significance

- **The slain children were honored, not merely victims.** Their deaths are described as being "in such a cause" that they became "heirs of eternal life." In other words, dying in connection with Christ turned tragedy into glory.
- **Rachel's grief is complex.** She mourns not only from sorrow but from a kind of holy longing. Her own line had no share in this honor, and seeing her sister's children so blessed made her loss feel sharper.

## Limitations

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Thessalonians 5: A Summary

These excerpts focus mainly on Paul's teaching about the coming "day of the Lord" in the opening verses of the chapter: its suddenness, its unknown timing, and how believers should live in light of it.

## Augustine of Hippo: Becoming "the Day" Through Holy Living

Augustine reads Paul's day-and-night language morally rather than literally. His central point is direct: "So what is this day which the Lord has made? Live good lives, and you will be this day yourselves."

- **The "day" is a way of life, not a time of day.** He says the apostle was not talking about the day which begins with sunrise and ends with sunset. Drunkenness belongs to "night" even if it happens at noon, because it is a matter of the night, not of the day which the Lord has made.
- **Two kinds of people.** The "day" is realized in those who live godly, holy and righteous lives, marked by moderation, justice, sobriety. For those who live in an ungodly, loose-living, proud and irreligious manner—for that sort of night, the night will undoubtedly be a thief.

**Key insight:** Whether the Lord's coming is a threat or not depends on the moral condition of the person. Those who already live "in the day" are not ambushed. One caution: the phrase Augustine quotes, "Let us walk honorably, as in the day," is from Romans 13, not 1 Thessalonians 5. He appears to be combining related Pauline passages.

## John Chrysostom: Urgency, Uncertainty, and Readiness

Chrysostom applies the "thief in the night" theme to each person's own death and to complacency.

- **Do not presume on time.** He warns: "Do not place your confidence in your youth, nor think that you have a very fixed term of life".
- **Hidden timing has a purpose.** God has made our end invisible, so that we might demonstrate clearly our diligence and forethought. The uncertainty is meant to call forth faithfulness.
- **Do not delay repentance.** Since people are taken away prematurely day after day, one should not put off turning to the Lord. This applies to everyone: "Let the old man keep this admonition; let the young man heed this advice."
- **Prosperity is false security.** He addresses those who are wealthy and free from trouble, using Paul's warning that "when they say peace and safety, then sudden destruction comes upon them."
- **What we can control.** His summary is memorable: Affairs change often. We are not masters of our end. Let us be masters of virtue. Our Master Christ is loving.

**Key insight:** Since we cannot control when our end comes, we should give our effort to virtue, trusting in Christ's love.

## Theodoret of Cyrus: Certain Event, Uncertain Hour

Theodoret uses the image of pregnancy, which likely reflects Paul's comparison to labor pains in this chapter. The woman who is pregnant knows that she has a fetus in the womb but does not know when birth will occur. Likewise, we know that the Lord will come, but we do not teach the time itself with certainty.

**Key insight:** Christians can be confident that the Lord will return while staying humble about when. This implicitly cautions against speculating about dates.

## Irenaeus: A Citation Without Commentary

The Irenaeus excerpt only quotes the verse: "When they shall say, Peace and safety, then sudden destruction shall come upon them." It contains no interpretation, so no theological insight can be drawn from it without going beyond the text. The surrounding argument in *Against Heresies* Book V is not included here.

## Common Themes

- **Certainty of the Lord's coming:** All the commentators treat it as sure.
- **Uncertainty of its timing:** Theodoret and Chrysostom stress that the hour is hidden.
- **Moral readiness:** Augustine and Chrysostom both see holy living as the proper response.
- **Warning against complacency:** Chrysostom and Irenaeus both cite the "peace and safety" warning.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 20: A Summary

The excerpts cover Acts 20:1–12: Paul's travels through Macedonia and Greece, his stay at Troas, and the long night gathering where a young man fell from a window. Three commentators are represented, and their excerpts vary greatly in theological depth.

---

## John Chrysostom

### On Paul's ministry of encouragement (Acts 20:1–2)
This short excerpt highlights Paul's pastoral care. Chrysostom notes that by this again he refreshed them, giving them much consolation. He stresses that Paul's travels were full of personal encouragement: having exhorted the Macedonians, with much discourse, he came into Greece.

### On the gathering at Troas (Acts 20:7–12)
This is the richest excerpt in the collection. Chrysostom offers several insights:

**1. The meal came first, and the teaching grew out of it.** Chrysostom observes that it was not primarily to hear his teaching that they came together but to break bread; however, once [Paul] began speaking, he prolonged the teaching. He sees a lesson in this: even while seated at the table he was speaking, thus teaching us to consider all the rest secondary. He also emphasizes fellowship: See how at Paul's table all partook.

**2. He invites the reader to picture the scene.** Chrysostom calls his listeners to picture to yourself, please, that house with the lights, with the crowd, with Paul in the middle, speaking, with even the windows occupied by many people.

**3. Why Paul preached through the night.** Chrysostom's answer is pastoral: Because [Paul] was about to depart and never see them again. He adds that Paul held this back out of tenderness: This he does not tell them, since they are too weak, but he did tell the others.

**4. God's purpose in the young man's fall.** Chrysostom reads the accident as providential. The miracle that took place made them remember that evening forever. The interruption extended the gathering rather than ending it: Great was the pleasure experienced by his audience; though interrupted, it was further extended. He concludes that the fall took place to the benefit of the teacher.

**5. A rebuke to the indifferent.** Finally, he holds up the young man as an example of eagerness for the Word: all who were indifferent were about to be censured by that young man who underwent death to hear Paul.

---

## Bede (on Acts 20:7–8)

Bede reads the passage allegorically, treating the details of the scene as symbols.

**1. The symbolic meaning of the setting.** The upper room is the loftiness of spiritual gifts; night is the obscurity of the Scriptures; the abundance of lamps is the explanation of the more enigmatic sayings; the Lord's day is the remembrance of either the Lord's resurrection or our own.

**2. A lesson for teachers: make hard things clear.** Bede draws a practical warning for preachers. When a teacher stirs listeners toward higher things and touches on difficult passages, he should very soon, for the sake of weak listeners, shed light on those same [enigmas] by the lamp of plain explanation, just as the apostle did.

**3. Paul as the model.** Bede gives an example of Paul doing this himself: When he said, "Abraham had two sons, the one by a slave girl and the other by a free woman," he soon added by way of explanation, "These are the two covenants," showing a difficult image followed at once by its meaning.

---

## Irenaeus (Against Heresies, Book III)

This excerpt contains no theological commentary. It simply quotes the biblical text: "But we sailed from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread, and came to Troas, where we abode seven days." The excerpt does not say why Irenaeus cites the verse, so no interpretive insight can fairly be attributed to him from this passage alone.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Chrysostom** reads Acts 20 pastorally. He emphasizes Paul's care for the churches, the shared meal at the center of worship, and God's providence even in the young man's fall.
- **Bede** reads the Troas scene allegorically and draws a lesson for teachers: difficult truths should always be followed by clear explanation for the sake of weaker listeners.
- **Irenaeus's** excerpt only quotes the narrative and offers no commentary.

# Summary of Commentaries on Hebrews 6

The excerpts come from two commentators: **Thomas Aquinas** (his verse-by-verse commentary on Hebrews 6:1–8) and **John Chrysostom** (Homilies 9 and 10 on Hebrews). Both spend most of their attention on the hard passage in verses 4–6 about the impossibility of "renewal."

---

## I. Thomas Aquinas

### 1. Moving from the basics to maturity (vv. 1–2)
Aquinas reads the chapter's opening as the author's plan: passing over the things which pertain to the beginning of Christian doctrine, he may go on to loftier matters. He then answers two objections.

- **Should we really "leave" the beginning?** He distinguishes two senses. In one, a man should always be a beginner tending to what is higher. In the other, a man should always strive to pass to the perfect state. He cites Bernard: not to progress in the way of God is to fall behind.
- **Is everyone called to perfection?** He separates outward perfection, such as virginity and voluntary poverty, from inward perfection, which consists in the love of God and neighbor. His conclusion is that all are bound to tend toward it; because if a person no longer desired to love God more, he would not be doing what charity requires.

### 2. The six "foundations"
Aquinas arranges the six items listed in verses 1–2 as stages of a spiritual journey.

- **Repentance from dead works.** This comes first because penance is a departure from sin and is, as it were, the foundation of that life. Works done in mortal sin are "dead." Good works done in love are deadened by later sin, but penance makes them revive; hence they are then once more counted for eternal life.
- **Faith toward God.** Faith is assent based on someone else's testimony. When that testimony comes from God, it is most true and firm, because it comes from the Truth itself, which cannot deceive or be deceived.
- **Baptisms (plural).** He explains the plural through three kinds of baptism, namely, of water, of desire, and of blood. Martyrdom washes away all guilt and punishment, but it does not imprint a character. Penance does not take away all punishment, although it takes away all guilt. Even so, it can be so great that it would remove all guilt and punishment, as happened to the good thief and to Magdalene.
- **Laying on of hands.** He takes this as confirmation, in which the Holy Spirit is given for strength to enable a man to boldly confess Christ's name before men.
- **Resurrection and eternal judgment.** These are the journey's goal. He notes that the judgment is "eternal" not because it lasts a long time, as Lactantius taught, but because the sentence passed then will last for ever.

### 3. "If God permit" (v. 3)
Aquinas says the author says less than he means, for it is not only necessary that God permit, but He must do all things.

### 4. The blessings received (vv. 4–5)
- "Enlightened" refers to baptism, because it is the beginning of spiritual rebirth, in which the intellect is enlightened by faith.
- The word "tasted" is chosen because it not only enlightens the intellect, but also refreshes the affections.
- "The powers of the age to come" are partly already present. The soul's future gifts are possessed inchoatively inasmuch as faith, hope and charity, which correspond to them, are possessed in the present.

### 5. The "impossibility" of renewal (vv. 4–6)
- **What the passage does not mean.** Aquinas rejects the reading of Novatian, a Roman priest, who declared that no one could rise to penance after baptism. Following Athanasius, he calls this false because Paul himself received the incestuous Corinthians.
- **What it does mean.** With Augustine, he holds that the text does not say that it is impossible to repent, but that it is impossible to be renewed again, i.e., baptized. He suggests the author is correcting a practice, since according to the Law, the Jews were baptized frequently.
- **"Crucifying the Son of God again."** He offers two readings:
  1. Baptism is configuration to Christ's death, and that death is not repeated, so those who are repeatedly baptized crucify Christ again.
  2. The emphasis falls on the falling away of the sinner, who, as far as in him lies, crucifies Christ again.
- **An alternative explanation.** He also reports a reading in which the author shows that the baptized cannot be renewed again to penance in another life, that is, after death.

### 6. The parable of the land (vv. 7–8)
He considers the baptismal reading the most literal one: Just as the cultivated earth, if it brings forth thorns again, is not cultivated but is burned, so a man who sins after baptism is not washed again.

- **The image.** This earth is the human heart, and the rain is the doctrine of faith falling on those who hear preaching.
- **Who cultivates it.** The heart is tended by God, by church leaders, and by the man himself.
- **"Often."** On the rain falling "often," he quotes Augustine: 'If always, then it becomes worthless; if rarely, then it is not enough and is neglected'.
- **Thorns and briars.** These represent minor sins, and the briars, i.e., graver sins.
- **A sobering conclusion.** the fact that a person is frequently watered with salutary precepts is a sign of reprobation, if he continues to sin.

---

## II. John Chrysostom, Homily 9

### 1. Repentance remains; a second baptism does not
Chrysostom reads verse 6 the same basic way Aquinas does. He asks, What then, is repentance excluded? Not repentance, far from it! But the renewing again by the laver. ("Laver" means the washing of baptism.) He draws a careful distinction: to make men new is [the work] of the laver only, while repentance frees those who have afterwards become old through sins. However, To bring them to that former brightness however, is not possible; for there the whole was Grace.

### 2. Baptism as a cross
His reasoning is that Baptism is a Cross. Therefore If therefore it is necessary to be baptized [again ], it is necessary that this same [Christ] should die again. Repeating Christ's death would make his victory meaningless: all those things become a fable and a mockery. He also applies the phrase to careless living. Whoever lives carelessly acts in all respects as if there were another baptism.

### 3. Why a second baptism is impossible
He gives two reasons, first, because he who has been deemed worthy of such [blessings], and who has betrayed all that was granted to him, is not worthy to be again renewed; neither is it possible that [Christ] should again be crucified afresh. He adds a practical argument: if a second washing existed, there is also a third, and a fourth; for the former one is continually disannulled by the later. He also worries that a repeatable baptism would breed spiritual laziness.

### 4. The "medicine of repentance"
This is the pastoral heart of the homily. Chrysostom insists that repentance has great force, and is able to set free from the burden of his sins, even for someone in the very depth of wickedness. He lists its ingredients:

- **Condemning one's own sins.** First, of the condemnation of our own sins.
- **Humility.** He describes it as a chain: great humbleness of mind: For it is like a golden chain; if one have hold of the beginning, all will follow.
- **Intense prayer and tears.**
- **Almsgiving.** He calls this the essential herb, yea, it may be everything.
- **Forgiving others**, turning straying brethren back, and defending the wronged.

He also urges specific confession. Someone who only says "I am a sinner" without naming his sins will be confessing indeed continually, but never caring in earnest for amendment.

### 5. The emptiness of worldly glory
The homily closes with a reflection that moves away from the text of Hebrews 6. Chrysostom compares worldly honors, such as being consul, to a dream, and sets them against Paul's lasting glory. This section is moral exhortation rather than direct commentary on the chapter.

---

## III. John Chrysostom, Homily 10 (brief excerpt)

This short excerpt covers only verse 9. Chrysostom notes the author's confident wording: he did not say, We think, or, we conjecture, or, we expect, or, we hope, but "we are persuaded." He contrasts this with Galatians, where Paul could praise his readers only in view of the future. In Hebrews, by contrast, he encourages them from things present. The excerpt breaks off before his further comments.

---

## Points of Agreement

- **"Renewal" means baptism.** Both commentators read the "impossible renewal" of verses 4–6 as a ban on repeating baptism, not as a denial that sinners can repent.
- **The same proof text.** Both cite Paul's words in Galatians 4:19, "my little children, of whom I travail in birth again," as evidence that restoration after falling is possible.
- **Baptism and Christ's death.** Both ground the unrepeatable nature of baptism in Romans 6 and in Christ's once-for-all death.

*A note on the sources:* several Scripture references in the Aquinas excerpt appear to contain transcription errors. For example, "Without me you can do nothing" is labeled Jn. 16:5, and "These shall go into eternal punishment" is labeled Mt. 15:46. Readers may want to check verse numbers against a Bible.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 15:1–2

All of the provided excerpts focus on the opening of Matthew 15, where religious leaders from Jerusalem challenge Jesus about his disciples' conduct. Jerome quotes the verse directly: "Then came to him from Jerusalem scribes and Pharisees, saying: Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders?" The excerpts do not address the rest of the chapter.

---

## Origen of Alexandria

**1. The leaders came with the wrong motive.** Origen contrasts the visitors' attitude with the miracles that had just taken place. They did not come because they were amazed at the power in Jesus that healed people even if they "only touched the edge of his cloak." Instead, they came with a faultfinding attitude and brought an accusation before the teacher.

**2. The charge concerned human tradition, not God's law.** Origen points out that the accusation did not concern the transgression of a commandment of God but rather the transgression of one tradition of the Jewish elders.

**3. The accusation actually shows the disciples' faithfulness.** This is Origen's most original insight. He argues that the charge of the faultfinders itself displays the piety of the disciples of Jesus, because they offered no grounds at all for criticism by the Pharisees and scribes in regard to transgressing the commandments of God. If the critics could have found a real violation of God's commands, they would have raised it. Instead they had to rely on a lesser charge.

---

## John Chrysostom

*Two of the provided documents appear to be different translations of the same passage from Chrysostom's Homily 51 on Matthew. They are summarized together here.*

**1. The timing reveals the leaders' hardness of heart.** Chrysostom focuses on the word "then." The confrontation came when he had worked thousands of signs, when he had healed the sick with the touch of his tassel. According to Chrysostom, it is for this reason that the Evangelist indicates the time, so that he might show that their unspeakable wickedness is second to none. The other translation conveys the same point: their wickedness was by nothing repressed. In other words, even overwhelming evidence of divine power did not soften their opposition.

**2. "From Jerusalem" is significant.** Chrysostom asks why Matthew notes where these leaders came from. He explains that scribes and Pharisees were scattered everywhere throughout the tribes and were divided into twelve parts. However, the ones who were in charge of the mother city were more wicked than the others, because they enjoyed more honor and had become extremely arrogant. His spiritual lesson is that greater prestige and honor can breed greater pride.

---

## Jerome

Jerome's comment is brief and pointed, and it emphasizes who Jesus is. He writes that the stupidity of the Pharisees and scribes is evident as they accuse the Son of God of not keeping the traditions and precepts of men. For Jerome, the absurdity of the scene lies in the gap between the accusers and the accused. Mere human customs were being used to judge the Son of God himself.

---

## Common Threads

- **Divine command versus human tradition:** Origen and Jerome both stress that the charge involved human tradition rather than God's law. Origen makes the point through the disciples' blamelessness, Jerome through the identity of Christ.
- **Hostility despite miracles:** Origen and Chrysostom both connect this scene to the preceding healings, in which people were healed by touching Jesus' garment. They see the leaders' faultfinding as all the more striking in light of those healings.
- **Pride and spiritual blindness:** Chrysostom's remarks about Jerusalem's leaders suggest that honor and status can harden the heart against the truth.

**Note on scope:** These excerpts cover only the opening confrontation (Matthew 15:1–2). They do not comment on Jesus' response or on later events in the chapter.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 6: Summary of Key Insights

Almost all of the provided material comes from **Bede**, and it covers Luke 6:1–4: the disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath and Jesus' appeal to David. The **Clement of Alexandria** excerpt is very short and does not clearly comment on Luke 6.

---

## Bede: *On the Gospel of Luke*

### 1. The Disciples' Hunger and Simplicity
Bede explains the disciples' hunger with a detail from Mark: because of the great number of those who came to be healed, the disciples did not even have time to eat, and thus were as hungry men. He also sees a moral lesson in how they ate. Plucking grain by hand is an indication of a more austere life, not seeking prepared feasts, but simple food.

### 2. The Meaning of the "Second-First Sabbath"
Bede's main theological contribution is his treatment of Luke's unusual phrase "second-first Sabbath." He offers several complementary readings:

- **The end of the legal Sabbath:** Luke uses this term for the day when the letter of the Sabbath began to be dissolved, signaling that the observance of the legal Sabbath ought henceforth to cease, and the freedom of the natural Sabbath, which was similar to the other days up to the times of Moses, ought to be restored.
- **A spiritual Sabbath:** He draws a parallel with salvation by faith. Just as the Church is saved not by circumcision or the ceremonies of the law, but by the faith of Abraham, the true Sabbath is a spiritual Sabbath, in which even Abraham always rested from servile, that is, sinful action.
- **Both second and first:** The New Testament Sabbath is second, because it is observed by us after the legal Sabbath. It is also first, because it was observed by the ancient just ones before the decrees of the law.
- **Superior rather than earlier:** Alternatively, the phrase may mean that the superior Sabbath is understood to be above the inferior.
- **Christ as the "second-first Adam":** Bede extends the idea to Christ himself, saying it is not wrong to call the Lord Jesus Christ the second-first Adam, who by merit and grace certainly preceded the first Adam by no human birth order.

Bede also uses the passage against a contemporary error. He notes that the first apostles of the Savior break the letter of the Sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, while accepting the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law. If the original apostles set aside the letter of the Sabbath, Paul cannot be singled out for doing so.

### 3. The Spiritual Meaning of the Grain Fields
Reading the scene allegorically, Bede links the fields to the "fields white for harvest" of John 4. He connects the disciples' eating to Peter's vision in Acts 10, observing that there, beasts are ordered to be killed and eaten, and here the ears of corn are reported to be rubbed and nonetheless eaten. In his reading, each action pictures the work of evangelism:

- To pluck the ears of corn is to remove men from an earthly intention.
- To rub them with hands is to strip the purity of mind from carnal concupiscence, like husks and chaff.
- To eat the grains is for each person cleansed from all filthiness of flesh and spirit to be incorporated into the members of the Church through the mouths of preachers.

### 4. Jesus' Defense of the Disciples
Bede addresses a difference between the Gospels. In Luke the Pharisees question the disciples, but other Evangelists narrate that this was rather objected to the Lord Himself. He resolves this by noting that whatever is done by the disciples, reflects upon Him whose teaching they follow. Christ therefore overcomes the false defenders of the law with true examples of the saints.

### 5. David and the Showbread
Bede retells how the priest Abimelech gave David the consecrated bread, deeming it better, in the prophet's words: I desire mercy and not sacrifice, to save men from the danger of hunger than to offer a sacrifice to God. His central principle is that the sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of men.

Christ's argument, as Bede paraphrases it, exposes the Pharisees' inconsistency: why do you not approve the same hunger in the apostles as you approve in others?

Bede also finds a figurative meaning here. David's taking of the loaves figuratively showed that the priestly food was to be transferred to the use of the people. He suggests two reasons: Whether because we all ought to imitate the priestly life, or because all the children of the Church are priests.

---

## Clement of Alexandria

This excerpt does not clearly address Luke 6. It criticizes Jewish worship, claiming that the Jews, thinking that they only know God, do not know Him, adoring as they do angels and archangels, the month and the moon. It also states that if the moon be not visible, they do not hold the Sabbath, which is called the first.

The phrase "the Sabbath, which is called the first" may explain why the excerpt was grouped with Luke 6's "second-first Sabbath." However, the passage itself never mentions Luke or interprets that verse, and it breaks off mid-sentence. It would be speculative to draw a firm interpretation of Luke 6 from it.

---

## Summary
Bede's commentary has three main threads:
1. **Christian freedom:** The legal Sabbath gives way to a spiritual "Sabbath" of resting from sin.
2. **Mercy over ritual:** God's preferred sacrifice is human salvation.
3. **Allegory:** The grain fields picture the work of preaching and bringing people into the Church.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 34: A Summary

The excerpts come from two early Christian writers with very different approaches. Jerome focuses on the wording of the text, and Cyril of Alexandria reads the story spiritually for its moral lessons.

---

## Jerome: *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*

Jerome compares the Greek translation (the Septuagint) and other versions with the Hebrew text. His comments are textual rather than theological, but they show how translation choices shape the story.

**1. "Peaceful" or "perfected" (v. 20)**
When Hamor ("Emor") and Shechem address their townsmen, they describe Jacob's family as peaceable: "these men are peaceful with us." Jerome notes that where the Septuagint translated it as 'peaceful', Aquila interpreted it as 'consummated' or 'perfected', for which in Hebrew it is read Salamim. He concludes that from this it is clear that what we said above about Salem is true. That earlier discussion of Salem is not included in these excerpts, so his full argument cannot be reconstructed here. The point is that the Hebrew word carries a sense of wholeness or completion as well as peace.

**2. "Diligently" or "boldly" (v. 25)**
On the attack by Jacob's sons, where they entered the city diligently, and they killed every male, Jerome observes that it is read in Greek as ἀσφαλὼς, which means diligently: it is written in Hebrew as Bete, which means boldly and confidently. By his reading, the Hebrew stresses the brothers' confident boldness rather than their carefulness.

*Note:* The Hebrew characters themselves are missing from the excerpts (shown as empty parentheses), so only Jerome's transliterations and explanations are available.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria: *Glaphyra on Genesis* 5.4–5

Cyril reads the chapter allegorically, treating its characters as figures for the Church and the Christian life. He draws three main lessons.

**1. Restraint instead of revenge**
Cyril sees Simeon and Levi as types of believers. Levi represents those in the priestly order, and Simeon represents the faithful generally, since Simon, in fact, is interpreted as "obedience". He grants that such people are extremely displeased if somebody who is their intimate friend according to faith is offended. Still, they should not proceed to demand blood, nor should they expect extremely severe punishments for the corruptors.

To support this, Cyril quotes the rebuke *"You have made me hateful… in the eyes of all the inhabitants of the land"* and attributes it to Christ. In Genesis these are Jacob's words to his sons, so Cyril is reading Jacob as a figure of Christ. He also cites Jesus' words to Peter: "Put up again your sword into its sheath: all those who take the sword shall perish with the sword."

**2. Patient but not silent**
Cyril says that it is not fitting for us, who are inclined toward piety in God, to be armed with swords but rather to be patient. Patience is not passivity, though: We must be patient but never silent, as we must refer to him who judges rightly. Believers should rebuke wrongdoing and leave final judgment to God.

**3. Staying within "the father's tabernacle"**
Cyril reads Dinah's going out as a warning. Those who want to avoid destruction must be careful not to leave the tabernacle of the father, that is, the house of God, in order not to be received into the herds of the heretics and other strangers. He notes that after moving out of the father's tabernacle, Dinah was brought to the house of Shechem, and argues she would have never been reproached if she had stayed in the paternal houses.

He supports this with Psalm 27, quoting David's longing "that I should dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life" and the assurance that "in the days of my affliction he hid me in his tabernacle." The house of God is a place of safety.

*A note for modern readers:* Cyril's reading of Dinah serves his allegory about remaining in the Church. Many readers today would want to stress that the narrative places responsibility for the wrong done to her on Shechem.

---

## Summary

| Commentator | Approach | Key Insight |
|---|---|---|
| **Jerome** | Textual and linguistic | The Hebrew adds meaning: "peaceful" also suggests completeness, and the brothers acted "boldly" rather than merely "diligently." |
| **Cyril** | Allegorical and moral | Christians should answer wrongs with patience and rebuke rather than violence, and should stay within the protection of God's house. |

Together, the excerpts show two sides of early Christian reading of Genesis: Jerome's close attention to the original language, and Cyril's effort to draw lessons for the life of the Church.

# Summary of Commentary on 1 Corinthians 9

**A note on the sources:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, **John Chrysostom**, in his *Homily 21 on First Corinthians*. Documents 2 and 4 are shorter, condensed versions of passages that also appear in Documents 1 and 3, so the summary below treats them as one body of teaching.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 21)

### 1. Chapter 9 as proof that Paul practices what he preaches
Chrysostom reads chapter 9 as continuing Paul's argument from chapter 8. Paul had said, "If meat make my brother to stumble I will eat no flesh forever;" a thing which he had not yet done, but professed he would do if need require. To avoid being accused of empty talk, Paul is compelled to enter on the proof of this also, and to point out how he was used to forego even things permitted that he might not give offense, although without any law to enforce his doing so.

### 2. Giving up rights for the sake of others
The heart of the chapter, for Chrysostom, is Paul's refusal of financial support. Paul reasons this way: although Christ had enjoined that those who preach the Gospel should live at the charge of their disciples, I did not so, but chose, if need were, to end my life with famine and die the most grievous of deaths, so I might avoid receiving of those whom I instruct. Chrysostom stresses that Paul did this not because they would otherwise be made to stumble, but because his not receiving would edify them : a much greater thing for him to do. Accepting support would have been legitimate, for it would but have been a law which he was fulfilling. But for all this, by a sort of supererogation he used to spare them. In other words, Paul went beyond what was required.

### 3. The application: an argument from the greater to the lesser
Chrysostom draws a pointed lesson for the Corinthians: if he did more than was enacted lest they should take offense, and abstained from permitted things to edify others; what must they deserve who abstain not from idol sacrifices? And that, when many perish thereby? He adds that eating idol sacrifices is something even apart from all scandal one ought to shrink from, as being "the table of demons." He also notes Paul's step-by-step approach. At first Paul argues, "Though it were lawful, your brethren's harm should keep you from doing so;" and afterwards he proves that it is not even lawful.

### 4. Why Paul first defends his own dignity
Chrysostom explains why Paul opens with questions about his status. He wants to block the objection, "True; thou did not receive, but the reason thou did not was its not being lawful;" he sets down therefore first the causes why he might reasonably have received. Paul is also careful not to seem to criticize Peter and the other apostles, for they did not use to decline receiving.

Chrysostom especially admires Paul's restraint. He limits his self-praise not by what he knew of himself, but by what the subject of necessity required. Paul could have claimed he had worked harder than the others, but this he omits, being a point wherein he surpassed them; and those points wherein they were great and which were just grounds for their receiving, those only he sets down.

### 5. The four questions (9:1)
- **"Am I not free?"** Chrysostom paraphrases this as "have I not authority over myself? Am I under any, to overrule me and forbid my receiving?"
- **"Have I not seen Jesus Christ?"** This answers the claim that the other apostles had an advantage from having been with Christ. Chrysostom calls it no small dignity.
- **"Are you not my work in the Lord?"** For Chrysostom this question is decisive: For this is the great thing; and those others avail nothing, apart from this. Even Judas himself was "an Apostle," and "free," and "saw Christ;" but because he had not "the work of an Apostle," all those things profited him not. In short, office and privilege mean nothing without fruitful ministry.
- **"In the Lord"** Chrysostom reads this phrase as an act of humility. Because Paul had made a great claim, he softens it: "the work is God's, not mine."

### 6. The Corinthians as the "seal" of Paul's apostleship (9:2)
Chrysostom notes that Paul argues "by concession," claiming less than he could. He could have spoken of his ministry across the world, however, he mentions none of these things, but carries his point by concession, and even granting more than he need. For the whole world had him for its Apostle. Instead, Paul points only to the Corinthians as the proof of his apostleship. The irony is sharp: from whom I had most right to receive, even you whose teacher I was, from those I received not. Chrysostom summarizes the evidence Paul offered them: "For I both exhibited miracles, and taught by word, and underwent dangers, and showed forth a blameless life."

---

## Key Takeaways
1. **Love limits liberty.** True Christian freedom includes giving up legitimate rights for the good of others.
2. **Example over words.** Paul earns the right to instruct the Corinthians by having already lived out what he asks of them.
3. **Fruit over status.** Apostolic credentials are worthless without real gospel work, as the case of Judas shows. Even that work belongs to God.
4. **Humility in self-defense.** Paul defends himself only as much as necessary and avoids comparisons that would elevate him over others.

**Limitation:** These excerpts cover only roughly verses 1–2 of chapter 9 and the overall argument Chrysostom sees in it. They do not offer detailed comment on later sections of the chapter, so this summary cannot speak to Chrysostom's treatment of those verses.

# Patristic Insights on 2 Timothy 4

All four excerpts focus on the opening of the chapter: Paul's solemn charge to Timothy and his command to preach. None of them address the rest of the chapter.

## John Chrysostom: The Judgment That Frames the Charge

Chrysostom explains the weight behind Paul's charge in verse 1.

- **Two readings of "the quick and the dead":** Paul either means the wicked and the just, or the departed and those that are still living; for many will be left alive.
- **A deliberate escalation:** Chrysostom contrasts this letter with 1 Timothy. There Paul invoked God "Who quickens all things" [1 Timothy 6:13]: but here he sets before him what is more dreadful, "Who shall judge the quick and the dead," meaning the One Who shall call them to account "at His appearing and His kingdom."
- **A different kind of coming:** The phrase may be meant to show that He will not come in the way that He now has come. In other words, Christ's return in glory will differ from His first, humble coming.
- **The link to preaching:** For Chrysostom, this vision of judgment is the foundation for what comes next. After it, Paul turns to teaching him how he ought to preach the word.

## Theodoret of Cyrus: No Wrong Time to Teach

Theodoret's comment is brief and practical. He reads "in season and out of season" to mean that every occasion is appropriate for teaching, so long as this is done boldly and with forethought. His point is balance: the preacher should be both courageous and wise.

## Augustine of Hippo: Many Words, Yet Not Too Many

In a personal, prayerful reflection, Augustine works through a tension between warnings against excessive speech and Paul's command to preach constantly.

- He acknowledges the warning that "In the multitude of words you shall not avoid sin."
- He argues that speaking God's word is a different matter. If he spoke only to preach and praise God, not only would I avoid sin, but I would obtain a good reward, no matter how many words I spoke in this way.
- His reasoning is that the blessed Paul would not command a sin to his own true son in the faith when he wrote "Preach the word, be urgent in season, out of season."
- He resolves the tension this way: even someone who preaches constantly does not truly speak "many words," because they were only what was necessary.

## Athanasius of Alexandria: Faithfulness in Sacred Timing

Athanasius uses the verse in a notably different way from the others. Writing in a letter about the church calendar, he applies it to observing holy days:

- It is our duty and obligation to remember and heed the special day of Easter Sunday every year.
- He reads Paul as teaching his disciple Timothy to be aware of dates, so that Timothy would do things when they were supposed to be done and avoid the blame for doing things at the wrong time.

This is a pastoral application of the verse to liturgical life rather than an explanation of its immediate context, which concerns preaching.

## Summary

| Commentator | Key Emphasis |
|---|---|
| Chrysostom | Christ's coming judgment gives the charge its seriousness |
| Theodoret | Teach at every opportunity, with boldness and forethought |
| Augustine | Preaching God's word, however much, is not sinful excess |
| Athanasius | Faithfulness includes keeping sacred times, such as Easter |

Taken together, these Fathers show how one passage can support several insights: the motive for ministry (judgment), the manner of ministry (bold and wise), the measure of ministry (only what is necessary), and the rhythm of the church's life (its appointed seasons).

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 17:1–4: Offenses, Rebuke, and Forgiveness

The excerpts cover only the opening verses of Luke 17 (vv. 1–4), which address stumbling blocks, the "millstone" warning, and the duty to rebuke and forgive. They do not discuss later parts of the chapter, such as the ten lepers or the coming of the Kingdom.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria: Distinguishing Kinds of Offense

Cyril clarifies which kind of "offense" Jesus means. He identifies two categories: "of which the one resist the glory of God, but the other serve only to cause a stumbling-block to the brethren." The first type includes the inventions of heresies, and every word that is spoken against the truth.

His key point is that Jesus is not primarily talking about doctrinal error here. Instead, He means offenses which occur between friends and brethren, as strifes, slanders, and the like. Cyril supports this reading from the flow of the passage itself: Therefore He adds afterwards, If your brother trespass against you, rebuke him. For Cyril, then, the passage is about relationships within the community of believers.

---

## Bede: Scandal, the "Little Ones," and Ordered Mercy

Bede offers the most extensive commentary, developing several themes.

### 1. Scandals are inevitable, but responsibility remains
Bede connects Jesus' words to Paul's statement that There must be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest among you. He reasons that it is therefore impossible in this world, so full of errors and afflictions, that scandals will not come very often; but woe to him who, by his fault, causes what is inevitable to come through him.

### 2. Reading the passage in context
Unlike Cyril, Bede ties the warning to the preceding chapter. He grants that some false brother or Judas himself, who was preparing his mind for betrayal, may be understood here by the general sense. However, he argues that the passage looks back to the previous context, where the Lord, speaking about giving alms, is mocked by the Pharisees. His insight is that he who reproaches one speaking rightly certainly provides a scandal, that is, a stumbling block and ruin to weak listeners, especially if he, like the Pharisees, appears to possess knowledge of the law. Religious authority used to mock the truth is especially harmful.

### 3. The millstone and the "little ones"
Bede explains that Jesus speaks according to the custom of the province, by which this punishment was for greater crimes among the ancient Jews. The image underscores a moral priority: it is better for the innocent to end their bodily life with a punishment, however atrocious, than to deserve the eternal death of the soul by harming a brother.

He also reflects on why the vulnerable are called "little." For he who is great, whatever he sees, whatever he suffers, does not turn away from the faith. Therefore, it is most appropriate for us to consider those who are small in faith, that they not be offended by anything of ours, and leave the faith, and fall from salvation.

### 4. When scandal must be accepted
Bede adds an important qualification. Insofar as we can without sin, we must avoid scandalizing our neighbors. Yet if a scandal arises from the truth, it is better to permit the scandal to arise than to forsake the truth. Concern for others' sensitivities never overrides fidelity to the truth.

### 5. Rebuke and forgiveness as a single command
Bede links Jesus' instruction to Leviticus 19: You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your neighbor and not bear sin because of him. He sees a three-part path for avoiding scandal: if we take care not to offend anyone, if we rebuke the sinner with the zeal of justice, if we open the bowels of mercy and compassion to the penitent.

He stresses that we are commanded not to forgive indiscriminately but to forgive the one who repents. His most striking claim is that silence is itself disobedience: whoever sees his brother sin and remains silent is no less a transgressor of the Lord's command than he who refuses to grant pardon to the penitent. The goal is balance, lest forgiveness be either too difficult or indulgence too lax.

---

## Summary of Key Insights

| Commentator | Central Insight |
|---|---|
| **Cyril** | The "offenses" in this passage are interpersonal sins among believers, such as strife and slander, rather than heresy. |
| **Bede** | Scandal is inevitable, yet personally culpable. The spiritually weak deserve special care, but truth must not be abandoned to avoid offense. Loving rebuke and forgiveness of the repentant are inseparable duties. |

Both commentators read the passage as guidance for life within the Christian community. Cyril emphasizes the relational nature of the offenses. Bede develops a fuller pastoral framework that balances protecting the weak, holding to truth, and practicing mercy that is neither harsh nor lax.

# Patristic Insights on 1 Thessalonians 3

## John Chrysostom: Homily 3 on First Thessalonians

This excerpt deals most directly with the chapter. Chrysostom explains why Paul sent Timothy (1 Thess 3:2–3).

- **Why the Thessalonians were shaken:** Chrysostom observes that the temptations of the teachers trouble their disciples, and he had then fallen into many temptations. He points to Paul's repeated complaint that "Satan hindered us," noting that Paul's inability to come was a proof of great violence.
- **The general and the soldier:** His central insight is that believers are not so much troubled at their own temptations, as at those of their teachers; as neither is the soldier so much troubled at his own trials, as when he sees his general wounded.
- **"To establish you" is not a rebuke:** Chrysostom stresses that Timothy's mission did not imply weakness in the church. It was not that they were at all deficient in faith, nor that they required to learn anything.

## Theodore of Mopsuestia: Commentary on 1 Thessalonians

Theodore focuses on the purpose of Timothy's visit.

- **Strengthening through presence:** Paul says that Timothy is coming to strengthen the Thessalonians with his words, stabilizing the thinking of the Thessalonians by his presence with them, lest they collapse under the weight of their tribulations. Theodore thus sees both Timothy's words and his physical presence as means of support.
- **The danger of being "moved":** He interprets the threatened collapse as inner turmoil: Paul describes this collapsing as a "commotion," being caught up in the passions of your persecutors. The risk was not only fear but being drawn into the hostile spirit of the persecutors.

## John Chrysostom: Homilies on Acts 42

This excerpt comes from Chrysostom's homilies on Acts, not from a commentary on 1 Thessalonians. It does open with the words of 1 Thess 3:1, but it then blends in language about Paul sending "two of those who ministered to him," which is drawn from the Acts narrative. Its reflections are relevant to the chapter's themes but are not strictly an exposition of it.

- **God's purpose in trials:** Chrysostom asks, Do you see how God permits trials, and by them stirs up and awakens the disciples and makes them more energetic? He therefore urges, let us not sink down under trials.
- **Affliction builds fellowship:** Nothing so makes friends and rivets them so firmly as affliction; nothing so fastens and joins the souls of believers.
- **Suffering makes hearers receptive:** When the hearer is living an easy life, listless and indolent, those who try to teach him only annoy him. In contrast, when he is in affliction and distress, he longs to hear his teachers.

## Theodoret of Cyrus: Letter 78

This is a pastoral letter, not a commentary. Theodoret uses Timothy's mission only as an illustration, and the excerpt does not interpret the chapter's text in detail.

- **Stepping in without seizing power:** He compares Timothy to a ship's officer who takes the helm not because he becomes a self-appointed helmsman but because he looks out for the safety of the ship. In the same way, the thrice blessed Timothy when sent by the divine Paul took his place.
- **Application to church leadership:** He urges his recipient to accept the responsibilities of helmsman, of captain, of shepherd, gladly to run all risk for the sake of the sheep of Christ.

## Common Threads

Several themes run through these excerpts:
1. **Timothy's mission** is a stabilizing ministry of presence and encouragement, not a correction of deficient faith.
2. **Affliction is expected and purposeful.** It can strengthen believers and deepen their bonds rather than destroy them.
3. **Teachers and congregations are bound together.** The sufferings of leaders affect their people, and faithful leaders step in for the flock's sake rather than for their own standing.
