# Augustine of Hippo on Matthew 5: The Opening of the Sermon on the Mount

**Note on sources:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, **Augustine of Hippo**. Documents 1 and 3 appear to be two translations of the same passage (*Sermon on the Mount* 1.1.2), so their insights are combined below. Document 2 discusses the Sermon as a whole and quotes its closing parable of the wise and foolish builders, which comes from the end of the Sermon in Matthew 7 rather than chapter 5. It is included because Augustine uses it to frame how the Sermon, beginning in chapter 5, should be read.

## 1. The Sermon as a Complete Guide to Christian Living
Augustine makes a bold claim about the Sermon's scope. Anyone who reads it carefully will find in it, so far as regards the highest morals, a perfect standard of the Christian life. He says this is not his own assumption but something he draws from the very words of the Lord Himself.

His evidence is a small detail in the wording. Jesus has not simply said, Whosoever hears my words, but has made an addition, saying, Whosoever hears these words of mine. For Augustine, this shows that these sayings which He uttered on the mount so perfectly guide the life of those who may be willing to live according to them, that they may justly be compared to one building upon a rock.

## 2. The Meaning of the Mountain
Augustine reads the setting symbolically. The mountain may well be understood as meaning the greater precepts of righteousness; for there were lesser ones which were given to the Jews. He supports this with a prophetic text: Your righteousness is like the mountains of God: and this may well mean that the one Master alone fit to teach matters of so great importance teaches on a mountain.

## 3. One God, Two Stages of Revelation: Fear and Love
This is Augustine's most significant theological point. He insists that the Old and New Covenants come from the same God, who revealed his will in stages suited to his people. It is one God who, through His holy prophets and servants, according to a thoroughly arranged distribution of times, gave the lesser precepts to a people who as yet required to be bound by fear; and who, through His Son, gave the greater ones to a people whom it had now become suitable to set free by love.

He describes God as a wise physician. God alone knows how to present to the human race the medicine suited to the occasion. He also links the two sets of precepts to their purposes: the greater precepts are given for the kingdom of heaven, and the lesser for an earthly kingdom, by that one and the same God, who made heaven and earth.

This view affirms continuity between the Testaments while still recognizing that the Gospel brings something higher.

## 4. The Posture of Teacher and Disciples
Augustine also finds meaning in the physical details of the scene. Jesus teaches sitting, as behooves the dignity of the instructor's office; and His disciples come to Him, in order that they might be nearer in body for hearing His words, as they also approached in spirit to fulfil His precepts. The disciples' physical approach mirrors the inner response of obedience.

## 5. "And He Opened His Mouth"
Augustine offers two readings of this phrase:
- **A practical one:** the pause it creates perhaps gracefully intimates by the mere pause that the sermon will be somewhat longer than usual.
- **A theological one:** it may signify that now He is said to have opened His own mouth, whereas under the old law He was accustomed to open the mouths of the prophets.

The second reading fits his larger theme. The same God who once spoke through the prophets now speaks directly in the person of his Son.

## Summary
Augustine presents the Sermon on the Mount as the complete standard of Christian morality. It is delivered by Christ as the one true Teacher of a "greater righteousness." Its central idea is a single God who guided his people first by fear through the Law and the prophets, and now by love through his Son, speaking in his own voice.

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on Matthew 28

**Note on scope:** Only one excerpt was provided, from **Augustine of Hippo's *Harmony of the Gospels* (3.65)**. It focuses on a single question from the opening verse of Matthew 28: *when* the women came to the tomb. It does not address other parts of the chapter, such as the angel's message, the guards, or the Great Commission, so this summary is limited to that one issue.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: Reconciling the Timing of the Women's Visit

### 1. The Apparent Problem
Augustine treats a possible discrepancy between the Gospels as a serious matter. He insists that one must not dismiss lightly the question concerning the exact hour at which the women came to the tomb. The tension is that Matthew places the visit "In the evening of the sabbath, at the dawn of the first day of the week," while Mark says "And early in the morning on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb at the rising of the sun".

### 2. Mark, Luke, and John Agree
Augustine first shows that the other Gospels fit together. Luke says "early in the morning," and John says "in the morning when it was still dark." He reads Mark's "rising of the sun" as the moment when the heavens in the east were brightening, which customarily is called the dawn.

- **Mark and John:** There is no contradiction with John's "still dark," for as day is breaking the remaining shadows of darkness diminish only in proportion to the sun's rising.
- **Luke:** "Early in the morning" need not be understood to imply that the sun had already appeared above the horizon. It is an everyday expression used to signal that something happened earlier, at dawn.

### 3. Matthew's "Evening" Means the Whole Night
The key insight concerns Matthew's wording. Augustine argues that Matthew's own phrase resolves the difficulty. Reading "evening" as only early nightfall would be impossible, because it is not the beginning of the night which "dawns on the first day of the week" but the night which begins to be terminated by the coming of the light.

He therefore concludes that we cannot say that the evening is "at the dawn of the first day of the week" unless by "evening" we intend "night," which the light brings to an end. He presents this as a regular feature of biblical language: by saying "evening" it signifies the whole night, the end of which is the dawn.

### 4. Conclusion
All four accounts describe the same moment: the women came to the tomb at dawn, and therefore they came at night, which is signified in Scripture by the designation of evening. Even if they came at the very end of the night, the fact remains without a doubt that they came at night.

---

## Why This Matters
Augustine's contribution here is interpretive rather than doctrinal. He shows how to read the resurrection narratives as complementary accounts instead of conflicting ones. He pays close attention to ordinary speech and to biblical idiom, and he takes apparent tensions seriously rather than dismissing them. The excerpt does not comment on the theological meaning of the resurrection itself.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 2:2: Summary of Key Insights

**Scope:** The provided excerpts focus almost entirely on one verse, 2 Corinthians 2:2, and briefly on the background of verse 1. They do not address the rest of the chapter, so this summary is limited to that passage.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. The setting: avoiding another painful visit
Chrysostom explains the background to Paul's words. Paul had obviously had one bad experience at Corinth and wanted to avoid another one, for a second occasion would be even worse. In Paul's own reasoning, as Chrysostom paraphrases it: "I would not, he says, come unto you, lest I should increase your sorrow, rebuking, showing anger and disgust."

### 2. Paul softens a potential accusation
Chrysostom sees verse 2 as a pastoral correction. Paul realized that even this was strong and implied accusation that they so lived as to make Paul sorry, he applies a corrective with the question, "Who then is he that makes me glad, but he that is made sorry by me?"

### 3. Sorrow as proof of love
This is Chrysostom's central insight. The Corinthians' grief at being rebuked shows how much they value their relationship with Paul. He paraphrases Paul this way: 'Even though I were to be in sorrow, being compelled to rebuke you and to see you sorry, still nevertheless this very thing would have made me glad. For this is a proof of the greatest love, that you hold me in such esteem as to be hurt at my being displeased with you.' His homily summarizes the point the same way: even if he were to make the Corinthians sorry he would be glad, since their sorrow would be proof of how much they held him in esteem.

### 4. Paul's pastoral wisdom and tenderness
Chrysostom praises Paul's "prudence." Paul takes something ordinary, their doing what all disciples do, namely, smarting and feeling it when rebuked, and presents it as an instance of their gratifying him.

Chrysostom also notes how Paul phrases the sentence. The expected logic would have been 'For if I make you sorry, who then is he that can make you glad?' Instead, Paul turns his speech back again, dealing tenderly with them. In effect, Paul tells them that their being hurt by his words is itself a great favor to him.

---

## Basil of Caesarea

### Correction as spiritual medicine
Basil applies the verse to the relationship between believers and their spiritual leaders, using the image of a physician. He observes that the physically sick trust doctors even when treatment is painful. He finds it shameful that we do not share this attitude toward the physicians of our souls when they secure our salvation for us by laborious discipline.

He cites Paul's words in 2:2 as the model and concludes: It behooves one who looks to the end, therefore, to consider him a benefactor who causes us pain which is according to God.

---

## Common Thread

Both writers see godly sorrow as constructive rather than destructive, but they approach it from different angles:

- **Chrysostom** looks at the relationship. The disciples' grief over rebuke reveals their love, and Paul handles it with tenderness.
- **Basil** looks at the practical lesson. Believers should welcome painful correction as healing that serves their salvation, and should regard those who give it as benefactors.

# Patristic Insights on Colossians 3

The excerpts focus mainly on the chapter's opening call to "seek the things that are above." Each commentator develops that theme differently.

## Augustine of Hippo: Resurrection as Inner Renewal

Augustine reads the chapter as describing a transformation that begins inside the believer.

- **Renewal implies a prior "oldness."** He argues that the inner man, too, if he is certainly renewed from day to day, is surely old before he is renewed.
- **"Putting off the old man" is an interior act.** He writes that that is done inwardly, which the same apostle says: "Put off the old man and put on the new man."
- **Truthfulness is the example.** He connects this to the command "Wherefore putting away lying, speak the truth." He insists that lying can only be put away inwardly, in order that he may dwell in the holy mountain of God who speaks the truth in his heart.
- **Rising with Christ is a present, inward mystery.** He calls this an inner resurrection and says the apostle's words fit it: "But if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; mind the things that are above."

Augustine attributes these sayings to "the same apostle" without naming the letter each comes from. His excerpt therefore weaves together several Pauline phrases rather than commenting on Colossians 3 verse by verse.

## John Chrysostom: The Mind Lifted to God's Throne

Chrysostom (in two excerpts) emphasizes how high Paul directs the believer's attention.

- **Union with Christ's death and resurrection.** Chrysostom notes that He brings them together, having above established that He died. He adds a short remark on the heavenly realm: No observances are there. The excerpt does not explain this further, but it appears to contrast heavenly realities with religious observances.
- **The significance of "seated at the right hand."** Chrysostom sees Paul deliberately raising his readers as far as possible: Whither has he led our minds aloft! How has he filled them with mighty aspiration! He observes that it was not enough to say, "the things that are above," nor yet, "where Christ is," but what? "seated on the right hand of God."
- **Passing beyond all heavenly powers.** In his second excerpt, he says Paul cut a path through the midst of all the angels, archangels, thrones, dominations, principalities, virtues, all those invisible powers, the cherubim and seraphim and set the thoughts of the faithful right before the very throne of the King.
- **Earthly people standing in spirit before God.** Through this teaching, Paul has persuaded those who walk the earth to sever the bonds of the body, to take flight and to stand in spirit by the side of him who is the Lord of all.

The final line of the homily excerpt, "From that point he was preparing them henceforward to see the earth," is cryptic without its surrounding context, so I won't guess at its exact meaning.

## Gregory of Nyssa: Transforming the Passions

Gregory's excerpt is mainly about human emotions. He cites Colossians 3 in support of his point rather than commenting on the chapter directly.

- **Emotions governed by reason become virtues.** He teaches that if reason instead assumes sway over such emotions, each of them is transmuted to a form of virtue. His examples: anger produces courage, terror caution, fear obedience, hatred aversion from vice, the power of love the desire for what is truly beautiful.
- **A healthy "high spirit" lifts the mind.** He says that high spirit in our character raises our thought above the passions and keeps it from bondage to what is base.
- **The link to Colossians 3.** He finds Paul endorsing this: the great apostle praises such a form of mental elevation when he bids us constantly to "think those things that are above."
- **Restoring the divine image.** He concludes that every such motion, when elevated by loftiness of mind, is conformed to the beauty of the divine image.

## Common Threads

All three writers treat the call to set one's mind "above" as central, but they stress different aspects:

| Commentator | Main emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Augustine** | Inward moral renewal: resurrection with Christ begins in the heart, as seen in truthfulness. |
| **Chrysostom** | How high the believer's attention is directed: past every heavenly power to Christ enthroned beside God. |
| **Gregory of Nyssa** | Practical transformation: redirected emotions become virtues and reflect God's image. |

Together they present "seeking the things above" as an inner reality, a spiritual ascent, and a reshaping of character.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Peter 3: A Summary

The excerpts come from two commentators: **the Venerable Bede**, who gives the most extended treatment, and **Eusebius of Caesarea**, whose catena excerpt reflects on related themes.

---

## Bede: *Commentary on the Catholic Epistles*

### 1. Peter's Second Letter (v. 1)
Bede's note on the opening verse is brief and mainly clarifies wording. He explains that the phrase "in which" means in the Epistles, or to those to whom he writes the epistles. It is a grammatical clarification rather than a major theological point.

### 2. The Earth Formed Out of Water and Through Water (v. 5)
Bede's most developed reflection concerns how creation depends on water by God's word. He makes two points:

- **Origin:** The earth consists out of water, for at the beginning of creation God said: "Let the waters be gathered together in one place, and let the dry land appear;" and it was so (Gen. I).
- **Ongoing sustenance:** The earth also continues to exist through water. By divine arrangement the veins of water fill the whole depth within, just as we see the bodies of living creatures overflowing with veins of blood, lest they fail in dryness if the irrigation of water ceases. He gives an everyday example: with the heat of summer, the lands with their absorbed moisture wither away, and soon are turned into dust which the wind casts.

**Insight:** For Bede, God's word did not only create the world in the beginning. It continues to hold the world together, and the world's stability depends entirely on God's ordering.

### 3. What "Heavens" Means
Bede notes a textual variant: Another Edition has: "The heavens existed long ago out of water and through water." He takes "heavens" here to mean this humid and cloudy air. He explains that Scripture is accustomed to call this air, and sometimes the heavens, and supports this with Jeremiah 8: "The hawk in heaven knows its appointed time" (Jerem. VIII).

### 4. The World That Perished in the Flood (v. 6)
Bede asks in what sense "the world perished." He answers carefully that the destruction was real but limited:

- The higher parts of the world were in no way touched by the flood.
- The earth perished because, being submerged and covered by waters, it not only lost the state of fruitfulness inherent to it for such a long time, but also, as we have taught above, in many places it received a different face from that which it had initially.
- The heavens likewise perished to the extent of this airspace. Here Bede draws on Augustine: "For the water increased," as Saint Augustine says, "and occupied this entire space where birds fly."

### 5. An Open Question About the Coming Fire
Bede, following Augustine, raises the question of the final judgment by fire without settling it. There are also the heavens of the heavens higher in the firmament, but whether they too are to perish by fire, or if only these which perished by the flood will do so, is a rather more precise debate among the learned.

**Insight:** Bede reads the flood as a precedent for the coming judgment, which is Peter's own argument in this chapter. He also shows humility about how far that judgment will extend, leaving the question open rather than claiming certainty.

---

## Eusebius of Caesarea: *Catena*

**Note on relevance:** This excerpt does not explicitly mention 2 Peter 3. It comments on a psalm verse: "In the beginning you, O Lord, laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands," said the psalmist. Its placement in a catena on this chapter suggests it was linked to Peter's teaching that the heavens and earth will pass away, but that connection is implied, not stated.

Eusebius's main points:

- **Created things can be changed:** Because the heavens and earth are God's work, they are subject to his will. Since you were their maker, you can do whatever you want to with them.
- **Creation is perishable:** They are made of destructible matter and did not exist at all until you made them by your will and power.
- **Only God is eternal:** There is only one that is eternal and can never be removed and that is you, the only maker of everything that exists.

**Insight:** Eusebius contrasts a temporary creation with an eternal Creator. This provides a theological basis for believing that the present heavens and earth can be transformed or brought to an end.

---

## Common Ground

Both commentators stress that creation depends completely on God. Bede emphasizes that God's word both formed the world and continues to sustain it, and that the flood shows how that world can be judged. Eusebius emphasizes that creation is perishable because it was made, while God alone endures forever. Together they support Peter's warning that the present world is not permanent and remains under God's sovereign word.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 26: A Summary

The excerpts come from two early Church commentators. **John Chrysostom** focuses on how Jesus prepares His disciples for the Passion and on the religious leaders' plot. **Jerome** focuses on the anointing scene at Bethany.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. The Passion follows the promise of glory
Chrysostom notes that Jesus chooses His moment carefully. He speaks of His coming suffering right after teaching about the final judgment. In good season again does He speak of the passion, when He had reminded them of the kingdom, and of the recompense there, and of the deathless punishment; as though He had said, Why are you afraid at the dangers that are for a season, when such good things await you?

**Insight:** Present suffering should be seen in light of eternal reward.

### 2. The Passover frames the Passion as a saving mystery
Chrysostom points out that Jesus softens painful news by how He phrases it. For He said not, You know that after two days I am betrayed, but, You know that after two days is the passover, to show that what is done is a mystery and that a feast and celebration is being kept for the salvation of the world, and that with foreknowledge He suffered all.

The Passover connection also carries meaning of its own. Jesus shows that even His very passion is a deliverance from countless evils, having by the passover reminded them of the ancient benefits in Egypt. Chrysostom also explains why Jesus does not mention the resurrection here: it was superfluous, after having discoursed so much about it, to speak of it again.

**Insight:** Christ's death is not a defeat but a foreknown, saving "feast," much as the Exodus Passover brought deliverance.

### 3. The plot of the high priests
Chrysostom's language about the religious authorities is sharply critical. He sees irony in the conspirators desiring to obtain their authority from that quarter, whence they ought to have found hindrance. He also comments on the plural "high priests." For the law wills there should be one, but then there were many. Whence it is manifest, that the Jewish constitution had begun to dissolve. He explains that they were afterwards made for a year, and that the evangelist here call high priests, who had been high priests.

**Insight:** For Chrysostom, the multiplied priesthood and the leaders' misuse of their office show a religious order in decline.

---

## Jerome

### 1. Bethany and the meaning of Simon's name
Commenting on verse 6, Jerome sees symbolism in the setting. Jesus, about to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations with his blood, he stayed in Bethany, the house of obedience, which was once Simon the leper's.

### 2. Why "the leper"? A testimony to the Healer
Jerome explains that Simon was no longer a leper. Rather, he who was formerly a leper was cleansed by the Savior, with his former name remaining, so that the power of the healer may be apparent. He offers a parallel: in the list of apostles, with his former vice and occupation, Matthew is called a tax collector, who had certainly ceased to be a tax collector.

**Insight:** A person's former label can stand as a lasting witness to Christ's transforming power.

### 3. A spiritual (allegorical) reading
Jerome also reports a symbolic interpretation held by others. "They," he says, take Simon's house to mean a part of the people, which has believed in the Lord, and has been cured by him. He adds that Simon can be interpreted in another sense as the world, in whose house the Church is healed.

**Insight:** The house at Bethany can symbolize the healed community of believers, a picture of the Church restored by Christ.

---

## Summary

- **Chrysostom** reads Matthew 26 pastorally and historically. Jesus comforts His disciples by presenting the Passion as a foreknown, Passover-like act of salvation, while the leaders' plotting shows a corrupted religious order.
- **Jerome** reads the Bethany scene both literally and spiritually. Simon's retained title testifies to Christ's healing power, and his house can symbolize the Church healed by the Savior.

# Patristic Insights on 2 Timothy 2

The excerpts focus mainly on the chapter's opening verses: Paul's charge to Timothy as his "son" and the command to pass on what was heard "among many witnesses" (v. 2).

## John Chrysostom

**1. Paul's suffering as encouragement**

Chrysostom explains why Paul points to his own hardships when he exhorts Timothy. He uses two illustrations:
- At sea, the young sailor at sea is inspired with great confidence if the master of the ship has been preserved in a shipwreck. The sailor sees that the danger comes not from the master's inexperience but from the nature of things.
- In battle, the captain, who sees his general wounded and recovered again, is much encouraged.

The lesson is that believers are comforted to see that the apostle should have been exposed to great sufferings and not been rendered weak by the utmost of them. Paul's reasoning is simple: If the master much, more the disciple. Suffering is not a sign of failure. It is the normal path of faithful service, and Paul has already walked it.

**2. Affection in the exhortation**

Chrysostom notes the tenderness of Paul's language. This exhortation he introduces with much affection, calling him "son," and not only so, but "my son." The family language also carries a challenge: If you are a son, he implies, imitate your father. In Chrysostom's reading, Christian discipleship works like a family likeness passed from spiritual parent to child.

**3. The public nature of the teaching**

Commenting on "among many witnesses," Chrysostom paraphrases Paul's meaning: You have not heard in secret, nor apart, but in the presence of many, with all openness of speech. His point is that the apostolic teaching was open and publicly attested, not a hidden or private tradition.

## Basil of Caesarea

Basil quotes the same verse, "what you have heard from me before many witnesses entrust to faithful men", in a discussion about the Holy Spirit and the angels. He insists that one does not speak of the Spirit and of angels as if they were equals. The Spirit is the Lord of life. By contrast, the angels are our helpers, our fellow servants, faithful witnesses of the truth.

He cites 2 Timothy 2:2 as an example of a wider practice: It is customary for the saints to deliver God's commandments in the presence of witnesses. He then speaks of Paul calling on angels as witnesses: He asks the angels to testify with him, because he knows that angels will be present when the Lord comes in the glory of his father to judge the world in righteousness.

Basil's use of the verse is therefore part of a larger theological argument about the Spirit's divine status. The excerpt does not say which Pauline passage the angels-as-witnesses idea comes from. Verse 2 itself speaks only of "many witnesses," so the angelic application is best read as Basil's broader theme rather than a direct interpretation of this verse.

## Clement of Alexandria

The excerpt from Clement's *Stromata* quotes the verse: "And the things which thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." However, it includes no commentary, so it shows only that Clement knew and used this verse. His interpretation cannot be determined from what was provided.

## Summary of Themes

- **Endurance modeled by the teacher** (Chrysostom): Paul's survival of severe suffering gives Timothy and all believers courage to endure.
- **Spiritual sonship** (Chrysostom): Paul's affectionate "my son" calls Timothy to imitate his spiritual father.
- **Open, attested teaching** (Chrysostom): The faith was handed on publicly, before many witnesses.
- **Witnesses and divine order** (Basil): The practice of entrusting teaching before witnesses supports Basil's distinction between the Spirit as Lord and the angels as fellow servants and witnesses.

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on 1 Corinthians 14

All of the provided excerpts come from a single commentator, **John Chrysostom** (Homily 35 on First Corinthians). They cover the opening verses of the chapter. Document 3 appears to be a condensed rendering of material that also appears more fully in Document 4, so the two are treated together below.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. Love must be actively pursued
Chrysostom focuses on Paul's word "follow after," reading it as the language of a hunt. He explains that "he that is in chase beholds that only which is chased, and towards that he strains himself, and leaves not off until he lay hold of it."

He then applies this image to the Christian life. When we cannot reach love by ourselves, we should ask those who are near her to hold her until we catch up. Once we have grasped her, we should not let her go again, so that she does not escape us. He also explains why love tends to slip away: "continually she springs away from us, because we use her not as we ought, but prefer all things unto her."

His encouraging conclusion is that, once love is firmly held, "we require not henceforth much labor, nay rather scarce any; but taking our ease, and keeping holiday, we shall march on in the narrow path of virtue."

### 2. Love does not cancel spiritual gifts
Chrysostom notes that Paul guards against a misunderstanding. Readers might suppose that he brought in the discourse of charity for no other end than to extinguish the gifts. That is why Paul immediately adds, "Yet desire earnestly spiritual gifts." In Chrysostom's reading, love governs the gifts but does not replace them.

### 3. Why the Corinthians overvalued tongues
Chrysostom explains that the Corinthians were greatly puffed up on account of this, because the gift was considered to be a great one. They esteemed it because it was the one which the apostles received first, and with a great display. Yet this was no reason to think it was the greatest gift of all.

The gift had a specific missionary purpose. The apostles received it first "Because they were to go abroad every where." Chrysostom draws a vivid contrast with Babel: as at the building of the tower the one tongue was divided into many, so now many tongues frequently met in one man. The same person could speak in Persian, Roman, Indian, and many other languages, the Spirit sounding within him.

### 4. Paul's balanced treatment of tongues
Chrysostom sees Paul as carefully showing it to be neither altogether useless, nor very profitable by itself. Paul does this in two moves:
- **He lowers it.** By saying that the speaker in tongues "speaks not unto men, but unto God, for no man understands," he depressed it, implying that the profit of it was not great.
- **He raises it again.** By adding "in the Spirit he speaks mysteries," he again elevated it, that it might not seem to be superfluous and useless and given in vain.

### 5. Prophecy is greater because it benefits others
This is Chrysostom's central theological principle. Paul measures the value of a gift by the common benefit, and every where he gives the higher honor to that which tends to the profit of the many.

Chrysostom grants that both gifts share the same source: being moved by the Spirit is common to the one who prophesies and the one who speaks in tongues. The prophet, however, has the advantage because he is also profitable to the hearers. The reason is that those who spoke with tongues were not understood by those who did not have the gift.

He then asks whether tongues edified anyone at all. His answer is "Yes," says he, "themselves alone". The excerpt ends here, just as Chrysostom moves on to the next verse, so his fuller development of this point is not included in the provided material.

---

## Key Takeaways
- **Love comes first** and must be pursued with single-minded effort, sometimes with the help of others who already possess it.
- **Spiritual gifts remain desirable.** Love orders the gifts rather than abolishing them.
- **Tongues had a missionary purpose**, a reversal of Babel for spreading the gospel. This is not grounds for ranking it above other gifts.
- **Building up the community is the test of a gift's worth.** Prophecy surpasses tongues because it brings edification, exhortation, and comfort to others, not just to the speaker.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 6: A Summary

## Jerome: Who Are the "Sons of God"? (Genesis 6:2)

Jerome's excerpt deals with the language of verse 2. He reports how earlier translators handled the phrase rather than giving his own verdict.

- **The ambiguity of *Elohim*:** He notes that the Hebrew word Elohim is of common gender: and both God and gods are called by this name.
- **Aquila's angelic reading:** For this reason, Aquila, in the plural number, dared to call them Sons of gods, understanding them to mean the Holy Ones or Angels. Jerome supports this usage with "For God stands in the assembly of gods: but in the midst of them He judgeth gods."
- **Symmachus's alternative:** Symmachus took a similar interpretive approach but rendered it differently: "The sons of the powerful saw the daughters of men".

**Key insight:** The identity of the "sons of God" depends partly on how one understands the flexible Hebrew word *Elohim*. Ancient translators already offered more than one option: heavenly beings or powerful men.

## Bede (Drawing on Jerome): The 120 Years as Mercy (Genesis 6:3)

Bede comments on the verse "My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years." He relies heavily on Jerome.

- **Mercy rather than severity:** Bede quotes Jerome's reading of the Hebrew: "My Spirit shall not judge these men forever, because they are flesh; that is, because human nature is fragile, I will not condemn them to eternal torment; but here I will render to them what they deserve." On this reading, the verse denotes not the severity, as it is read in our texts, but the clemency of God, while a sinner is punished here for his crime. In other words, punishment in this life is presented as an act of mercy that spares people from eternal condemnation.
- **A time for repentance:** After the quotation, Bede explains that lest He seem to be cruel in not giving sinners a place for repentance, He added: "And his days shall be one hundred and twenty years" (Gen. VI), that is, they will have one hundred and twenty years to repent.
- **The period cut short:** Bede adds that because they despised repentance, God did not want to wait for the appointed time, but cutting short the span of twenty years, He brought the flood in the hundredth year appointed for repentance.

**Key insight:** God's words in 6:3 express patience and mercy. Human frailty becomes a reason for God's restraint. However, people who scorn that mercy can lose it sooner than expected.

## Ephrem the Syrian: Shortened Lives and Grace Beyond Justice (Genesis 6:3)

Ephrem reads the 120 years in two complementary ways.

- **A shortened lifespan:** This generation will not live nine hundred years like the previous generations, for it is flesh and its days are filled with the deeds of flesh.
- **A window for repentance:** If they repent during this time, they will be saved from the wrath that is about to come upon them. If they do not, by their deeds they will call down wrath upon themselves. Judgment is therefore the result of their own choices.
- **Undeserved grace:** His most striking statement is that Grace granted one hundred and twenty years for repentance to a generation that, according to justice, was not worthy of repentance.

**Key insight:** Ephrem sets grace against strict justice. The opportunity to repent is itself an unearned gift.

## Augustine: "Flesh" and Humanity's Fallen Condition

Augustine's excerpt is mainly about Genesis 3 (the curse after the Fall), not Genesis 6. It touches chapter 6 only through one cross-reference.

- He argues that by the justice of God the whole human race was delivered into the power of the devil, the sin of the first man passing originally into all persons of both sexes.
- He connects the curse "earth you are" to Genesis 6:3, saying it shows that the whole man has been changed into something worse, for "earth you are" is just the same as saying "My spirit shall not remain in those men, because they are flesh."

**Key insight:** For Augustine, "flesh" in 6:3 describes humanity's corrupted condition after the Fall. Readers should note that this is a side connection within a larger argument about original sin, not a full commentary on Genesis 6.

## Common Threads

- **Bede (with Jerome) and Ephrem** both read the 120 years mainly as a merciful period for repentance. Ephrem adds that it also shortens human life.
- **Jerome/Bede and Augustine** both reflect on the word "flesh." For Jerome it signals fragility that calls forth God's clemency. For Augustine it signals the degraded state of fallen humanity.
- Taken together, the commentators present Genesis 6 as a chapter where God's judgment is real but is preceded and shaped by patience and grace.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 5

All four excerpts center on the opening of the chapter: Paul's image of the "earthly house" contrasted with "a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." Each Father draws a different lesson from it.

## Origen of Alexandria: The Same Body, Transformed

Origen stresses **continuity** between our present body and our resurrection body. He teaches that there is not one body which we now use in lowliness and corruption and weakness and a different one which we are to use hereafter in incorruption and power and glory, but that this same body, having cast off the weaknesses of its present existence, will be transformed into a thing of glory and made spiritual. The result is that what was a vessel of dishonor shall itself be purified and become a vessel of honor and a habitation of blessedness. He uses Paul's phrase "a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" to support his claim that our body remains in this condition forever unchangeably by the will of the Creator.

## Augustine of Hippo: The Body Is Not the Problem

Augustine uses this passage to argue against blaming the flesh for sin. Anyone who claims that the cause of vices and evil habits lies in the flesh has not, he says, sufficiently considered human nature as a whole. He grants that our corruptible body may be a burden on our soul, but insists that the cause of this encumbrance is not in the nature and substance of the body.

So the Christian hope is not escape from the body but its renewal: we do not desire to be divested of the body but rather to be clothed with its immortality. In immortal life we shall have a body, but it will no longer be a burden since it will no longer be corruptible.

## Didymus the Blind: Two Worlds and the Soul's Journey

Didymus reads the passage cosmologically: Paul is talking here about two different worlds. One is the earthly, made with hands and visible. The other is invisible, made without hands and heavenly. He describes a sequence. On earth, our soul is clothed in flesh and blood. Then, once this body is left behind, the soul will move to the heavenly realm, where it will receive its body back, but one that has been transformed into a heavenly body.

## John Chrysostom: Suffering, Resurrection, and the Language of Contrast

Chrysostom gives the fullest pastoral and literary reading.

**Pastoral context.** He sees Paul encouraging believers facing hardship, because many trials drew on. His message is that one ought not to wonder that we suffer affliction; nor to be confounded, for we even reap many gains thereby. He makes a striking claim: not only ought not one to grieve at its perishing now in part, but even earnestly to seek for the completion of that destruction, for this most conducts you to immortality.

**Doctrinal purpose.** Chrysostom believes Paul is urging again the doctrine of the Resurrection in respect to which they were particularly unsound.

**Interpreting "earthly house."** He notes a different view from Didymus's: Some indeed say that the 'earthly house' is this world; But I should maintain that he alludes rather to the body.

**Paul's word choices.** Chrysostom observes how Paul's terms show the superiority of the future things to the present. "Earthly" is set against "heavenly," and "tabernacle" (tent) against "eternal," for the name "tabernacle" often times denotes temporariness. On "not made with hands," he denies that the body itself is handmade. Paul either alludes to the houses here that are made with hands, or if not this, then he called the body which is not made with hands, 'a house of tabernacle.'

## Key Takeaways

- **Points of agreement:** Origen, Augustine, and Chrysostom all read the passage as being about the body and resurrection hope. Each affirms that the future involves a glorified, imperishable body, not escape from bodily existence.
- **A notable difference:** Didymus interprets the "houses" as two worlds. Chrysostom explicitly mentions this kind of reading and prefers to see the body as the main reference.
- **Distinct emphases:** Origen stresses the continuity of the same body. Augustine defends the goodness of the body against blaming it for sin. Chrysostom draws pastoral comfort for those who suffer.

**A note on scope:** These excerpts focus almost entirely on the opening verse of chapter 5. They do not address the chapter's later themes, so this summary cannot speak to how these Fathers interpreted those sections.

# Augustine of Hippo on Matthew 7:1–5

All four excerpts come from **one commentator, Augustine of Hippo**. They focus on the opening verses of Matthew 7: the command "Judge not" and the image of the mote and the beam. The rest of the chapter is not discussed in these excerpts.

## 1. "Judge not" means giving others the benefit of the doubt

Augustine reads Jesus' command narrowly. He says that in this passage, I am of opinion that we are taught nothing else, but that in the case of those actions respecting which it is doubtful with what intention they are done, we are to put the better construction on them.

This is not a ban on all moral judgment. He explains that the saying "By their fruits you shall know them" has reference to things which manifestly cannot be done with a good intention; such as debaucheries, or blasphemies, or thefts, or drunkenness, and all such things, of which we are permitted to judge. What we must not do is presume to judge the secrets of the heart, of which God alone is Judge. His summary principle is: Let us judge, therefore, with respect to those which are manifest; but respecting those which are concealed, let us leave the judgment to God.

## 2. Two forms of rash judgment

Augustine identifies two things, moreover, in which we ought to beware of rash judgment; when it is uncertain with what intention any thing is done; or when it is uncertain what sort of a person he is going to be, who at preset is manifestly either good or bad. He gives an example of each:

- **Judging motives:** If, therefore, any one, for example, complaining of his stomach, would not fast, and you, not believing this, were to attribute it to the vice of gluttony, you would judge rashly.
- **Judging someone's future:** Even when sin is obvious, reproving as if the man could never be amended and changed, you would nevertheless judge rashly.

In short, rash judgment means either assuming the worst about hidden motives or giving up hope that a sinner can change.

## 3. How "the measure you use" comes back to you

Augustine asks whether rash judgment on our part means God will judge us rashly in return. He answers: By no means does God either judge rashly, or recompense to any one with an unjust measure; but it is so expressed, inasmuch as that very same rashness wherewith you punish another must necessarily punish yourself.

His point is that sin damages the sinner more than its target. Injustice often does no harm to him who suffers the injury, but it must necessarily do harm to him who inflicts it. He uses the martyrs as an example: persecution did them no harm, but very much to the persecutors themselves. He interprets "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword" the same way, as meaning that the soul dies by that very sin, whatever it may be, which it has committed.

## 4. The mote and the beam: anger versus hatred

Augustine says the warning is aimed especially at those who love rather to censure and to condemn than to amend and to improve, which is a fault arising either from pride or from envy. He interprets the image psychologically. There is as much difference between anger and hatred as between a mote and a beam. For hatred is inveterate anger, which, as it were simply by its long duration, has acquired so great strength as to be justly called a beam.

What makes hatred so serious is that it rules out the goal of correction: though you are angry with a man, you wish him to be turned from his error; but if you hate a man, you cannot wish to convert him. So the instruction is: First cast the hatred away from you, and then, but not before, shall you be able to amend him whom you love.

## 5. "Thou hypocrite" and how to correct others

Augustine explains that to make complaint against vices is the duty of good and benevolent men; and when bad men do it, they are acting a part which does not belong to them, much like actors wearing masks. He warns against people who, while they take up complaints against all kinds of faults from hatred and spite, also wish to appear counsellors.

He offers a practical self-examination before rebuking anyone:
- If we have never had the fault, we should reflect that we are men, and might have had it.
- If we once had it, we should remember our shared weakness, that not hatred but pity may go before that fault-finding or administering of rebuke.
- If we still have the same fault, let us not censure nor rebuke; but yet let us mourn deeply over the case, and let us invite him not to obey us, but to join us in a common effort.

## 6. A related point: love versus pretense (somewhat beyond Matthew 7)

The final part of the excerpts turns to Paul's statement "I am made all things to all men." This does not comment directly on Matthew 7, but it extends Augustine's discussion of hypocrisy. He insists Paul did not certainly so act in the way of pretence, as some wish it to be understood, in order that their detestable pretence may be fortified by the authority of so great an example; but he did so from love. True love requires that each one reckon the infirmity of another as his own, so as to bear it with equanimity, until the party for whose welfare he is solicitous is freed from it.

## Key Takeaway

For Augustine, "Judge not" does not forbid moral discernment. It forbids presumption: claiming to know hidden motives, despairing of someone's repentance, and correcting others out of hatred instead of love. Rash judgment harms the judge most. Legitimate correction must come from humility, an awareness of our shared weakness, and a genuine desire for the other person's restoration.

## Key Takeaway

For Augustine, "Judge not" does not forbid moral discernment. It forbids presumption: claiming to know hidden motives, despairing of someone's repentance, and correcting others out of hatred instead of love. Rash judgment harms the judge most. Legitimate correction must come from humility, an awareness of our shared weakness, and a genuine desire for the other person's restoration.

For in reference to such matters as can be done with a good and single and noble intention, although they may also be done with an intention the reverse of good, those parties wished, howbeit they were [mere] men, to pronounce judgment upon the secrets of the heart, of which God alone is Judge.

Let us judge, therefore, with respect to those which are manifest; but respecting those which are concealed, let us leave the judgment to God: for they also cannot be hid, whether they be good or evil, when the time shall come for them to be manifested.

There are two things, moreover, in which we ought to beware of rash judgment; when it is uncertain with what intention any thing is done; or when it is uncertain what sort of a person he is going to be, who at preset is manifestly either good or bad.
If, therefore, any one, for example, complaining of his stomach, would not fast, and you, not believing this, were to attribute it to the vice of gluttony, you would judge rashly.

Likewise, if you were to come to know the gluttony and drunkenness as being manifest, and were so to administer reproof as if the man could never be amended and changed, you would nevertheless judge rashly.

By no means does God either judge rashly, or recompense to any one with an unjust measure; but it is so expressed, inasmuch as that very same rashness wherewith you punish another must necessarily punish yourself.

Unless, perchance, it is to be imagined that injustice does harm in some way to him against whom it goes forth, but in no way to him from whom it goes forth; but nay, it often does no harm to him who suffers the injury, but it must necessarily do harm to him who inflicts it.
None; but very much to the persecutors themselves.
For what else is meant by the statement, For all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword, but that the soul dies by that very sin, whatever it may be, which it has committed?

And inasmuch as the Lord is admonishing us in this passage with respect to rash and unjust judgment,— for He wishes that whatever we do, we should do it with a heart that is single and directed toward God alone; and inasmuch as, with respect to many things, it is uncertain with what intention they are done, regarding which it is rash to judge; inasmuch, moreover, as those parties especially judge rashly respecting things that are uncertain, and readily find fault, who love rather to censure and to condemn than to amend and to improve, which is a fault arising either from pride or from envy; therefore He has subjoined the statement: And why do you behold the mote that is in your brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in your own eye?
So that if perchance, for example, he has transgressed in anger, you should find fault in hatred; there being, as it were, as much difference between anger and hatred as between a mote and a beam.
For hatred is inveterate anger, which, as it were simply by its long duration, has acquired so great strength as to be justly called a beam.

First cast the hatred away from you, and then, but not before, shall you be able to amend him whom you love.

For to make complaint against vices is the duty of good and benevolent men; and when bad men do it, they are acting a part which does not belong to them; just like hypocrites, who conceal under a mask what they are, and show themselves off in a mask what they are not.

And there is, in fact, a class of pretenders much to be guarded against, and troublesome, who, while they take up complaints against all kinds of faults from hatred and spite, also wish to appear counsellors.

And therefore we must piously and cautiously watch, so that when necessity shall compel us to find fault with or rebuke any one, we may reflect first whether the fault is such as we have never had, or one from which we have now become free; and if we have never had it, let us reflect that we are men, and might have had it; but if we have had it, and are now free from it, let the common infirmity touch the memory, that not hatred but pity may go before that fault-finding or administering of rebuke: so that whether it shall serve for the conversion of him on whose account we do it, or for his perversion (for the issue is uncertain), we at least from the singleness of our eye may be free from care.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 22: Summary of Key Insights

All of the excerpts focus on the **parable of the wedding feast** at the beginning of Matthew 22. The excerpts do not address the rest of the chapter. Two commentators are represented: John Chrysostom (three excerpts) and Jerome (one brief excerpt).

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. The parable continues the parable of the vineyard
Chrysostom reads this parable alongside the preceding parable of the wicked tenants. He notes both the great affinity between both parables, and the great difference also. Like the earlier parable, it indicates God's long-suffering, and His great providential care, and the Jews' ingratitude.

He argues that this parable goes further than the first: it proclaims beforehand both the casting out of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles; and it indicates together with this also the strictness of the life required, and how great the punishment appointed for the careless. Having said the kingdom would be given to another nation, Christ now declares next to what kind of nation.

### 2. God keeps inviting, even after rejection
A central theme for Chrysostom is God's persistence. In the earlier parable, Christ appears before His crucifixion bidding them; but here even after He is slain, He still urges them, striving to win them over. Strikingly, when they deserved to have suffered the most grievous punishment, then He both presses them to the marriage, and honors them with the highest honor. The order of the invitation matters too. God calls not the Gentiles first, but the Jews, and only when they were not willing to be present at the marriage, then He called others.

### 3. Who issued the invitation
Chrysostom identifies the many messengers. The invitation came by all the prophets; by John again; for unto Christ he would pass all on, saying, He must increase, I must decrease; John 3:30 by the Son Himself again. It also continued after the ascension, not by words only, but also by actions did He bid them, after His ascension by Peter, and those with him. The repeated invitations show that the call came not suddenly but long before, which circumstance makes the charge against them heavier.

### 4. Why a *wedding*? The joy of the kingdom
Chrysostom asks why the kingdom is pictured as a marriage. His answer is that you might learn God's tender care, His yearning towards us, the cheerfulness of the state of things, that there is nothing sorrowful there, nor sad, but all things are full of spiritual joy. He connects this to other Scripture, noting that John calls Him a bridegroom and that Paul speaks of the mystery of Christ and the Church.

The invitation itself is generous. God calls people not to labors, and toils, and sweat? Nay but unto pleasure. The slaughtered oxen and fatlings show how complete His banquet, how great His munificence.

### 5. Theological depth: the Trinity and the resurrection
- **The Father and the Son:** Chrysostom asks why the bride is espoused to the Son rather than to the Father. He answers that she that is espoused to the Son, is espoused to the Father. For it is indifferent in Scripture that the one or the other should be said, because of the identity of the substance.
- **The resurrection:** The parable also proclaims the resurrection. Having spoken of the death, Christ shows that even after the death, then is the marriage, then the bridegroom.

### 6. A threefold accusation and a practical lesson
Chrysostom sees a building case against those who refused. The first that they killed the prophets; then the son; afterwards that even when they had slain Him, and were bidden unto the marriage of Him that was slain, by the very one that was slain, they come not, but feign excuses.

He draws a lesson for every reader. He admits that the excuses seem to be reasonable; but hence we learn, though the things which hinder us be necessary, to set the things spiritual at a higher price than all.

---

## Jerome

Jerome's excerpt is short. It focuses on identifying the "servant" sent in verse 3. He offers two readings, depending on the manuscript tradition:

- **Singular "servant":** There is no doubt that it refers to Moses, through whom the Law was given to the invited guests.
- **Plural "servants":** But if we read it in reference to the servants, as most copies have it, it should be understood as referring to the prophets, who were ignored by those invited through them.

Jerome's contribution shows close attention to the wording of the text. He recognizes that differences between manuscripts can shape how a passage is interpreted.

---

## Points of Agreement

Both commentators read the parable as a story of God's repeated invitations through His messengers, and both include the prophets among those messengers. Chrysostom develops this into a broad picture of God's patience, the joy of the kingdom, and the seriousness of refusing the invitation. Jerome concentrates on the textual and historical identity of the messengers.

# Patristic Commentary on John 7: Summary of Key Insights

All three commentators address the same question: **why did Jesus avoid Judea if He had divine power?** Each answers it differently and draws out further themes.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

**1. Christ's withdrawal was an example for believers, not a sign of weakness.**
Augustine begins with Christ's two natures: Christ became man in such manner that He ceased not to be God. So when Jesus hid Himself, He must not be thought to have lost His power, but only to have offered an example to our infirmity. Persecuted believers would sometimes need to hide, and lest the concealment should be objected to him as a crime, that occurred first in the head, which should afterwards be confirmed in the member. As proof of Christ's power, Augustine points to the arrest in the garden, where at His word going backwards, they fell to the ground.

**2. Christ is united with His people as Head and Body.**
A theme throughout the commentary is that Christ is not simply in the head and not in the body, but Christ whole is in the head and body. This is why Christ could say "Saul, why do you persecute me?", because Saul was not persecuting Himself on earth, but His members, namely, His believers.

**3. "His brethren."**
Augustine reads this as kinship in a broader sense: The blood relations of the Virgin Mary used to be called the Lord's brethren. He cites Abraham and Lot as a precedent, since they are called brothers, while Abraham was Lot's uncle.

**4. The brothers' unbelief and "My time is not yet come."**
Why did the brothers not believe? Because they sought human glory. In a memorable phrase, The flesh spoke to the flesh; but the flesh without God, to the flesh with God. Augustine takes Jesus' reply to mean the time of my glory is not yet come. The deeper point is that He would have loftiness preceded by humility, and willed to prepare the way to elevation itself through humility. He sums it up: the fatherland is on high, the way there lies low.

**5. The present is a time of patience; judgment comes later.**
For at present it is not the time of judging, but of tolerating the wicked. Augustine defines the "upright in heart" as those to be upright in heart who bear the evils of the world, and do not accuse God. He contrasts this with the crooked heart: When you get any good, you praise yourself; when you suffer any evil, you accuse God.

**6. The Feast of Tabernacles is a picture of the Christian life.**
Augustine treats the feast as a "shadow" fulfilled in Christ. Believers have been delivered from bondage, led out by baptism as through the Red Sea, and now, before we come to the land of promise, namely, the eternal kingdom, we are in the wilderness in tabernacles. This explains why Jesus went up "in secret": Christ was hid in that same festal-day; for that very festal-day signified Christ's members that were to sojourn in a foreign land.

**7. Divided opinion about Jesus, and about His followers.**
The crowd's split ("He is a good man" versus "he deceives the people") applies to believers too: whoever becomes eminent in some spiritual grace, of him some will assuredly say, He is a good man; others, Nay; but he deceives the people. Augustine uses the image of a fruit tree in winter that looks dead, adding that the summer proves, the judgment proves. He ends hopefully: the Church has spread so widely that "he deceives the people" is now only whispered.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

**1. The move to Galilee was a rebuke to Israel.**
Cyril sees Jesus' stay in Galilee as a judgment: in these words no less is Israel found fault with for its extreme perverseness, if indeed the being found among the Gentiles was shown to be far better than living with it. He links this to Jeremiah's words, I have forsaken Mine House, I have left Mine heritage; I gave My loved Soul into the hand of her enemies. The act carried a warning: if they did not desist from persecuting Him, and from destroying with their mad folly their Benefactor, Christ would wholly give Himself to those without, and remove unto the Gentiles. A separate excerpt from Cyril's commentary makes the same point in nearly the same words.

**2. An Old Testament foreshadowing.**
Cyril connects this to the Levitical sacrifice slain on the north side of the altar. Since Galilee lies to the north (Galilee of the Gentiles), and since Christ was about, after His saving Passion, to depart out of the country of the Jews, and go into Galilee, that is, to the church of the Gentiles, the sacrificial lamb faced northward as a sign of this.

**3. Withdrawal was not cowardice.**
Like Augustine, Cyril denies any weakness: we do not consider the withdrawal of Christ as an imputation of cowardice, nor yet will we therefore accuse of weakness Him That is mighty unto all things, but we will accept the mode of the economy. The reason was timing: it beseemed Him not before His time, but in His own time to endure the Cross for all.

*Note:* Cyril's chapter heading says the Feast of Tabernacles signifies the restitution of the hope due to the Saints, and the resurrection from the dead, but the excerpt ends before he develops this idea, so his full interpretation of the feast cannot be summarized from this material.

---

## John Chrysostom

**1. Envy as the root of the plot.**
Chrysostom traces the hostility to envy: Nothing is worse than envy and malice; through these death entered into the world. The same root led to Abel's murder, and from this also the Jews became Christ-slayers.

**2. "He had not power": the two natures.**
Chrysostom's text says Jesus had not power to walk in Jewry. He resolves the apparent difficulty by pointing to the two natures: as man He fled, as God He appeared, and in both cases the Evangelist speaks truly. This balance protects against error: Christ's yielding strengthened and authenticated the Dispensation, that neither Paul of Samosata, nor Marcion, nor those affected with their maladies, might have anything to say.

**3. The Evangelists' honesty.**
Chrysostom notes that John skips about five months between Passover and Tabernacles, because it was impossible to recount everything fully, and moreover, because they were anxious to mention those points which were followed by any fault-finding or gainsaying of the Jews. The report that Jesus' own brothers did not believe in Him shows the writers' integrity: they are not ashamed to relate things which seem to bring disgrace upon their Teacher.

---

## Common Threads

- **Power and humility:** All three insist that Jesus' withdrawal from Judea was not weakness. Augustine treats it as an example for persecuted believers, Cyril as part of God's plan and timing, and Chrysostom as evidence of Christ's true humanity alongside His divinity.
- **Divine timing:** Augustine and Cyril both stress that Christ acted according to His appointed "time," whether the time of glory (Augustine) or the time of the Cross (Cyril).
- **Distinctive emphases:** Augustine applies the chapter to the Church's life as pilgrims; Cyril reads it as foreshadowing the gospel's movement to the Gentiles; Chrysostom focuses on doctrinal precision and the honesty of the Gospel writers.

# Commentary on John 17: Augustine of Hippo

**A note on the sources:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, Augustine of Hippo. Documents 2–4 are shorter, differently worded translations of the same passages in Document 1 (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 104), so this summary treats them as one body of teaching. The excerpts cover only the opening of the chapter, centering on John 17:1 ("Father, the hour has come; glorify Your Son").

---

## 1. The Bridge into the Prayer: Peace as the Goal

Augustine's first section looks at the words just *before* John 17, the end of the Farewell Discourse. It helps explain how the prayer begins.

- **Peace is the purpose of Christ's teaching and of the Christian life.** Jesus gave this as the cause of His discourse, that in Him they might have peace, just as it is wholly on this account that we are Christians. This peace will have no temporal end, but will itself be the end of every pious intention and action that are ours at present.
- **Everything in the Christian life serves this peace:** for its sake we are endowed with His sacraments, for its sake we are instructed by His works and sayings, for its sake we have received the earnest of the Spirit.
- **The move from teaching to prayer:** Having told the disciples that in Him they might have peace while having distress in the world, and had exhorted them to be of good cheer, because He had overcome the world; having thus finished His discourse to them, He then directed His words to the Father, and began to pray.

## 2. Why Jesus Prayed Out Loud

Augustine asks why the Son, who is one with the Father, prayed audibly at all.

- Christ could have prayed in silence if need be. But by praying out loud he wanted to show himself as one who prayed to the Father; he remembered that he not only had to pray but to teach.
- **The prayer is itself a lesson:** the prayer that he offered for us, he also made known to us. For it was not only his discourse but also his prayers that were a source of edification for his disciples—and for us who read it today.

*Takeaway:* For Augustine, John 17 is meant to be overheard. Later readers receive it as instruction, just as the first disciples did.

## 3. "The Hour Has Come": Divine Appointment, Not Fate

Augustine strongly rejects any idea that Christ's death was forced on him by fate or the stars.

- The words "the hour has come" show that all time, and every occasion when he did anything or suffered anything to be done, was arranged by him who was subject to no time.
- It was no necessary law of the heavenly bodies that tied the passion of Christ to its timetable. How could anyone think that the stars compelled their own maker to die?
- His key line: It was not the time, therefore, that drove Christ to his death, but Christ who selected the time to die.
- **The Son and the Father chose the hour together.** Augustine paraphrases Jesus' words as: "Father, the hour," which we fixed together for the sake of humanity and of my glorification among them, "is come; glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you."
- He supports this with Scripture, citing Paul: But when the fullness of the time had come, God sent forth His Son; Galatians 4:4

## 4. What "Glorify Your Son" Means: Humility, Then Glory

- **Resurrection more than the cross.** Augustine notes that some take the Son's glorification to be the Father giving him up for us. He answers: if he was glorified by his passion, how much more was he glorified by his resurrection? For his passion showed his humility more than his glory. He concludes, This is the glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ, that took its commencement from His resurrection.
- **The pattern of Philippians 2.** Augustine reads John 17 through Paul's hymn. Christ's humility begins where Paul says He emptied Himself, and took upon Him the form of a servant; and reaches even to the death of the cross. His glory begins with Wherefore God also has exalted Him.
- **The central principle:** Humility is the earning of glory. Glory is the reward of humility. In his words, had He not died, He would not have risen from the dead.
- **Seed and harvest.** Augustine's memorable reading of the prayer: the hour is come for sowing the seed—humility. Do not defer the fruit—glory.

## 5. Christ's Eternal Glory

Augustine makes clear that this glorification concerns Christ's human nature, not any lack in his divinity. This, however, was done in the form of a servant; but He was always in the form of God, and always shall His glory continue. In his divine nature, without beginning and without end, His glory is everlasting.

He also adds a short word study. The Greek *doxa* ("glory") underlies the command "glorify," and the Latin translator renders by clarifica (make illustrious), although he might as well have said glorifica (glorify), which is the same in meaning.

## 6. A Question Left Open

Augustine raises a puzzle he does not answer in these excerpts: how can the Son glorify the Father, whose eternal glory could neither appear diminished through human form, nor be enlarged in the divine? He sets it aside for later: I will not confine such a question within the present discourse, or draw the latter out to greater length by such a discussion. His answer is not included in the material provided.

---

## Summary of Key Insights

| Theme | Augustine's Insight |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Christ's teaching aims at eternal peace in him, the goal of the Christian life |
| **Prayer** | Jesus prayed aloud to teach; the prayer still instructs readers today |
| **The Hour** | Christ chose the time of his death with the Father; it was not fate or the stars |
| **Glorification** | Glorification comes mainly through the resurrection, after the humility of the cross |
| **Core principle** | Humility earns glory; glory rewards humility (seed and fruit) |
| **Christology** | Glorification concerns Christ's human nature; his divine glory is eternal |

**Limitations:** Since only Augustine is represented and the excerpts cover mainly John 17:1, this summary cannot speak to other commentators or to later themes in the chapter, such as Jesus' prayer for his disciples or for the unity of believers.

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Timothy 3: Summary

The relevant excerpts focus on the opening of the chapter, Paul's statement about desiring the office of bishop. Augustine engages it directly in three passages. The Chrysostom excerpt mostly addresses other material.

## Augustine of Hippo

### 1. The episcopate is work, not dignity (*City of God* 19.19)
Augustine places Paul's statement within a broader reflection on the Christian life. He describes three ways of life, the contemplative, the active, the contemplative-active, and holds that a man can live the life of faith in any of these three and get to heaven. What matters is that he love truth and do what charity demands.

For those in active leadership, he warns that one should not love worldly position or power, for all is vanity under the sun, but only what can be properly and usefully accomplished by means of such position and power, namely the salvation of those in one's care. He reads Paul's words this way: Paul wanted to make clear that the office of bishop, episcopatus, implies work rather than dignity.

**Insight:** Church leadership is a call to service directed toward others' salvation, not a platform for status.

### 2. Seeking the name versus the reality (*Sermon* 340A.6)
Augustine imagines someone exclaiming, "I want to be a bishop; oh, if only I were a bishop!" and asks, Are you seeking the name or the real thing? If it's the real thing you're seeking, you are setting your heart on a good work. If it's the name you're seeking, you can have it even with a bad work but with a worse punishment.

He then makes a bold claim: there are no bad bishops; because if they are bad, they aren't bishops. To anyone who objects that a man is a bishop simply because he occupies the bishop's throne, he replies with a vivid image: And a straw scarecrow is guarding the vineyard.

**Insight:** A true bishop is defined by faithfully doing the work, not by holding the title or the seat. An unfaithful officeholder only looks like a guardian.

### 3. The good work and the unwilling candidate (*Letters* 173.1.2)
Writing to someone who believes no one should be forced to do good, Augustine points to this verse as a counterexample. Although Paul calls the episcopate a good work, how many are forced against their will to undertake the episcopacy. Some are dragged in, locked up and kept under guard, suffering all this unwillingly until there arises in them a will to undertake this good work.

**Insight:** Augustine reflects the practice of his era, in which reluctant men were sometimes pressed into office. In his view, the willing desire Paul describes can grow after the call rather than precede it. This complements the first two passages: the right attitude toward the office is not eager ambition but willingness to take on its labor.

## John Chrysostom (*Homily 9 on First Timothy*)

This excerpt connects to 1 Timothy 3 in only one sentence. Chrysostom explains that the "true saying" Paul affirms relates to the present subject, not to what follows, respecting the office of a Bishop. In other words, he attaches the affirmation to the preceding discussion about parents being benefited by the virtue of their children, rather than to the bishop passage that follows. This is a point of interpretation about where the chapter's opening statement belongs.

The rest of the excerpt is a moral exhortation on raising children, citing 1 Timothy 5:10 rather than chapter 3. Its main points:
- Parenting carries eternal weight: if the basis, the foundation which they lay be good, great will be their reward; as great, if they neglect it, will be their punishment. He cites Eli, who from his unwillingness to give them pain he destroyed both himself and them.
- Character matters more than inheritance: Form the soul of your son aright, and all the rest will be added hereafter.
- Good formation spreads outward, benefiting the husband who is destined to marry them, and not the husband only, but the children, not the children only, but the grandchildren.

Chrysostom does not link this teaching to the qualifications for church leaders in 1 Timothy 3, so it is best treated as background rather than commentary on that chapter.

## Summary
Augustine offers the most direct and substantial reflections on 1 Timothy 3. Across three works, he consistently holds that the episcopate is a good *work*, not an honor to be grasped. Its legitimacy rests on faithful service rather than title, and even those who come to it reluctantly may grow into a genuine desire for it. Chrysostom's excerpt contributes only a brief interpretive note on how the chapter's opening "true saying" should be read.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 4: The Temptation in the Wilderness

All four excerpts address the opening of Luke 4: Jesus' time in the desert, his forty-day fast, and the devil's first temptation. Three come from the Venerable Bede and one, much shorter, from Gregory of Nazianzus.

---

## Bede, *On the Gospel of Luke*

### 1. Jesus Went Into the Desert by His Own Will (Luke 4:1)

Bede says Luke's wording was deliberate. Lest anyone should doubt by which spirit he was led or driven into the desert, Luke prudently wrote first that Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and then added, and was led by the Spirit into the desert. His conclusion is that Jesus is not driven into the desert by the power of any evil spirit, but by the will of His own good Spirit, He enters the place of combat, certain of victory, to defeat the adversary.

He also reads the passage as a pattern for believers. It shows the order of virtuous living, so that after receiving in baptism the remission of sins and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may gird ourselves more tightly against new snares of the ancient enemy, withdraw our mind from the world.

### 2. The Meaning of the Forty-Day Fast (Luke 4:2)

**Continuity with Scripture:** For Bede, the fast connects Jesus to Moses and Elijah, demonstrating that the Gospel does not dissent from the law and the prophets. He explains that the law is perceived in the person of Moses, and the prophets in the person of Elijah.

**The symbolism of forty:** Bede gives a numerical reading. There are ten commandments of the law, now diffused by the grace of Christ throughout the world, and the world is fourfold, and ten times four makes forty.

**Two sets of forty days:** Bede pairs the fast before Christ's death with the forty days after his resurrection. The Lord fasted while he was tempted before death, still needing food. However, he ate and drank after the resurrection, already not needing food. In this reading, here he was showing our labor in himself, but there his consolation in us.

**Application to the Christian life:** Fasting and feasting represent two sides of discipleship that believers live out together. Bede ties this to Paul's words "Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation (Romans 12)". He concludes that we fast from the vanity of the present age, and are refreshed by the promise of the future, not setting our hearts here, but feeding our hearts above. He also uses this framework to explain why Lent falls just before Easter. It signifies this laborious life, which requires continence, to fast from the friendship of this world.

### 3. Why Jesus Was Hungry

Bede notes that Scripture records nothing of the sort about Moses or Elijah. He interprets Christ's hunger as a strategic concealment, so that the devil would not be scared off from the contest. In his words, the humble God-man was hungry, so that he might not reveal to the enemy the sublime man-God.

### 4. The Devil's Uncertainty and Christ's Unshaken Mind (Luke 4:3)

Bede says the devil had already recognized Jesus as his conqueror. However, when he first saw Him as vulnerable, observed Him able to endure mortal things due to His humanity, everything he suspected about His divinity came into doubt out of the pride of his arrogance.

He also draws a sharp distinction between Christ's temptation and ours. Unlike humans, often shaken by attacking temptation, Christ graciously endured all these things outwardly, such that His mind inwardly, remaining attached to His divinity, remained unshaken. Even Christ's human emotions remained under his divine control: He Himself divinely arranged how much He would be troubled humanly.

---

## Gregory of Nazianzus

Gregory's excerpt is brief and comments on the fast in Luke 4:2. He affirms the full reality of the fast: He fasted in truth forty days, eating nothing. (For He was God.)

His main insight is pastoral. Christ's total fast was possible because of his divinity, so believers should not try to copy it literally. But we regulate our fasting according to our strength, although the zeal of some persuades them to fast beyond what they are able.

The final line, "For the body nourishes not our immaterial nature", stands without surrounding context. Its exact connection to the argument is not clear from this excerpt alone.

---

## Summary of Key Themes
