**A note on scope:** All of these excerpts focus on one verse, 1 Corinthians 11:1 ("Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ"). None of them addresses the rest of the chapter, such as head coverings or the Lord's Supper. Chrysostom reads the verse as the conclusion of Paul's preceding argument about food sacrificed to idols.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 25 on First Corinthians)

Chrysostom's homily is by far the most substantial excerpt. (Document 3 is a shorter rendering of the same passage.)

### 1. Imitating Christ means caring for one's neighbor
Chrysostom calls Paul's command a rule of the most perfect Christianity, this is a landmark exactly laid down, this is the point that stands highest of all; viz. the seeking those things which are for the common profit. His central claim is that nothing can so make a man an imitator of Christ as caring for his neighbors.

### 2. Spiritual discipline without love falls short
Chrysostom warns that personal piety alone is not enough: though you should fast, though you should lie upon the ground, and even strangle yourself, but take no thought for your neighbor; you have wrought nothing great, but still standest far from this Image. He points to the parable of the talents, arguing that no virtuous action can be very exalted, when it does not distribute its benefit to others also.

### 3. Paul's example of self-giving
Chrysostom notes that Paul gave up his rights for others' benefit. Paul even accepted practices such as circumcision and sacrifice, saying I submitted even to these on account of the advantage therefrom. Chrysostom sums up Paul's example in a memorable phrase: being above all in perfection, he became beneath all in condescension.

### 4. Old Testament examples
Chrysostom traces this principle through Scripture:
- **Positive examples:** Moses, David, Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph. Of the early saints he writes that none of them ever looked to his own things, but each one to the things of his neighbor, whence also they shone the brighter.
- **Cautionary examples:** Lot, who chose the better land for himself, sought his own profit, did not even find his own. Jonah not seeking the profit of many, but his own, was in danger even of perishing.

### 5. Paul surpasses them all
Chrysostom gives three reasons Paul's self-giving exceeds even these saints:
- **He suffered so others could flourish.** Rather than simply sharing others' hardships, he chose himself to be at all extremities that other men might enjoy blessings.
- **He risked eternal loss, not only earthly danger.** Paul prayed [Romans 9:3] that he might fall from the glory of the world to come for the sake of others' salvation.
- **He did this for people outside his own charge.** Paul wished to be accursed in the stead of those with whose guardianship he was not entrusted. For to the Gentiles was he sent.

### 6. God built mutual dependence into creation
Chrysostom argues that God, willing to bind us all to each other, has imposed upon things such a necessity, that in the profit of one neighbor that of the other is bound up. He illustrates this with neighbors who ignore a house fire and lose their own homes, a helmsman in a storm, and ordinary trades such as farming and commerce. God suffers them not to arrive at their own profit except they first travel through the profit of others.

### 7. The right motive is love and pleasing God
Self-interest is not the ideal motive. Chrysostom says one ought to be persuaded not from this reason, but from what pleases God. Citing 1 Corinthians 13:3, he insists that even generous deeds must be done with sincerity and much sympathy. He concludes that neither voluntary poverty nor martyrdom, nor any other thing, can testify in our favor, unless we have the crowning virtue of love.

### 8. Answering an objection
Someone might ask about God telling Lot to "escape for your life." Chrysostom replies that this came when the people were already condemned and incurably diseased, and that it was not spoken of vice and virtue but of the chastisement inflicted by God. He does not call for reckless self-sacrifice apart from the will of God.

---

## Basil of Caesarea (The Long Rules 43)

Basil's excerpt does not quote or explicitly mention 1 Corinthians 11. It does share the verse's theme of imitating Christ. Basil says that the goal of Christianity is the imitation of Christ according to the measure of his incarnation, insofar as is conformable with the vocation of each individual. He applies this to leaders, saying those entrusted with the guidance of many others are obliged to animate those still weaker than themselves, by their assistance, to the imitation of Christ. Like Paul in this verse, the leader serves as a model and a help to others.

---

## Clement of Alexandria

Clement's excerpt only quotes the verse, noting that openly and expressly the apostle, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians says, "Be ye followers of me, as also I am of Christ". Because the surrounding context is not provided, his interpretation cannot be determined from this excerpt.

---

## Key Takeaway

Taken together, these commentators read Paul's call to imitate him as a call to imitate Christ's self-giving love. For Chrysostom especially, the measure of Christian maturity is not personal austerity but active, sincere care for others.

# Patristic Commentary on Ephesians 1: A Summary

The excerpts come from three early Church Fathers: Irenaeus, John Chrysostom, and Jerome. Jerome and Irenaeus comment directly on verses in Ephesians 1. Chrysostom's excerpt introduces the letter as a whole.

---

## Irenaeus: The Holy Spirit as a "Down Payment" (Eph. 1:13–14)

*Note: The excerpt begins mid-sentence and the text appears slightly garbled at the start, but its main point is clear.*

Irenaeus focuses on the Spirit as the "earnest," or pledge, of our inheritance. His key insights are:

- **Gradual growth toward God:** He describes the Spirit's work in believers as tending towards perfection, and preparing us for in corruption, being little by little accustomed to receive and bear God. The text likely means "incorruption." The idea is that the Spirit trains us step by step to be able to bear God's presence.
- **A foretaste of what is promised:** He explains that Paul calls this gift "an earnest "that is, a part of the honour which has been promised us by God. He links this directly to Paul's words that believers have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance.

**Takeaway:** The Spirit we receive now is a real share in our future glory, not just a promise of it. It also prepares us over time to receive that glory fully.

---

## John Chrysostom: Setting the Scene for the Letter

*Note: This excerpt is an introduction to Ephesians as a whole, not a comment on chapter 1. The passages Chrysostom quotes as examples come from chapters 2, 3, and 6.*

**The city's background:**
- Ephesus is the metropolis of Asia. It was dedicated to Diana, whom especially they worshipped there as their great goddess.
- It had strong apostolic ties. The blessed John the Evangelist spent the chief part of his time there, and it was there too that Paul left Timothy.
- It was also a center of learning, the resort also of the disciples of Parmenides, and Zeno, and Democritus.

**Why this matters:** Chrysostom says he mentions these facts with a view of showing that Paul would needs take great pains and trouble in writing to these Ephesians. Paul is said indeed to have entrusted them, as being persons already well-instructed, with his profoundest conceptions; and the Epistle itself is full of sublime thoughts and doctrines.

**Circumstances of writing:** Chrysostom states that Paul wrote the Epistle from Rome, and, as he himself informs us, in bonds.

**Takeaway:** Ephesians is unusually lofty. In it Paul openly states thoughts which he scarcely so much as utters any where else, because he was writing to a sophisticated audience.

---

## Jerome: Close Reading of the Opening Greeting

### On Ephesians 1:1 — "Saints" and "Faithful in Christ Jesus"

- **Two sides of the Christian life:** Jerome explains why Paul calls the readers both saints and faithful. He writes that it is because faith derives from the choice of our own minds, but sanctification we receive meanwhile from the abundance of the Sanctifier, not from our own will. Faith involves our response, while holiness is God's gift.
- **Faithfulness is not enough on its own:** Jerome notes that there are those who have genuine faith but not faith in Jesus Christ. His example is someone who returns a deposit and does not deny another's trust shows himself a faithful friend.… This person is indeed faithful but not "in Christ."

### On Ephesians 1:2 — "Grace and Peace"

- Jerome considers two readings. In the first, both grace and peace apply no less to God the Father than to our Lord Jesus Christ. In the second, grace is referred to God the Father and peace to Christ.
- He prefers the second, since the words immediately following are to the praise of the glory of God's grace.
- His conclusion: the "grace" of the Father lies in his willingness to send the Son for our salvation, while the "peace" of the Son lies in the fact that we are reconciled to the Father through him.

**Takeaway:** Jerome treats even the greeting as theology. Each word reflects the distinct roles of the Father and the Son in salvation.

---

## Common Threads

Each writer takes a different approach. Chrysostom focuses on historical context, Jerome on careful reading of individual words, and Irenaeus on spiritual growth. Still, they share a theme: salvation begins with God. For Jerome, holiness comes from the Sanctifier and grace comes from the Father who sends the Son. For Irenaeus, the Spirit is God's pledge that prepares us for the promised inheritance.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 23: Paul and the "Whitewashed Wall"

**A note on scope:** All four excerpts focus on one episode in Acts 23: Paul's response after Ananias the high priest orders him struck (roughly vv. 2–5). None addresses the rest of the chapter, such as the Pharisee–Sadducee dispute, the Lord's appearance to Paul, the plot against him, or his transfer to Caesarea. This summary is therefore limited to that single scene.

---

## Origen of Alexandria: The Ongoing Persecution of Christ's Body

Origen reads the incident as a pattern that continues into his own day. He recounts that someone, ordered by Ananias the high priest, struck Paul because he said, "God will strike you, oh whitewashed wall." He then applies it to his own opponents: even to this day, the Ebionites, under orders from their illegitimate high priest, strike the apostle of Jesus Christ with their calumnies. Such a high priest, he says, is beautiful from without and a whitewashed wall but "within full of dead bones and every filth."

From there Origen moves beyond Acts 23 to Christ's own sufferings. He contrasts two kinds of readers. The simple know of these things as happening at one particular time, when Pilate scourged him, but Origen says, I, however, see Jesus daily giving his back to scourgings. In his view, Christ is still mistreated whenever the Word of God is insulted, reviled, hated by unbelievers.

**Key insight:** Paul's mistreatment becomes a model for how Christ and his messengers are attacked in every age. This latter part of the excerpt, however, is a broader meditation and does not comment directly on Acts 23.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: A Prophecy, Not an Insult

Augustine addresses the apparent problem of Paul losing his temper. He acknowledges that those who do not understand him think that [Paul] uttered a reproach when he had been slapped by order of the high priest, for, with seeming insolence, he then said, "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall." He offers a different reading: those who understand him take this as a prophecy.

He explains the image this way: The "whitewashed wall" stands for hypocrisy; it is pretense, veiled beneath the priestly dignity, and under this title—as though beneath a white covering—it conceals, as it were, an inner slimy filthiness.

**Key insight:** Paul's words expose religious hypocrisy, a holy office used to cover inner corruption. They are not a personal insult.

---

## Bede: The Grammar of Prophecy and the End of the Old Priesthood

Bede agrees that Paul was prophesying and gives two supporting arguments.

1. **Theological:** [Paul] did not say this because he was stirred by passion in his mind. Rather, that high priesthood that had been compared to the likeness of a whitewashed wall was to be struck and destroyed, since the true priesthood of Christ had now come with the apostles' preaching of the gospel.
2. **Grammatical:** That is why he said, "God will strike you." He did not say, "May God strike you." Bede notes that he signified by the indicative mood that this thing was going to happen; he did not utter a curse by using the optative mood.

**Key insight:** Paul's statement announces the passing of the old priesthood, which gives way to Christ's true priesthood. The grammar shows it is a prediction, not a curse.

---

## John Chrysostom: Holy Boldness with a Practical Purpose

Chrysostom takes a more direct and realistic approach. He questions the view that Paul did not recognize the high priest: Some say that he [Paul] did not know that he was the high priest. Then why does he defend himself as if there was an accusation and adds, "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people."

He also admits the tension with Paul's own teaching. Paul says, "When we are cursed we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it." But here he does the opposite. He not only reviles but also curses him. Yet Chrysostom concludes that these are words of boldness rather than anger.

He explains Paul's reasoning in practical terms. He did not wish to appear contemptible to the tribune. Had he been struck by the servants, it would have rather emboldened the tribune. For this reason he directs his attack not at the servant but at the one who gave the order. The outcome supported Paul: See how they were thunderstruck by his boldness. The point was to undermine him completely, but they commended him instead.

**Key insight:** Paul's sharp words were a deliberate act of courage, meant to keep the Roman authorities from treating him with contempt. They were not an outburst of temper.

---

## Points of Agreement and Difference

- **Agreement:** All four commentators defend Paul's integrity, and none treats his words as sinful anger. Origen, Augustine, and Bede all read "whitewashed wall" as an image of a corrupt or hypocritical priesthood.
- **Difference:** Bede argues that Paul did *not* curse, pointing to the grammatical mood of the verb. Chrysostom openly says Paul *did* curse but that the curse came from justified boldness. Augustine and Bede stress prophecy, while Chrysostom stresses the practical situation. Origen applies the scene to the ongoing persecution of Christ and his followers.

# Patristic Insights on Genesis 37: Joseph, Jacob, and the Favored Son

## John Chrysostom (*Homilies on Genesis* 61.2–3)

Chrysostom focuses on Joseph's character and on the real reason for Jacob's preference.

**Joseph's youth and virtue.** Chrysostom asks why Scripture mentions Joseph's age. His answer is that it shows that his youth constituted no obstacle to virtue, and it highlights the young man's obedience to his father and his sympathy for his brothers despite their savagery.

**The roots of the brothers' envy.** Joseph was kindly disposed toward his brothers, yet they saw from the outset the youth's inclination to virtue and the father's favor for him and were prompted to envy him. Chrysostom finds evidence of this envy in the fact that "they brought false reports about Joseph to their father Israel."

**The "son of his old age."** Chrysostom grants that children born to one in old age seem particularly dear. However, he argues this cannot be the full explanation, because even after him another son was born. If natural affection alone were at work, that last son would have been loved more for being truly a son of his old age.

**Grace as the true cause.** Chrysostom concludes that it was a kind of grace from on high that made the young man amiable and rendered him preferable to all the others on account of the virtue of his soul. He also suggests why Scripture names old age as the reason instead: in case the real reason might increase the brothers' envy.

## Ambrose of Milan (*On Joseph* 2.5–6)

Ambrose draws practical lessons for family life while still defending Jacob.

**A warning about parental favoritism.** Ambrose says the story teaches the proper nature of parental love and filial gratitude. He warns that often even parental love does harm to the children unless it is practiced with restraint, because by preference shown to one child, [it] may alienate the others from the spirit of brotherly love. He adds a memorable maxim: That son gains more who gains the love of his brothers.

**A sobering observation.** Ambrose remarks: What wonder if quarrels arise among brothers over an estate or a house, when enmity blazed up among the sons of holy Jacob over a tunic?

**Jacob defended as a prophet.** Ambrose does not simply condemn Jacob. He holds that we cannot take from parents their freedom to love the more those children whom they believe to be the more deserving. In his view, Jacob loved the more that son in whom he foresaw the greater marks of virtue; thus he would not appear to have shown preference so much as father to son but rather as prophet to a sacred sign.

**The tunic as a symbol.** Ambrose reads the famous garment symbolically. Jacob made it to indicate by it that Joseph was to be preferred to his brothers with his clothing of manifold virtues.

## Cyril of Alexandria (*Glaphyra on Genesis* 6.4)

**A note on this excerpt:** Cyril's passage does not mention Joseph, Jacob, or the events of Genesis 37 by name. It appears to take up the phrase "son of his old age" and apply it to Christ. Without the surrounding text, his full reasoning cannot be confirmed.

**Christ as the "Son of old age."** Cyril states that the Immanuel was born to the Father as a Son of his old age, because he appeared in the latter times of the world, that is, in these times, and after him there will be no other. In this reading, "old age" refers to the final era of history rather than literal age.

**Christ's sufficiency for salvation.** Because Christ is this final Son, Cyril affirms that He alone is sufficient, because we say that the salvation and life of the world is placed in no one else.

**Christ's eternal divinity.** Cyril takes care that his reading of "latter times" does not imply Christ began to exist late. Christ appeared in the latter times of the world... after he had assumed the flesh and who preexisted as God. Cyril affirms that he is coeternal with the Father.

## Common Threads

- **Jacob's love was not mere sentiment.** Chrysostom attributes Joseph's favored status to divine grace and the virtue of his soul. Ambrose sees Jacob acting as a prophet who perceived Joseph's virtue.
- **Envy is a central moral theme.** Chrysostom and Ambrose both trace how favor toward Joseph provoked his brothers' hostility.

# Patristic Insights on Acts 4: A Summary

These excerpts come from three early Church writers. Each highlights a different part of the chapter: the content of the apostles' preaching, the hostility it provoked, and the symbolic meaning of the growing number of believers.

---

## Irenaeus: The Continuity of God's Promise

Irenaeus focuses on **what** Peter and John preached and stresses that it was consistent with Israel's faith:

- **Fulfillment, not novelty:** Peter, together with John, preached to them this plain message of glad tidings, that the promise which God made to the fathers had been fulfilled by Jesus.
- **The same God, revealed in the Son:** The apostles were not certainly proclaiming another god, but the Son of God, who also was made man, and suffered.
- **Purpose of the preaching:** They were thus leading Israel into knowledge, and through Jesus preaching the resurrection of the dead.

**Key insight:** The work's title, *Against Heresies*, suggests Irenaeus is countering teachers who separated the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus. He presents the apostolic message as the completion of God's promises to the patriarchs, not a break from them.

---

## John Chrysostom: The Power of the Resurrection and the Hardening of Sin

Chrysostom has two separate insights.

### 1. Why the authorities were disturbed
He explains that the opposition was about more than the apostles' authority to teach. They were annoyed, not only because the apostles were teaching, but because they declared that not only was Jesus Christ himself risen from the dead but that through him we too rise again.

**Key insight:** Christ's resurrection makes the resurrection of believers possible. In Chrysostom's words, so powerful was his resurrection that he is the cause of resurrection for others as well.

### 2. The growing boldness of the persecutors
Chrysostom contrasts the arrest of Jesus with the arrest of the apostles: in the case of Christ they sought out a traitor, but now arrest the apostles with their own hands, having grown more audacious and more impudent since the crucifixion.

**Key insight:** He draws a moral lesson about how sin develops: sin, while it is yet struggling to the birth, is attended with some sense of shame, but once fully formed, it makes those who practice it more shameless. The authorities' open hostility shows how unrepented wrongdoing grows bolder over time.

---

## Bede: The Five Thousand as a Spiritual Sign

Bede comments on Acts 4:4 and reads the number of believers symbolically, linking it to the feeding of the five thousand in the Gospels.

- **Two groups of five thousand:** Bede suggests that if we take the five thousand men fed by the Lord in the wilderness as [standing for] the people established under the law, but created anew by Christ's favor, they and this five thousand, who were instructed by the teaching of the apostles, can designate the people of the nations who would spiritually follow the mysteries of the same law.
- **The significance of evening:** He also sees meaning in the timing: it was well done that both [groups of five thousand] were granted their heavenly favor in the evening, for when "the fullness of time came God sent his Son."

**Key insight:** Bede uses allegory, a traditional method of reading Scripture for deeper spiritual meaning. For him, the miracle in the wilderness and the apostolic preaching together point to God's people, renewed by Christ, and extended to the nations. Both happened "in the evening," matching God's timing in sending His Son.

---

## Common Threads

- **Continuity with God's plan:** Irenaeus and Bede both stress that the apostolic message fulfills, rather than replaces, what God established with Israel.
- **The centrality of resurrection:** Irenaeus and Chrysostom both identify the resurrection of the dead, through Jesus, as the core of the apostles' preaching. Chrysostom adds that this was the very teaching that provoked opposition.
- **Different approaches:** Irenaeus is doctrinal, Chrysostom is pastoral and moral, and Bede is allegorical. Together they show the range of early Christian ways of reading Acts 4.

# Patristic Insights on Genesis 30: A Summary

These excerpts come from two early Church Fathers, **Ephrem the Syrian** and **John Chrysostom**. All of them address Genesis 30, focusing on Rachel's barrenness, Jacob's response, the birth of sons through Bilhah, and the mandrakes episode.

---

## Ephrem the Syrian

### 1. Rachel's plea grew out of a family pattern of prayer
Ephrem explains Rachel's desperation by connecting it to the earlier patriarchs. He notes that Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah and then ceased giving birth, whereas Rachel was barren. Rachel heard Jacob say that Abraham had prayed over the barren Sarah and was heard and that Isaac had also prayed for Rebekah and was answered. As a result, she thought that it was because Jacob had not prayed for her that her closed womb had not been opened. Ephrem therefore reads her outburst, "Give me children, or I shall die!", as a cry spoken in anger and in tears. It was rooted in her belief that intercessory prayer had been withheld from her.

**Insight:** Ephrem treats Rachel's frustration as theologically informed. She knew that God had answered the prayers of the patriarchs for their barren wives, and she longed for the same intercession.

### 2. Why Jacob took Bilhah
Ephrem offers two reasons for Jacob's union with Rachel's maidservant:
- **A practical reason:** lest she nag him, asking him every day for children, Jacob, who was sent from his parents to take a daughter of Laban, agreed to take the foreign woman.
- **A reason concerning inheritance:** it was also so that the sons of the maidservants might become joint heirs with sons of the freewomen that Jacob took maidservants and freewomen.

The result: he took Bilhah, and she conceived and bore Dan and Naphtali.

**Insight:** Ephrem sees a larger purpose behind this domestic arrangement. The sons of the servant women were meant to share fully in the inheritance alongside the sons of the free wives.

### 3. Leah and the mandrakes
Ephrem reports a view about the plant without fully endorsing it: Some say that the mandrake is a plant whose fruit resembles apples, which have a scent and are edible. More significantly, he describes Leah's motives positively: by means of these mandrakes, with cheerfulness seasoned with faith, Leah made Jacob take her that night.

**Insight:** Ephrem does not read Leah's bargain as mere rivalry or manipulation. He describes it as an act marked by cheerfulness and faith.

---

## John Chrysostom

### God alone is the Lord of the womb
Chrysostom expands on Jacob's reply to Rachel and presents it as a lesson in divine sovereignty. In his paraphrase, Jacob asks: Why, Jacob says, do you ignore the Lord of nature and fix the blame on me? He continues: Why not make your request to him, who can open nature's workplace and quicken the womb to childbirth? Chrysostom stresses that God is the one who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb and granted your sister such fertility.

He also brings out Jacob's tenderness toward Rachel: if it lay in my power, I would certainly give you pride of place ahead of your sister by securing greater respect for you. Because Jacob is powerless, Rachel should address your request to him who inflicted the sterility and has the power to remedy it.

### Jacob as a model of wise response
Chrysostom praises Jacob's conduct: See the good man's common sense in that, though provoked to anger by her words, he replied to her with great wisdom, instructing her precisely in everything and making the responsibility clear to her, lest by ignoring the Lord she might seek from another what God alone was able to provide.

**Insight:** For Chrysostom, the episode teaches that people must look to God, not to other humans, for what only God can give. Jacob's restraint while provoked is a model of wise, instructive speech.

---

## Comparing the Two Perspectives

- **On Rachel:** Ephrem's account is sympathetic. Her anger stems from knowing that God had answered earlier patriarchal prayers. Chrysostom's account is more corrective. Rachel needed to be redirected from Jacob to God.
- **On Jacob:** Ephrem focuses on Jacob's practical and inheritance-related reasons for taking Bilhah. Chrysostom presents Jacob as a teacher who points Rachel back to the Lord.
- **A shared theme:** Both see God as the true source of fertility. Ephrem implies this through the patriarchs' answered prayers, and Chrysostom states it outright.

*Note:* These excerpts are brief and cover only certain episodes in Genesis 30. This summary does not represent either commentator's full treatment of the chapter.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 1: Summary

All of the provided excerpts deal with the **opening greeting** of the letter (2 Corinthians 1:1). None of them address the rest of the chapter, such as Paul's discussion of comfort in suffering or his travel plans, so this summary covers only the salutation.

---

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom offers the most theologically developed reflections, in two excerpts.

**1. Why Timothy is named as co-sender**
Chrysostom notices an apparent puzzle: in his first epistle, Paul said that he would send Timothy with the letter, but now he associates Timothy with him. His explanation is that Timothy had already accomplished his mission and returned to be with Paul. He also places the letter's composition geographically: having been for some time in Asia, they had crossed into Macedonia, from which he wrote this letter.

**2. Humility and love in leadership**
The key theological insight is that naming Timothy was an act of humility and affirmation. By associating Timothy with himself, Paul increased respect for him and displayed his own great humility, since Timothy was far less well known than Paul. Chrysostom sums up the point in a short phrase: love brings all things together. For Chrysostom, even the wording of a greeting shows how Christian love closes gaps in status between ministers.

**3. "Church" and "saints" as words with meaning**
Chrysostom sees Paul's terms for the recipients as deliberate. Paul calls the Corinthians a church, in order to bind them together, and "saints," implying that if anyone is impure he is not included in this greeting. The word "church" calls a divided congregation to unity. The word "saints" carries a quiet moral challenge: holiness is the expected identity of those being addressed.

---

## Didymus the Blind

Didymus focuses on Paul's habits in his greetings and on a question of interpretation.

**1. Why Paul sometimes names companions**
He observes that Paul does not always mention other people besides himself in his salutations. His proposed reason is that Paul does so when one of his associates is well-known to the intended recipients.

**2. The meaning of "with all the saints"**
Didymus admits honestly that "with all the saints" is ambiguous. He offers two readings: either it means all the saints who were with Paul, or else it means all the saints who were at Corinth. He leaves the question open rather than forcing a single answer.

---

## Theodoret of Cyrus

Theodoret's contribution is mainly historical. He explains who is and is not named in the greeting: Timothy and Titus were both sent to Corinth, but Paul did not mention Titus in the letter because he was the one who actually carried it there. His comment is less theological than Chrysostom's, but it reflects the same interest in why Paul names the people he names.

---

## Points of Comparison

- **A shared question:** All three commentators ask why Paul includes or leaves out particular companions in his greeting.
- **Different explanations:** Didymus suggests companions are named when they are already well known to the readers. Chrysostom stresses the opposite case, arguing that Paul named Timothy precisely because Timothy was *less* well known, in order to raise his standing. Theodoret gives a practical reason for Titus's absence: Titus was delivering the letter.
- **Theological depth:** Chrysostom draws out the most spiritual lessons, namely humility, love, unity, and holiness. Didymus and Theodoret concentrate on interpretation and historical circumstances.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 16: Jesus and the Demand for a Sign

All four excerpts address the episode at the start of Matthew 16, where religious leaders ask Jesus for a sign from heaven. Documents 1 and 2 are two translations of the same passage from John Chrysostom's Homily 53, so they are treated together below.

---

## John Chrysostom: The Motive Behind the Question

**1. Christ responds with compassion, not anger.**
Chrysostom notes that their inquiry was rightly deserving of anger and great displeasure. Yet the benevolent and provident one is not angry. He pities them even as they tempt him. He draws on Mark's parallel account, where Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit, to show that Christ laments them as incurably diseased after so full a demonstration of his power.

**2. The problem was their intent, not the request itself.**
Chrysostom's central point is that they did not seek him out in order to believe but to lay hold of him. He insists that had they come with any readiness to believe, he would have given such a sign. As evidence of Christ's willingness to give to sincere seekers, he points back to the Canaanite woman of the previous chapter: he who said to the woman, "It is not fair," and afterwards gave, much more would he have shown his bounty to these officials.

**3. Why Jesus calls them "hypocrites."**
Since they did not seek to believe, he therefore calls them hypocrites, because in another place they said one thing and meant another. Chrysostom adds that if they had believed, they would not even have asked.

**4. Their response proves their unbelief.**
Their lack of faith became clear afterward: when reproved and exposed, they did not remain with him, nor did they admit "We are ignorant and seek to learn."

**5. What kind of sign did they want?**
Chrysostom suggests they wanted a cosmic spectacle: either that he should stay the sun, or curb the moon, or bring down thunderbolts, or work a change in the air, or some other such thing.

---

## Theodore of Mopsuestia: Miracles Have Their Own Order

Theodore focuses on Jesus' comparison between reading the weather and reading the signs of the times. He paraphrases Jesus as exposing the rashness of their question: they could read the sky's patterns to tell when the weather will be fair and when stormy. But in the case of miracles you recognize no order at all.

The theological point is that divine wonders are not random or performed on demand. The leaders failed to recognize any occasions on which doing or not doing wonders is appropriate. You assume that such a thing happens completely without order and without any reason. God's miracles, like nature, follow purpose and timing.

---

## Jerome: Missing the Fulfillment of Prophecy

**A textual note.** Jerome opens by observing, "This is not found in many codices." The excerpt does not say exactly which words he means, though the context suggests the weather saying. He considers the meaning clear regardless: the meaning is clear from the order and harmony of the elements.

**The theological point.** Jerome stresses the irony: both fair and rainy days can be forecast. But the scribes and Pharisees, who were viewed as doctors of the law, could not discern the coming of the Savior from what the prophets had predicted. The experts in Scripture failed to recognize the very Messiah their Scriptures foretold.

---

## Common Threads

| Commentator | Main Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Chrysostom** | The leaders' insincere motive. Christ responds with pity, and would gladly give to those ready to believe. |
| **Theodore** | Miracles follow a divine order and purpose; they are not spectacles on demand. |
| **Jerome** | The religious experts failed to read the prophetic "signs" pointing to Christ. |

Together, these Fathers suggest that the leaders' problem was not a lack of evidence but a lack of willingness. Chrysostom locates it in their hearts, Theodore in their misunderstanding of how God works, and Jerome in their blindness to prophecy.

**Note on scope:** These excerpts cover only the opening episode of Matthew 16. They do not address the rest of the chapter, such as Peter's confession or Jesus' teaching on taking up the cross, so no summary of those passages can be drawn from them.

# Summary of Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Genesis 2

**A note on scope:** The excerpts only address **Genesis 2:1–3**, the completion of creation and God's seventh-day rest. They do not cover the rest of the chapter (the garden of Eden, the forming of Adam, or the creation of Eve), so this summary does not either. The first excerpt attributed to Aquinas simply quotes the opening verse: "In recapitulating the Divine works, Scripture says (Genesis 2:1): 'So the heavens and the earth were finished and all the furniture of them'". It offers no commentary of its own.

---

## Thomas Aquinas

**1. The two meanings of "rest."** Aquinas defines the key term: rest is taken in two senses, in one sense meaning a cessation from work, in the other, the satisfying of desire. He argues that in either sense God is said to have rested on the seventh day.
- God stopped creating, since He made nothing afterwards that had not existed previously, in some degree, in the first works.
- God's desire was fulfilled, because He Himself had no need of the things that He had made, but was happy in the fruition of Himself.

**2. Resting "from" His works, not "in" them.** Aquinas draws a careful distinction from the wording of the text. God is not said to have rested "in" His works, as though needing them for His own happiness, but to have rested "from" them, as in fact resting in Himself, as He suffices for Himself and fulfils His own desire.

**3. Eternal rest and the seventh-day rest.** He addresses an apparent puzzle: even though from all eternity He rested in Himself, yet the rest in Himself, which He took after He had finished His works, is that rest which belongs to the seventh day. He credits this reading to Augustine.

**4. Was creation finished on the sixth or seventh day?** Aquinas notes a difference between translations. In his version the completion of the works is attributed to the seventh day, though according to another (Septuagint) it is assigned to the sixth. He reconciles them: the completion of the universe as to the completeness of its parts belongs to the sixth day, but its completion as regards their operation, to the seventh.

**5. Does God still work?** He raises the objection from John 5:17, "My Father worketh until now, and I work." His answer is that God indeed "worketh until now" by preserving and providing for the creatures He has made, but not by the making of new ones.

---

## Bede

**1. Divine rest is not weariness.** Bede rules out a human picture of tiredness. God did not rest like a weary man from excessive labor through human frailty after completing the world's creation; but He is said to have rested from all His work, because He ceased to create any new creature thereafter. He points out that Scripture often uses the term "rest" to indicate the cessation of work or speech, citing the living creatures in Revelation 4:8. From this he draws a lovely conclusion: the greatest and only rest for the saints in heaven is to declare the praise of the highest Trinity.

**2. Creation exists so that creatures may rest in God.** Like Aquinas, Bede says God did not need His works. Bede adds that God made His works solely for the sake of His goodness, so that they might rest in Him. He contrasts this with human life, where labor is driven by need, recalling Genesis 3:19: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. God, by contrast, rests perfectly in Himself while offering rest to rational creatures.

**3. Blessing the seventh day is itself a divine work.** Bede offers another way to understand how God "completed His work on the seventh day": God completed His work on the seventh day, which He had made, even in that He blessed and sanctified that day itself. For blessing and sanctification are not no work. He compares this to Solomon dedicating the temple.

He then links it to Christ's parable of the faithful servants in Luke 12:37, where the master serves them at table. This shows that the Lord blesses and sanctifies His saints forever, that is, He rewards them with the vision of His glory after their good works which He gave.

**4. The "eighth day."** Bede gives the seventh day a forward-looking meaning:
- **The final judgment:** the day of judgment and consummation of the world, because it is to come after the seventh Sabbath, is called the eighth in the Scriptures. He supports this from the title of Psalm 6.
- **The Resurrection:** the day of the Lord's Resurrection is also called the eighth, because naturally it follows the seventh, so that it exists as the first of the following week, that is, the same one in which God said in the beginning: Let there be light and there was light.

---

## Common Ground

Both commentators agree on several points:
- God's "rest" means He stopped creating new kinds of things, not that He grew tired or stopped acting entirely.
- God rested *from* His works, not *in* them, because He is complete in Himself.
- God's ongoing activity continues after the seventh day. Aquinas describes it as preservation and providence. Bede describes it as blessing and sanctifying His saints.

Their emphases differ:
- **Aquinas** is more analytical. He defines terms, reconciles translations, and answers objections.
- **Bede** is more pastoral and forward-looking. He reads the Sabbath as pointing to the saints' eternal rest, the Resurrection, and the final judgment.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Peter 1: Summary of Key Insights

## Bede (Commentary on the Catholic Epistles)

Bede comments most extensively on the opening verses of 2 Peter 1, focusing on the greeting (vv. 1–2) and on God's gifts and calling (v. 3).

### 1. The Audience and the Equality of Faith (v. 1)
Bede identifies the letter's recipients by connecting it to Peter's first epistle. He notes the later reference to a "second Epistle" and concludes that he wrote this to the same elect proselytes dispersed in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, to whom he had sent the first Epistle.

He also explains why Peter treats them as spiritual equals. Peter considers them equals to himself, not because they had received circumcision according to the Law, which, being a Jew by nature, he himself held, but because they had received the same faith he had obtained through the illuminating grace of Christ. His central principle is that it is not legal circumcision, but only evangelical faith that unites the peoples of the nations with the ancient people of God.

### 2. Faith Joined with Righteousness
Bede reads the phrase "in the righteousness of our God and Savior" as a necessary complement to faith: since the same faith cannot save without works, it is rightly added: In the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. He specifies that this righteousness is not human or legal in origin. It is the righteousness which human prudence has not discovered, nor legal institution teaches, but the Lord and our Savior speaking through the Gospel has shown, and he points to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5) as an example.

### 3. Grace and Peace "Fulfilled" (v. 2)
Bede contrasts the greeting of the two letters. In his text of the first epistle, grace and peace are "multiplied," while here they are fulfilled to you, because, of course, he wrote the former letter to those beginning, and this one to those more perfect. He gives this distinction an eschatological meaning: peace and grace are multiplied to those advancing well in this life through faith, but will be fulfilled for those arriving in the other life through vision.

He ties this fulfillment to the "knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ" and supports it with John 17: this is eternal life (he says), that they know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

*Note:* In a later section, Bede paraphrases the greeting using "multiplied" (Grace and peace be multiplied to you as you come to know our Lord Jesus Christ perfectly). This suggests he was working with variant wordings of the text.

### 4. Divine Power Gives Everything Needed (v. 3)
Bede connects verse 3 grammatically to the greeting. He explains that believers should know that all things of His divine power have been given to us through His grace, which are sufficient for attaining life and preserving piety.

He also discusses a manuscript variant. Under that reading, the sense is that the Lord has given all things of His divine power to us according to the measure of our capacity. He explains the verse's compressed grammar as ellipsis, that is, the omission of a necessary word, which he describes as common in Scripture.

### 5. Called by Christ's Own Glory, Not Our Merit
On "Him who called us by His own glory and virtue," Bede stresses that salvation is entirely God's initiative. Christ did not send an angel to our salvation, nor an archangel, nor did He find in us any merit for which we were to be saved, but rather seeing us as weak and inglorious, He redeemed us by His own power and glory. He supports this with John 15: You did not choose Me, but I chose you.

---

## John Chrysostom (Catena)

**A note on relevance:** This excerpt does not mention 2 Peter or quote any of its verses. Its placement among the chapter's commentary suggests it relates to the word "peace" in the greeting of verse 1:2, but that link is inferred rather than stated.

Chrysostom offers a reflection on the supreme value of peace. He observes that everywhere we pray for peace in the churches—in the prayers, in the supplications and in the sermons. His central claim is that peace is the mother of all good things and the foundation of our joy. He notes that Christ taught his disciples that when they entered people's houses they were to say: "Peace be unto you." He concludes simply: Without peace everything else is useless.

---

## Summary of Themes

- **Bede** treats the opening of 2 Peter as a theology of grace:
  - Faith, not the Law, unites Jew and Gentile.
  - True faith is expressed in Gospel righteousness.
  - God supplies everything needed for life and godliness.
  - Salvation springs wholly from Christ's own glory and power, not human merit.
  - His contrast between grace "multiplied" in this life by faith and "fulfilled" in the next by vision is perhaps his most distinctive insight.
- **Chrysostom**, assuming his remarks bear on the greeting, highlights peace as the foundation of every other spiritual good.

# Commentaries on Romans 5: Key Theological Insights

All four excerpts focus on the **opening verses of Romans 5** (roughly vv. 1–5): peace with God, access to grace, hope, tribulation, and God's love poured into our hearts. None of them discusses the later Adam–Christ section (vv. 12–21) in detail. Aquinas only mentions it as part of his outline.

---

## Origen of Alexandria: Peace as Victory in Spiritual Warfare

**Peace means a change of allegiance.** Origen describes conversion as switching sides in a war: we who once were enemies of God, following the devil, that great enemy and tyrant, now, if we have thrown down his weapons and in their place taken up the sign of Christ and the standard of his cross, have peace with God. This peace is made possible by Christ, who has reconciled us to God through the offering of his blood.

**Peace is both inner and communal.** For Origen, peace with God includes harmony within the person, so that the flesh will no longer war with the spirit, and harmony with others: let there be no dissension either among ourselves or between us and others outside our ranks. In contrast, anyone in whom the vice of wickedness is found can never have peace.

**His most striking insight: fighting the devil is evidence of peace with God.** Origen asks how a righteous person can have peace while under attack, and answers that such a man has greater peace than anyone else, because war against the devil is a guarantee of peace with God. He supports this with James: "Resist the devil and he will flee from you; draw near to God and he will draw near to you."

---

## John Chrysostom: Peace as a Call to Holy Living

**"Let us have peace" is a moral exhortation.** Chrysostom notes that some read the phrase as a warning against insisting on the Law. He prefers a different reading. Paul has just stressed faith over works, so to prevent any one from supposing what he said was a ground for listlessness, he says, "let us have peace," that is, let us sin no more, nor go back to our former estate. Returning to sin is making war with God.

**Keeping peace is easier than gaining it.** To the objection that sinlessness is impossible, Chrysostom argues from the greater to the lesser: if when liable for so many sins we were freed from all by Christ, much more shall we be able through Him to abide in the estate wherein we are. He explains that to acquire surely is harder than to keep.

**Faithfulness is a fitting response to grace.** He also stresses that this is reasonable, not just possible: if He reconciled us when we were in open war with Him, it is reasonable that we should abide in a state of reconciliation, so that Christ may not seem to have reconciled untoward and unfeeling creatures to the Father.

---

## Theodoret of Cyrus: Preserving the Gift Received

Theodoret's brief excerpt reaches a conclusion similar to Chrysostom's. He links faith with baptism: Faith has given you forgiveness of sins and made you spotless and righteous by the washing of regeneration. The practical result is that you ought to keep the peace by which you have been united with God. He grounds this reconciliation in the Incarnation: when you were still enemies, the only begotten Son of God reconciled you by taking on human flesh and putting sin to death in it.

---

## Thomas Aquinas: A Structured Theology of Grace, Hope, and Love

*(Aquinas is a medieval rather than patristic writer, but his excerpt fits well alongside the others.)*

**Context and structure.** Aquinas places Romans 5 within Paul's larger argument. Having shown humanity's need for grace, the Apostle now begins to extol the power of grace. Paul shows what goods we obtain through grace; secondly, from what evils we are freed by it, the latter beginning at verse 12.

**Peace through submission and mediation.** Aquinas interprets having peace with God as submitting ourselves and obeying him. Christ is the one through whom we have access as through a mediator.

**Grace comes before faith.** Aquinas clarifies that we obtain grace through faith, not because faith precedes grace, since it is rather through grace that there is faith, because the first effect of grace in us is faith.

**The greatness of hope.** The hope Christians glory in is that we hope to obtain the glory of sons of God. This glory which will be completed in us in the future, is in the meantime begun in us through hope.

**Why believers glory in suffering.** Aquinas compares this to medicine: anyone who vehemently hopes for something endures difficult and bitter things for it, as a sick person who strongly desires health gladly drinks a bitter medicine to be healed by it. He then traces Paul's chain of tribulation, patience, trial, and hope:
- Tribulation does not directly produce patience. Instead, suffering is the material and occasion for exercising the act of patience.
- Patient endurance proves one's priorities: it is sufficient proof that such a person loves eternal blessings more than temporal.
- He resolves the apparent conflict with James 1:3 by distinguishing two senses of "trial." Here it means the fact of having been tested.
- Thus it is clear that suffering paves the way to hope.

**Why hope does not disappoint.** Hope does not confound, i.e., does not fail, unless the man fails it. Aquinas reads "the love of God" in two ways: God's love for us and our love for God. He teaches that Both these loves of God are poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Indeed, The fact that we love him is a sign that he loves us. Either reading confirms the certainty of hope, since God does not deny himself to those whom he loves.

---

## Common Threads

- **Reconciliation of former enemies:** Origen, Chrysostom, and Theodoret all stress that believers were once God's enemies and have been reconciled through Christ.
- **Peace as a responsibility:** The early commentators especially read "let us have peace" as a call to *keep* the peace received. Origen frames this as resisting the devil and discord, while Chrysostom and Theodoret frame it as not returning to sin.
- **Distinctive emphases:** Origen offers the paradox that spiritual warfare is a sign of peace with God. Aquinas provides the most systematic treatment of grace, hope, suffering, and the Holy Spirit's gift of love.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Acts 5: Summary of Key Insights

The excerpts focus on the episode of Ananias (and his wife) in Acts 5. Below are the main insights from each commentator, from most to least developed.

## John Chrysostom: The Sin as Sacrilege

Chrysostom gives the fullest theological reading. He argues that **the core offense was sacrilege**, not simply dishonesty about money.

- **The money had become sacred.** This money was sacred. He reasons that the person who withdraws his possessions after he has chosen to sell them and distribute them would be guilty of sacrilege. He summarizes the charge: that having made the money sacred, he then took it.
- **The offering was voluntary.** Chrysostom stresses that the sin lay in breaking a freely made commitment. Paraphrasing Peter, he writes: We neither forced you to sell, says the apostle, nor to give the money after you have sold. You chose to do so of your own free will. Ananias was not forbidden to keep the proceeds, so the question becomes Why then after you had promised?
- **The judgment was severe.** He draws an argument from lesser to greater: If for gathering sticks one could be stoned to death, much more, it may be argued, ought he be stoned for committing sacrilege. He calls sacrilege a most grievous crime, insolent and full of contempt.
- **Spiritual warning.** He notes how the devil made his attack from the very beginning, how in the midst of such signs and wonders this man became insensible as a rock. He also warns his own hearers: do not think that because the consequence now is not the same, the crime will go unpunished.

## Thomas Aquinas: How Satan "Fills the Heart"

Aquinas comments on Peter's question, why has Satan tempted your heart. He uses it to explore a theological problem: can the devil put anything into our hearts?

- **The "heart" defined.** what is in a person's thought and will is said to be in his heart.
- **Only God moves the will directly.** Something can be placed in the heart directly only by one who has the power to move our will from within, and Only God can do this.
- **The devil works by suggestion.** Since the will is drawn by what appears good, others can influence it indirectly. Aquinas distinguishes an external suggestion, and then one person can put something into another's heart; or by an interior suggestion, which is the way the devil puts something into our heart. The devil does this through the imagination, which is subject to the power of the devil when God allows it.
- **Conclusion:** the devil puts something into our heart, not directly by moving our heart, but indirectly, by suggestion. This keeps God sovereign and leaves human beings responsible, since temptation persuades but does not compel.

## Clement of Alexandria: Peter's Word of Judgment

Clement mentions Acts 5 only in passing, as a comparison within a discussion of Moses. He notes that the mystics say that he slew the Egyptian by a word only; as, certainly, Peter in the Acts is related to have slain by speech those who appropriated part of the price of the field, and lied. His point is that the judgment came through Peter's spoken word alone. He does not develop this further theologically.

## Jerome: The Meaning of the Name

Jerome's excerpt offers only an etymology: The name Ananais means "grace of the Lord." The excerpt does not explain the significance he drew from it. One might see an irony between the name and the man's fate, but that would go beyond what the text says.

## Summary

| Commentator | Key Insight |
|---|---|
| **Chrysostom** | Ananias's sin was sacrilege: taking back what he had freely dedicated to God |
| **Aquinas** | Satan tempts by suggestion, not by direct control of the will |
| **Clement** | Peter's judgment came by word alone (a brief comparison with Moses) |
| **Jerome** | The name Ananias means "grace of the Lord" (etymology only) |

Chrysostom and Aquinas provide the substantive theological reflection. Chrysostom focuses on the moral seriousness of breaking a sacred vow, and Aquinas on the psychology of temptation. The Clement and Jerome excerpts are brief and offer limited interpretation of the chapter.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 14: Bede and Jerome

**Scope:** These excerpts cover only the opening verses of Genesis 14 (vv. 1–5): the war of the kings, the gathering in the valley, and the defeat of the giant peoples. They do not address the rest of the chapter. Bede reads the passage mainly for its spiritual and moral meaning. Jerome focuses on Hebrew language, place names, and translation.

---

## Bede — *Commentary on Genesis*

### 1. The story's purpose is theological, not just historical
Bede insists that it is not to be supposed that the sacred author of Scripture recorded these only for the sake of historical study but rather to commend to us the grace of heaven. Abraham's victory shows what the power of faith is, with which he himself was armed, and how great the grace of divine blessing was, with which he was endowed. He sees Abraham as a model for later believers, who through this faith, overcome kingdoms, perform righteousness, and obtain promises.

### 2. Sodom's capture was a warning and a chance to repent
Bede reads the defeat of Sodom as divine discipline. Seeing their wickedness, God first chastised them with hostile slaughter and captivity. Then, through Abraham, God rescued them for the sake of the blessed Lot, who served God faithfully among them, so that they might learn, leaving their errors, to serve God. Because they neither wished to be corrected by divine chastisements nor by gifts to abandon their iniquity, their final destruction followed.

### 3. The pattern applies to all history and to the end of the world
Bede sees the same pattern operating universally: those who care neither for heavenly benefits nor chastisements are subsequently condemned by heavenly vengeance. He extends it to the end of the age, when people ungrateful for heavenly gifts and insensitive to chastisements, will suddenly be swept to eternal destruction by the whirlwind of the last judgment.

### 4. The enemy's strength magnifies Abraham's faith
Bede explains why the text describes the invaders' campaign in detail: so that the greater the power of the adversaries is shown, the mightier the faith of Abraham appears, by which he easily broke all their strength. The names of the defeated peoples serve the same point. Rephaim in Hebrew, in Greek are called Giants, and Zuzim are called "The Terrible Ones," Emim are called "The Horrifying Ones."

### 5. Geography as a lasting sign of judgment
Bede identifies the wooded valley as the region of Pentapolis, that is, the province of Sodom and neighboring cities. Now, however, after being overflowed following the fire with waters from the Jordan, it is called the Salt Sea or the Dead Sea. The landscape itself thus bears witness to the judgment he describes.

---

## Jerome — *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*

### 1. Place names carry the memory of judgment
Jerome notes that Bale in the Hebrew language is called κατάποσις, which means swallowing. He reports a Hebrew tradition that the city was swallowed up by the third movement of the earth. After the destruction of the other cities by fire, it is called that little one, that is, Segor, which in Syriac became a small place called Zoara.

### 2. The Dead Sea as the result of God's wrath
Like Bede, Jerome links the valley to later judgment. It was a place in which there were previously pits of bitumen, after the wrath of God and the rain of sulfur, was turned into the Dead Sea.

### 3. Translating meaning, not just words
Jerome observes that because the Zuzim and the Emim are interpreted as terrifying and horrifying, the Seventy [translators], conveying the sense rather than word for word, translated them as the strongest nations.

### 4. Correcting a textual reading
Jerome explains that the Greek translators misread one Hebrew letter. They thought it was written with He (), guided by the similarity of the elements, while it is written with Heth. With He the word means 'in them'; but if it has Heth, as in the present case, it signifies a place, that is, 'in Hom ()'. So the text names a location ("in Hom") rather than saying "with them."

---

## Comparison

- **Agreement:** Both connect the battle valley with the later Dead Sea and with God's judgment on Sodom. Both interpret the names Zuzim and Emim as signs of a fearsome people.
- **Different emphases:** Bede draws out faith, grace, repentance, and the final judgment. Jerome offers little explicit theology in these excerpts. His contribution is to clarify the Hebrew text, the place names, and the reliability of the Greek translation, which supports careful reading of Scripture.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on 2 Thessalonians 1

The excerpts vary in how directly they address Chapter 1. Thomas Aquinas comments verse by verse on the opening greeting (1:1–2). John Chrysostom's homily gives the letter's background and then moves to themes from Chapters 2–3 and a long moral exhortation. Ambrose cites 1:1 only in passing, within a separate argument about the Trinity.

---

## 1. Thomas Aquinas: The Greeting (1:1–2)

**Paul's humility and his companions.** Aquinas notes that Paul, in writing to these good people, does not mention his title, but supplies only his humble name which is Paul. He also names his co-workers: Silvanus, who is Silas, and Timothy, whom he circumcised, as is mentioned in Acts 16.

**A Trinitarian greeting.** Paul addresses the church, which is the assembly of believers. Aquinas reads the phrase "in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" as meaning in the faith of the Trinity and of the divinity and humanity of Christ, because our beatitude will consist in knowing them. The Holy Spirit is not named, but Aquinas argues the Spirit is implied: Paul mentions only the person of the Father and the incarnate Son, in which two is understood the Holy Spirit who is the bond between the Father and the Son.

**Grace and peace as beginning and end.** Aquinas sees the two blessings as framing the whole Christian life. Grace is the source of all good things, and he supports this with 1 Corinthians 15:10. Peace is our end: for there is peace when desire is totally at rest.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: Why the Letter Was Written, and a Warning Against Pride

*Note: this excerpt reads as an introductory homily. It explains why the letter was written and draws on Chapters 2–3, rather than commenting closely on the text of Chapter 1.*

**Why a second letter.** Chrysostom suggests Paul had been unable to visit and to complete their instruction, so he adds a second Epistle, filling up by his writings what was wanting of his presence.

**The threat to Christian hope.** Chrysostom's central insight is that hope in Christ's return sustained the persecuted believers. For since that hope supported them, and did not allow them to yield to the present evils, the devil wishing to cut it off, as being a kind of anchor, the devil used deceivers to persuade them that the promised events had already been fulfilled. These false teachers said that the Judgment and the coming of Christ were at hand. Their aim was to suggest there is hereafter no retribution, nor judgment-seat, nor punishment and vengeance for those who had done them evil. Some went further and even to forge Epistles as written by him.

**Comfort for the suffering.** This connects most directly to Chapter 1's themes. Chrysostom says Paul comforts them, as being excessively pinched by their troubles; both praising them from their present state, and encouraging them from a prospect of the futurity, and from the punishment, and from the recompense of good things prepared for them.

**Pride and its cure.** Most of the excerpt turns to moral exhortation. Starting from the Antichrist's self-exaltation (2:4), Chrysostom argues that as the devil fell by pride, so he who is wrought upon by him is anointed unto pride. He calls pride the root of all sin: every sin begins from it, and is maintained by it. The remedy is knowing God: he who knows God as he ought to know Him, he who knows that the Son of God humbled Himself so much, is not lifted up. He ends by pointing to Christ's example: He washed the feet of His disciples, affording us an example of humility.

---

## 3. Ambrose of Milan: 1:1 as a Proof-Text

*Note: this is not a commentary on the chapter. It comes from Ambrose's treatise* On the Holy Spirit*, where he quotes 2 Thessalonians 1:1 as supporting evidence.*

Ambrose is answering opponents who argued that because the same kind of language is used of the Spirit as of the Son, the Son's honor is reduced. Ambrose's response is that I am contending against the argument that because the same is written of the Spirit, therefore the Son's honor is lessened because of the Spirit. To show that the phrase "in God" applies to the Father as well, he lists several passages, ending with "Paul and Silvanus and Timothy to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."

---

## Summary

- **Aquinas** reads the brief greeting as rich in theology: it shows Paul's humility, contains an implied Trinitarian faith, and presents grace and peace as the beginning and goal of the Christian life.
- **Chrysostom** explains the letter's pastoral purpose: protecting persecuted believers' hope in Christ's coming against deception. He then turns that discussion into a warning against pride.
- **Ambrose** uses only the opening verse, as evidence in a debate about the equal honor of the divine Persons.

None of the excerpts comments in detail on the chapter's later verses, such as the thanksgiving for the Thessalonians' faith or the description of righteous judgment. Chrysostom's general remarks about comfort and future reward come closest to those themes.

# Patristic Insights on 1 John 3

## Augustine of Hippo

Augustine's commentary is the most extensive of the excerpts and covers roughly verses 1–3.

**1. Being, not just being called, children of God**
Augustine stresses that the title must match reality: "For whoso are called sons, and are not sons, what profits them the name where the thing is not?" He gives everyday examples: "How many are called physicians, who know not how to heal!" In the same way, many are called Christians, and yet in deeds are not found such; because they are not this which they are called, that is, in life, in manners, in faith, in hope, in charity.

**2. Why the world does not know believers**
For Augustine, "the world" here refers to people, not creation. When you hear the word world, in a bad signification, you know that you must understand it to mean only lovers of the world because through love they inhabit, and by inhabiting have become entitled to the name. The world shows that it does not know believers when they deride them that live good lives. He traces this back to Christ, who was not recognized because He reproved all sins in men. He uses a medical image: through loving that which the fever prompted, they did wrong to the Physician.

**3. "Now" and "not yet"**
Augustine notes that our sonship is real now but still awaits its fulfillment: Already we are begotten of Him; but because we are such in hope, he says, Beloved, now are we sons of God.

**4. Seeing God "as He is"**
Augustine reflects on the word "Is." That which is called Is, and not only is called but is so, is unchangeable: It ever remains, It cannot be changed, It is in no part corruptible. He then draws a distinction about who will see what. To see Christ in this sort, Christ in the form of God, Word of God, Only-Begotten of the Father, equal with the Father, is to the bad impossible. The ungodly will see Christ at the judgment, but they will see but the form of a servant, the form of God they will not see. The vision promised to believers surpasses all created beauty, because from it are all things beautiful.

**5. The Christian life as holy desire**
This is perhaps Augustine's best-known insight in this passage: The whole life of a good Christian is an holy desire. He compares it to stretching a bag so it can hold more: so God, by deferring our hope, stretches our desire; by the desiring, stretches the mind; by stretching, makes it more capacious. This desire requires first being emptied of worldly love: Suppose that God would fill you with honey: if you are full of vinegar, where will you put the honey?

**6. Purifying oneself: grace and free will**
On verse 3, Augustine notes that John's wording has not taken away free-will, in that he says, purifies himself. He balances this carefully with grace: God does not purify you if you be unwilling. Thou purifiest yourself, not by yourself, but by Him who comes to inhabit you. Our part is real, yet it consists in asking for help: If you say, Be my helper, you do somewhat: for if you be doing nothing, how should He be said to help you?

## Bede

**1. The greatness of adoption**
Bede marvels that God lets us love Him as children rather than servants. That alone would be great, if we could love Him as faithful servants love masters. Drawing on John's Gospel together with this epistle, he concludes that it is certain that through faith and love we become children of God.

**2. A doctrinal defense against heresy**
Bede reads verse 1 as refuting two errors:
- **Pelagius**: The heresy of Pelagius (who dared to say that men can be saved without the grace of God) is condemned in that it is said that love or the power is given to us by God, by which we receive the adoption of sons.
- **Arius**: In this epistle the Father gives the love that makes us children, while in the Gospel the Son gives the power to become children. Bede concludes that it is certain that they are of one substance and the same power, who equally and indifferently bestow heavenly gifts upon men.

**3. The world's eventual recognition**
Like Augustine, Bede reads "the world" as the lovers of the world. He adds a look ahead to the judgment: those who scorned the saints will lament, These are they whom we once had in derision, and in a likeness of a reproach. He cites Wisdom 5 as his source for this.

## Clement of Alexandria

Clement's two fragments are very brief and address only the phrase about the world not knowing believers (verse 1). In the Cassiodorus translation, He means by the world those who live a worldly life in pleasures. The *Adumbrations* says the same thing even more briefly: The "world" means those who live in pleasure. No further theological development appears in the excerpts provided.

## Common Thread

All three commentators agree that "the world" in 1 John 3:1 refers to people who love the world and its pleasures, not to creation itself. Augustine offers the richest pastoral and spiritual reflection, especially on longing for God and on how grace and free will work together. Bede emphasizes adoption as a gift of grace and uses the passage to defend orthodox doctrine.

# Patristic Commentary on Revelation 21: Key Insights

These excerpts come from two commentators, **Augustine of Hippo** and **Bede**. Most focus on the opening of the chapter: the new heaven and new earth, and the statement that "the sea is no more."

---

## Augustine of Hippo

### *City of God* 20.16: The Sequence and Nature of Renewal

**1. Judgment comes before renewal.** Augustine reads Revelation 21 as the positive counterpart to the preceding vision of judgment. Having concluded his prophecy of the judgment awaiting bad people, John has to speak of what is to befall the good. He sets out an order of events: first, to be sure, will come the judgment of those uninscribed in the Book of Life and their consignment to eternal fire.… Afterwards, this world as we see it will pass away, burned away by terrestrial fires, just as the flood was caused by the overflowing of terrestrial waters.

**2. The world is transformed, not destroyed.** For Augustine, the fire purifies rather than annihilates. It will utterly burn away the corruptible characteristics proper to corruptible bodies, so that the world, remade into something better, will become fit for people now remade, even in their bodies, into something better. The renewed creation and resurrected humanity are made to fit each other.

**3. The puzzle of the sea.** Augustine is frank about the limits of his understanding. He admits it is hard to know whether [the sea] will be dried up by the terrible heat of those flames or will itself be transformed into something better. He notes that Scripture speaks of a new heaven and earth but not clearly of a new sea. He therefore offers a figurative reading: as prophecy is prone to intermingle the literal and metaphorical and so veil its meaning, the sea may stand for this world of ours, made restless and stormy by the lives of men (and, hence, figuratively, called the sea), which will have passed away.

### *Of True Religion* 23.44: An Indirect Connection

This excerpt is mainly about the nature of evil and the soul, not a commentary on Revelation 21. It touches the chapter only through a passing reference: There will be, as it is written, a new heaven and a new earth, and there souls will not have to do their part in toiling but will reign over the universe.

Its contribution is to describe the renewed person who will live in that new creation:
- **Restoration of soul and body.** When the soul is regenerated by the grace of God and restored to its integrity, its body too will be restored to its original strength, and it will receive power to possess the world, not to be possessed by the world.
- **Freedom from evil and change.** Then it will have no evil. For the lowly beauty of temporal changes will not involve it, for it will have been raised above change.

---

## Bede: *Commentary on Revelation*

Bede follows Augustine's interpretation closely, often nearly word for word, which shows how much Augustine shaped later reading of this chapter.

**1. Same order of events.** Bede also links the new creation to the earlier vision in which heaven and earth fled, implying the judgment of the wicked.

**2. Renewal matching the resurrected saints.** The figure of this world will pass away with the conflagration of the heavenly fires, so that, with heaven and earth transformed for the better, the quality of the transformation will correspond to the incorruption and immortality of the bodies of the saints. One difference in wording is worth noting: Augustine speaks of "terrestrial fires," while Bede speaks of "heavenly fires."

**3. The sea as a symbol.** Bede shares Augustine's uncertainty: Whether it will be dried up by that great heat, or whether it will also be transformed for the better, I cannot easily say. He gives a somewhat clearer figurative reading, suggesting that the turbulent life of this age, which will then cease, is symbolized by the sea.

---

## Common Themes

- **Transformation, not annihilation:** Both writers understand the "new" heaven and earth as the present creation purified and renewed.
- **Creation and the resurrection body belong together:** The renewed world is fitted to the incorruptible, resurrected bodies of the redeemed.
- **Interpretive humility:** Both openly admit uncertainty about the literal fate of the sea. Both suggest it may symbolize the restless, stormy life of the present age, which will end.
