# Patristic Insights on Matthew 4: The Temptation of Christ

All four excerpts address the opening of Matthew 4, where Jesus is led into the wilderness, fasts forty days, and is tempted by the devil. The two Chrysostom excerpts are different translations of overlapping material, so they are treated together below.

---

## 1. Theodore of Mopsuestia: Christ Reverses Adam's Fall

Theodore's brief fragment frames the temptation as a deliberate reversal of Eden:

- **Paradise versus wilderness:** Since Adam met with luxury in paradise and, through deception, deteriorated to what is worse, it was necessary that [the Spirit] lead Christ into the wilderness in order to enfeeble the devil's force by someone greater in strength.

The insight is that the setting is not incidental. Adam fell amid abundance, so Christ confronts the devil amid deprivation, and the one who is "greater in strength" undoes what Adam lost.

---

## 2. Hilary of Poitiers: The Divine Plan and the Victory of Christ's Humanity

Hilary offers the most theologically developed reading, emphasizing God's sovereignty and the importance of Christ's real humanity.

**The temptation is part of God's plan.** The journey into the desert, the forty-day fast, the hunger after the fast, the temptation by Satan and the Lord's response—all these are full of the effects of the great heavenly counsel. The devil had no power of his own here. Being led into the desert signifies the freedom of the Holy Spirit to offer his man to the devil and to permit the occasion of temptation and conquest, which the tempter would not have had unless he had been given it.

**The devil's ignorance.** According to Hilary, there was in the devil therefore suspicious fear but no knowledge of the true identity of the One suspected. The forty-day fast unsettled him because he had knowledge of the poured-out waters of the abyss in just as many days and of the exploration of the promised land, so apprehensive of that time therefore in tempting him whom he considered to be a man, he acted rashly.

**Defeated by the same humanity he ruined.** Hilary's central insight is that the devil, who had enticed Adam and by deceiving him led him to death, should be defeated by that same humanity in whose death and misfortunes he gloried. In the same way, the devil was not to be defeated by God but by the flesh.

**The meaning of Christ's hunger.** Hilary reads the hunger carefully:
- Jesus did not hunger for human food but for human salvation.
- It was after forty days and not during forty days that he hungered.
- His strength was not depleted by his forty days of fasting. He did not abandon his nature as a man.

**A warning for believers.** Because the Lord was therefore tempted immediately after being baptized, Hilary concludes that his temptation indicates how sinister are the devil's attempts especially against those who have been sanctified, for he eagerly desires victory over the saints.

---

## 3. John Chrysostom: The Temptation as Instruction for the Baptized

Chrysostom's emphasis is pastoral. He reads the temptation as a lesson for Christians, especially the newly baptized.

**Timing matters.** The word "then" refers to the moment after the descent of the Spirit, after the voice that was borne from above had said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Christ submitted to this in order that each of those who are baptized, if after his baptism he have to endure greater temptations may not be troubled as if the result were unexpected, but may continue to endure all nobly.

**Why God permits temptation.** Chrysostom gives a list of reasons. Temptations teach believers that you have become much stronger; next, that you may continue modest neither be exalted even by the greatness of your gifts. They also show that you may in this way be made stronger, and better tempered than any steel. Temptation can even be a sign of honor: the devil would not have assailed you, unless he had seen you brought to greater honor.

**"Led up," not rushing in.** Chrysostom reconciles this passage with Jesus' command to pray against temptation. Matthew shows Jesus not simply going up, but led up according to the principle of the Economy; signifying obscurely by this, that we ought not of ourselves to leap upon it, but being dragged thereto, to stand manfully.

**The danger of isolation.** The wilderness setting teaches a practical lesson: For then most especially does the devil assail, when he sees men left alone, and by themselves. Hence we have the greatest need on this very account to be flocking together continually, that we may not be open to the devil's attacks.

**Fasting as a shield.** The devil approaches not in his fast, but in his hunger, which shows how great a good fasting is, and how it is a most powerful shield against the devil. Christ fasted, not as needing it Himself, but to instruct us. Chrysostom ties this to the fall: Adam by the incontinence of the belly was cast out of paradise.

**Why exactly forty days.** Christ fasted forty days yet proceeds no further, lest on the other hand, through the exceeding greatness of the miracle the truth of His Economy should be discredited. Had he gone further, His assumption of our flesh would have seemed incredible to many.

---

## Common Threads

| Theme | Theodore | Hilary | Chrysostom |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Christ as the reversal of Adam** | ✓ Luxury vs. wilderness | ✓ Defeated by the humanity he ruined | ✓ Fall through the belly, remedied by fasting |
| **The Spirit's deliberate leading** | ✓ | ✓ Sovereign permission | ✓ "Led up," not self-sought |
| **Christ's genuine humanity** | — | ✓ Victory through the flesh | ✓ Forty-day limit protects belief in the Incarnation |
| **Lesson for the baptized** | — | ✓ Saints especially targeted | ✓ Central emphasis |

**In brief:** All three see Christ in the wilderness as undoing Adam's defeat in the garden. Hilary stresses the hidden divine plan and the significance of Christ conquering *as a man*. Chrysostom draws the most practical lessons: temptation after baptism should be expected, fasting and Christian fellowship protect believers, and trials should be endured rather than sought out.

# Bede on Revelation 17: Summary of Key Insights

**A note on sources:** All four excerpts come from a single commentator, **Bede**, so this summary presents his insights only. No other patristic voices appear in the material provided.

## 1. The Harlot: The Community of the Lost

Bede reads the "great harlot" as a collective figure rather than an individual. She represents the multitude of the lost, who, forsaking the Creator, surrendered themselves to demons to be defiled. Her seat "on the waters" is interpreted as the discord of the peoples.

He then contrasts her with the Church: the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, the community whom the Apostle betrothed to one man to present a chaste virgin to Christ. The harlot embodies division and unfaithfulness. The Church embodies unity and faithful devotion to Christ.

## 2. The Kings' Fornication: Inner Spiritual Corruption

Bede does not limit "the kings of the earth" to literal rulers. He applies the phrase to individuals. He notes that the universality prevails over the parts, explaining that the kings and inhabitants of the earth are each individually those arrogantly seeking earthly things, whom the allurements of the world, with the lust of vices, defile and intoxicate with the madness of mind. In his reading, the "fornication" is the soul's attachment to worldly things.

## 3. The Wilderness: Separation from God

On John being carried into the wilderness, Bede writes that the wilderness represents the absence of divinity, whose presence is paradise. The setting itself becomes a theological statement about life apart from God.

## 4. The Scarlet Beast and Its Heads and Horns

Bede identifies the beast as the devil. He describes it as bloody with impiety, blasphemous, inflated, one who exalts the corruption of the wicked with the pride of presumption.

The seven heads and ten horns signify the kings of the world and kingdoms, whose glory he also showed to the Lord on the mountain. Bede also notes that the number seven and ten often indicate universality. The beast's dominion therefore represents the full scope of worldly power under the devil's influence.

## 5. The Harlot's Appearance: Deceptive Splendor

Bede interprets the harlot's adornments as symbols of deception:
- **Purple and scarlet:** In purple is shown the pretense of feigned rule, in scarlet the bloody habit of impiety is demonstrated.
- **Gold, precious stones, and pearls:** these represent all the allurements of simulated truth.

## 6. The Golden Cup: Hypocrisy Exposed

This may be Bede's most striking insight. He explains that a golden cup full of impurities is hypocrisy, because hypocrites outwardly appear to people as just, but inside they are full of all filth. He concludes: For what poison is in gold, this is the beast hidden under the guise of the harlot.

## Overall Theological Thrust

Several themes run through Bede's reading of Revelation 17:
- **Moral and spiritual interpretation:** He reads the vision mainly as a portrait of spiritual realities, such as unfaithfulness to God, worldly desire, and demonic influence, rather than as a set of specific historical events.
- **Contrast between two communities:** The divided, defiled multitude of the lost stands against the united, faithful Church.
- **Deception as the core danger:** The harlot's power lies in her attractive appearance, which hides corruption and the devil within. Her most dangerous quality is that evil looks like truth and righteousness.

## Overall Theological Thrust

Several themes run through Bede's reading of Revelation 17:

# Commentary Summary: Mark Chapter 7

## Bede

Bede's commentary is the most substantial of the provided excerpts. His central concern is the contrast between **outward ritual cleanliness and inward purity of heart**.

### 1. The humble receive what the learned miss
Bede contrasts the people of Gennesaret with the religious leaders. He sees in this scene a fulfillment of Christ's words, "you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to the little ones." The men of the region of Gennesaret, who seemed less learned, not only come themselves but also bring their sick, and as a result they immediately obtain the reward of the desired healing.

The Pharisees and scribes, by contrast, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, come to the Lord not to hear the word, nor to seek a cure, but only to stir up debates. Bede finds an irony here: they should blame themselves more, who, having hands washed with water, bore a conscience defiled with malice.

### 2. Human tradition versus divine authority
Bede is blunt about the confrontation: The stupidity of the Pharisees and scribes is astonishing. They argue with the Son of God, why he does not observe the traditions and precepts of men. He calls the ritual washing practice a superstitious tradition of men.

### 3. "Hands" as works: a spiritual interpretation
Bede reads the washing of hands symbolically: The hands, that is, works, of course, not the hands of the body, but of the soul, must be washed, so that the word of God may be done in them. In his view, the true teaching orders those who wish to participate with the bread of life descending from heaven to often cleanse their works with the washing of alms, tears, and other fruits of righteousness, so that they may be able to communicate with heavenly mysteries with a pure heart and body.

He applies this to everyday life: It is necessary to purge the defilements that anyone has contracted from the cares of temporal business with the following diligence of good thoughts and acts, if he desires to enjoy the feasts of internal refreshment.

### 4. Misreading the Old Testament
Bede argues the Pharisees misunderstood their own Scriptures. They took the spiritual words of the prophets carnally, which commanded them concerning the chastisement of heart and works, citing Isaiah, yet these only observed the washing of the body. He insists that Moses and the prophets who ordered the vessels of the people of God to be either washed with water, or purged by fire, or sanctified with oil for whatever reason, did not command in this the cleansing of material things, but rather the chastisement and holiness of minds and works, and the salvation of souls.

### 5. Cleansing comes through Christ
Finally, Bede treats Christ as the true source of purification. All ritual washing is futile apart from Him: Pharisees in vain, all Jews in vain, wash their hands, and are baptized from the market, as long as they despise being washed by the fountain of the Savior.

## Clement of Alexandria

The excerpt attributed to Clement consists only of a single quotation: "this people honoureth Me with their lips "it is said, "but their heart is far from Me." This line fits the chapter's theme of outward religion versus inward devotion. However, the excerpt contains no interpretation, explanation, or context from Clement. It is therefore not possible to identify any distinct theological insight of his own from this material, and drawing conclusions about how he understood or applied the verse would go beyond the provided text.

## Summary

Bede provides nearly all the interpretive substance here. His key insight is that Mark 7 exposes a religion of external ritual that neglects the heart. He reads "washing" as moral and spiritual cleansing through works of righteousness, repentance, and ultimately Christ Himself. The Clement excerpt echoes this lips-versus-heart theme, but offers no commentary of its own.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 14: Herod and John the Baptist

All four excerpts address the opening of Matthew 14, where Herod hears about Jesus and concludes that John the Baptist, whom he had executed, has risen from the dead.

## Theodore of Mopsuestia: Clarifying Who Herod Is

Theodore makes a historical clarification to prevent confusion between two rulers. He notes that Herod the king is one person, Herod the tetrarch, his son, is another. He explains that after King Herod's death the Romans divided his kingdom into a tetrarchy, and one part of the tetrarchy went to his son. This son is the Herod of Matthew 14, the man who beheaded the Forerunner and who, for this reason, received his due punishment not long afterward.

**Key insight:** Theodore's contribution is mainly historical, but it carries a moral and theological point: sin against God's messenger does not go unpunished.

## John Chrysostom: The Psychology of a Guilty Ruler

Chrysostom focuses on Herod's inner state, drawing moral lessons from his character.

- **Pride delays spiritual awareness:** Chrysostom argues the evangelist mentions the timing deliberately, to make you observe also the haughtiness of the tyrant, and his thoughtlessness, in that not at the beginning did he inform himself about Christ, but after a very long time. He presents this as a pattern among the powerful: they learn these things late, because they do not make much account of them.

- **The power of virtue, even after death:** Chrysostom invites readers to mark how great a thing virtue is, that he was afraid of him even when dead, and out of his fear he speaks wisely even concerning a resurrection. John's righteousness still troubles his murderer.

- **A guilty conscience:** He observes that Herod did not dare speak of it openly, but he still speaks apprehensively to his own servants. Yet Chrysostom calls Herod's theory absurd, since even though many were thought to have risen from the dead, no one had done anything like what was imagined of John.

- **Mixed passions:** Chrysostom diagnoses Herod's words as the language both of vanity and of fear, adding that such is the nature of unreasonable souls; they often accept a mixture of opposite passions.

**Key insight:** Chrysostom's lasting contribution is spiritual and psychological. Worldly power dulls spiritual attention, a guilty conscience produces irrational fear, and genuine virtue has a force that outlives death.

## Origen of Alexandria: The Theology Behind Herod's Mistake

Origen places Herod's statement within Jewish debates about resurrection. He notes that the Jews had different opinions about the resurrection. He calls the Sadducees' denial false and affirms as true the Pharisees' teaching about the resurrection of the dead—that they rise.

He then examines Herod's particular error: the belief that John had risen from the dead after he had been beheaded and that this person who had risen was the same person under a different name, one now called Jesus. Origen explains the logic: Herod imagined that Jesus possessed the same powers that formerly worked in John.

Origen traces this idea to expectations about Elijah: it was the spirit and power of Elijah that had returned in John. By analogy, Herod reasoned that John's powers had passed to Jesus. Origen observes a telling detail: Herod thought John's powers had a miraculous effect in Jesus, even though John did not do miracles. He suggests the same reasoning was the underlying thought of those who said that Elijah had appeared in Jesus or that one of the old prophets had risen.

**Key insight:** Origen treats Herod's statement as a theological error rather than simple superstition. It is a distorted use of real ideas about resurrection and prophetic succession, and it helps explain the confused popular opinions about who Jesus was.

## Summary

Together, these commentators illuminate the passage from three angles:
- **Theodore** supplies the historical identity of Herod and points to divine justice.
- **Chrysostom** explores Herod's moral psychology: pride, fear, and the lingering power of a righteous man's witness.
- **Origen** analyzes the theological reasoning behind Herod's mistaken belief and links it to wider confusion about Jesus' identity.

Note that these excerpts cover only the Herod and John the Baptist episode at the start of Matthew 14. They do not address the chapter's later events, such as the feeding of the five thousand or Jesus walking on the water.

# Patristic Commentary on John 16: Key Theological Insights

These four early Church commentators focus mainly on the opening verses of John 16, where Jesus warns his disciples about coming persecution. Their main questions are why Jesus warned them in advance, what the persecutors were thinking, and how the disciples would find the strength to endure.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

Augustine's commentary is the most extensive of the excerpts. It develops several themes.

**1. Example alone is not enough; the Spirit is needed.**
Augustine links this chapter to Christ's promise of the Spirit at the end of chapter 15. He explains the dual witness this way: because He shall bear witness, you also shall bear witness: He in your hearts, you in your voices; He by inspiration, you by utterance. His central point is that it would have been to little purpose to have exhorted them by His example, had He not also filled them with His Spirit. Peter illustrates this. Before Pentecost, he had got instruction to stand, but not the strength to keep him from falling. Once the Spirit supplied that strength, he preached Christ even to the death, whom, in his fear of death, he had previously denied.

**2. Peace that prevents stumbling.**
Augustine connects Jesus' words "that you should not be offended" with love poured out by the Spirit: when the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit given unto us, Romans 5:5 they have great peace who love God's law, so that nothing may offend them.

**3. Expulsion from the synagogue.**
Augustine reflects that, had Israel received Christ, nor would the churches of Christ have been different from the synagogues of the Jews, for they would have been one and the same, had they also desired to abide in Him. He contrasts the Spirit-filled disciples with those who loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.

**4. A close reading of "but the hour comes."**
Augustine notices that Jesus says "*but* the hour comes" rather than "*and* the hour comes," a phrasing that would normally introduce good news. He resolves the puzzle this way: the disciples would gain so many to Christ, by being driven out of the Jewish congregations, that it would be found insufficient to expel them, and they would not suffer them to live for fear of all being converted by their preaching. In other words, the coming persecution is itself a sign of the gospel's success. He paraphrases Jesus' meaning: They will put you out of the synagogues; but have no fear of solitude: inasmuch as, when separated from their assembly, you will assemble so many in my name.

**5. Misguided zeal.**
Augustine distinguishes Jewish from Gentile persecutors. Gentiles thought not that it was to the true God, but to their own false deities, that they were doing service. By contrast, every Jew that slew the preachers of Christ reckoned that he was doing God serv ice; believing as he did that all who were converted to Christ were deserting the God of Israel. He exclaims: Is it thus you would please God by striking down the God-pleaser; and is the living temple of God by your blows laid level with the ground, that God's temple of stone may not be deserted? He also stresses that Israel's blindness is only partial: not all, but only some of the branches have been broken off, that the wild olive might be ingrafted.

**6. Why Jesus warned them in advance.**
Christ foretold these trials lest their minds, left ignorant and unprepared, should be cast into trouble by evils, however transient, that were unexpected and unprovided for; but rather by knowing of them beforehand, and sustaining them with patience, might be led onward to everlasting blessing.

---

## Theodore of Mopsuestia

Theodore's excerpt is a single sentence. It focuses on the purpose of Jesus' warning, which he presents as spiritual training: I predicted these things to you, he says, so that when sudden unexpected tribulations would occur, your resolve might not turn and fail but instead, through constant meditation, you might be trained through these difficulties. His distinctive contribution is the idea that dwelling on Christ's warnings ahead of time prepares the believer to persevere.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

Cyril's excerpt focuses on the transition from chapter 15 into chapter 16. It concerns what Jesus chose *not* to say, rather than directly expounding the persecutions described in chapter 16.

**1. Pastoral restraint.**
Cyril suggests Jesus could have revealed that the Jews would reject even the combined testimony of the Spirit and the disciples. He held back because doing so would have produced in them an immoderate grief, and, breaking the hearts of His disciples even to despair, would have made the entrance of faint-heartedness and cowardice into their hearts absolutely certain. The disciples might have asked, Why should they not rid themselves of their troubles, and choose silence in preference to teaching men unwilling to hear? So Christ skilfully conceals what was too grievous to be told and instead turns the drift of His speech into an exhortation to hold themselves in readiness and make vigorous preparation.

**2. The psychology of foreknowledge.**
Like Theodore, Cyril sees value in advance warning: whatever comes to men suddenly and unexpectedly is likely to disturb even the mind that is stable. Suffering that has been anticipated has lost its edge by the expectation of certain suffering.

---

## Bede

Bede's homily centers on the persecutors' sincere but misdirected zeal, and on how that understanding should shape the disciples' response.

He notes that Christ warned that they would not only be driven away from fellowship with their fellow citizens but also that they would suffer death at their hands. His distinctive pastoral insight is that the disciples should accept them the more steadfastly in the realization that you are afflicted with them not so much out of hatred toward yourselves as out of zeal for the divine law. He gives a concrete example of this attitude: Mindful of this advice, the blessed martyr Stephen prayed for his slayers.

---

## Common Threads

- **Foreknowledge as preparation:** Augustine, Theodore, and Cyril all agree that Jesus warned the disciples in advance so that trials would not catch them unprepared and shake their faith.
- **Zeal without knowledge:** Augustine and Bede both read the persecutors' belief that they were "doing God service" through Paul's description of zeal "not according to knowledge."
- **Distinctive emphases:**
  - Augustine stresses the necessity of the Spirit's power, and he sees persecution as evidence of the gospel's fruitfulness.
  - Cyril highlights Christ's pastoral care in what he chose to leave unsaid.
  - Bede draws from the passage a call to forgive one's persecutors, as Stephen did.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 8: A Summary

The excerpts come from two early Christian commentators, **Bede** and **Jerome**. Bede reads the text both literally and symbolically. Jerome's excerpt is brief and deals with wording and translation.

---

## Bede: Commentary on Genesis

### 1. The Wind as God's Spirit (Genesis 8:1)
Bede connects the wind that dried the floodwaters to the creation account. He reads it in the name of the Vivifying Spirit of God, of which it is said at the beginning: "And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters" (Genesis 1:2). His key point is that God acts the same way in both events: just as then, when the waters were gathered to one place, making the land dry, so also now, with the waters of the flood taken away, He once again revealed the face of the earth.

**Insight:** The receding flood is a kind of new creation, brought about by the same life-giving Spirit.

Bede also allows a more natural reading of the wind. He points to the Exodus crossing as a parallel, where "the Lord caused it to go back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided" (Exodus 14:21).

### 2. The Returning Waters: Literal and Mystical Readings (Genesis 8:2–3)
**Literally**, Bede says the waters "going and coming" show that all the courses of rivers and streams return through the hidden veins of the earth to the matrix of the abyss. He supports this with Ecclesiastes 1:7.

**Mystically**, the end of the rains after 150 days points to the end of history. Scripture's teaching will one day stop, because they will have nothing greater to promise, after having perfected us in the immortal glory of flesh and spirit and led us to the blessed vision of our Creator.

### 3. The 150 Days and the 150 Psalms
Bede links the 150 days to the number of Psalms: it is well that the book of Psalms, which is contained in the number of one hundred and fifty, is completed in divine praise. The Psalter begins with obedience to God's law (Psalm 1) and ends in pure praise (Psalm 150). For Bede this reflects the shape of the Christian life, because evidently the sum of all our blessedness is in this, that dwelling in His house we may endlessly praise Him.

**Insight:** The end of the flood anticipates the believer's final destiny, which is endless worship in God's presence.

### 4. The Ark at Rest: Symbolic Numbers (Genesis 8:4)
- **The seventh month** refers symbolically to that seventh rest about which it has often been spoken, the rest toward which the spiritually mature move.
- **The twenty-seventh day** is, in Bede's arithmetic, a solid squared trinity, since 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. The number three corresponds to the soul's devotion to God through the memory by which we recall God, the understanding by which we know Him, and the will by which we love Him. The ark therefore stands for the Church, which in the stability of its mind and action, as if squared, both expects rest in this life and receives eternal rest in the future.
- **The mountains of Armenia** show that the Church, renouncing the summit of the world's pomp, even in this pilgrimage, leading a life, it approaches heavenly joys with the mind.

**Insight:** The ark's resting place is a picture of the Church: stable, devoted to the Triune God, and already reaching toward heaven while still on its earthly journey.

---

## Jerome: Hebrew Questions on Genesis

Jerome's excerpt is short and focuses on wording rather than theology. He notes that the interpreters have translated the phrase 'fountains of the deep were revealed' as 'the closed and sealed fountains were opened'. Like Bede, he connects the returning waters to Ecclesiastes and teaches that all waters and torrents return to the hidden veins of the abyss.

**Note on the text:** This excerpt has some difficulties, possibly from translation.
- Its version of verse 2 says the fountains were "revealed" and the floodgates "opened." That runs opposite to the sense of the passage in Bede's text, where the fountains were closed.
- It attributes the phrase "the waters returned from the earth, going and coming" to Ecclesiastes 1:7, though that wording matches the Genesis verse quoted by Bede.

Readers should treat this excerpt cautiously. Its main contribution is its attention to translation and its agreement with Bede's literal explanation.

---

## Summary

| Commentator | Main Approach | Key Insight |
|---|---|---|
| **Bede** | Literal and allegorical | The flood's end echoes creation through the Spirit's work. The 150 days point to final praise of God. The ark's rest pictures the Church's stability and heavenly hope. |
| **Jerome** | Textual and philological | Notes differences in translation and agrees that the waters return to the hidden depths. Offers little theological development. |

Taken together, Bede supplies most of the theological reflection on Genesis 8 in these excerpts. He presents the end of the flood as a picture of renewal, rest, and eternal worship.

# Patristic Insights on Genesis 40: A Summary

The excerpts come from three Church Fathers: Jerome, Ambrose of Milan, and John Chrysostom. Each approaches the story of Joseph and the two imprisoned royal officials from a different angle. Jerome focuses on language, Ambrose on moral warning, and Chrysostom on Joseph's character.

## Jerome: Clarifying the Hebrew Text

Jerome's comments are mainly about words and translation rather than theology, but they help explain the story's background.

- **The cupbearer's title:** Jerome notes that where he has placed 'chief of the wine cellar' in Hebrew it is written 'Masec', that word which we have recently read in the name of Abraham's servant, whom we can call the cupbearer according to the custom of the common people.
- **The dignity of the office:** He cautions readers not to underestimate this role. He writes that this office should not be considered lowly, since it is of the utmost dignity even among barbarian kings to offer a cup to the king. He supports this with a classical example: poets have written about Ganymede and Jove, that he entrusted his beloved to this very duty.
- **The vine in the cupbearer's dream (v. 10):** Jerome observes that the words in Hebrew, which are called Sarigim, signify three scourges and three branches or shoots. He points out this double meaning in the Hebrew but does not develop a theological interpretation of it in this excerpt.

## Ambrose of Milan: The Fragility of Worldly Status

Ambrose draws a moral lesson from the downfall of the two officials, whom he identifies as eunuchs.

- **A warning about dependence on earthly power:** He writes that they ought to serve as an example to other eunuchs that their standing is fragile and weak and all their hope lies in the will of the king; for them a slight offense is a very great danger, while prosperity is a paltry condition of service.
- **Pride before the fall:** Ambrose highlights their self-importance: One boasted because he was the chief butler, the other because he was the chief baker. Yet both committed offenses, were put into prison and were entrusted to the holy Joseph by the jailer of the prison.

His key point is that worldly rank offers no real security. The men who took pride in their positions ended up in the care of Joseph, whom Ambrose calls "holy."

## John Chrysostom: Joseph's Compassion in Suffering

Chrysostom focuses on Joseph's virtue, especially his attentiveness to others while he himself was suffering.

- **Noticing others' distress:** Chrysostom describes how Joseph, concerned for their comfort, noticed that they were dismayed by the experience of the dreams and confused in mind; so he asked, "Why so downcast today?"
- **The face reveals the heart:** He explains that the dejection on their faces, you see, betrayed the apprehension within them. He supports this with a proverb: a sage too has said, "When the heart is free from care, the face beams, but when it is in mourning the face falls."
- **Virtue that persists through hardship:** His main insight is the moral example Joseph sets: See how, even when he found himself in prison, he gave evidence of his characteristic virtue and was concerned to relieve the sadness of others.

## Summary

All of these excerpts address Genesis 40, and together they offer complementary perspectives:

| Commentator | Focus | Key Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Jerome** | Language and context | Explains Hebrew terms and defends the dignity of the cupbearer's office |
| **Ambrose** | Moral warning | Shows how fragile status is when it rests on a ruler's favor |
| **Chrysostom** | Character and virtue | Presents Joseph as a model of compassion amid his own suffering |

Jerome's contributions are mostly philological rather than theological. Ambrose and Chrysostom offer the more directly spiritual lessons. One warns against trusting in worldly position, and the other holds up Joseph's selfless care for others as an example to follow.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 25: The Parable of the Ten Virgins

All four excerpts focus on the parable of the wise and foolish virgins. None addresses the rest of Matthew 25, so this summary covers only that parable.

---

## Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 93.5)

**1. What it means to "go and meet the bridegroom."** Augustine asks what this phrase means and answers that it means to go with all the heart, to eagerly await his coming. For him, the virgins' journey describes wholehearted spiritual longing for Christ.

**2. The parable applies to the whole Church.** Augustine insists that this parable relates to us all, that is, to the whole church together, not to the clergy only, of whom we spoke yesterday, nor to the laity only but generally to all.

**3. Division exists among those who appear faithful.** Augustine's sharpest point is that the virgins are not just any souls but such souls as have the catholic faith and seem to have good works in the church of God. Yet even of them it is said, "Five are wise, and five are foolish." His warning is that orthodox belief and outward good works do not by themselves guarantee readiness.

---

## Hilary of Poitiers (Commentary on Matthew 27.3)

**1. The parable is about the final judgment.** Hilary reads the story eschatologically: The whole story is about the great day of the Lord, when those things concealed from the human mind will be revealed through our understanding of divine judgment. On that day, the faith true to the Lord's coming will win the just reward for unwavering hope.

**2. The parable marks a complete separation.** He writes that in the five wise and five foolish virgins, a complete separation between the faithful and unfaithful is established.

**3. A comparison with the two tablets of Moses.** Hilary links the five-and-five structure to the Ten Commandments: Moses had received the Ten Commandments written on two tablets. He interprets this so that the double column represented, under a single testament, the division between the good and the bad, between the designation of right and left. For Hilary, the number symbolism points to a single covenant community that will ultimately be divided.

---

## John Chrysostom (Commentary)

**1. The parable belongs to a group of teachings on mercy.** Chrysostom connects it with the former parable of the faithful servant, and of him that was ungrateful and devoured his Lord's goods. He sees these parables as admonishing us about the same things, I mean about diligence in almsgiving, and about helping our neighbor by all means which we are able to use, since it is not possible to be saved in another way.

**2. Neglect alone is judged.** He notes a progression in severity. The earlier parable punishes active wrongdoing, but here even him that does not help, nor spends abundantly his goods upon the needy. The foolish virgins had oil indeed, but not in abundance, wherefore also they are punished.

**3. The lamps and the oil.** Chrysostom offers a clear key to the imagery: by lamps here, He means the gift itself of virginity, the purity of holiness; and by oil, humanity, almsgiving, succor to them that are in need.

**4. Why the characters are virgins.** Chrysostom explains that Christ had spoken highly of virginity, citing Matthew 19:12 and Paul's remark in 1 Corinthians 7:25, both of which appear in the excerpt. Because virginity was so highly honored, Christ told this parable lest any one attaining to this should feel as though he had attained to all, and should be careless about the rest. The lesson is that virginity, though it should have everything else, if destitute of the good things arising out of almsgiving, is cast out with the harlots, and He sets the inhuman and merciless with them.

**5. Why they are called "foolish."** Chrysostom reasons that the love of money is a weaker temptation than the love of carnal pleasure, and the weaker the antagonist, the less excusable are these that are overcome thereby. So Christ calls them foolish, for that having undergone the greater labor, they have betrayed all for want of the less.

---

## Common Threads

- **Separation within the community of believers.** Augustine and Hilary both stress that the division in this parable runs through those who appear faithful, not between the Church and outsiders.
- **Different emphases.** Augustine focuses on eager, wholehearted waiting. Hilary focuses on the final judgment and its symbolism. Chrysostom gives the most practical reading: mercy and almsgiving are the "oil" that no other spiritual achievement can replace.

# Patristic Insights on Ephesians 5: A Summary

The excerpts focus mainly on Ephesians 5:1–2, the call to be "imitators of God." Chrysostom's homily begins with the preceding verse, Ephesians 4:32, and reads it together with 5:1–2. The excerpt titled for this homily ("HOMILY ON EPHESIANS 17.4.32-5.2") makes the same connection.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 17 on Ephesians)

**1. Paul grounds his appeal in what God has already done.**
Chrysostom notes that the events which are past have greater force than those which are yet to come, and appear to be both more wonderful and more convincing. Promises of future reward or punishment carry weight, but Paul appeals to the conscience not by these arguments only, but also by things already done for us. He sees a difference in what each kind of motive achieves: In the former way we may escape punishment, whereas in this latter we may have our share of some positive good.

**2. Forgiveness is how we imitate God.**
For Chrysostom, this alone is enough to recommend virtue, that it is "to imitate God." He states it plainly: Forgive another, and you are "imitating God," you are made like God. Because human relationships always involve hurt, Paul offers a practical remedy. Inasmuch as it cannot be that, being men, we shall avoid either giving pain or suffering it, he does the next thing, he devises a remedy — that we should forgive one another.

**3. Our forgiveness cannot compare with God's.**
Chrysostom stresses the gap between the two. Thou indeed art forgiving a fellow-servant; whereas God is forgiving a servant, and an enemy, and one that hates Him. God's forgiveness was also costly. He forgave not simply, he would say, … and at no risk or cost, but at the sacrifice of His Son. People, by contrast, often refuse to pardon even when you see pardon to be both without risk and without cost.

**4. Christ gave himself freely, and we should love as far as we can.**
The phrase "gave Himself up" shows that Christ's sacrifice was voluntary: That you may not then think it an act of necessity, hear how He says, that "He gave Himself up." Chrysostom admits we cannot fully match this love, yet still urges the effort: As your Master loved you, love thou your friend. Nay, but neither will you be able so to love; yet still do so as far as you are able.

**5. Forgiving wrongs is a form of wealth.**
Chrysostom argues that it is more our duty to forgive trespasses than debts of money; for if you forgive debts, you have not "imitated God"; whereas if you shall forgive trespasses, you are "imitating God." Forgiving costs nothing in the end: is it not rather wealth, is it not abundance, is it not a plentiful store?

**6. Being God's beloved children is a further motive.**
Believers have another reason to imitate God, not only in that you have received such good at His hands, but also in that you are called His children. Chrysostom notes that not all children imitate their fathers, but those which are beloved. A second translation of the same homily (Document 2) adds that becoming like God can happen when you are reconciled with him.

---

## Jerome (Commentary on Ephesians 5:1)

**1. Paul's wording reflects the Ephesians' spiritual maturity.**
Jerome contrasts this verse with Paul's words to the Corinthians. There, though they could not instantaneously become imitators of Christ, it was still a great thing for them if they could be imitators of the imitator. The Ephesians were addressed differently: since they are those to whom he has revealed such great mysteries, he neither says "be imitators of me" nor "be imitators of Christ" but "be imitators of God."

**2. Imitating Christ is not a lesser calling.**
Jerome guards against misreading this contrast. It does not imply that it is less to be an imitator of Christ than of God, for Christ is God.

**3. We imitate God by showing mercy to everyone.**
Jerome acknowledges limits: much that God has done we humans can hardly be said to imitate. He points to one area where imitation is possible: in the way that he is merciful to all and rains on good and bad, so we may pour out mercy upon all we meet. When we do this, we shall be beloved children.

---

## Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, Book III)

This excerpt contains no commentary or interpretation. It consists only of two quoted passages. The first is an exhortation to masters: Ye masters, treat your servants well, forbearing threatening: knowing that both their and your Lord is in heaven. That verse belongs to Ephesians 6 rather than chapter 5. The second is a Latin text warning against fornication, impurity, and greed (Fornicatio autem, et omnis immunditia, vel avaritia, ne nominetur quidem in vobis, sicut decet sanctos), which corresponds to Ephesians 5:3. Since Clement's own reflections on these verses are not included, no theological insight can fairly be attributed to him from this excerpt.

---

## Common Threads

Chrysostom and Jerome agree on three points:
- **Imitating God means showing mercy.** Both draw on the image of God sending sun or rain on the just and the unjust ("for He makes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.").
- **"Beloved children" names both a gift and a calling.** Being loved by God is what moves believers to resemble him.
- **Divine love sets the standard, and we follow it as far as we can.** Both admit that full imitation of God is beyond human ability, yet both insist believers should still pursue it.

# Patristic Insights on Acts 17:1–3

**Scope note:** These excerpts cover only the opening verses of Acts 17, which describe Paul's arrival and synagogue preaching. They do not address the later parts of the chapter, so this summary is limited to those first few verses.

---

## John Chrysostom

### 1. Missionary strategy: reaching the centers
Chrysostom sees a deliberate plan in the apostles' route. They pass through the small towns and hurry to the biggest, since the word was to flow to nearby cities as from a source. Major cities served as hubs from which the gospel could spread to the surrounding region.

### 2. Paul's enduring love for his own people
Chrysostom notes that Paul went to the synagogue "as was his custom," even after earlier turning toward the Gentiles. Although he had said, "We turn to the Gentiles," he did not abandon these people, for great was his desire toward them. To show this, Chrysostom cites Paul's own words: "Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved," and, "I wished myself accursed from Christ for my brothers." He offers several motives for Paul's practice: because of the promise and the glory of God and because he did not wish to offend the Gentiles.

### 3. Persuasion through Scripture rather than miracles
On Paul arguing from the Scriptures for three weeks, Chrysostom adds a practical detail: this was when they were not at work. His main point is about method. Paul followed Christ's example: he often made his argument from the Scriptures and not by miracles. The reason is credibility: it is natural for him who tries to persuade people by miracles alone to be suspected, but one who persuades by the Scriptures does not arouse this suspicion.

He also suggests that persuasive teaching is itself a kind of wonder. Recalling that in Antioch "the whole city gathered together" to hear his teaching, he concludes: it is not a small but an exceedingly great miracle.

---

## Bede

### 1. A twofold argument from Scripture
Bede identifies two linked claims in Paul's preaching. He made both things known from the Scriptures at the same time, that the Christ had to suffer and to rise and that this suffering and resurrection pertained to none other than Jesus of Nazareth.

### 2. Why the second claim mattered
Bede explains that some listeners accepted the first claim but rejected the second. Although they could not deny that the suffering and resurrection of the Christ were present in the Scriptures, they nevertheless entirely denied that these things pertained to Jesus. He regards this as a problem in his own day as well.

### 3. From prophecy to fulfillment
For Bede, Paul's preaching went beyond describing the Messiah in the abstract: Paul not only preached the mysteries of the Christ, but he also taught that these mysteries were accomplished in Christ Jesus. Prophecy and its fulfillment in Jesus belong together.

---

## Common Thread
Both commentators stress that Paul grounded his preaching in Scripture. Chrysostom emphasizes the credibility of this method and Paul's love for his audience. Bede emphasizes the content of the argument: Scripture foretold a suffering and rising Messiah, and that Messiah is Jesus.

# Patristic Insights on Acts 24

The excerpts come from two commentators, John Chrysostom and Bede. Most of the material focuses on the trial of Paul before the Roman governor Felix, and especially on the tactics of his accuser, Tertullus.

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom reads the trial closely, exposing the rhetorical strategies Tertullus uses against Paul.

**1. Flattery and urgency (Acts 24:2–3)**
Chrysostom notes that Tertullus opens by trying to win over the judge before making his case. He observes, "See how [Tertullus] approaches the judge with praises from the start and wants to hand Paul over as a revolutionary and a rebel." He also points to the speaker's haste: "notice how he hastens as if he has many things to say." The implication is that the accusation depends more on rhetorical posture than on substance.

**2. Vague charges and selective framing (Acts 24:7–9)**
Chrysostom highlights several flaws in Tertullus's speech:
- **Unsupported accusations:** Paul is charged with trying "to profane the temple," but [Tertullus] does not say how.
- **Exaggeration and minimization:** Tertullus magnified what concerned Paul, but see how he diminished what concerned him.
- **Shifting blame to Lysias:** The accusers present themselves as reluctant litigants. Chrysostom summarizes that Tertullus claims that it was unpleasant to them to come to foreign courts and that they would have not given trouble to [Felix], if he had not forced them, and that it was not right for Lysias to take Paul away.
- **The irony of "violence":** On Tertullus's complaint that Lysias acted "with great violence," Chrysostom remarks pointedly, "That, indeed, was violence."

**3. Accusers acting as witnesses**
Chrysostom says Tertullus puts Paul in the position to become his own accuser. He also exposes a basic unfairness in the proceedings: the very witnesses of the things that were said, they are the accusers—they are the witnesses and the accusers. The point is that Paul faced a trial in which his opponents both brought the charges and supplied the testimony.

**4. Felix's political motives (likely Acts 24:27)**
A brief, fragmentary excerpt concerns Felix's treatment of Paul. Even after speaking with him, for it was towards the end of his government— he left him bound, willing to show the Jews a pleasure. The excerpt is short and lacks context, but it appears to stress that political expediency, not justice, kept Paul in chains.

## Bede

**The term "Nazarenes" (Acts 24:5)**
Bede explains the background of Tertullus's description of Paul as a leader of the "sect of the Nazarenes." He notes that at that time Christians were called Nazarenes as an insult. He then distinguishes this early usage from a later group: Afterwards, however, a heretical sect arose among the Jews, which was called the Nazarenes.

The rest of the passage appears in quotation marks, which suggests Bede is citing an earlier source rather than writing in his own words. That source affirms the group's orthodox beliefs: "They believed in Christ as the son of God, born of the virgin Mary, and they said that it was he who suffered under Pontius Pilate and rose from the grave." It nevertheless faults them: "But while they wanted to be both Jews and Christians, they were neither Jews nor Christians." The theological point is that right belief about Christ was not enough for this group, because their attempt to hold on to both identities left them belonging fully to neither.

## Summary

- **Chrysostom** presents Acts 24 as a study in unjust accusation. Paul's opponents use flattery, unsupported charges, and blame-shifting, and they act as both accusers and witnesses. Felix keeps Paul imprisoned to please the Jewish leaders.
- **Bede** clarifies that "Nazarene" was originally an insult aimed at Christians. He separates this from a later sect whose divided loyalties left them, in the view of the source he quotes, neither truly Jewish nor truly Christian.

# Patristic Commentary on Mark 13: A Summary

The excerpts come from two commentators, Origen of Alexandria and the Venerable Bede. They focus on the opening of Mark 13: Jesus's prophecy of the temple's destruction, the disciples' private question on the Mount of Olives, and his warning against deceivers.

**A note on sources:** Origen's excerpt comes from his *Commentary on Matthew*, not a commentary on Mark. It is included here because it discusses the "stone upon stone" prophecy, which appears in both Gospels (Mark 13:2).

---

## Origen of Alexandria: The Soul as a Temple

Origen reads the temple's destruction as a picture of the believer's spiritual life.

- **The temple fell gradually.** He observes that the temple was not overthrown all at once, but gradually as time went by.
- **The believer is a temple.** Every one who welcomes the Word of God into himself is something like a temple.
- **Sin damages the temple partially or completely.**
  - A person who sins but keeps traces of faith and accountability to God's commands, he is a temple partly destroyed, partly standing.
  - A person who keeps drifting till he completely departs from the living God, he is a temple in which no stone of doctrine is left upon any stone and not thrown down.

**Key insight:** Origen turns a historical prophecy into a warning about the soul. Spiritual ruin, like the temple's, usually happens step by step through neglect.

---

## Bede: Three Themes

### 1. Why the Temple Had to Fall

Bede accepts the plain historical meaning, noting that according to history, the meaning is clear. He then draws out several theological points:

- **The Law lost its center.** When the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures of the law and the composition of the commandments were so destroyed that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews; and with the head removed, all the members clashed among themselves.
- **The narrative sequence matters.** Bede links this passage to the widow's offering just before it. It was fitting for the Lord, after praising the devotion of the Church in the poor widow, to leave the temple, and to predict its future ruin.
- **The destruction protected new believers.** Bede sees the temple's removal as a provision of God. Otherwise someone still young and suckling in the faith, seeing those things which were made by the holy prophets and instituted by the Lord remaining, might wonder at the secular sanctity and gradually slip from the sincerity of the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
- **The shadow gives way to the truth.** God removed the temple so that with the shadow and type ceasing, the truth now declared throughout the world might hold the greater palm.

### 2. The Mount of Olives as a Symbol of the Church

- **Jesus's position fits his words.** Jesus sits opposite the temple so that even in the very position of his body he aligns with the words he speaks, mystically indicating that while resting in the holy, he detests the madness of the proud.
- **The mountain signifies the Church.** Bede asks, who does not see that the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful height of the holy Church, which the Lord always delights to dwell in?
- **Olives carry meaning.** They provide light to dispel the shadows of the night, cures for infirmities, and rest for the weary. Bede connects this to Psalm 52: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God; I trust in the mercy of God forever.

### 3. Warning Against Deceivers

Bede applies Jesus's warning that many will come in my name saying, I am he, and they will lead many astray at several levels:

- **Historically:** as the destruction of Jerusalem approached, there were leaders who claimed they were christs, and reported that the time of liberation was near at hand.
- **Within the Church:** Many heresiarchs appeared in the Church even in the times of the apostles, who, among many other things contrary to truth, proclaimed that the day of the Lord was imminent. Bede notes that these the Apostle condemns in the Epistle to the Thessalonians.
- **The first antichrist:** Bede names Simon Magus as the first of many antichrists. Citing Acts 8, he says all in Samaria followed him because he had for a long time bewitched them with his magical arts.

---

## Comparing the Two

| | **Origen** | **Bede** |
|---|---|---|
| **Main focus** | The individual soul | Salvation history and the Church |
| **The temple stands for** | The believer who receives the Word | The old order of the Law, now replaced by the Gospel |
| **Main concern** | Gradual personal falling away | New believers being drawn back to the old forms, and false teachers |

Both readers see more than a historical prediction in Mark 13. Both are also concerned with the danger of slowly slipping from faith: Origen through personal sin, Bede through attraction to outdated religious forms and false teachers.

**Scope:** These excerpts cover only the first part of Mark 13. The later sections of the chapter, such as the coming of the Son of Man, the fig tree, and the call to watchfulness, are not addressed in the material provided.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 48: A Summary

## Jerome: Close Reading of the Text

Jerome's notes are textual and historical rather than allegorical.

**Joseph's two sons (v. 1).** Jerome uses this verse to support an argument he made earlier: that Joseph had only two sons in that place, Ephraim and Manasseh. He reasons that if many years later, when Jacob his father died, he led only two sons for the blessing, surely at that time, when his sons were unable to beget children, being young and nursing infants, he could not have grandchildren from them at the entrance of his father and brothers. His point is about the chronology and makeup of Jacob's family when it arrived in Egypt.

**"Bed" or "rod" (v. 2).** On the phrase "And Israel, strengthened, sat upon the bed," Jerome points out an inconsistency in the Greek Septuagint. He admits he does not know why the translators rendered one Hebrew word in two ways, but says the word itself, Meta, which they translated here as bed, in the place where we have said above that Jacob worshipped on it, they have rather called a rod than a bed. This reflects his concern with reading the Hebrew original rather than relying only on the Greek translation.

## Cyril of Alexandria: Adoption into God's Family

Cyril reads the chapter as a picture of the Gentiles being brought into God's people through Christ.

**The last become first.** The excerpt opens in the middle of his argument with the claim that we the last became the first through faith, and the nation of the Gentiles inherited the glory of the firstborn. He says they obtained that honor through obedience and faith. The excerpt does not say which detail of Genesis 48 prompts this point, so its exact link to the narrative is implied rather than stated.

**Jacob's adoption as a type.** Cyril's main image is Jacob adopting his grandsons: see how through Jacob's love for Joseph he placed the sons of Joseph among his own sons. In the same way, we are also beloved in Christ, and after we were born again through him in a spiritual generation, we are received by the Father and added to the saints who preceded us.

**Christ as mediator.** Believers come from many nations, but Christ is sufficient for us as a mediator, who unites us to God the Father. Cyril concludes that even though we are called children of God, nonetheless we will be children of Christ, and he links this to Christ's words to the Father: "Those whom you gave me from the world were yours, and you gave them to me, and I have been glorified in them."

## Ambrose of Milan: The Thirteenth Tribe and the Apostle Paul

Ambrose offers a symbolic reading based on numbers. After noting that Joseph presented his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, and Jacob blessed them, he draws a parallel: because Jacob had twelve sons, and Paul, as one chosen later, was going to be the thirteenth apostle, a thirteenth tribe would thus be sanctified from the descendants of Manasseh and Ephraim, and divided between them both.

For Ambrose, this means Paul would not appear outside the enumeration of the tribes of the fathers. As a preacher of both Testaments, Paul could affirm that the inheritance of a father's blessing was of help to himself as well.

## Common Thread

Cyril and Ambrose both treat Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh as a sign that people who come "later" can be fully included in God's family. For Cyril, this means the Gentile church. For Ambrose, it means the apostle Paul. Jerome, by contrast, focuses on the literal text, its chronology, and the accuracy of its translation.

# Patristic Commentary on Hebrews 13: A Summary

All four excerpts relate to **Hebrews 13:4**, the verse on honoring marriage and God's judgment of sexual immorality. Each Father uses it differently.

---

## 1. Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 32.11)
**Focus: The verse as a warning against excusing sexual sin**

Augustine uses the verse pastorally, to confront people who downplay sexual sin.

- **Rejecting rationalizations:** He describes people who hunt about for heaven knows what null and worthless proofs in their support, and say, "God does not mind the sins of the flesh."
- **Scripture as the answer:** He counters with the text itself: "what about what we have heard today, 'God will judge the immoral and adulterous'?"
- **God's voice over self-justification:** He urges listeners to listen to what God is saying, not to what your own prejudice is saying in favor of your sins, or to your friend, perhaps, chained with the same shackles of wickedness as yourself—though in fact he is more your enemy and his own.

**Key insight:** Sin rationalizes itself, often with the help of companions in the same sin. Augustine treats such "friends" as enemies in disguise.

---

## 2. Eusebius of Caesarea (Proof of the Gospel 1.9)
**Focus: Marriage among laity and clergy**

Eusebius uses the verse to show that the new covenant affirms marriage while also making room for clerical continence.

- **Marriage affirmed:** According to the laws of the new covenant, the producing of children is certainly not forbidden, but the provisions are similar to those followed by the ancient men of God.
- **Higher standard for priests:** He holds that it is fitting that those in the priesthood and occupied in the service of God should abstain after ordination from the intercourse of marriage.
- **Hebrews 13:4 applied to everyone else:** To all who have not undertaken this wondrous priesthood, Scripture almost completely gives way, when it says, "Let marriage be held in honor, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the immoral and adulterous."

**Key insight:** Eusebius reads the verse as Scripture's broad permission of marriage for those not in priestly service. This reflects an early two-tiered view of Christian vocation.

---

## 3. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, Book IV)
**Focus: The verse as a decisive word on marriage**

The excerpt is brief. Clement presents the verse as settling a debate, saying that as putting the finishing stroke to the question about marriage, he adds: "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

**Key insight:** Clement treats Hebrews 13:4 as conclusive in defending marriage's honor. The excerpt does not identify who "he" is or what the surrounding argument was, so little more can be drawn from it.

---

## 4. Ephrem the Syrian (Commentary on Tatian's Diatessaron 10–11)
**Note: This excerpt does not clearly address Hebrews 13.**

Ephrem is mainly interpreting Matthew's statement that Joseph "knew her not until she had borne a son," and defending Mary's perpetual virginity:

- He argues that "until" is not the end limit, citing Psalm 110 as a parallel.
- He explains the "brothers of our Lord" by noting that "Because our Lord entrusted his mother Mary to John, it is clear that these are not her sons, nor is Joseph her husband."

The only possible connection is his question, "Is not marriage pure, according to the testimony of the apostle, 'The fruit of their womb is pure'?" The quotation does not match the wording of Hebrews 13:4, and the excerpt does not say it refers to Hebrews. It may share the theme of marriage's purity, but linking it firmly to Hebrews 13 would be speculation.

---

## Summary of Themes

| Commentator | Main use of Hebrews 13:4 |
|---|---|
| **Augustine** | A warning against excusing sexual sin; God's judgment is real |
| **Eusebius** | Affirms marriage for laity, with continence fitting for clergy |
| **Clement** | The decisive scriptural word on marriage's honor |
| **Ephrem** | No clear connection; concerned with Mary's virginity |

The Fathers in these excerpts hold together two sides of the verse: the **honor of marriage** (stressed by Eusebius and Clement) and the **seriousness of God's judgment on sexual immorality** (stressed by Augustine).

# Bede on Revelation 15: Summary of Key Insights

**A note on sources:** All four excerpts come from a single commentator, the Venerable Bede, so this summary covers only his views. The excerpts address verses 1, 5, 6, and 7. Bede's comments on verses 2–4 (the sea of glass and the song of Moses and the Lamb) and verse 8 are not included.

## 1. The "Great and Marvelous Sign" and the Last Plagues (v. 1)

- **A call to attention:** Bede sees the chapter as returning to an earlier theme. With the order again restored, about to narrate the same plagues of the final persecution, he wanted the listener to be attentive by saying: A great and marvelous sign.
- **The angels as the Church:** Bede reads the seven angels symbolically, as the Church full of sevenfold grace.
- **Why "seven" and why "last":** Bede links the plagues to a biblical pattern of complete judgment. Because in them the wrath of God is completed, he called them the last: for the wrath of God always strikes the rebellious people with seven plagues, that is, perfect ones, as frequently in Leviticus. He adds a timing point: These will be the last when the Church has departed from its midst.

## 2. The Opened Temple (v. 5)

- Bede connects this vision to the song in the preceding verses: The vision harmonizes with the song.
- He reads the opened temple as the spread of God's revelation beyond Israel: For the Lord to be worshipped by all nations, that temple of God's secrets, once enclosed within the walls of a single city, has now begun to be spiritually opened to the whole world.

## 3. The Angels Going Out and Their Clothing (v. 6)

- **Going out as mission:** Bede links the angels leaving the temple to the apostolic mission: This is what Mark says: But they went out and preached everywhere.
- **Clothing as putting on Christ:** He interprets the angels' garments through baptism, citing Paul: As many (the Apostle says) as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. He also calls Christ the supreme cornerstone chosen, though the excerpt does not fully explain how this image connects to the clothing.
- **Alternative readings:** Bede offers more than one interpretation. Or if you understand the singular number for the plural, it signifies various ornaments of virtues. Following another translation, he sees the white linen as indicating the mortification of the heart for teachers, supported by Paul's words about disciplining his body so that, having preached to others, he would not himself be disqualified.
- **Golden belts as wisdom and love:** For Bede, preachers need more than self-discipline: Whoever wants to preach strong things should not only mortify the body but also gird the chest with the gold of wisdom. Alternatively, to gird the chest with golden belts is to restrain all the movements of mutable thoughts with the bonds of God's love alone.

## 4. The Bowls: Prayer and Judgment Together (v. 7)

- Bede identifies these bowls with the earlier bowls of incense, again seeing the Church in the imagery: These are the bowls which the living creatures and elders, who are the Church, bear with odors, who are also the seven angels.
- This leads to perhaps his most striking insight: the same bowls hold both prayer and wrath. For the same bowls are said to contain both the sweetness of supplications and the wrath of punishments, when they are poured out by the saints for the coming of God's kingdom, when God's judgments, no longer hidden like an abyss, but open as bowls, bring salvation to the righteous, but are proclaimed to bring ruin to the wicked. He supports this with Paul's description of believers as the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.

## Overarching Themes in Bede's Reading

1. **Ecclesial interpretation:** The angels, living creatures, and elders all point to the Church.
2. **Judgment through proclamation:** The angels' going out is the Church's preaching, and God's judgments are revealed, not hidden, as the gospel goes out.
3. **Character of the preacher:** The angels' clothing and belts describe the discipline, wisdom, and love required of those who teach.
4. **The double effect of the gospel:** One message brings salvation to some and judgment to others, as shown by the bowls that hold both prayers and wrath.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 3: A Summary

**Note on scope:** All four excerpts deal with the opening verses of the chapter (3:1–2), where Paul asks whether he needs "letters of commendation." They do not address the rest of the chapter, so this summary covers only that opening theme.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 6 on Second Corinthians)

Chrysostom gives the fullest treatment, focusing on Paul's humility and pastoral skill.

**1. Paul answers an objection before anyone raises it.**
Chrysostom notes that Paul anticipates and puts himself an objection which others would have urged against him, 'You vaunt yourself;' He does this even though he had already guarded against that charge with the words "Who is sufficient for these things?" (2:16–17). Howbeit he is not satisfied with these.

**2. Paul's character shows deep humility.**
For Chrysostom, this reflects who Paul is: From appearing to say anything great of himself he is far removed, and avoids it even to great superfluity and excess.

**3. Paul transforms suffering into glory.**
Chrysostom highlights Paul's wisdom in how he presents hardship: For a thing of woeful aspect, I mean tribulations, he so much exalted and showed to be bright and lustrous, that out of what he said the present objection rose up against him. The context is that Paul spoke of his trials and his perils, and that every where he is conducted as in procession by God in Christ, and that the whole world knows of these triumphs. Having said such great things, he worries they will sound like self-praise.

**4. Paul adjusts his tone to the situation.**
Chrysostom contrasts this passage with later ones in the letter. In chapter 3, the words are those of love, "Need we, as do some, epistles of commendation?" Later, his tone is full of a kind of pride even, necessarily and properly so, of pride, I say, and anger. The later sharpness serves to prevent all appearance of a wish to flatter, as though he desired honor from them. That sharper language comes after many accusations ; But in the beginning he speaks not so, but more gently.

**5. The Corinthians themselves are Paul's credentials.**
Paul's answer to the suspicion of boasting is: We desire not this, that is, to boast and exalt ourselves; yea, so far are we from needing epistles of commendation to you that you are to us instead of an epistle. In another homily, Chrysostom paraphrases Paul this way: "If we needed to be commended to others," he says, "we would have produced you before them rather than a letter."

---

## Theodoret of Cyrus

Theodoret's brief comment shifts responsibility onto the congregation. In his reading, Paul is telling the Corinthians that they should have been commending him without any reminders of this kind. Paul's question carries a mild rebuke: the church he founded should have spoken up for him.

---

## Didymus the Blind

Didymus emphasizes Paul's tone. He observes that Paul gently expresses his surprise that the Corinthians are still unaware of the implication of his apostleship. The Corinthians should have understood what Paul's apostolic ministry among them already showed.

---

## Common Threads

- **Gentleness:** Chrysostom and Didymus both describe Paul's approach here as gentle rather than harsh.
- **The church as evidence:** Chrysostom and Theodoret both suggest that the Corinthian believers should themselves vouch for Paul's ministry, without needing to be prompted.
- **Humility in ministry:** Chrysostom shows Paul working to defend his ministry without exalting himself.

# Patristic Insights on Philippians 4

The excerpts address two passages in the chapter: Paul's call to "stand fast" (v. 1) and his appeal on behalf of his co-workers, including the "yokefellow" (vv. 2–3).

## John Chrysostom

### On standing firm (Homily 13)
Chrysostom focuses on how Paul encourages the Philippians and what steadfastness means.

- **Steadfastness means being unshaken.** He explains Paul's "so" by asking: "So." How? Unmoved.
- **Exhortation paired with affection.** He notes Paul's pastoral method: See how he adds praise after exhortation, "my joy and my crown," not simply joy but glory too, not simply glory but my crown too. He adds that this is a glory nought can equal, since it is the crown of Paul.
- **The ground of firmness.** He interprets "in the Lord" as "So stand fast in the Lord, my beloved," i.e. in the hope of God. Christian stability rests on hope in God, not human strength.

### On the women who labored with Paul (Homily 14)
The excerpt does not name the women, but Chrysostom clearly honors their role.

- **High spiritual standing.** He compares Paul's praise of them to Christ's words to the apostles: Do you see how great is the virtue of these women, according to his testimony? As great as that which Christ told his apostles … "your names are written in the book of life."
- **Real partners in ministry.** They contributed in no small part. Even though there were many fellow workers, yet in many affairs they also took a hand.
- **Honor and church unity.** He links mutual respect to the church's health: Great therefore was the cohesion of the church at that time when the most respected, whether men or women, enjoyed such honor from the rest.

## Theodoret of Cyrus

### On the identity of the "yokefellow" (4:3)
Theodoret rejects one interpretation directly: Now some have been foolish enough to suppose that the yokefellow was his wife, not considering that when he wrote to the Corinthians he reckoned himself among the unmarried. He reads Paul's letters together, using one to clarify another. His conclusion is that the term describes a spiritual partnership: the yokefellow is so called because he bore the same yoke of piety.

## Clement of Alexandria

### On the "yokefellow"
Clement takes a different angle: Paul at least is not afraid in one of his letters to give the name yokefellow to the one whom, for the convenience of his ministry, he did not lead about with him.

It suggests Clement saw the yokefellow as a close companion whom Paul chose not to bring along for the sake of his ministry.
