# Patristic Commentary on John 3: Nicodemus's Night Visit

**A note on scope:** All four excerpts focus on the opening of John 3, which covers Nicodemus's coming to Jesus by night and his first words to Him. None of them discuss the later parts of the chapter, such as Jesus's teaching on new birth or His reply to Nicodemus. Chrysostom's excerpt ends just as he is about to turn to Jesus's answer, so this summary covers only Nicodemus's approach and opening statement.

---

## Bede

Bede gives a short, generous reading. He sees Nicodemus as a genuine believer whose night visit reflects spiritual immaturity rather than bad faith. Nicodemus was one of the many who believed in Jesus, and therefore he came at night, and not during the day because he was not yet illumined with the gracious heavenly light. In this reading, the darkness of the hour mirrors the incomplete enlightenment of the man.

---

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom gives the fullest treatment. His main insights are these:

**1. Nicodemus's whole story.** Chrysostom places this scene within Nicodemus's later actions in the Gospel. He notes that Nicodemus appears also in the middle of the Gospel, making defense for Christ, and that after the crucifixion he bestowed great care upon the burial of the Lord's body.

**2. Well-disposed but fearful.** At this point Nicodemus was disposed towards Christ, but not as he ought, nor with proper sentiments respecting Him, for he was as yet entangled in Jewish infirmity. Unlike Bede, Chrysostom names fear as the reason for the night visit: he came by night, because he feared to do so by day.

**3. Christ's mercy toward weak faith.** Jesus did not turn Nicodemus away. Yet not for this did the merciful God reject or rebuke him, or deprive him of His instruction, but even with much kindness conversed with him and disclosed to him very exalted doctrines, enigmatically indeed, but nevertheless He disclosed them. Chrysostom separates fear from malice: far more deserving of pardon was he than those who acted thus through wickedness. He supports Christ's gentleness by citing the prophecy that A bruised reed shall He not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench.

**4. What Nicodemus's confession gets wrong.** Nicodemus's words ("a Teacher come from God") sound respectful, but Chrysostom finds them inadequate. Nicodemus yet lingers below, has yet human thoughts concerning Him, and speaks of Him as of a Prophet, imagining nothing great from His miracles. Saying that "God is with him" implies that Christ depends on outside help. Here Nicodemus speaks like the heretics, in saying, that He has a power working within Him, and has need of the aid of others to do as He did.

**5. Why Jesus speaks indirectly.** Chrysostom explains why Jesus does not simply declare His divinity. He refrained for a while from saying, I need not the help of others, but do all things with power, for I am the Very Son of God, and have the same power as My Father, because this would have been too hard for His hearer. Chrysostom contrasts Christ's careful words with His commanding deeds. In miracles He does all with power, and he lists examples from the Gospels. So with Nicodemus, Jesus utters nothing openly, but by dark sayings leads him up from his low thoughts, teaching him, that He has sufficient power in Himself to show forth miracles.

**6. How far Nicodemus has to go.** Chrysostom closes with a vivid image. Nicodemus had not yet set foot even on the threshold of right knowledge, nor stood in the porch, but was yet wandering somewhere without the palace.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

Cyril is the sharpest critic of Nicodemus's motives. His two excerpts address both the man's divided heart and his mistaken view of Christ.

**1. A divided heart.** Cyril sees a man pulled in two directions. His conscience pushed him toward belief by reason of the exceedingness of the miracles, yet he regarded the loss of rulership over his own nation a thing not to be borne, for he was a ruler of the Jews. The night visit was therefore a deliberate strategy. Deeming that he can both preserve his repute with them, and be a disciple secretly, he cometh to Jesus, making the darkness of the night an aider of his scheme, and by his secret coming convicted of double mindedness.

**2. Admiration is not saving faith.** Cyril warns that Nicodemus imagines that he can become pious enough to attain salvation merely by marveling at the wonders Jesus had done.

**3. A deficient Christology.** Like Chrysostom, Cyril finds Nicodemus's confession too small. By calling Jesus a teacher from God and a co-worker with him, he does not yet know that Jesus is by nature God, nor does Nicodemus understand the plan of salvation according to the flesh. Instead, he still approaches Jesus as a mere man and has only a slight conception of who he is.

---

## Common Threads and Differences

- **Why Nicodemus came at night:** Bede points to incomplete spiritual enlightenment. Chrysostom points to fear and treats it as pardonable weakness. Cyril points to calculated double-mindedness aimed at protecting his status.
- **What his confession reveals:** Chrysostom and Cyril agree that calling Jesus "a Teacher come from God" falls short. Nicodemus sees a prophet or empowered man, not the divine Son.
- **Christ's response:** Chrysostom alone stresses Christ's gentle, step-by-step teaching. Jesus meets a weak believer where he is and leads him upward rather than rebuking him.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 11: A Summary

## John Chrysostom: Why Jesus Withdrew

Two excerpts are attributed to Chrysostom. They are essentially two translations of the same passage, so they are treated together here. The passage concerns the transition after Jesus sent out his apostles.

- **Making room for the disciples' ministry:** After Jesus commissioned the apostles, he proceeded to separate himself from them, to give them room and opportunity to do what he had called them to do.
- **The practical reason:** For while he was present with them and healing others, no one would be inclined to approach them.

**Insight:** Chrysostom reads Jesus' departure as a deliberate act of empowerment. Jesus steps back so his followers can grow into the work he has given them.

## Theodore of Mopsuestia: John the Baptist's Question from Prison

Theodore addresses why John sent his disciples to question Jesus. His argument is dense and at times hard to follow, but its main points are:

- **John was not ignorant of who Jesus was.** Theodore points out that John had already said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." He already knew very well that the Messiah would offer his suffering up to God for the sake of all humanity. He concludes that it is hardly conceivable that John was ignorant about the Christ but now was guessing and wanted to find out for sure from him.
- **The question was about life beyond death.** In Theodore's reading, when John was about to die and join the departed, he sent them to ask whether he was the one who was to come and free those who had been vanquished by death.
- **The question also served his disciples.** In this way the good news was delivered to his disciples as well.

**A broader theological digression:** Theodore then signals that there is another point being made here. From there he moves into wider questions of salvation that go beyond the immediate text of Matthew 11:

- The present life is the time when we must conduct ourselves responsibly. After death there is judgment and punishment.
- He holds that Christ's death did not universally redeem the sins of all those who had already died.
- He sees a change between the eras before and after Christ. Before Christ it was enough to refrain from idolatry and to worship the one true God in order to be saved. But now that alone is not enough. We must also know Christ personally.

**Insight:** Theodore defends John's prophetic understanding. He also uses the episode to reflect on death, judgment, and the necessity of knowing Christ, although this second section connects only loosely to the chapter itself.

## Hilary of Poitiers: John as a Figure of the Law

Hilary offers a symbolic, or allegorical, reading. He states that a fuller spiritual meaning is to be found in these actions, which were being accomplished in and through John.

- **John represents the Law.** The law rose up and took shape in John. For the law announced Christ, predicted the forgiveness of sins and promised the kingdom of heaven.
- **John's imprisonment symbolizes the Law held back by sin.** The law was oppressed as it was by the sins of the common people and held in chains by the vicious habits of the nation, so that Christ could not be perceived.
- **Sending the disciples symbolizes the Law pointing to the Gospel.** The law (i.e., John) sent others to behold the good news. In this way unbelief would be confronted with the accomplished truth of what had been prophesied.
- **The Law is freed through the Gospel.** By this means the part of the law that had been chained by the misdeeds of sinners would now be freed through the understanding of the good news freely expressed.

# Patristic Commentary on John 2: The Wedding at Cana

All four excerpts address the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11). Augustine's sermon is by far the most extensive, so it receives the most attention below.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

### 1. The miracle points to God's everyday wonders
Augustine argues that turning water into wine should not surprise anyone who knows it was God's doing. He who made wine on that day at the marriage feast, in those six water-pots, which He commanded to be filled with water, the self-same does this every year in vines. We overlook the yearly miracle because it happens every year: it has lost its marvellousness by its constant recurrence. So God has, as it were, reserved to Himself the doing of certain extraordinary actions, that, by striking them with wonder, He might rouse men as from sleep to worship Him. He gives a striking example: A dead man has risen again; men marvel: so many are born daily, and none marvels.

### 2. The same Word creates and works the miracle
The Creator and the miracle-worker are the same person. The former miracles He did by His Word, God with Himself; the latter miracles He did by the same Word incarnate, and for us made man. In the Incarnation, He was not made man in such manner that He lost His being God. Man was added to Him, God not lost to Him. The right response is therefore not mere amazement: Let us not therefore wonder that God did it, but love Him because He did it in our midst, and for the purpose of our restoration.

### 3. Our spiritual transformation
Augustine sees the miracle as a picture of what Christ does in believers: for we were water, and He made us wine, made us wise; for He gave us the wisdom of His faith, while before we were foolish.

### 4. Christ the Bridegroom
Christ's presence at a wedding reflects His mission. What wonder if He came to that house to a marriage, having come into this world to a marriage? The Church is His bride, whom He has redeemed by His blood, and to whom He has given the Holy Spirit as a pledge. Augustine contrasts this with earthly gifts: men offer jewels and estates, but will any give his own blood? He also applies the image to the Incarnation: the Word was the Bridegroom, and human flesh the bride, and the womb of the Virgin Mary, in which He became head of the Church, was His bridal chamber.

### 5. "Woman, what have I to do with you?" (against the heretics)
Some heretics, whom Augustine later identifies as the Manichæans, used this verse to argue that Jesus was not truly born of Mary. Augustine answers that the same Gospel writer reports both facts: The mother of Jesus was there, said the evangelist; and it is the same evangelist that has told us what Jesus said to His mother. One cannot accept one statement and reject the other. He insists that Christ's full humanity matters, since Christ is true man, true God, true nativity, true passion, true death, true resurrection. For those still puzzled, his counsel is: Let him first have the piety to believe, and he will then have fruit in understanding. He distinguishes honest inquiry from unbelief: It is one thing to be willing to understand what is shut up, another thing to be unwilling to believe what is open.

### 6. The meaning of Jesus' reply
Augustine's own interpretation rests on Christ's two natures. According as He was God, He had not a mother; according as He was man, He had. She was the mother, then, of His flesh, of His humanity, of the weakness which for our sakes He took upon Him. Because the miracle would be done through His divine nature, Jesus was saying in effect, That in me which works a miracle was not born of you, you gave not birth to my divine nature; but because my weakness was born of you, I will recognize you at the time when that same weakness shall hang upon the cross. This is fulfilled at the crucifixion, when Jesus entrusts Mary to the disciple: That hour had now come, the hour of which He had then said, Mine hour is not yet come. He sums up the point this way: Christ is Mary's son after the flesh, and Mary's Lord after His majesty.

### 7. "My hour" is not fate (against the astrologers)
Astrologers claimed that "Mine hour is not yet come" showed Christ was subject to fate. Augustine responds with Christ's own words about having power to lay down His life and take it up again, and reasons that even if fate were from the stars, the Maker of the stars could not be subject to their destiny. The "hour" refers instead to the fitting time Christ Himself chose: having it in His power when to die, He did not yet see it fit to use that power. First disciples had to be called, the kingdom of heaven to be proclaimed, the Lord's divinity to be shown forth in miracles, and His humanity in His very sympathy with mortal men. When the time came, His hour came, not of necessity, but of will,— not of condition, but of power.

*Note:* Augustine raises the symbolic meaning of the water-pots, the master of the feast, and the marriage itself, but let us defer until tomorrow what pertains to the hidden meaning. That interpretation is not included in this excerpt.

---

## Eusebius of Caesarea

Eusebius reads the Cana miracle as fulfilled prophecy. He suggests the miracle is foretold in the beginning of this prophecy where it says, "Drink this first. Act quickly, land of Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles." The excerpt does not say which prophetic book he is quoting. Theologically, he sees the miracle as a sign of the mystic wine—that wine of the faith of the new covenant that is transformed from bodily joy to a joy of mind and spirit.

---

## Theodore of Mopsuestia

Theodore addresses the chronology of the opening phrase "the third day" (John 2:1) rather than its theology. It is evident that this third day should be calculated as the third day after the baptism. He counts the days: the first was when Andrew and his companion followed him and then passed the night with him, the second relates the events concerning Philip and Nathanael, and the third day points to the events of this wedding party. His contribution is a framework that connects Cana to the calling of the first disciples in John 1.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

Cyril finds significance in where the wedding took place. The wedding was not held in Jerusalem but outside of Judea, as it were, in the country of the Gentiles—"Galilee of the Gentiles," as the prophet said. He interprets this as a sign of salvation history: the synagogue of the Jews rejected the Bridegroom from heaven and that the church of the Gentiles [gladly] received him.

---

## Common Threads

- **Christ as Bridegroom:** Augustine and Cyril both read the wedding as pointing to Christ's union with His people.
- **"Galilee of the Gentiles":** Eusebius and Cyril both cite this prophetic phrase. Eusebius uses it to show the miracle was foretold, and Cyril uses it to point to the Gentiles' reception of Christ.
- **Transformation:** Augustine (water made wine, "made us wise") and Eusebius (bodily joy transformed into spiritual joy) both treat the change of water into wine as an image of spiritual renewal.

# Patristic Commentary on Jude 1: A Summary

**A note on scope:** These excerpts focus mainly on **who Jude was**, not on the content of his letter. Only Bede addresses the letter's purpose, and only briefly. Origen and Eusebius are concerned chiefly with Jude's family ties to Jesus and James.

---

## 1. Origen of Alexandria: Jude in the Family of Jesus

Origen's comments on Jude come within a larger discussion of Jesus' relatives in Matthew 13:55–56.

**Jude among the "brethren" of Jesus.** Origen quotes the townspeople's question: "Is not His mother called Mary? And His brethren, James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?" He notes that they thought, then, that He was the son of Joseph and Mary.

**How the "brethren" were related to Jesus.** Origen reports, without fully endorsing it as fact, a view held by others. Some say, basing it on a tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is entitled, or "The Book of James," that the brethren of Jesus were sons of Joseph by a former wife, whom he married before Mary. He explains that those holding this view wish to preserve the honour of Mary in virginity to the end. His own sympathy is clear: I think it in harmony with reason that Jesus was the first-fruit among men of the purity which consists in chastity, and Mary among women.

**The importance of James.** Since Jude calls himself "brother of James," Origen's remarks on James help set the context. He cites Paul's reference to "James the Lord's brother." He also cites Josephus, who said the people's misfortunes came in accordance with the wrath of God in consequence of the things which they had dared to do against James the brother of Jesus who is called Christ. Origen finds it remarkable that though he did not accept Jesus as Christ, he yet gave testimony that the righteousness of James was so great.

**His assessment of the letter.** Origen's one direct comment on the epistle is warm praise. He describes Jude as one who wrote a letter of few lines, it is true, but filled with the healthful words of heavenly grace, and cites its opening: "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ and the brother of James."

---

## 2. Eusebius of Caesarea: Jude's Descendants

Eusebius does not comment on the epistle itself. He passes on traditions from the earlier writer **Hegesippus** about Jude's family, which bear on Jude's identity and the faithfulness of his household.

**Persecution for their Davidic lineage.** Eusebius records that when Domitian ordered that those of the race of David be slain, an ancient story holds that some of the heretics accused the grandchildren of Jude (the brother of the Savior, according to the flesh), on the ground that they really were of the family of David and were related to Christ himself.

**Faithful witness.** He adds that, according to Hegesippus, other descendants of one of the so-called brothers of the Lord, Jude by name, lived until the reign of Trajan [98-117], after giving testimony of their faith in Christ in the time of Domitian [81-96].

The cautious phrase "so-called brothers" fits the debate Origen describes over how these relatives were related to Jesus.

---

## 3. Bede: Jude's Identity and Purpose

Bede's brief comment is the only one that speaks to the **purpose** of the letter.

**Identity.** Bede identifies the author as Jude the apostle, whom Matthew and Mark call Thaddeus in the Gospel.

**Purpose.** He says Jude writes against the same corruptors of the faith whom both Peter and John condemn in their Epistles. In Bede's view, Jude joins other apostolic writers in a shared defense against false teaching.

---

## Overall Observations

- **Common focus on identity:** All three commentators care about who Jude was. Origen and Eusebius stress his kinship with Jesus and James. Bede stresses his apostolic standing.
- **Different identifications:** Origen and Eusebius place Jude among the Lord's "brethren." Bede identifies him with the apostle Thaddeus. These excerpts do not try to reconcile the two views.
- **Limited comment on content:** None of the excerpts discusses specific verses beyond Jude's opening greeting. Bede's note about opposing "corruptors of the faith" is the closest any comes to the letter's message.

# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 1: Key Insights

The main concern of the relevant excerpts is a well-known puzzle: Matthew and Luke give **different genealogies for Jesus**. Augustine and Hilary offer two different but complementary solutions. The excerpts attributed to Athanasius and Cyril do not clearly address Matthew 1.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: *Harmony of the Gospels* 2.3.5

**The problem:** Augustine acknowledges that some might be perplexed by the fact that Matthew enumerates one series of ancestors, descending through David to Joseph, while Luke specifies a different succession, tracing the ancestry from Joseph backwards through David.

**His solution is adoption.** Augustine proposes that Joseph was able to have two fathers, one blood father by whom he was born and another adoptive father by whom he was adopted. He notes that this was the custom of adoption even among that people of God, so that they could endow sonship upon those whom they had not given birth.

**Biblical precedents:**
- Moses: Pharaoh's daughter adopted Moses (and she was a foreigner).
- Jacob's grandsons: Augustine cites Jacob's words, "And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt, before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are." He adds that because of this, there were thirteen tribes, although there had been twelve sons of Jacob.

**Conclusion:** Luke included Joseph's father in his Gospel, not by whom he was begotten but by whom he was adopted. By implication, Matthew gives the line of natural descent.

**Key insight:** In Scripture, adoption confers real sonship and inheritance. Two genealogies can therefore both be true without contradiction.

---

## Hilary of Poitiers: *Commentary on Matthew* 1.1

**Two lineages, two offices.** Hilary interprets the genealogies theologically: What Matthew publishes in order of kingly succession, Luke has set forth in order of priestly origin. While Matthew recounts his paternal origin that began in Judah, Luke teaches that his ancestry was taken from the tribe of Levi.

**The Christological point.** Each in his own way demonstrates the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is both the eternal king and priest, as seen even in the fleshly origin of both of his ancestries. Hilary says the royal and priestly tribes were joined: the association of the priestly and royal tribes that was begun through David from marriage is now confirmed out of the descent from Shealtiel to Zerubbabel.

**Why Joseph's line counts for Jesus.** Hilary addresses the objection that Joseph was not Jesus' biological father. It does not matter that the origin of Joseph instead of Mary is recounted, for indeed there is one and the same blood relationship for the whole tribe. Joseph and Mary belonged to the same kinship line.

**Clan over strict lineage.** The evangelists name fathers in order not so much by their lineage as by their clan. What matters is that Christ is shown to be the son of David and Abraham.

**The levirate law.** Hilary also points to the law under which, if the oldest of a family should die without sons, the next oldest brother of the same family would take the dead man's wife in marriage. The children would count as the dead brother's, so a person could legitimately be reckoned to two "fathers."

**Key insight:** The two genealogies present Christ as both **King** (through Judah and David) and **Priest** (through Levi), even in his human ancestry.

---

## Excerpts That Do Not Clearly Address Matthew 1

**Athanasius of Alexandria:** This excerpt is introduced with a reference to Vigil. Tapsens., which suggests it may come from Vigilius of Thapsus rather than Athanasius himself. Its theme is the distinct personhood and divinity of the Son, argued from Genesis: In Genesis we find God saying, "Let Us make man in Our own Image." By this plural number showing, that there was some other person to whom He spoke. This is Trinitarian theology. It may relate in a general way to the divine identity of the child in Matthew 1, but the excerpt does not discuss that chapter.

**Cyril of Alexandria:** These excerpts from Cyril's letters address the unchanging divine nature of the Word. He writes that we account those persons mad who have suspected that so much as the shadow of change could take place in the nature of the Divine Word; it abides what it ever was, neither is nor can be changed. This teaching bears on how the incarnation is understood, but the excerpts do not mention Matthew 1 or its genealogy and birth narrative.

---

## Summary

| Commentator | Main Contribution to Matthew 1 |
|---|---|
| **Augustine** | Reconciles the genealogies through adoption: one line natural, one adoptive |
| **Hilary** | Reads the genealogies as presenting Christ as both King and Priest; stresses the shared kinship of Joseph and Mary and the levirate law |
| **Athanasius (attrib.)** | Trinitarian argument; not directly about Matthew 1 |
| **Cyril** | The immutability of the divine Word; not directly about Matthew 1 |

Augustine and Hilary agree that the genealogies do not contradict each other. Augustine's explanation is legal and historical, while Hilary's draws out the meaning of Christ's royal and priestly identity.

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Corinthians 13: Summary of Key Insights

All of the provided excerpts deal with the opening verses of the chapter: the "tongues of men and of angels," the "sounding brass," and the gifts that are worthless without love. None of them address the later parts of the chapter.

---

## Theodoret of Cyrus

**Why Paul starts with tongues:** Theodoret explains Paul's choice from the Corinthians' point of view. Paul chooses speaking in tongues as his example because the Corinthians thought that it was the greatest of the gifts. Their high regard had a historical basis: it had been given to the apostles on the day of Pentecost, before any of the others. On this reading, Paul deliberately targets the gift the Corinthians prized most.

**The nature of angelic tongues:** Theodoret gives a brief spiritual interpretation: The tongues of angels are those which are perceived by the mind, not by the ear.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 32)

Chrysostom's treatment is the most detailed of the excerpts.

**1. Exalting the gift in order to humble it.** Chrysostom reads "tongues of men" as meaning tongues of all nations in every part of the world. Paul then goes further by adding "of angels." Chrysostom stresses the rhetorical strategy: Do you see to what point he first exalted the gift, and to what afterwards he lowered and cast it down? Paul inflates the gift as much as possible so that its emptiness without love is all the more striking.

**2. "Sounding brass": worse than useless.** Chrysostom observes that Paul did not simply say, "I am nothing," but, "I have become sounding brass," a thing senseless and inanimate. Such brass emits a sound at random and in vain, and for no good end. A loveless person is not merely unprofitable but is counted by most men as one giving impertinent trouble, an annoying and wearisome kind of person. Elsewhere in the same homily he puts it bluntly: if I have no love I am not just useless but a positive nuisance.

**3. "Tongues of angels" is not a literal claim about angelic bodies.** Paul is not investing angels with a body, but what he means is this: "should I even so speak as angels are wont to discourse unto each other, without this I am nothing, nay rather a burden and an annoyance." Chrysostom supports this with a parallel from Philippians 2:10, where "every knee shall bow" in heaven does not attribute physical knees to angels. In the same way, Paul calls it "a tongue" not meaning an instrument of flesh, but intending to indicate their converse with each other by the manner which is known among us. In other words, Paul describes heavenly realities in human terms.

**4. The structure of Paul's argument.** Chrysostom notes that Paul does not stop at tongues: having depreciated all in the absence of love, he then depicts her image. The order is deliberate. He begins from the less and ascends to the greater. Chrysostom points to a reversal: whereas, when he indicated their order, he placed the gift of tongues last, this he now numbers first; by degrees, as I said, ascending to the greater gifts.

---

## Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, Book IV)

This excerpt is very brief and fragmentary. It contains only a citation of Paul: "If I give my body, and have not love, I am sounding brass, and a tinkling cymbal." Clement's wording appears to combine phrases that occur separately in the chapter: "give my body" and "sounding brass." The surrounding argument is cut off, so the excerpt does not show what point Clement draws from the verse. It confirms that he used the passage, but it offers no developed commentary that can be summarized reliably.

---

## Points of Comparison

- **Why tongues come first:** Theodoret and Chrysostom give complementary explanations. For Theodoret, it is because of the Corinthians' high (Pentecost-rooted) esteem for the gift. For Chrysostom, it reflects Paul's rhetorical method of building from lesser gifts to greater ones.
- **Angelic tongues:** Both interpret the phrase non-physically. Theodoret calls it speech perceived by the mind. Chrysostom calls it Paul's way of expressing angelic communication in human terms.
- **The central lesson:** Chrysostom states it most forcefully. Even the most exalted spiritual gifts, without love, leave a person not only empty but burdensome to others.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 5: A Summary

The excerpts come from two commentators, the Venerable Bede and Jerome. Bede reads the chapter theologically and symbolically. Jerome focuses on the language and text.

---

## Bede: *Commentary on Genesis*

### 1. The Divine Likeness: Given, Lost, and Restored
Bede treats the opening verses as the story of humanity's original dignity. Genesis 5 is the book of the first creation of man, which God made in His likeness, that he might be perpetually good, immortal, and happy by participation in His goodness. In his view, humanity's goodness and happiness come from sharing in God's goodness, not from itself.

He then traces how that likeness was progressively corrupted over the generations:
- **Adam** defiled the likeness of God by believing the enemy rather than the Creator.
- **Cain**, the firstborn, contracted the heavier punishment of a curse by envying and killing his brother.
- **Lamech**, the seventh from Adam, corrupted the established law of male and female, of which it was said, "They shall be two in one flesh" (Gen. II, 24), by taking two wives and uniting three in one flesh.

The result was that humanity so departed from the likeness of its Creator and the first blessing that by the tenth generation, except for a few whom the ark held, it deserved to be entirely destroyed.

Bede does not end in despair. He sees the restoration of the likeness in Christ: the Creator Himself granted that we might return to that likeness and blessing, being born and dying in the likeness of our nature. Believers can therefore hope to say, "We know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is", and to hear, "Come, you blessed of My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world". For Bede, Genesis 5 is a narrative of creation, fall, and redemption in miniature.

### 2. The Meaning of the Name "Adam"
Bede explains why both man and woman are called "Adam." The word is able to be applied to both sexes; hence it is rightly said that he called their names Adam, that is, Man.

He also connects the name to humanity's origin. Just as the Latin word for man relates to soil, so among the Hebrews Adam is named from the earth because man was formed from the clay of the earth; hence also Adam can be interpreted as Earthly, or red earth. He contrasts this with the Greek word *anthropos*, explained as man being one who ought to look above and lift the eyes of the mind to view the heavens. Taken together, these etymologies present humanity as formed from the earth but meant to look toward heaven.

### 3. A Symbolic Reading of the Name
Bede also sees a "mystery" in the four letters of ADAM. They match the first letters of the Greek names for the four directions: anatole (east), dysis (west), arctos (north), and mesembria (south). He concludes that it was very fitting that the name of the first man should mystically contain all the regions of the world, through whose progeny the whole world was to be filled.

# Patristic Commentary on Ephesians 6: Key Insights

The four excerpts come from three early church writers: Theodoret of Cyrus, John Chrysostom, and Jerome. Together they focus on the household instructions in Ephesians 6, especially the relationship between children and parents and the overall order of Paul's teaching.

---

## 1. Theodoret of Cyrus: The Logic of Paul's Ordering

Theodoret's main contribution is structural. He argues that Paul's sequence of instructions is intentional and theologically meaningful. He writes that the order in which he gives his injunctions is worthy of admiration.

**The sequence he traces:**
- **Husbands and wives first:** for marriage comes before childbirth.
- **Fathers and children next:** for childbirth is the fruit of marriage, since it is only after the birth that one is called a father and one called son.
- **Servants and masters last:** Finally he has set forth his instructions to servants and masters.

**Key insight:** Theodoret distinguishes between kinds of relationships. He sees marriage and parenthood as natural bonds. The master–servant relationship, by contrast, arises from the social environment, as distinguished from those arrangements that come about under the laws of nature. This suggests that the relationships Paul addresses do not all carry the same standing.

He also notes that, having given all these specific injunctions, he once again gives them a common one. The excerpt does not say what that shared instruction is, so it cannot be identified from this source alone.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: Healthy Marriages Support Faithful Children

Chrysostom also notes Paul's progression: Paul has spoken first about the husband, second about the wife; now he moves along this path to children.

**Responsibility in the household:**
He describes layered responsibility: The husband is responsible for the wife. Both the husband and the wife are responsible for the children.

**Pastoral sensitivity:**
He observes that Paul adapts his tone to his audience: He speaks to children in an infant voice.

**Key insight: the marriage shapes the home.**
Chrysostom believes that obedient children grow out of a well-ordered marriage. Paul is well aware that if husband and wife are well disposed according to the commands he has laid down, there will be little difficulty in eliciting the cooperation of children.

**The limits of obedience:**
He raises a hard question: But what if the parents command foolish things? His answer is that generally parents do not command foolish things. If they do, the apostle has a remedy when he says that parents are to be obeyed "in the Lord." In other words, they are to be obeyed in whatever way they are not offending against God.

---

## 3. Jerome: Two Readings of "In the Lord" and the Commandment's Origins

**Interpreting an ambiguous phrase:**
Jerome notes a grammatical ambiguity in Ephesians 6:1: It is not clear whether this saying means that children are to obey their "parents in the Lord" or that in the Lord children are to obey their parents. Rather than choose one, he says, I take it both ways.

- **Spiritual parents:** We are to obey those parents who gave birth to us in the Lord, as through Paul and the apostles they were spiritually born, and do what they say.
- **Natural parents:** we should submit in the Lord to our own parents, from whom we were born according to the flesh, performing all their commands that are not contrary to the Lord's will.

**Key insight:** Jerome widens the idea of "parents" to include those who bring others to faith. He also agrees with Chrysostom that obedience to earthly parents is limited by God's will.

**The commandment with a promise:**
In a second excerpt, Jerome comments that a promise is attached to this commandment.… It is found in the Decalogue. He places it within the Ten Commandments: It is the first command in the second table of the law. He also notes its historical setting: It was given to the people as they were leaving Egypt. The excerpt does not quote the commandment itself, though from context it refers to the commandment about parents that Paul cites.

---

## Common Threads

- **Order matters:** Theodoret and Chrysostom both see Paul's sequence (marriage, then children, then wider household) as deliberate, with each relationship building on the one before.
- **Obedience has limits:** Chrysostom and Jerome independently read "in the Lord" as a safeguard. Children owe obedience to parents, but never in ways that go against God.
- **Rooted in Scripture and nature:** Jerome ties Paul's teaching back to the Ten Commandments, while Theodoret distinguishes natural family bonds from relationships created by social arrangement.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 15: The Parable of the Lost Sheep

All four excerpts deal with one passage, the Parable of the Lost Sheep. None of them addresses the other parables in the chapter, the lost coin or the prodigal son, so this summary covers only the lost sheep.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

**1. The hundred sheep represent all rational creation.**
Cyril reads the parable as a picture of the scope of Christ's rule: "We may hence understand the extent of our Savior's kingdom." The hundred sheep mean the number of rational creatures subject to Him, since the number hundred is perfect, being composed of ten decades.

**2. The lost sheep is humanity.**
The one that strayed is the race of man which inhabits earth.

**3. God's care for the one does not neglect the many.**
Cyril asks whether God was angry with the rest, and moved by kindness only to one? His answer is no, because they are in safety, the right hand of the Most Mighty being their defense.

**4. Rescuing the lost makes creation whole again.**
For Cyril, saving humanity restores God's whole creation. It behoved Him rather to pity the perishing, that the remaining number might not seem imperfect. For the one being brought back, the hundred regains its own proper form.

---

## Bede

**1. A parable about both us and God.**
Bede quotes the opening question, "Which one of you, having a hundred sheep, and if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one which is lost until he finds it?" He sees it as working on two levels: it is something man can recognize in himself, and it also particularly pertains to the very Creator of men.

**2. Angels and humans together form the hundred.**
Like Cyril, Bede treats one hundred as a perfect number. He says God had a hundred sheep when He created the substance of angels and men. But one sheep was lost when man, by sinning, abandoned the pastures of life.

**3. Heaven as the "wilderness."**
Bede's most distinctive point is his reading of the "wilderness." The ninety-nine are left there because He left those lofty choirs of angels in heaven. He explains why heaven would be called a wilderness: because it is said to be abandoned, for Man deserted heaven when he sinned.

**4. The search completes heaven's number.**
The company of rational creatures, namely angels and men, made to see God, was diminished by the loss of man, and in order to complete the perfect number of sheep in heaven, the lost man was sought on earth.

**5. The shepherd's shoulders point to the Incarnation and Atonement.**
On the verse "And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing," Bede gives a Christ-centered reading: He laid the sheep on his shoulders because, taking on human nature, He Himself bore our sins.

---

## Irenaeus of Lyons

The Irenaeus excerpt needs careful reading. It is fragmentary, and much of it reports the views of opponents he is arguing against rather than his own interpretation.

**1. Describing a misuse of the parable.**
Irenaeus reports that certain teachers claimed the parable referred to their figure "Achamoth." They said that Achamoth wandered beyond the Pleroma, and received form from Christ, and was sought after by the Saviour, and that Christ meant this when He said, that He had come after that sheep which was gone astray. He charges them with blending in one the production of their own Aeons, and the straying and recovery of the sheep. These are his opponents' ideas, not his own.

**2. His own view: Adam is the lost sheep, and he has been found.**
In his own voice, Irenaeus links the lost sheep to Adam and defends Adam's salvation: All therefore speak falsely who disallow his (Adam's) salvation, shutting themselves out from life for ever, in that they do not believe that the sheep which had perished has been found. Because the excerpt is brief, its full argument cannot be reconstructed from this passage alone.

---

## Common Threads

- **The lost sheep is humanity.** Cyril says the human race, Bede says man who sinned, and Irenaeus says Adam.
- **A perfect number restored.** Cyril and Bede both treat one hundred as a symbol of wholeness. In their reading, Christ's search for the lost completes God's whole creation, not just one part of it.
- **Christ as the Shepherd.** Each reads the shepherd as Christ. Bede in particular connects carrying the sheep to the Incarnation and to Christ bearing our sins.
- **Reading the parable faithfully.** Irenaeus's excerpt shows that even in the early church, how this parable was interpreted mattered and could be disputed.

# Patristic Commentary on Ephesians 3

**Scope note:** All of the excerpts deal with the **opening verse of Ephesians 3**, where Paul calls himself a prisoner "for you Gentiles." None of them address the rest of the chapter, so this summary covers only that verse.

---

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom reads Paul's imprisonment as **an expression of love that follows Christ's example.**

- **From Christ's care to Paul's:** Chrysostom notes that Paul, having mentioned Christ's great and affectionate care, now passes on to his own, insignificant indeed as it is, and a very nothing in comparison with that, and yet this is enough to engage them to himself. Paul's suffering is small next to Christ's, but it still binds his readers to him.

- **The servant shares the Master's suffering:** Chrysostom reasons, "For if my Lord was crucified for your sakes, much more am I bound." Christ not only was bound Himself, but allows His servants to be bound also. Being imprisoned is a way of sharing in Christ's own path.

- **Reconciliation between Jew and Gentile:** Chrysostom hears strong emphasis in the phrase "for you Gentiles." Paraphrasing Paul, he writes: not only do we no longer loathe you, but we are even bound, says he, for your sakes and of this exceeding grace am I partaker. Another rendering puts it more sharply: "Not only do we not hate you. We are even imprisoned on your account!"

- **Suffering as grace:** Paul does not treat his chains as a misfortune. He calls them an "exceeding grace" in which he is privileged to share.

---

## Jerome

Jerome takes two approaches: one about grammar and one about spiritual meaning.

### 1. An unfinished sentence
Jerome observes that Paul's sentence never finishes its thought: "After a diligent search I have found nothing that answers to his prior clause.… For he does not say, 'For this reason I, Paul, have done this or that or have taught this or that.' Instead, leaving the thought in suspense, he goes on to other matters."

He responds charitably. He suggests that perhaps we ought to pardon him for what he himself has admitted when he said, "if unschooled in speech, at least not in knowledge," and look for order in his meaning rather than in his words. In other words, readers should look for the meaning even when the grammar is untidy. Jerome offers this reconstruction: "I, Paul, in the chains of Jesus Christ and in chains for you Gentiles, have learned the mystery so that I may hand it on to you."

### 2. "Prisoner" as life in the body
Jerome also offers a more figurative reading of Paul's imprisonment. He draws on the idea that the body is called the prison of the soul. The soul is confined as if in a cage. On this reading, Paul was constrained by the ties of the body and did not return to be with Christ so that the preaching to the Gentiles might be perfectly accomplished through him.

He also mentions an alternative view held by others: Paul before his birth was predestined and sanctified from his mother's womb for the purpose of preaching to the Gentiles. For this vocation he took on the bonds of flesh. Here Paul's very life in the body becomes a kind of "imprisonment" accepted for the sake of his calling.

---

## Common Thread

Both commentators connect Paul's "chains" to **his mission to the Gentiles**:

- **Chrysostom** stresses the *relational and moral* side: Paul's suffering is an act of love that follows Christ and overcomes old hostility between Jew and Gentile.
- **Jerome** stresses the *textual and vocational* side: he works through Paul's awkward sentence and suggests that Paul's earthly life itself was a "bondage" accepted for preaching to the nations.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Romans 15: A Summary

The four excerpts differ greatly in length. Thomas Aquinas's commentary is extensive and covers most of the chapter. John Chrysostom's is a short passage on the opening verses. The excerpts from Origen and Theodore of Mopsuestia are only one sentence each, so only limited conclusions can be drawn from them.

---

## Thomas Aquinas

Aquinas reads Romans 15 as a continuation of Paul's teaching on the strong and the weak. He traces it through Christ's example to the inclusion of the Gentiles.

**1. Moving from avoiding offense to bearing burdens (vv. 1–2)**
Aquinas sees a progression from the previous chapter: the Apostle taught above that the stronger should avoid scandalizing the weak; here he teaches that the stronger should bear with the failings of the weak. He uses an architectural image: as in a material edifice certain stronger material is selected to support the edifice's entire weight, upon which weaker material is set, as are the foundation and pillars, so in the spiritual edifice of the Church stronger men are not only chosen but made stronger to support the weight of the others. In practice, the stronger support the failings of the weak, when they endure the shortcomings of the weak patiently and, so far as they can, try to help them.

**2. Pleasing one's neighbor has limits**
Aquinas carefully qualifies the call to please others. We should condescend to him in matters that please him, but not in matters that are evil. The motive also matters: we should not have the intention of pleasing men for the sake of human favor or glory, but act for the honor of God and the benefit of our neighbor.

**3. Christ as the model of self-denial (v. 3)**
Aquinas writes that Christ, Who is our head, did not please himself, when he chose to suffer for our salvation and do things contrary to His own will, namely, His natural human will, in order to accomplish the divine will. He offers two readings of "the reproaches fell on me." The first is that the reproaches came from those who opposed Christ's teaching. The second is broader: this can also refer to the sins of the whole human race, because all sins in a way reproach God. On this reading, the reproaches of those reproaching God fell on Christ, inasmuch as He died for the sins of all.

**4. Scripture produces hope (v. 4)**
Aquinas explains that Scripture contains both the patience of the saints and the consolation God gave them. The result is hope: by the instruction from Sacred Scripture that those who suffered tribulations patiently for God were divinely consoled, we receive the hope that we ourselves will be consoled, if we have been patient in them.

**5. Why Paul turns to prayer (vv. 5–6)**
Aquinas notes that Paul prays at this point because it seemed exceedingly difficult for a mere man to be able to imitate the example of Christ. The unity Paul prays for is principled, not consenting in sin, but in accord with Christ.

**6. God's truth and God's mercy (vv. 8–9)**
This is one of Aquinas's most distinctive points: the Apostle attributes the conversion of the Jews to God's truth but that of the Gentiles to His mercy. He does not let this become a strict either/or. Regarding the Jews, it was also an act of mercy that God made the promises to the patriarchs about the salvation of their descendants. Regarding the Gentiles, it also pertained to divine truth that He should fulfill His intention concerning the salvation of the Gentiles. The real difference is that one form of truth, namely, the fulfillment of promises, is considered in the call of the Jews, that is not considered in the call of the Gentiles, to whom the promises were not made.

**7. The four Old Testament quotations (vv. 9–12)**
Aquinas observes that although the call had not been promised to the Gentiles, it was not unplanned but was foretold by the predictions of the prophets. He gives each of Paul's quotations a distinct theme:
- Christ's thanksgiving to the "Father for the conversion of the Gentiles achieved by Him
- The coalescence of Gentiles and Jews
- The devotion of the Gentiles to God
- The reverence of the Gentiles toward Christ

**8. Faith joined with love (v. 13)**
Aquinas sees in the closing blessing a wish that believers have not only faith but charity, through which faith works, as it says in Gal (5:6) lest their faith be unformed and dead.

*A note on the text:* A few Scripture references in this translation appear to be garbled. For example, the references labeled "Is 14:4" and "Is. 1:4" seem to be misattributed, and "2 Cor 7:8" appears to be in error. These look like transcription or editorial slips, so readers checking the references should keep that in mind.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 27)

Chrysostom focuses on Paul's pastoral strategy in verse 1, particularly how Paul motivates the strong.

**1. Paul motivates through affirmation**
Chrysostom points out how Paul has roused their attention by his praises, not only by calling them powerful, but also by putting them alongside of himself.

**2. The stakes are unequal**
The strong lose nothing, but the weak risk a great deal: thou, he says, art powerful, and art no whit the worse for condescending. But to him the hazard is of the last consequence, if he is not borne with.

**3. Paul's careful wording**
Chrysostom notices a subtle phrasing: he does not say the infirm, but the "infirmities of the weak," so drawing him and bending him to mercy.

**4. Strength comes from grace and should be repaid**
This is Chrysostom's central theological point. Strength is a gift to be repaid by serving others: Render a return to God for making you so. But render it you will if you set the weakness of the sickly right. For we too were weak, but by grace we have become powerful.

**5. Wider application**

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Timothy, Chapter 1: Summary

## Theodoret of Cyrus

The excerpt from Theodoret is a single sentence, but it captures the key point about Paul calling Timothy his son: It is not nature but faith that has made Timothy a son. The bond between Paul and Timothy is spiritual, not biological.

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom's excerpts are much fuller. They fall into four themes.

### 1. Introduction: Timothy's Character and the Purpose of the Letter

Much of this material introduces the epistle as a whole rather than commenting on chapter 1 verse by verse. Several of the passages he cites come from later chapters or other books.

- **Timothy's character:** Chrysostom notes that testimony is borne by Luke, who informs us, that he was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium. He praises Timothy's prudence: although Paul preached without insisting on circumcision, Timothy chose not only not to preach against it, but to submit to that rite.
- **Paul's affection:** The affection of Paul for him is a sufficient evidence of his character.
- **Why letters to Timothy and Titus alone?** Paul wrote only to them because he had already committed the care of churches to these, and certain marked places had been assigned to them, but the others were in attendance upon him.
- **Virtue over age:** So preëminent in virtue was Timothy, that his youth was no impediment to his promotion. Chrysostom states the principle behind this: where there is virtue, all other things are superfluous, and there can be no impediment. This point draws on 1 Timothy 3–5, not chapter 1.
- **A letter written to a teacher:** Why write to someone already appointed? Because the instruction which he needed was not that which was suited to a disciple, but that which was proper for a Teacher. Chrysostom finds this in chapter 1 itself. At the very beginning, Paul does not say, Do not attend to those who teach otherwise, but, Charge them that they teach no other doctrine.

### 2. "My True Child in the Faith"

Like Theodoret, Chrysostom reflects on Paul's address to Timothy as his son. He notes that Timothy is not the biological son of Paul. The qualifier "in the faith" settles the question. It shows that he was really his own son, and truly from him, there being no essential difference between father and son in the faith.

He then develops an analogy. Human fathers and sons may differ in many particulars, as in color, figure, understanding, age, bent of mind, endowments of soul and body. In contrast, in the relation of the divine Father and Son there is no such dissimilarity. In other words, spiritual sonship in faith points toward a likeness deeper than biological kinship.

### 3. Why "Mercy" Appears in the Greeting

Chrysostom asks Why is mercy mentioned here, and not in the other Epistles? He offers two answers:

- **Paul's fatherly concern:** This is a further mark of his affection. Upon his son he invokes greater blessings, with the anxious apprehension of a parent. As evidence of this care, he cites Paul's unique advice about Timothy's bodily health (1 Timothy 5:23).
- **The burden of teaching:** Teachers indeed stand more in need of mercy.

### 4. God as Father

On the phrase "From God our Father," he says, "and Jesus Christ our Lord.", Chrysostom finds comfort: Here too is consolation. For if God is our Father, He cares for us as sons. He supports this with Christ's words about a father who would not give his son a stone instead of bread.

## Common Thread

Both commentators stress that Timothy's sonship rests on **faith rather than nature**. Chrysostom builds on this to show Paul's parental tenderness toward Timothy, which he sees reflected in the fatherly care God shows to believers.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 5: A Summary

These excerpts come from two commentators, the Venerable Bede and Gregory of Nazianzus. Bede's comments focus on the opening verses of Luke 5, where Jesus teaches by the lake and the fishermen are washing their nets.

## Bede: *On the Gospel of Luke*

### 1. The Setting: The Lake of Gennesaret

Bede starts with the geography. The lake of Gennesaret is said to be the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. He explains that the name Tiberias comes from a city restored by Herod the tetrarch and named Tiberias in honor of Tiberius Caesar. He also notes why a freshwater lake is called a "sea": by the custom of the Hebrew language, any gathering of waters, whether sweet or salty, is called a sea.

### 2. The Lake as This Present Life

Bede's main insight is allegorical. He reads the lake as a symbol of the world. Since the present age is designated by the lake or the sea, the Lord stands by the sea, after overcoming the mortality of the fleeting life, having attained in the same flesh in which He suffered the stability of eternal rest. In this reading, Christ standing on the shore represents the risen Lord, who stands firm beyond the restlessness of mortal life.

### 3. The Crowd as the Gathering of the Nations

The crowd pressing around Jesus points beyond its own moment. The gathering of the crowd to Him is a type of the nations running together in faith. Bede supports this with a passage from Isaiah 2: "And all nations will flow to Him, and many peoples will go and say: Come and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord".

### 4. The Two Boats: Jew and Gentile

Bede also reads the two boats symbolically. The two boats placed by the lake symbolize the circumcision and the foreskin, meaning Jewish and Gentile believers. He stresses that Christ knows His people: It is well said that Jesus saw them, for the Lord knows who are His in both peoples. Christ leads their heart from the waves of this world to the tranquility of future life, as if to the solidity of the shore. The end of this sentence ("by living, that is by mercifully avoiding") is unclear in this translation and may be garbled.

### 5. The Fishermen as Teachers of the Church

Bede sees the fishermen as a picture of Christian ministry. The fishermen are the teachers of the Church, who, having caught us in the net of faith and raised us from the depths to the moon, bring us to the land of the living like fish to the shore. The phrase "to the moon" reads oddly and may be a translation error, so it is best not to build much on it. The nets stand for the preachers' message: just as the nets are entwined, so are the words of the preachers, which do not lose those they have caught in faith.

### 6. Washing the Nets: Rhythms of Ministry

Bede draws a practical lesson from the fishermen washing their nets. The nets are sometimes let down for a catch, sometimes washed and folded, because not every time is suitable for teaching, but now the teacher's tongue must be exercised, now he must take care of himself. Ministry needs times of active preaching and also times of rest and personal renewal.

## Gregory of Nazianzus

The excerpt from Gregory is a short fragment. It speaks of Christ condescending to all, in order that He might draw forth a fish from the deep, with the "fish" glossed as man swimming in Or the ever changing scenes and bitter storms of this life.

The text appears corrupted; the stray "Or" suggests an editor's note has been mixed into it. The excerpt also does not mention Luke 5 or any detail of the passage. It is grouped with Luke 5 commentary, and its fishing imagery fits the chapter's themes. Even so, it would go beyond the evidence to say Gregory was commenting on this passage. What it does express is that Christ humbles Himself to rescue people from the instability of earthly life.

## Common Thread

Both writers use similar imagery. The sea stands for the restless present life, and Christ draws people out of it toward stability and salvation. Bede develops this most fully, reading the lake scene as a picture of the risen Christ, the gathering of all nations, and the teaching work of the Church.

# Bede on Luke 21: A Summary of Key Insights

All four excerpts come from one commentator, **the Venerable Bede**, in his commentary *On the Gospel of Luke*. They cover the opening section of Luke 21: the widow's offering, the disciples' question about the temple's destruction, and Jesus' warning against deceivers.

---

## 1. The Temple Treasury and God's Watchful Gaze

Bede starts with background on the word "treasury." He explains that in the Greek language, φυλάσσειν means to guard, and gaza in the Persian language means riches, the treasury was called the place where riches were kept. He describes it physically as a chest with a hole on top, placed near the altar to the right of those entering the house of the Lord, into which the priests who guarded the doors put all the money brought to the temple of the Lord and its upkeep. (He also tells readers to read the words of the days, apparently pointing to another scriptural source, though the excerpt does not say which.)

He then applies the scene to the present. Christ still watches worshippers today: even now, those who pray running into the house of the Lord, He too looks upon those bringing gifts, and whom He sees as worthy, He praises; whom He sees as reproachable, He condemns. The scene becomes a reminder that Christ examines the hearts of those who give and worship.

## 2. The Widow's Offering: An Allegory of Grace

Bede reads the contrast between the rich givers and the poor widow allegorically.

- **The rich represent self-righteousness.** The Jew casts into the gifts of God out of his abundance, who, presuming on his own righteousness, prays thus with himself: "God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, etc." Bede links this to the Pharisee's prayer in Luke 18.
- **The widow represents the Church.** The Church casts her whole livelihood into the gifts of God, understanding that everything she lives by is not of her own merit, but the gift of God, saying, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." This echoes the tax collector of Luke 18.

Bede supports this with a Psalm: "My strength I will guard for you, for you, O God, are my protector, my God, His mercy will go before me."

**The theological point:** The widow's "whole livelihood" stands for the humble recognition that everything we have comes from God's grace, not our own merit. Giving out of "abundance," by contrast, stands for relying on one's own righteousness.

## 3. The Disciples' Question About the Temple

Bede places the disciples' question in context and harmonizes Luke with the other Gospels. While some were praising the buildings of the temple, the Lord openly responded that all these things would be destroyed, the disciples secretly, as he sat on the Mount of Olives, asked about the time and the signs of the predicted destruction, as Matthew and Mark testify. He notes the contrast between Jesus' public prophecy and the disciples' private question.

## 4. Warning Against Deceivers: A Threefold Fulfillment

On Jesus' warning that many will come in my name, saying, "I am he" and "the time is near", Bede sees the prophecy fulfilled on three levels:

1. **Historically, around Jerusalem's fall:** Many, at the imminent destruction of Jerusalem, rose up as leaders and claimed to be the Christs, asserting that the time of freedom was now approaching.
2. **Within the early Church:** Many in the Church, even in the times of the apostles, arose as heresiarchs who, among numerous other things contrary to the truth, preached that the day of the Lord was at hand. He notes that the Apostle condemns these in the letter to the Thessalonians.
3. **As Antichrists in Christ's name:** Many in the name of Christ came as Antichrists, the first of whom was Simon the Magician, to whom, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, all those in Samaria listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called great". Simon gained this following because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

**The theological point:** Christ's warning is not limited to one moment in history. It applies wherever false teachers claim divine authority or announce that the end is near, and impressive signs do not prove a message is true.

---

## Overall Observations

Bede's approach moves from the literal and historical (word meanings, the temple's layout, events around Jerusalem's fall) to spiritual and moral application (the widow as the humble Church, Christ still watching worshippers, warnings that apply to every age). He interprets Scripture by Scripture, connecting Luke 21 to Luke 18, the Psalms, Acts, Thessalonians, and the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark.

Because all the excerpts come from Bede, this summary cannot compare him with other commentators. The excerpts also cover only the opening part of Luke 21, not the rest of the chapter's teaching about the end times.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 32: A Summary

## John Chrysostom: God's Care for Jacob's Fears

Chrysostom focuses on God's pastoral care for Jacob. Jacob faces one threat after another: once fear of Laban faded and was no more, then fear of his brother took hold of Jacob; so the loving Lord wanted to give the good man heart and drive out all his apprehension. The vision of angels is God's answer to that fear: he caused Jacob to see the angels' camp.

He also explains why Jacob named the place. When Jacob called it "Camps," the result was that from the name there was a constant reminder of the vision that occurred to him there. The name served as a lasting memorial of God's encouragement.

**Key insight:** God anticipates the anxieties of the faithful and strengthens them in advance.

## Ephrem the Syrian: Angelic Protection and God's Faithfulness

Ephrem sees three purposes in the angelic encounter:

1. **Protection from Laban:** The angels met Jacob to make known to him that if Laban did not obey God, who had appeared to him in the evening, he and those with him would be destroyed at dawn by the hands of those angels who protect Jacob.

2. **Confirmation of God's promise:** Ephrem links this scene to Jacob's earlier journey. Just as God had shown Jacob the angels that accompanied him when he went down, he also showed him angels when he was going up to make him know that the word was true which God had spoken to him, namely the promise to go down with him and bring him back up.

3. **Courage before Esau:** The army of angels that God had shown Jacob was so that he would not fear Esau, for there were many more [angels] with Jacob than were with Esau.

**Key insight:** The angels show that God's promises hold at both ends of Jacob's journey, and that those who belong to God are never outnumbered.

## Augustine of Hippo: A Prophetic Reading of Jacob and Esau

Augustine addresses Jacob's approach to Esau. He notes that Jacob did not want to see Esau before he had appeased him with presents, and he only saw him afterward when the presents had been accepted. Jacob sends the gifts in chapter 32, but the meeting and bowing Augustine describes come in the narrative that follows.

Augustine raises a theological puzzle. Since Jacob bowed down to him from a long way off, he asks: how shall the elder be slave to the younger, when the younger manifestly bows down to the elder? He answers that the reason why these things were not fulfilled in the actual history of the two men is to make us understand that they were said of a future Jacob. In his reading, the younger son received the first place, and the elder son, the people of the Jews, lost the first place. He concludes: See how Jacob has filled the whole world, has taken possession of nations and kingdoms.

**Key insight:** When a prophecy seems unfulfilled in the literal history, Augustine reads it as pointing to a later fulfillment, here in the Church spread among the nations. Readers should note that his identification of the "elder son" with the Jewish people reflects a supersessionist framework common in early Christian interpretation, one that many theologians today approach critically.

## Jerome: An Excerpt Outside Chapter 32

Although Jerome's excerpt is labeled "Chapter XXXII, Verse 2," its content does not concern Genesis 32. It discusses Sarah's death: And Sara died in the city of Arboc, which is in the valley: this is Chebron, in the land of Canaan. Sarah's death is not part of the Genesis 32 narrative, so this appears to be a mislabeling or a different numbering system.

The excerpt is mainly textual criticism. Jerome notes that the phrase "which is in the valley" is not found in authentic codices, and that the name "Arboc" has also gradually been corrupted by scribes and readers. He argues the proper name means "four," because there Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried, and also the first of the human race, Adam. This is interesting for the history of the text but offers no insight into Genesis 32 itself.

## Common Thread

Chrysostom and Ephrem both read the angelic encounter as God's reassurance to a frightened Jacob, which shows God's faithfulness and protective presence. Augustine moves from the historical narrative to a prophetic reading about God's purposes in later history.

# Patristic Insights on Genesis 1:1

The excerpts center on Genesis 1:1, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Origen and Augustine are represented by short passages, while Basil of Caesarea's commentary is much longer. The summary is weighted accordingly.

---

## Origen of Alexandria: "The Beginning" Is Christ

Origen reads "beginning" as a reference to Christ rather than to time.

- **Christ as the Beginning:** He asks, "What is the beginning of all things except our Lord and 'Savior of all,' Jesus Christ 'the firstborn of every creature?'"
- **Link to John's Gospel:** He connects Genesis to John's prologue: "In this beginning, therefore, that is, in his Word, 'God made heaven and earth' as the evangelist John also says in the beginning of his Gospel".
- **Not a moment in time:** He holds that Scripture is not speaking here of any temporal beginning, but it says that the heavens and the earth and all things that were made were made "in the beginning," that is, in the Savior.

**Key takeaway:** For Origen, Genesis 1:1 points to Christ as the one through whom everything was made.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: "Heaven and Earth" as Unformed Matter

Augustine's brief excerpt focuses on what the phrase "heaven and earth" refers to.

- **Raw material of creation:** He explains that Scripture called heaven and earth that formless matter of the universe, which was changed into formed and beautiful natures by God's ineffable command.
- **Ready to be shaped:** This matter, though confused and mixed up, were suited to receive forms from God their maker.

**Key takeaway:** Augustine reads "heaven and earth" in verse 1 as the unformed material that God's word then shapes into an ordered and beautiful world. The excerpt is too short to say much more about his wider reading of the chapter.

---

## Basil of Caesarea: A Wide-Ranging Reflection on Genesis 1:1

### 1. Approaching the Text with Reverence
Basil begins with the attitude the reader should bring. He asks What ear is worthy to hear such a tale? and urges that the soul be pure it should be from carnal affections, how unclouded by worldly disquietudes. He grounds the text's authority in Moses, whom God judged worthy to behold Him, face to face, like the angels, who imparts to us what he has learned from God.

### 2. God, Not Chance, Is the Source
Basil contrasts Genesis with Greek philosophy. He notes that not one of their systems has remained firm and unshaken, each being overturned by its successor. Some imagined that atoms, and indivisible bodies, molecules and ducts, form, by their union, the nature of the visible world. Against such thinking, the writer on the creation, from the very first words, enlightens our understanding with the name of God; In the beginning God created.

### 3. A Beginning Implies an End
Basil argues that the world is not eternal. Moses first establishes a beginning, so that it might not be supposed that the world never had a beginning. From this he draws a conclusion about the future: That which was begun in time is condemned to come to an end in time. If there has been a beginning do not doubt of the end. He criticizes those who imagine that this visible world is co-eternal with the Creator of all things.

### 4. An Invisible Creation Before the Visible One
Basil suggests that even before this world an order of things existed of which our mind can form an idea, but of which we can say nothing. This invisible order included intellectual and invisible natures, all the orderly arrangement of pure intelligences. He therefore reads the verse as In the beginning God created; that is to say, in the beginning of time. In his view, Moses only wishes to tell us that, after the invisible and intellectual world, the visible world, the world of the senses, began to exist.

### 5. The World as a School for Souls
Basil sees a purpose in creation. The world was made for an useful end and for the great advantage of all beings, since it is really the school where reasonable souls exercise themselves, the training ground where they learn to know God; since by the sight of visible and sensible things the mind is led, as by a hand, to the contemplation of invisible things.

### 6. The Many Meanings of "Beginning"
Basil lists several senses of "beginning": the first movement in time, the foundation of something, and its guiding purpose. He then asks the reader to see if we have not all the meanings here. He also proposes that creation was instantaneous: at the will of God the world arose in less than an instant.

### 7. "Created": A Free and Intentional Act
Basil stresses the verb "created." He does not say God worked, God formed, but God created. Some philosophers claimed that God is the world's involuntary cause, as the body is the cause of the shadow and the flame is the cause of the brightness. Basil answers that the verse corrects this error. Being good, He made it an useful work. Being wise, He made it everything that was most beautiful. Being powerful He made it very great.

### 8. "Heaven and Earth" Includes Everything
By naming the two extremes, Moses suggests the substance of the whole world, so that All intermediate beings were created at the same time as the extremities.

### 9. Humility Before Speculative Questions
Basil warns against getting lost in physical speculation, such as what holds up the earth. Instead, we must still remain faithful to thought of true religion and recognise that all is sustained by the Creator's power. He sums up: let us prefer the simplicity of faith to the demonstrations of reason. The goal is worship: by the beauty of visible things let us raise ourselves to Him who is above all beauty.

---

## Comparing the Commentators

- **What "beginning" means:** The excerpts disagree. Origen denies that "beginning" refers to time and reads it as Christ. Basil reads it, among other senses, as "the beginning of time."
- **What "heaven and earth" means:** Augustine sees formless matter awaiting form. Basil sees the two extremes that stand for the whole created order.
- **Common ground:** All three affirm that the world owes its existence to God's deliberate, purposeful action rather than to chance or necessity.

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 13

All of the excerpts come from **John Chrysostom** (Homily 29 on Second Corinthians). Two of them (labeled 29.1) read like condensed paraphrases of the same homily rather than direct quotations, but they are consistent with the fuller text. Chrysostom's comments focus on the opening verses of chapter 13 (vv. 1–2), where Paul announces his third visit and warns that he "will not spare."

## 1. Paul's Patience: Quick to Warn, Slow to Punish

Chrysostom sees Paul's wisdom and love chiefly in how he handles discipline. He notes Paul's being so abundant and vehement in his admonitions, but so tardy and procrastinating in his punishments. Paul did not chastise them immediately on their sinning, but warned them once and again, and even when they ignored him, he warned them again.

**Theological insight:** This patience mirrors God's own character. Paul is imitating the Lord of all: because that God also threatens indeed continually and warns often, but not often chastises and punishes.

## 2. Patience Without Complacency

Chrysostom also recognizes that delayed punishment could breed indifference. Paul guards against this by threatening continually and holding the blow suspended over them. In Chrysostom's view, Paul neither kept silence nor punished, but he both foretells often, and continues ever threatening, and puts off the punishment, and if they should continue unamended, then he threatens to bring it to the proof. He presents this balance as forethought becoming a teacher.

## 3. "Two or Three Witnesses": A Creative Use of Scripture

Chrysostom explains that Paul applies the legal principle of witnesses to his own visits and warnings. Paul is setting his comings and his warnings in the place of witnesses. He compares this to Paul's adaptation of the "one flesh" text in 1 Corinthians 6:16, which was spoken of lawful marriage; but he diverted its application unto this thing conveniently, so as to terrify them the more.

Chrysostom paraphrases Paul's reasoning this way: 'For if at the mouth of two witnesses or three every word shall be established, and I have come twice and spoken, and speak now also by this Epistle; it follows, I must after this keep my word.' He also stresses that Paul's letter carries the same authority as his presence: 'For think not, I pray you, that my writing is of less account than my coming; for as I spoke when present, so now I write also when absent.'

## 4. "I Will Not Spare": Discipline in a Father's Voice

Chrysostom notices that even Paul's sternest warning is softened by affection. Paul did not say, 'I will avenge and punish and exact satisfaction:' but again expresses even punishment itself in paternal language; showing his tender affection, and his heart to be grieved along with them. Drawing on 2 Corinthians 12:21, Chrysostom says Paul had already shown that he is unable to do this unless he is compelled, and having called the thing a mourning, and a humbling.

The paraphrased excerpt makes the same point. Paul's threats have been heard so widely that if he comes and nothing has changed he will have to carry them out. Yet he will see it more as a humbling and as a defeat than as anything else.

## 5. The Goal: Repentance, Not Punishment

For Chrysostom, the purpose of the warnings is to make punishment unnecessary. Paul takes great pains to write in advance of his coming, because he hopes that the church will put things right before he gets there, so that what he threatens to do will prove to be unnecessary. He sums up Paul's stance in Paul's imagined words: 'And if indeed ye attend to me, what I desired is accomplished; but if you pay no attention, it is necessary henceforth to stop speaking, and to inflict the punishment.'

## A Note on Scope

The final excerpt ends just as Chrysostom turns to Paul's response to critics who said "his presence is weak, and his speech of no account;". The commentary on those later verses of chapter 13 is not included, so this summary cannot address them.

## Key Takeaway

Chrysostom presents 2 Corinthians 13:1–2 as a model of pastoral discipline that reflects God's own character: generous with warnings, patient in waiting, grieved rather than vindictive when correction becomes necessary, and always aimed at repentance rather than retribution.
