# Patristic Commentary on John 18: Key Theological Insights

**Note on scope:** These excerpts cover only the opening of John 18 (the garden, the arrest, Peter's sword, and the binding of Jesus). They do not address the trials before Annas, Caiaphas, or Pilate, or Peter's denials. Also, the excerpt labeled *Tractates on the Gospel of John 112.1* is another translation of the opening paragraph of the first Augustine commentary, so the two are treated together below.

---

## Augustine of Hippo

### 1. The Gospels agree with one another
Augustine starts with a point about how to read the Gospels together. John's account of entering the garden did not take place immediately after Jesus had brought the prayer to a close. Instead, certain other incidents were interposed that are passed over by the present Evangelist and found in the others, just as in this one are found many things on which the others are similarly silent in their own narratives.

He asks readers to trust Scripture's unity even before they fully understand it. They should believe that there is nothing written by any one Evangelist, as far as regards those who have been received by the church into canonical authority, that can be contrary to his own or another's equally veracious narrative.

In his *Harmony of the Gospels*, he applies this principle to the setting. Matthew and Mark name Gethsemane, and Luke refers to it without naming it, and there, we understand, was also the garden that John brings into notice when he gives his narrative.

### 2. Judas and the armed crowd
Augustine pictures Judas vividly as the wolf, clad in a sheep's skin, and tolerated among the sheep by the profound counsel of the Father of the family. He notes that the cohort was not of Jews, but of soldiers.

The large show of force says something about Christ. His enemies thought such measures necessary against one for whose hurt nothing would have sufficed but what was pleasing to Himself; in His own goodness making a good use of the wicked.

### 3. "I am He": divine power within chosen weakness
This is the high point of Augustine's commentary. When the crowd falls back, he observes that His own single voice uttering the words, I am [He], without any weapon, smote, repelled, prostrated that great crowd. He explains it this way: For God lay hid in that human flesh; and eternal day was so obscured in those human limbs, that with lanterns and torches He was sought for to be slain by the darkness.

He then looks ahead to Christ's return: What will He do when He comes as judge, who did this when giving Himself up to be judged?

Augustine stresses that the arrest was voluntary. Had Jesus never allowed it, they would certainly not have done what they came to do, but no more would He be doing what He came to do. He sums up with a contrast: They, verily, in their mad rage, sought for Him to put Him to death; but He, too, in giving Himself to death, was seeking for us.

### 4. The Shepherd protects His disciples
When Jesus says "let these go their way," Augustine notes that He sees His enemies, and they do what He bids them: they let those go their way, whom He would not have perish. He explains that losing them at that moment would have been spiritual loss, because as yet they did not believe in Him, as all believe who perish not.

### 5. Malchus and Peter's sword
Augustine reads the episode symbolically. He says the interpretation of Malchus is, one who is destined to reign, and he takes the healed ear to represent the renewed hearing that has been pruned of its oldness, that it may henceforth be in the newness of the spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.

Peter's act was sincere but misguided. That disciple only sought to defend his Master, without any thought of what it was intended to signify.

On "the cup," Augustine draws out a Trinitarian point. The Father gave the cup, yet the originator of this cup is also one with Him who drank it. In other words, the Son was not simply a victim of the Father's will. He freely offered Himself.

### 6. The irony of the binding
Augustine highlights the tragic irony of the arrest: they bound Him by whom they themselves ought rather to have been loosed. Had they come to Him rightly, they would have taken Him, not with their hands for the purpose of murder, but with their hearts for the purpose of a welcome reception. He ends on a note of hope: perhaps there were those among them who then fastened their fetters on Christ, and yet were afterwards delivered by Him.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria

### The garden as a new Paradise
Cyril's short excerpt gives a typological reading of the setting in John 18. The place was a garden, typifying the paradise of old. He sees the location as fitting for salvation history: For the troubles of humanity began in paradise, while Christ's suffering, which brought us deliverance from all the evil that happened to us in times past, began in [this] garden. For Cyril, this is where our return to humanity's ancient condition was consummated.

---

## Summary of Major Themes

| Theme | Commentator |
|---|---|
| The Gospel accounts agree and complement one another | Augustine |
| Christ's divine power is hidden within His voluntary weakness | Augustine |
| The arrest was Christ's free choice, made in order to seek humanity | Augustine |
| Christ protects His disciples as a shepherd protects his flock | Augustine |
| Malchus's healed ear symbolizes spiritual renewal | Augustine |
| Father and Son are united in the offering of the "cup" | Augustine |
| The garden of the Passion reverses the fall in Eden | Cyril |

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Timothy 2: A Summary

Almost all of these excerpts focus on one verse, Paul's call to offer four kinds of prayer: supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings. Each commentator explains how these differ, and their answers vary widely. Chrysostom instead focuses on why Christians should pray for everyone.

**A note on the sources:** Document 1 is labeled "Origen — Conferences 9.11-14," but it actually contains excerpts from five writers: Origen, Ambrosiaster, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Augustine, and John Cassian. *Conferences* is Cassian's work. The Origen passage ends with a reference to ON PRAYER 14.2. Below, each insight is credited to the writer named within the text. The Augustine passage also appears twice (Documents 1 and 2), so it is summarized once.

---

## 1. Origen: Prayer Defined by Its Purpose
Origen distinguishes the four terms by what the person praying intends:
- **Supplication** is a prayer offered with a special request for something a person lacks.
- **Prayer** is more plainly offered with simple praise, not to obtain a request but simply to praise the nobility of great things.
- **Intercession** is a petition for certain things addressed to God by someone who has some greater boldness.
- **Thanksgiving** is gratitude for good things received from God, either when it is a great thing that is received and acknowledged with gratitude or when the greatness of the benefit is apparent only to the one who has benefited.

**Insight:** Origen separates asking from praising. He also says thanksgiving applies to private blessings that only the receiver recognizes, not just to obvious ones.

## 2. Ambrosiaster: Prayer for Society and Its Rulers
Ambrosiaster ties each term to a group being prayed for:
- "Supplications" are on behalf of secular rulers, that they may have obedient subjects, and thus peace and tranquillity.
- "Prayers" are for those to whom power has been entrusted, that they may govern with justice and truth, so that all may prosper.
- "Intercessions" are for those in dire necessity, that they may find help.
- "thanksgivings" refer to gratitude for God's daily providences.

**Insight:** For Ambrosiaster, the passage is about public life. Christian prayer is meant to support peace, just government, and help for people in need.

## 3. Theodore of Mopsuestia: Seeking Good and Escaping Evil
Theodore offers a short scheme: supplications express the desire for good things from God. Prayers express the desire to be released from various evils. Intercessions ask for freedom from undeserved consequences. And thanksgivings express gratitude for blessings.

**Insight:** Theodore treats the terms as ways of asking God for good and for rescue from harm. His idea that intercession seeks relief from undeserved consequences is distinctive.

## 4. Augustine: The Four Prayers as the Shape of the Eucharist
Augustine gives the most original reading. He links the four terms to the order of the Communion service, appealing to what the entire, or almost the entire, church observes:
- **Supplications** are those prayers which are said in celebrating the mysteries, before we begin to consecrate what lies on the table of the Lord.
- **Prayers** are said when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution; and the whole church, for the most part, closes this complete petition with the Lord's Prayer.
- **Intercessions** are offered while the blessing is being given to the people, for at that time, by the laying on of hands, the bishops, as intercessors, offer the members of their flock to the most merciful Power.
- **Thanksgiving** comes at the end: When this is completed and all have received the holy sacrament, the whole is ended by thanksgiving.

He supports this with the Greek. Paul's word for "prayer" (*proseuchē*) is connected to vowing, and all the things which are offered to God are vowed, especially the oblation at the holy altar, for in this sacrament we show forth that supreme offering, by which we vow to abide in Christ, even to the union of the body of Christ. The outward sign of this is that "we, being many, are one bread, one body."

**Insight:** Augustine reads Paul's list as a pattern for worship. In this view, the Eucharist expresses believers' commitment to remain in Christ and their unity as one body.

## 5. John Cassian: From Repentance to Wordless Gratitude
Cassian describes the four terms as stages in the spiritual life:
- "Supplication' is a beseeching or petition for sins.… "Prayers" are those by which we offer a vow to God.… "Intercession" is customarily offered, in moments of fervor, for other men and women—our family, the peace of the world. He links this to Paul's words that we pray "for all men, for kings and all in authority."
- **Thanksgiving** is when the mind recollects what God has done or is doing or looks forward to the good which he has prepared for those who love him, and so offers its gratitude in an indescribable transport of spirit. It can deepen further, when the soul contemplates in singleness of heart the reward of the saints and so is moved in its happiness to pour forth a wordless thanksgiving.

**Insight:** Cassian's reading is the most inward and contemplative. Prayer moves from confessing sin, to commitment, to love for others, and finally to joyful thanksgiving beyond words.

## 6. John Chrysostom: Praying for All Overcomes Hostility
*(Homilies on 1 Timothy 6)*
Chrysostom focuses on Paul's call to pray for everyone. The priest serves as the common father, as it were, of all the world. It is proper therefore that he should care for all, even as God, whom he serves cares for all. This has practical effects:
- hatred toward those who are outside the circle is transcended, for no one can feel hatred toward those for whom he prays.
- Those apart are made better by the prayers that are offered for them, by losing their ferocious disposition toward us.
- For nothing is so apt to draw men under teaching as to love and to be loved.

**Insight:** Praying for everyone reflects God's care for the whole world. It also changes both sides: it removes hatred from the one who prays and softens those outside the church, opening them to the faith through love.

### A Note on Chrysostom's *Homilies on Second Corinthians* 2.5
This excerpt is from a homily on 2 Corinthians, not 1 Timothy 2. Its theme of thanksgiving for others fits the chapter's call to thanksgiving, but it does not directly comment on 1 Timothy. In it, Chrysostom urges thanksgiving for shared blessings: Drawing near to God, we give thanks for the whole world and the good things we commonly share. He encourages believers to give thanks also for the faith that others have toward God, calling this an ancient one, planted in the church from the beginning.

---

## Summary of the Approaches

| Commentator | How he reads the four terms |
|---|---|
| **Origen** | By purpose: asking, praising, bold petition, gratitude |
| **Ambrosiaster** | By who is prayed for: rulers, those in authority, the needy, and God's daily care |
| **Theodore** | Seeking good, escaping evil, relief from undeserved consequences, gratitude |
| **Augustine** | The order of the Eucharistic service |
| **Cassian** | Inward progress from repentance to wordless thanksgiving |
| **Chrysostom** | Focuses on praying for *all*, which overcomes hatred and draws others to faith |

These early writers clearly did not agree on exact definitions. They did agree that Paul's instruction calls for prayer that is broad, generous, and full of gratitude.

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Corinthians 8: Knowledge and Love

These excerpts center on one theme from the chapter: the relationship between knowledge and love. John Chrysostom provides most of the material, Augustine offers a short supporting comment, and the Irenaeus excerpt is incomplete.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 20 on First Corinthians)

### 1. The problem in Corinth
Chrysostom first explains what had gone wrong. Many among them, having learned that "not the things which enter in defile the man, but the things which proceed out," and that idols of wood and stone, and demons, have no power to hurt or help, had made an immoderate use of their perfect knowledge of this to the harm both of others and of themselves. The harm went in two directions:
- **To the weak:** those who still retained the fear of idols and knew not how to contemn them, took part in those meals, because they saw the more perfect sort doing this, and the thing was becoming a way to idolatry.
- **To the "strong" themselves:** these very persons who pretended to be more perfect were injured in no common way, partaking in the tables of demons.

### 2. Paul's gentle approach
Chrysostom points to Paul's pastoral wisdom. Paul did not immediately begin to speak vehemently; for that which was done came more of folly than of wickedness: wherefore in the first instance there was need rather of exhortation than of severe rebuke and wrath. Paul also discourses with the strong first, for this is the sort of person that is able to receive rebuke also with readiness.

Chrysostom also explains why Paul could not simply reject their knowledge: what was done was of knowledge, and perfect knowledge. Nor was it safe to overthrow it, and yet in no other way was it possible to cast out the conceit which had resulted from it.

### 3. Three steps to humble pride
Chrysostom traces a progression in Paul's argument:

1. **Knowledge is shared by everyone.** By signifying that it was common, he curbs that swelling pride of theirs. Chrysostom notes that Paul says not, "I too have knowledge," but, "we know that we all have knowledge." If Paul had named only himself as a fellow possessor, that would still have flattered them.
2. **Knowledge without love is incomplete and harmful.** Paul shows that not even this thing itself was in all points complete, but imperfect, and extremely so. And not only imperfect, but also injurious, unless there were another thing joined together with it. When it is without love, it lifts men up to absolute arrogance.
3. **Even with love, our knowledge is not perfect.** Although charity be joined with it, yet not even in that case is this our knowledge perfect.

### 4. How love and knowledge relate
Chrysostom argues that love is the more basic of the two. He who loves, inasmuch as he fulfils the commandment which is most absolute of all, even though he have some defects, will quickly be blessed with knowledge because of his love; as Cornelius and many others. By contrast, knowledge is not productive of love, but on the contrary debars from it him that is not on his guard, puffing him up and elating him. For arrogance is wont to cause divisions: but love both draws together and leads to knowledge.

Paul does not forbid knowledge. Chrysostom paraphrases him: "I forbid not this," says he, "namely, your having perfect knowledge; but your having it with love, that I enjoin; else is it no gain, but rather loss." Love protects knowledge: "For although you may know something more than your neighbor, if you love him you will not set yourself up but lead him also to the same."

He also finds meaning in Paul's word choice. Paul did not say, "Behaves itself modestly," but what is much more, and more gainful. For their knowledge was not only puffing them up but also distracting them. On this account he opposes the one to the other.

### 5. The root of the Corinthians' problems
Chrysostom sees this chapter as part of a larger theme. The church's troubles came not from perfect knowledge, but from their not greatly loving nor sparing their neighbors. That is why Paul is continually providing for love; so correcting the fountain of all good things.

*(The second Chrysostom excerpt, from Homilies 20.2, summarizes these same points and adds nothing new.)*

---

## Augustine of Hippo (City of God 9.20)

Augustine's comment is brief but agrees with Chrysostom's main point: Paul means that knowledge only does good in company with love. Otherwise it merely puffs a man into pride.

---

## Irenaeus (Against Heresies, Book II)

This excerpt is cut off mid-sentence and does not explicitly mention Paul or 1 Corinthians 8. It does share the chapter's theme, since it holds that it is therefore better and more profitable to belong to the simple and unlettered class, and by means of love to attain to nearness to God, than, by imagining ourselves learned and skilful, to be found. Because the sentence is incomplete, its direct connection to this chapter should not be assumed.

---

## Common Thread

All three Fathers rank love above knowledge. Knowledge is not condemned, but without love it leads to pride and division. Chrysostom develops this most fully, showing how Paul humbles the "strong" believers in Corinth while still protecting the weaker ones.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Romans 16: A Summary

All four excerpts address Romans 16. Three focus almost entirely on **Phoebe**, the woman Paul commends at the start of the chapter. Thomas Aquinas's excerpt is the only one that goes through the chapter's list of greetings in detail.

---

## 1. Theodoret of Cyrus: Phoebe as Evidence of the Gospel's Spread

Theodoret uses Phoebe's home church to show how quickly the early church grew.

- **Geography:** He notes that Cenchreae is a village outside Corinth.
- **Rapid growth:** He finds it interesting to note how quickly the gospel was spreading, in that it had already reached the villages.
- **Phoebe's role:** He argues that the church at Cenchreae was so large that it even had a woman deaconess, and one who was famous and well known to boot.

**Key insight:** For Theodoret, a well-known deaconess in a village church shows that the Christian community there was mature and well established.

---

## 2. Origen of Alexandria: Women in Ordained Ministry

The excerpt does not name Phoebe, but it refers to "this passage" in a Romans 16 commentary, which most likely means Paul's commendation of her. Origen draws a strong conclusion about church ministry:

- He states that this passage teaches that there were women ordained in the church's ministry by the apostle's authority.
- He goes further, saying that they ought to be ordained into the ministry, because they helped in many ways and by their good services deserved the praise even of the apostle.

**Key insight:** Origen reads the passage as describing past practice and also as a model for the church. In his view, the faithful service of women justifies their ordination to ministry.

---

## 3. John Chrysostom: The Honor Paul Gives Phoebe

The excerpt says "her" rather than naming Phoebe, but the details (mentioned first, called "sister," a deaconess) match Romans 16:1. Chrysostom focuses on how deliberately Paul honors her:

- See how many ways he takes to give her dignity.
- For he has both mentioned her before all the rest, and called her sister.
- And it is no slight thing to be called the sister of Paul.
- Moreover he has added her rank, by mentioning her being "deaconess."

**Key insight:** Chrysostom shows that Paul's word choices (her place in the list, the family title "sister," and her official title) are intentional ways of affirming her standing.

---

## 4. Thomas Aquinas: A Systematic Reading of the Whole Chapter

Aquinas gives the longest commentary, treating the chapter as an orderly whole.

### The Chapter's Structure
He says Paul does three things: first, he suggests what they should do for others; secondly, he tells what other do to them [v. 23; n. 1221]; thirdly, he ends the epistle with thanksgiving.

### Phoebe
- Aquinas describes her service, noting she is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae, a port city of the Corinthians, where some Christians were gathered whom this woman had served, just as it was said of Christ Himself (Lk 8:3) that certain women provided for Him out of their means. He frames her work as practical service, comparing it to the women who supported Jesus. This differs in emphasis from Origen and Chrysostom, who stress her office or rank.
- He explains that the church should help her by affording advice and aid in any enterprise she may need you. He suggests she possibly had something to settle in Caesar's curia.

### Getting Involved in Others' Affairs
Aquinas addresses an apparent conflict with 1 Thessalonians 4:11 ("Take care of your own business"). He distinguishes two kinds of involvement:
- Helping in a worldly way, i.e., for the favor of men or for gain; and this does not befit God's servants.
- Helping out of piety; for example, to help the needy and the wretched, and this is religious. He concludes: It is in this way that the Apostle speaks here.

### Prisca and Aquila
- Paul names Prisca before her husband, perhaps because of the greater devotion of her faith.
- Their risking their lives for Paul is an indication of the greatest charity. Aquinas adds that Paul's life mattered mainly for the sake of others: the Apostle's life was necessary not so much for himself as for others.

### Andronicus and Junias
Aquinas notes four ways Paul honors them: their Jewish heritage, their imprisonment for Christ, and their standing, which he explains as men of note among the 599 apostles, i.e., noble among the preachers. (Aquinas reads both as men and takes "apostles" in the broader sense of "preachers.") Fourth, because they were believers before Paul, they had been converted before the Apostle and thus were owed greater respect.

### Other Notable Observations
- **Greeting only believers:** On the household of Narcissus, he notes there were some unbelievers in this family, and therefore to note the difference, he says: who are in the Lord, because he was asking only believers to be 600 greeted.
- **Service to the saints as service to Christ:** Tryphaena and Tryphosa labored in ministering to the saints, which the Lord regards as done to Himself.
- **Rufus's mother:** Paul calls her his own mother because she was his mother as a benefactor.
- **The holy kiss:** He says the holy kiss is given as a sign of the Blessed Trinity, and from this the custom arose in the Church whereby the faithful give one another the kiss of peace during the solemnities of the Mass.
- **The churches' greeting:** "All the churches of Christ greet you" reflects that all wish your salvation and pray for you.

**Key insight:** Aquinas reads the greetings as more than formalities. Each name becomes an occasion to teach about charity, respect, faithful service, and Christian community, and he connects the holy kiss to the church's liturgy.

---

## Common Threads

| Theme | Commentators |
|---|---|
| **Phoebe's importance** | All four discuss her. Theodoret, Origen, and Chrysostom stress her recognized role or rank; Aquinas stresses her service and hospitality. |
| **Women in ministry** | Origen speaks most directly of ordination. Chrysostom stresses her "rank," and Theodoret calls her a famous deaconess. |
| **Growth and unity of the church** | Theodoret (the gospel reaching villages) and Aquinas (house churches and the greetings of "all the churches"). |
| **Service as a mark of holiness** | Origen ("good services") and Aquinas (ministering to the saints as service to Christ). |

Together, these commentators show that the list of names in Romans 16 says a great deal about how the early church was organized, the roles women played in it, and the love that bound believers together.

# Patristic Insights on 1 Corinthians 10

The excerpts are very brief, so this summary is necessarily limited. Two of them offer real interpretation, and two mainly reproduce the apostle's words without visible commentary.

## Augustine of Hippo: *The Usefulness of Belief*
Augustine offers the broadest interpretive principle. He reads Israel's story as pointing forward to the Church, stating that the history of the exodus was an allegory of the Christian people that was yet to be. In this view, the Old Testament events Paul recalls in this chapter are not merely past history. They foreshadow the life and experience of Christians.

## Theodoret of Cyrus: *Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*
Theodoret applies that kind of reading to specific images, linking the exodus to Christian sacramental and spiritual life: The cloud is the grace of the Holy Spirit, while the sea represents baptism. The cloud that covered Israel and the sea they passed through become pictures of the Spirit's grace and of Christian baptism.

## Clement of Alexandria
Clement's excerpt quotes the apostle rather than commenting on him: For I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren "says the apostle, "that all were under the cloud, and partook of spiritual meat and drink; " The fragment shows Clement drawing on this passage and its theme of Israel's shared spiritual privileges. However, it does not reveal how he interpreted it.

## Irenaeus: *Against Heresies*, Book IV
Irenaeus's excerpt is also a quotation, a warning against overconfidence: Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall." The fragment is incomplete. The preceding text survives only as ) is come. His own commentary on the warning is not visible, so no further insight can responsibly be attributed to him from this excerpt.

## Summary of Key Themes
- **Exodus as a type of the Church:** Augustine supplies the principle, and Theodoret applies it concretely by connecting the cloud and sea to the Holy Spirit and baptism.
- **Privilege and warning:** Clement's and Irenaeus's quotations point to the chapter's twin emphases. Israel shared in spiritual blessings, and believers are cautioned against complacency. In these excerpts, however, both writers only cite the text rather than explain it.

# Bede on Revelation 10: A Summary

**A note on sources:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, **Bede**, so this summary presents his interpretation alone. Each excerpt clearly addresses Revelation 10.

---

## 1. The Mighty Angel as Christ Incarnate

Bede reads the "mighty angel" as Christ. On the text "And I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud," he comments that the Lord, the angel of great counsel, descended from heaven, clothed with the cloud of flesh.

- **Key insight:** The cloud represents the Incarnation, Christ's divinity veiled in human flesh.
- He supports this with Isaiah: "Behold, the Lord is riding on a swift cloud and will come to Egypt (Isaiah XIX)."
- The rainbow on the angel's head signifies mercy. Around the good, the promise of propitiation remains.

## 2. The Shining Face and Pillar-Like Feet

Bede reads the angel's radiant appearance as the risen Christ and his feet as the Church's preachers:

- The shining face is his knowledge manifested through the glory of the resurrection.
- The feet are prepared to evangelize and proclaim peace on the mountains (Romans X), illuminated by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and established like pillars.
- He identifies these pillars with the apostles: For James, Cephas, and John seemed to be pillars of the Church.

**Key insight:** Christ's glory reaches the world through Spirit-filled apostolic preaching, which gives the Church a firm foundation.

## 3. Sealing the Seven Thunders: Revealing and Concealing

John is ready to write because earlier he heard: What you see, write in a book (Revelation I). He is then told to seal up what the thunders said. Bede explains the tension with a pastoral principle:

> The mysteries of the Christian faith are neither to be shown to all indiscriminately, lest they become cheap, nor hidden from the worthy, lest they be entirely unknown.

- He sets this alongside the later command: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book (Revelation XXII).
- He finds both are comprehended in one verse in Daniel, where it is said to him through the angel: Seal the book and shut up the words until the appointed time (Daniel XII).

**Key insight:** Sacred truth should be shared with discernment. It must not be cheapened or withheld from those ready to receive it.

## 4. The Voice from Heaven and the Book of Preaching

Bede reads this scene on two levels:

- **For the Church:** As the Lord reveals the mysteries of the future time, saying: For the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matthew X), the Church is also admonished to take up the same book of preaching.
- **For John himself:** These words can also be fittingly applied to John himself, who would return to preach after exile.

## 5. The Sweet and Bitter Book: The Cost of Preaching

On the command "You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations," Bede says the verse explains what the book eaten and the sweetness mixed with bitterness signify, namely, that, being freed from exile, he would preach the Gospel to the nations, sweet indeed with love, but bitter with the persecutions to be endured.

**Key insight:** Preaching the Gospel is sweet because it is an act of love, and bitter because it brings suffering. Both come with the calling.

---

## Overall Themes in Bede's Reading

1. **Christ-centered interpretation:** The angel is Christ, clothed in flesh and shining with resurrection glory.
2. **The Church's mission:** The vision concerns apostolic preaching and the Church's duty to proclaim the Gospel.
3. **Discernment with sacred truth:** Revelation is balanced between disclosure and reserve.
4. **The cost of discipleship:** Proclaiming the Gospel joins the sweetness of love with the bitterness of persecution.

# Summary of Commentary on Matthew 9

**Note on scope:** Only one commentary excerpt was provided, from **Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 63B)**. This summary therefore covers a single commentator. Augustine does not name the passage directly, but his discussion of the synagogue ruler's daughter and the healed woman corresponds to the account in Matthew 9 of Jesus raising a ruler's daughter and healing a woman who touched him along the way.

---

## Augustine of Hippo: Sermon 63B

Augustine reads the story **allegorically**, treating the two people Jesus helps as symbols of two groups in salvation history.

### 1. The Two Figures as Two Peoples
Augustine's central claim is that the daughter of the synagogue ruler signifies the Jewish people, whereas the woman signifies the church of the Gentiles. The story becomes a picture of how the gospel reaches both Jews and Gentiles.

### 2. Christ's Mission to Israel and God's Faithfulness
Augustine stresses that the Lord Christ, born of the Jews in the flesh, was presented to those Jews in the flesh. However, he sent others to the Gentiles; he did not go himself. He supports this with the apostle's teaching that Christ served the circumcision "in order to show God's fidelity in confirming the promises made to our fathers." He connects this to God's promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, "that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy."

**Theological insight:** Christ's ministry to the Jews fulfills God's covenant promises, and those same promises also look ahead to blessing for the nations.

### 3. The Woman's Healing: Faith Without Sight
In the narrative, Christ went to restore life to the daughter of the synagogue ruler. Meanwhile, the woman appears on the scene, and she is healed. Augustine observes that she is healed first in faith, being practically ignored by the Savior, for he said, "Who touched me?"

He finds meaning in this apparent ignoring: "It means something when someone who cannot ignore, ignores." In his view, it points to the healed church of the Gentiles, the bodily presence of which is not seen by Christ. He links this to the psalm: "People whom I had not known served me. As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me."

*A small textual note:* the question "Who touched me?" appears in Mark's and Luke's versions of this story, not in Matthew's. Augustine seems to draw on the combined Gospel tradition.

**Theological insight:** The woman stands for the Gentiles, who never saw Jesus in the flesh but were healed by reaching out to him in faith.

### 4. Hearing Versus Seeing, and the Hope for Israel
Augustine contrasts how the two peoples responded: "The world heard and it believed. The Jewish people saw and at first they crucified." He does not end on rejection, though. He adds that later they too came to him, and he expresses hope that also the Jews will believe—but at the end of the world.

**Theological insight:** Just as the ruler's daughter is raised after the woman is healed, Augustine sees the Gentiles coming to faith first and Israel's full restoration following at the end of the age.

---

## Key Takeaway
Augustine turns Matthew's intertwined miracle stories into a map of salvation history. Christ comes first to Israel to keep God's promises. The Gentiles, unseen and unknown, are healed through faith in what they heard. Israel's "daughter" will ultimately be raised to life as well. His reading emphasizes God's faithfulness, the power of faith that has not seen, and hope for both peoples.

# Summary of Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Hebrews 9

The excerpts come from two commentators. **Thomas Aquinas** focuses mainly on the tabernacle and its furnishings (roughly Hebrews 9:1–5). **John Chrysostom** focuses on the priestly service and its meaning (roughly Hebrews 9:6–8).

---

## Thomas Aquinas

### 1. The purpose of Hebrews 9: showing the superiority of the New Covenant
Aquinas sees the chapter as a detailed follow-up to the argument of chapter 8. Having showed in general the dignity of the New Testament as compared to the Old, the Apostle now shows the same in particular by reaching down to the individuals in each Testament.

### 2. What both covenants aim at, and what the Old could not do
Aquinas starts from a shared goal: both the Old and New Testaments were instituted in order that by them the soul might come to God. But two things are needed for this, namely, withdrawal from sin and union with God.

However, the Old Covenant's rituals worked at a limited level. For in the Old there were washings, by which they were cleansed not from the stain of sin, but from certain irregularities, which hindered them from the worship of God. For example, after touching a corpse or anything unclean, they could not enter the tabernacle, until they were purified by certain washings.

### 3. "Earthly sanctuary": the absence of grace
Aquinas reflects on the word "worldly" (earthly) in 9:1. One reading is that that sanctification can be called 'worldly,' because it is temporal and not perpetual.

His more important point is about grace. Although both covenants use physical rites, the former contains grace and is holy, and in it the divine power works salvation under cover of visible things. This was not so in the Old Testament, because it contained no grace in itself.

### 4. The two parts of the tabernacle as "figures"
Aquinas offers two ways to read the division between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies:
- by the first tabernacle was signified the Old Testament, and by the second, the New.
- Alternatively, by the first tabernacle the present Church, and by the second, heavenly glory.

He neatly summarizes the layered symbolism: inasmuch as it signifies the Old Testament, it is a figure of a figure; but inasmuch as it signifies the present Church, which in turn signifies future glory, it is a figure of the truth in regard to each.

### 5. The tabernacle as a picture of creation and of God's incomprehensibility
At the level of the Old Covenant itself, Aquinas says the ceremonies were all instituted to represent God's magnificence. The Holy of Holies stood for the higher, spiritual world, while the Holy Place stood for the lower, sense-perceptible world.

His most striking insight concerns the mercy seat: God is utterly incomprehensible; therefore, there was a seat left unoccupied, because He cannot be comprehended by a creature except from his effects.

He also interprets the cherubim:
- There were two of them, to designate that they were not set there to be adored.
- The fact that they looked at the mercy seat shows that they do not cease contemplating God.

### 6. Christ prefigured in the furnishings
Aquinas reads each item in the tabernacle as pointing to Christ:
- **The lampstand:** He is a candlestick of light: 'I am the light of the world', and the seven lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
- **The table and loaves:** Christ is a table of refreshment. The twelve loaves are the doctrine of the Apostles and their successors.
- **The mercy seat:** Christ is the propitiation of our sins'.
- **The ark and its contents:** The ark made of sethim wood is Christ's pure and most precious flesh. The tablets are His wisdom. The rod is His eternal priesthood, or it is Christ's power; and the manna the sweetness of grace.

### 7. An apparent tension with 1 Kings
Aquinas also addresses a textual difficulty. In 1 Kg (8:9) it says that 'in the ark there was nothing else but the two tables of stone.' His answer is that this is true as regards its principal purpose, because that was what the ark was principally made for.

*Note:* Some passages in this translation of Aquinas are hard to follow, especially the detailed descriptions of the lampstand and of the objects between the cherubim. This summary avoids building on those passages.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 15 on Hebrews)

### 1. The furnishings belonged more to the future than to Israel
On the priests' daily service in the outer tent (9:6), Chrysostom makes a provocative point. These things indeed were [there], but the Jews did not enjoy them: they saw them not. So that they were no more theirs than [ours] for whom they prophesied. This excerpt is very brief.

### 2. The one annual entry foreshadows Christ's single sacrifice
On the high priest entering the Holy of Holies once a year (9:7), Chrysostom sees an answer to a likely objection. For, lest they should say, "how is there [but] one sacrifice?" he shows that this was so from the beginning, since at least the more holy and the awful [sacrifice] was [but] one.

### 3. "Not without blood": pointing to the Cross
Chrysostom finds the Cross anticipated in this phrase. He signifies that there shall be a sacrifice, not consumed by fire, but rather distinguished by blood. The Cross had neither fire, nor logs, nor was offered many times, but had been offered in blood once for all; he shows that the ancient sacrifice also was of this kind.

### 4. "Errors" rather than "sins": a pastoral note on humility
Chrysostom notices the author's choice of words. He said not "sins"; but "errors," that they might not be high-minded. For even if you have not sinned intentionally, yet unintentionally you have erred, and from this no man is pure.

### 5. "For himself": Christ's superiority
The high priest had to offer "for himself; and for the errors of the people." Chrysostom says the author keeps repeating "for himself," showing that Christ is much greater. Unlike the high priest, Christ did not need to offer for his own sins.

### 6. The Holy of Holies as heaven, not yet opened
On 9:8, Chrysostom notes that the author moves from description to deeper reflection: Thus far there is no speculation. He interprets the arrangement this way: For this cause (he says) have these things been thus "ordained," that we might learn that "the Holy of Holies," that is, Heaven, is as yet inaccessible.

He adds a word of reassurance: Let us not then think (he says) that because we do not enter them, they have no existence: inasmuch as neither did we enter the Most Holy [place].

---

## Brief Comparison

Both commentators read the tabernacle as pointing beyond itself, but they emphasize different things.

- **Aquinas** concentrates on the *structure and furnishings* of the tabernacle. He reads them in layers: as a picture of creation and of God's incomprehensibility, and as figures of the New Covenant, the Church, heavenly glory, and Christ himself.
- **Chrysostom** concentrates on the *priestly action*: the single annual entry, the blood, and the offering "for himself." He uses these to highlight the uniqueness of Christ's sacrifice on the Cross and to encourage humility.

Both identify the inner sanctuary with heavenly realities. Aquinas does so in one of his two readings ("heavenly glory"), and Chrysostom does so explicitly ("that is, Heaven").

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Timothy 4: Summary of Key Insights

These excerpts center on the warning at the opening of 1 Timothy 4, that some will depart from the faith in the "last times." Each Church Father applies this prophecy to the controversies of his own day.

## Augustine of Hippo: Letters 199

Augustine reads the passage in terms of the end times and the Lord's return. He argues that considering the signs mentioned by Gospel and prophecy which we see happening, Christians ought to hope for Christ's coming, which is nearer and nearer every day. He cautions, however, that the exact span of the nearness, that, as we said, "is not for you to know."

His main point about 1 Timothy 4 is that Paul's prophecy has come true over time. Citing the apostle's words that "The Spirit manifestly says that in the last times some shall depart from the faith," Augustine observes that those were not yet the times of heretics such as he describes them in the same sentence, but they have now come. He concludes that we seem to be in the last times, and the heretics seem to be a warning of the end of the world.

**Key insight:** Heresy is both a fulfillment of apostolic prophecy and a sign that the end is approaching. This should encourage watchful hope rather than speculation about dates.

## Augustine of Hippo: Reply to Faustus the Manichaean 15.10

This excerpt is a single sentence. Augustine claims that the fulfillment of these predictions in the Manichaeans is as clear as day to all that know them. The excerpt does not say which predictions he means. Its placement suggests he is applying the warnings of 1 Timothy 4 to the Manichaean sect, but the text itself does not confirm this, so it should be read cautiously.

## Athanasius of Alexandria: To the Bishops of Egypt 2.20

Athanasius applies the passage pastorally to the Arian controversy. He urges vigilance, warning that heretics might disguise error under the clothing of their phrases and they lead some away from the true faith. If they venture to advance the opinions of Arius, he says the faithful must respond with great boldness of speech.

He treats Paul's words as a deliberate warning to later generations: we are to remember the predictions of the apostle, which he wrote to forewarn us of such heresies and which it becomes us to repeat. He quotes the passage directly: "in the latter times some shall depart from the true faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of devils, that turn from the truth."

**Key insight:** The prophecy calls church leaders to discernment and courageous speech. Error often comes in orthodox-sounding language.

## Ambrose of Milan: Exposition of the Christian Faith 2.15.133–34

Most of this excerpt quotes other apostolic warnings against fruitless disputes, and only its final line corresponds to 1 Timothy 4. Ambrose begins with a charitable hope that his opponents would hear with true love and meekness, as men seeking what is true and not assailing all truth. He then identifies those who sow disputes—that is to say, heretics as people the apostle bids us leave alone. He links them to the 1 Timothy 4 prophecy that "certain shall depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and the doctrines of devils."

**Key insight:** Ambrose pairs a sincere desire for his opponents' conversion with practical caution. Believers should avoid quarrelsome debate with those who only seek to stir up disputes.

## Common Themes

- **Prophecy fulfilled:** All the commentators treat Paul's warning about departure from the faith as fulfilled in the heresies of their own time: Manichaeans, Arians, or heretics generally.
- **Spiritual roots of error:** Athanasius and Ambrose both stress the passage's teaching that false doctrine comes from deceitful spirits, not merely from human mistakes.
- **Different responses:** Augustine emphasizes hope and watchfulness for Christ's return. Athanasius calls for bold confrontation. Ambrose counsels charitable hope combined with avoiding pointless disputes.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 44: A Summary

These excerpts come from two commentators, Ambrose of Milan and Jerome. All of them address Genesis 44, the episode of Joseph's silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. The two writers approach the text very differently. Ambrose reads it spiritually and allegorically, while Jerome's excerpt deals with the wording of the text.

## Ambrose of Milan (*On Joseph*)

Ambrose's central idea is that **Benjamin prefigures the Apostle Paul**. The cup hidden in Benjamin's sack becomes a picture of Paul's calling and conversion. The excerpts assume this link between Benjamin and Paul without explaining it.

**1. Called without knowing it**
Ambrose draws a parallel between Benjamin's ignorance and Paul's: "And the silver cup is put in his sack alone. Benjamin did not know this. So Paul was in error, but he was called." He also gives the morning pursuit of the brothers a spiritual meaning: "They sent after him in the morning; indeed, the night of his blindness had advanced, and the day of faith was near at hand."

**2. A moral lesson and a divine choice in the search**
Ambrose sees two lessons in the order of the search:
- **Honoring elders:** Previously they sat at the banquet in Joseph's presence in order of age from the firstborn. You see that the place of honor is to be given to the eldest.
- **God's election:** The sacks of each are searched in order of age so that you may know that Paul has been chosen by the judgment of heaven. The rest were examined, but this man was given the preference.

He also reads Joseph's scheme on two levels. Joseph sent the cup so that he might by a holy trick recall the brother whom he loved; yet the light of God's mysterious plans is clearly reflected.

**3. Nature and grace as gifts from Christ**
Ambrose reads the returned money as a picture of divine gifts: "Christ finds this money in us which he has himself given us. We possess the money of nature; we also possess the money of grace. Nature is the work of the Creator, grace the gift of the Redeemer." These gifts are often hidden. Christ is working in a hidden way and is giving them to all people, but there are few who are able to keep them and not lose them.

**4. The cup as a special calling**
Ambrose distinguishes common gifts from particular ones: "Wheat is given to many, but the cup to one, who is presented with the prophetic and priestly function." To support this, he cites the prophet's words, "The cup of salvation I will take up, and I will call upon the name of the Lord."

**5. Opening the sack as Paul's conversion**
This is the fullest part of Ambrose's allegory:
- Paul already had divine truth before his conversion, but it was concealed. The word of heavenly teaching already shone in Paul's body, since he was instructed in the law. But because he was still not subject to the justice of God, the cup was within the sack, the teaching within the law, the lamp within the bushel.
- Ananias opens the sack. Ananias was sent to give a blessing and to lay on his hand and open the sack. When the sack was opened, the money shone forth, and when the scales fell, in a way like fastenings on the sack, Paul saw straightway.
- Ambrose sums up the meaning briefly: "His fetter was unbelief; the loosening of it became faith."
- He ends with freedom and transformation. Free of the bond, he obtained the grace of liberty and said, "But we all, beholding the glory of God with faces unveiled, are transformed into the same image."

## Jerome (*Hebrew Questions on Genesis*)

Jerome's excerpt is about words, not theology. Commenting on Verse 2 ("And put the silver of each one in the mouth of the bag, and put my silver cup in the mouth of the youngest one's bag"), he makes two notes:
- On "bag," he says the Hebrew term corresponds to a peronem or follem, words for a pouch or sack.
- On "cup," he notes the same word appears in Isaiah and that Aquila translated as scyphum, Symmachus as phialam. Aquila and Symmachus were translators who rendered the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek.

This excerpt contains no theological interpretation. Its value lies in clarifying the text's vocabulary and how early translators handled it.

## Concluding Observation

Most of the theological insight here comes from Ambrose. He turns a family drama into a picture of grace: God gives hidden gifts, chooses whom He will, and through human messengers like Ananias opens hearts closed by unbelief. Jerome complements this by attending to the precise wording of the text, a reminder that careful reading of the words supports spiritual interpretation.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Timothy 3: A Summary

The excerpts focus mainly on the chapter's opening warning about "dangerous times" in "the last days" and on the vice list that follows. Two commentators are represented: Augustine of Hippo (three excerpts) and John Chrysostom (one excerpt).

---

## 1. Augustine of Hippo: *Letters* 199. When Are the "Last Days"?

Augustine asks how Paul's prophecy about the last days applies to the present.

- **The warning is meant for now, not only for the future.** Augustine does not think Paul used his verbs in the present tense for the future, because, in fact, he was warning his correspondent to avoid these persons.
- **Evil increases as the end approaches.** Paul demonstrates that the times will be dangerous by prophesying that evil men will become more numerous as the end draws near. Augustine notes they are already numerous at present, and will be most numerous of all when the end itself is imminent, although it is not known how far off it is.
- **The Church has always lived in the "last days."** The last days were spoken of even in the first days of the apostles when the Lord's ascension into heaven was a recent happening. If that was true then, it is even more true now, even if there remained as many days to the end as have already passed from the ascension of the Lord to this day.

**Key insight:** Augustine avoids speculating about dates. He treats the "last days" as the whole period since Christ's ascension, so believers in every generation should take Paul's warning seriously.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: *Homilies on 2 Timothy* 7. Why Paul Foretells Evil

Chrysostom focuses on the pastoral purpose of Paul's warning.

- **A recurring theme.** Paul had already said in his earlier letter that "the Spirit speaks expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith." He repeats the point here.
- **Three kinds of support.** Paul makes his case not only from the future but from the past: "As Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses." He also argues from reasoning: "In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver."
- **The purpose is reassurance.** Paul does this in order that Timothy may not be troubled, nor any one of us, when there are evil men. As Chrysostom concludes, if there were such in the time of Moses and will be in later times, it is no wonder that there are such in our times.

**Key insight:** For Chrysostom, the prophecy is meant to steady believers, not frighten them. Evil people in the Church are a recurring reality, so their presence should not shake anyone's faith.

*(Note: The "great house" quotation comes from 2 Timothy 2, so here Chrysostom is drawing on the surrounding context of the letter.)*

---

## 3. Augustine of Hippo: *Sermons* 330. Self-Love as the Root of Evil

This is the most theologically developed excerpt. Augustine reflects on the first vice in Paul's list.

- **Not all self-love is wrong.** There isn't anyone, after all, who doesn't love himself. But we have to look for the right sort of love and avoid the wrong sort.
- **Self-love apart from God leads to losing oneself.** Anyone who loves himself by leaving God out of his life and leaves God out of his life by loving himself, doesn't even remain in himself but goes away from himself.
- **The core of the evil.** Of the phrase "people loving themselves," Augustine says: That's the core of the evil.
- **From self-love to love of money.** He notes that Paul's very next words are "lovers of money" and challenges his listeners: Are you, I'm asking you, are you money? His conclusion is that after loving yourself by neglecting God, by loving money you have even abandoned yourself.

**Key insight:** Augustine reads the order of Paul's list as a spiritual progression. Self-love cut off from God does not make a person more themselves. It pushes them outward toward lesser things like money, until they lose themselves entirely.

---

## 4. Augustine of Hippo: *City of God* 14.7.2. A Note on Vocabulary

This brief excerpt is a word study rather than an exposition of the chapter. Augustine uses the passage simply as an example of love language in a negative sense: someone wanting such an example should read the text, "Men will be lovers [amantes] of self, covetous [amatores pecuniae]."

**Key insight:** The excerpt shows that Augustine regarded 2 Timothy 3 as a standard example of disordered love. On its own, however, it offers little commentary on the chapter itself.

---

## Summary of Main Themes

| Theme | Commentator | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| The "last days" | Augustine (*Letters*) | The whole age since the ascension is the "last days," and evil grows as the end nears |
| Pastoral purpose | Chrysostom | Paul foretells evil so believers will not be troubled when it appears |
| Disordered self-love | Augustine (*Sermons*) | Loving oneself without God leads to loving money and losing oneself |
| Meaning of "love" | Augustine (*City of God*) | The passage illustrates love used in a bad sense |

Together, these Fathers read 2 Timothy 3 as a timeless and practical warning rather than a puzzle about the timing of the end. They see its relevance for every generation and trace the moral decline it describes back to love turned away from God.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 18: Key Theological Insights

All four excerpts address Genesis 18, specifically the Lord's appearance to Abraham at Mamre. Augustine's argument also draws on the related account of Lot in Genesis 19.

---

## 1. Origen of Alexandria: Mamre as a Place of Spiritual Vision

Origen reads the setting symbolically and focuses on the meaning of the name "Mamre."

- **The meaning of the place:** He notes that Mamre in our language is translated "vision" or "sharpness of sight."
- **Purity of heart:** Abraham's vision and sharpness of sight pleased the Lord. For he was pure in heart so that he could see God.
- **Application:** The place becomes a picture of the receptive soul: in such a place, therefore, and in such a heart the Lord can have a meal with his angels. He connects this to the prophetic tradition, observing that earlier prophets were called seers.

**Key insight:** God makes his dwelling, or "shares a meal," with those whose hearts are pure and spiritually perceptive.

---

## 2. Augustine of Hippo: The Visitors Were Angels, with God Present in Them

Augustine gives the most detailed argument about the *identity* of the three visitors.

- **His position:** God appeared in three men, who it is not to be doubted were angels, although some think that one of them was Christ and assert that he was visible before he put on flesh.
- **How the invisible God appears:** It belongs to the divine nature, without changing itself at all, to appear even to mortals, not by what it is but by what is subject to it.
- **Answering the "singular address" argument:** Some argue that Abraham's addressing one "Lord" proves one visitor was Christ. Augustine replies by pointing to Lot, who also in his conversation with them addressed the Lord in the singular even though two angels were present. He concludes that Abraham in the three men and Lot in the two recognized the Lord, addressing him in the singular number, even when they were addressing men.
- **God present in the messengers:** There was about them something so excellent that those who showed them hospitality as men could not doubt that God was in them as he was wont to be in the prophets and therefore sometimes addressed them in the plural, and sometimes God in them in the singular.
- **Scriptural support:** He appeals to Hebrews, where in praising hospitality it is said, "For thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

**Key insight:** God can genuinely manifest himself through created messengers without any change to his own nature. The shift between plural and singular in the text reflects the presence of God *in* the angels.

---

## 3. Eusebius of Caesarea: The Visitor Was the Preexistent Word

Eusebius takes a different view from Augustine and identifies the Lord at Mamre with Christ before the Incarnation.

- **Abraham's recognition:** Though Abraham saw a man with his eyes, he worshiped him as God, besought him as Lord and confessed that he was not ignorant as to who he was, calling him "Judge of all the earth."
- **His reasoning:** It would be unreasonable to think that God the Almighty's unbegotten and immutable substance was changed into human form, or that Scripture's account was a deception. So he asks who else could be proclaimed God and the Lord who judges all the earth and judges righteously, appearing in the shape of a man—if it be not proper to call him the first cause of all things—than his preexistent Word alone?

**Key insight:** The appearance at Mamre is read as a revelation of the Son (the Word), which protects both the unchangeableness of the Father and the truthfulness of Scripture.

---

## 4. Bede: Spiritual Symbolism and Moral Example

Bede offers both a moral reading and a rich allegorical one.

- **The significance of this appearance:** It is considered to be more sacred than all the previous ones. This is because, after circumcision and the change of his name, Abraham came to know the more secret mysteries of God, of which, notably, not only circumcision but also the uncircumcised were to be participants.

# Augustine on Matthew 15: The Canaanite Woman

All three excerpts come from one commentator, **Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 77)**, so this summary is organized by theme rather than by commentator. The sermon focuses on the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter in Matthew 15.

## 1. The Woman as a Gentile Outsider

Augustine first establishes who the woman is. Clearly this woman was not from that people but from the Gentiles. He grounds this in geography: Tyre and Sidon were not cities of the people of Israel but of the Gentiles, although they were close to that people. Her outsider status is the foundation for everything else he draws from the passage.

## 2. Why Jesus Delayed Answering Her

Augustine treats Jesus' initial silence as purposeful rather than dismissive. She was ignored, not that mercy might be denied but that desire might be enkindled; not only that desire might be enkindled but, as I said before, that humility might be praised. In his reading, the delay serves to deepen her longing and to display her humility.

## 3. "Sent Only to the Lost Sheep of Israel"

Augustine addresses the puzzle raised by Jesus' words in the passage: How is it that we have come from the Gentiles to the sheepfold of Christ if he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel? His answer concerns the order of God's plan. Jesus had to manifest in due sequence to that people first the presence of his body, his birth, the display of miracles and then the power of his resurrection. This was predetermined from the beginning. Yet the Lord's ultimate purpose was to have a church among all the Gentiles.

Augustine also uses a harvest image, saying a multitude of chaff was there, the hidden dignity of grain was there, and pointing out that the apostles themselves came from Israel: In fact, where were the apostles if not there? Where was Peter?

*A note of caution:* the excerpt reads The Gentiles were not to be condemned but to be winnowed like grain. Since the surrounding lines describe the people among whom the apostles were found, the winnowing image seems to refer to Israel. The wording may reflect a translation or transcription issue, so this sentence should be read carefully.

## 4. The Woman as a Figure of the Church

This is Augustine's central insight. The woman came from the Gentiles and represented a type (namely, a figure of the church), and her humility is what he praises most. He contrasts her with the pride he attributes to those who rejected Christ: they were unwilling to respond to Christ the author of humility, the restrainer of swellheadedness, the physician God.

## 5. Christ the Humble Physician

Augustine digresses on the Incarnation as the cure for pride: What great medicine! If this medicine does not cure pride, what could possibly cure it? The tragedy he describes is that a person does not recognize that he is weak, a sinner, sick, and that being a sick person, he should seek a physician!

## 6. The Olive Tree: Pride and Humility

Augustine draws on "the apostle's" image of the olive tree. This wild olive shoot represents the Gentile people. The key contrast is: They were broken because of pride; the wild olive shoot was grafted in because of humility. He sees the woman embodying this humility in her reply, which he paraphrases as "Yes, Lord, I am a dog. I desire crumbs."

## 7. A Parallel: The Centurion's Faith

To reinforce his point, Augustine links the woman to the centurion, an episode from elsewhere in Matthew rather than chapter 15. The centurion's words "Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed." show the same humility. Augustine observes that he did not receive the Lord under his roof; he received him in his heart.

From this comes one of the sermon's most memorable images: The more humble a person is, the more receptive and full he becomes. Hills repel water; valleys are filled up. When Jesus praised the centurion's "such faith," Augustine explains it as great in humility. "I have not found such faith": like a grain of mustard seed—the smaller it is, the more potent it is.

## Summary

For Augustine, the Canaanite woman's story is about **humility as the doorway to grace**. Her persistence, her acceptance of a lowly place, and her status as a Gentile make her a figure of the Gentile church grafted into God's people. Jesus' initial silence and his mission "to Israel first" are part of a deliberate divine order, not a refusal of mercy.

## Summary

For Augustine, the Canaanite woman's story is about **humility as the doorway to grace**. Her persistence, her acceptance of a lowly place, and her status as a Gentile make her a figure of the Gentile church grafted into God's people. Jesus' initial silence and his mission "to Israel first" are part of a deliberate divine order, not a refusal of mercy.

citations.citedText: Clearly this woman was not from that people but from the Gentiles.
Tyre and Sidon were not cities of the people of Israel but of the Gentiles, although they were close to that people.
But she was ignored, not that mercy might be denied but that desire might be enkindled; not only that desire might be enkindled but, as I said before, that humility might be praised.
A question arises here on that point: How is it that we have come from the Gentiles to the sheepfold of Christ if he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel?
We accordingly understand that he had to manifest in due sequence to that people first the presence of his body, his birth, the display of miracles and then the power of his resurrection.

It had thus been predetermined from the beginning, such and such had been foretold and fulfilled, that Christ Jesus had to come to the Jewish people and to be seen and killed and to win for himself those whom he knew beforehand.
The Lord knew why he came—certainly to have a church among all the Gentiles—and he yet said that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel?
A multitude of chaff was there, the hidden dignity of grain was there, burning was to take place there, and a storehouse to be filled there.

The Gentiles were not to be condemned but to be winnowed like grain.

# Patristic Commentary on 1 Corinthians 2: Summary of Key Insights

## Augustine of Hippo (*On the Trinity* 1.12)

Augustine's excerpt is a single sentence explaining why Paul spoke as he did. He says that Paul said this because he was speaking to those who were unable to grasp the more sublime teachings of the divinity of Christ.

**Insight:** Augustine sees Paul's simple message as a choice to fit the teaching to the listeners' spiritual maturity. It does not mean the gospel lacks depth.

*Note:* The excerpt does not say which verse of chapter 2 "this" refers to, so its exact connection to the text cannot be determined from what is provided.

## John Chrysostom (*Homily 6 on First Corinthians*)

Two of the excerpts are versions of the same homily, one an older translation and one a modern one. They are treated together here. Chrysostom focuses on Paul's words, "And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling."

**1. The many obstacles the gospel faced.** Chrysostom lists the disadvantages the Corinthian mission had to overcome. Not only are the believers unlearned persons; not only is he that speaks unlearned; not only is the manner of the teaching of an unlearned cast throughout; not only was the thing preached of itself enough to stagger people; (for the cross and death were the message brought;) but together with these there were also other hindrances, the dangers, and the plots, and the daily fear, and the being hunted about.

**2. "Weakness" means persecution.** Chrysostom argues that the word "weakness," with him in many places stands for the persecutions. He supports this by citing other passages from Paul's letters, including Galatians 4 and 2 Corinthians 11–12. One citation in the provided text, "2 Corinthians 5:32," appears to be a printing error, since the quoted words about Aretas match 2 Corinthians 11:32. He concludes that in this passage too, Paul did not stop at this point, but explaining the word "weakness" makes mention of his dangers.

**3. Paul's real fear makes his courage greater.** This is Chrysostom's most memorable point. He asks directly whether Paul feared danger and answers that he was, for even though he was Paul, he was still a man. He insists this is not to say anything against him but rather about the infirmity of human nature. Instead, it is to the credit of his sense of determination that even when he was afraid of death and beatings, he did nothing wrong because of this fear.

He then challenges those who would picture Paul as fearless: those who claim that Paul was not afraid of being beaten not only do not honor him, they diminish his greatness. For if he was without fear, what endurance or self-control was there in bearing dangers? He ends with personal admiration. Being in fear, and not simply in "fear," but even in "trembling" at his perils, he so ran as ever to keep his crown; and gave not in for any danger, in his task of purging out the world, and everywhere both by sea and land sowing the Gospel.

**Insight:** Courage is not the absence of fear but faithfulness in spite of it. Paul's honesty about his fear is part of what makes his example worth following.

## Origen of Alexandria (*On First Principles* 4.1.7)

Origen does not quote chapter 2 directly in this excerpt. However, his argument closely matches the chapter's contrast between human wisdom and God's power: If our Scriptures had persuaded people to believe because they had been written with rhetorical art or philosophical skill, there is no doubt that our faith would be said to depend on the art of words and on human wisdom rather than on the power of God.

**Insight:** For Origen, the plain style of Scripture is evidence of its divine source. Because the message did not win people over through eloquence, its success shows that faith rests on God's power rather than on human skill.

## Common Thread

The three commentators point in the same direction. The apparent weakness of the gospel's presentation serves a purpose:
- Augustine sees it as fitting the teaching to the listeners.
- Chrysostom sees God's work advancing through a fearful but faithful messenger.
- Origen sees proof that faith depends on God rather than on human wisdom.

# Bede on Revelation 3: The Letter to Sardis

All four excerpts come from one commentator, **the Venerable Bede**, and all address the letter to the church in Sardis (Revelation 3:1–6). The excerpts do not cover the letters to Philadelphia or Laodicea later in the chapter, so this summary is limited to Sardis.

## 1. The "Angel" as the Church's Leader

Bede reads the "angel" of the church as its human leader. He says Christ reproves this angel, that is, the priest, for being less diligent in correcting evils. In Bede's reading, the main fault in Sardis is not open wickedness. It is a leader's failure to deal with wrongdoing in the community.

## 2. The Danger of a Merely Apparent Life

On the words "you have a name that you live, and you are dead," Bede gives a warning: You appear to be alive, but if you do not watch in correcting the wicked, you will be counted among the dead. He links spiritual vitality to active vigilance. A reputation for being alive is not enough.

## 3. God's Standard Differs from Human Judgment

This may be Bede's sharpest insight. Commenting on "I have not found your works perfect before my God," he says: The works of a ruler are not perfect before God if he does not strive to rouse others, even if he seems blameless to men. Personal blamelessness does not satisfy God's standard for a leader. The pastoral duty to stir others up is part of what makes a leader's works complete.

## 4. The Call to Vigilance

On Christ's warning "I will come upon you as a thief," Bede connects the passage to Jesus' teaching in the Gospels: As in the parable of the gospel, so here by the example of a thief to be avoided, he warns to be vigilant. The theme of watchfulness runs through his whole treatment of Sardis.

## 5. The Faithful Few and the Significance of Names

Bede also notices the faithful remnant. Christ praises some who walk in white garments, to whom the name of the Sardis stone, indeed precious, is fitting. This is a wordplay connecting the city's name with a precious gem.

He also draws attention to the wording "a few names": He did not say a few people, but a few names. He explains why this matters: For he calls his own sheep by name; he knows Moses by name, and he writes the names of his saints in heaven. The point is that God knows his faithful people personally and individually, even within a church that is failing as a whole.

## Summary

Bede's commentary on Sardis has two main threads:
- **A pastoral challenge:** Leaders are accountable before God not only for their own conduct but for watching over and correcting others. Looking blameless to people is not the same as being complete before God.
- **A word of comfort:** Even in a spiritually sleepy church, God sees and personally knows the faithful few, and he values them as precious.

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on 1 Corinthians 16

**Note on scope:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, **John Chrysostom**, in his Homily 43 on First Corinthians. Documents 2 and 4 appear to be condensed paraphrases of passages in Documents 1 and 3. The excerpts cover only the opening verses of the chapter (16:1–3, the collection for the saints). They do not address the rest of 1 Corinthians 16, such as Paul's travel plans, Timothy, Apollos, or the closing greetings.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 43)

### 1. Why Paul ends with almsgiving
Chrysostom points out that Paul, moving from doctrine to moral teaching, dismisses every thing else and proceeds to the chief of good things, discoursing about alms. This is unusual, because in his other letters Paul addresses many virtues in the conclusion. Chrysostom explains that the greater part also of what had been spoken before was of an ethical nature, so Paul raises only the subject which most pressed on him, viz. the aid required for the saints.

He also notes the timing. When he had persuaded them concerning the resurrection, and made them more earnest, then and not till then he discusses this point also. Doctrine prepares the heart for generosity.

### 2. Paul's method of encouragement
- **Shared burden:** Paul calls the gift a "contribution" (*logia*), presenting it as easy from the start, for when contribution is made by all together, that becomes light which is charged upon each.
- **Holy rivalry:** By citing the Galatian churches first, Paul was kindling their emulation by the account of the well-doings of others. The Corinthians would surely feel ashamed ever afterwards to be found inferior to Galatians.
- **Apostolic authority:** He says not, "I advised," and, "I counselled;" but, "I gave order," which is more authoritative.

### 3. The Lord's Day and giving
Chrysostom finds deep meaning in Paul's instruction to set money aside "on the first day of the week." The day itself was enough to encourage them to give alms. For the Lord's day was the day on which we received all the blessings which we now have. It is the root and the beginning of our new life in Christ. It is also the day of rest, when our souls can relax from their toils and open themselves to show pity. Moreover, participation in holy Communion on that day instills great zeal in us. Resurrection, rest, and the Eucharist together make Sunday the natural setting for generosity.

### 4. Everyone gives, and the home becomes a church
"Each one of you" means the call is universal: whether poor or rich, woman or man, slave or free. Paul does not ask them to bring small sums to church, where they might feel embarrassed. Instead he tells them to save at home. Chrysostom paraphrases Paul as saying: make your house a church; your little box a treasury. Become a guardian sacred wealth, a self-ordained steward of the poor. Your benevolent mind assigns to you this priesthood. Ordinary believers thus take on a priestly role in caring for the poor.

### 5. Gentle, proportional giving
Chrysostom praises how Paul avoids being burdensome:
- No fixed amount is set: He said not, "so much," or "so much," but "as he may prosper," whether much or little.
- The wording points to God as the source: Paul said "as he may prosper:" signifying that the supply is of God.
- Saving gradually makes it easier, since the gathering little by little hinders all perception of the burden and the cost.

### 6. Chrysostom's own pastoral boldness
Chrysostom applies the text to his congregation. He refuses to be silent about almsgiving, because neither was Paul ashamed to be continually troublesome upon such points as these. He pleads mainly for the givers' benefit: it is for the poor that I make my supplication; nay, not so much for the poor, as for your sake who bestow the gift. He grounds this in Christ's identification with the needy: Your Lord is not ashamed before the whole world to speak thus: "I was an hungred, and you gave Me not to eat," He who is void of all want and requires nothing. He concludes that hesitating to ask for the poor is of the snare of the devil.

---

**Key takeaway:** For Chrysostom, the collection in 1 Corinthians 16 is far more than an administrative note. It is the practical result of resurrection faith. The giving should be rooted in Sunday worship, shared by every believer, proportioned to God's provision, and understood as a spiritual good for the giver as much as for the poor.
