# Patristic Commentary on Matthew 24: A Summary

**Scope note:** All four excerpts focus on the opening scene of Matthew 24, where the disciples point out the temple buildings and Jesus predicts their destruction (24:1–2). None address the later parts of the chapter, such as the signs of the end, the "abomination of desolation," or the coming of the Son of Man, so this summary covers only that opening passage.

---

## 1. Origen of Alexandria (*Commentary on Matthew* 29.6; 30–31)

Origen reads the passage on three levels.

**The believer as temple.** Origen applies the temple's destruction to each person's spiritual life. Everyone who receives the Word of God into himself is a temple. He describes degrees of ruin:
- A person who sins but does not fully abandon God, and retains some vestiges of faith and devotion to the commandments of God remains a temple, albeit partially destroyed.
- A person who keeps walking away from faith is progressively alienated until he has fully departed from the living God. Of such a person, Jesus' words apply fully: "there will not be left one stone" of the teaching of the commandments of God "upon another that will not be destroyed."

**Scripture as temple.** Origen also treats the temple as a symbol of the Old Testament read literally. The temple of God was a building composed of distinct words, every Scripture from the Old Testament plainly having been constructed according to the historical sense. When the disciples admired the building, Jesus answered that this first, merely physical building must be destroyed by the Word so that another, more divine, more mystical temple might be constructed in its place. For Origen, that other temple is the Scripture, understood in its deeper spiritual sense.

**Christ's departure from the temple.** On Jesus leaving the temple (24:1), Origen writes that he who had preserved the temple left it, lest it collapse while he was still in it. He argues that the temple stood safe and secure as long as the Word and the kingdom of God were with the Jews, and that afterward both Jesus and the kingdom of God were then established among the Gentiles.

## 2. Cyril of Alexandria (*Fragment* 266)

Cyril reads the passage mainly as historical prophecy.

**Misplaced admiration.** Cyril notes the irony of the disciples' sightseeing: they supposed that Jesus would admire with them all there was to see, although being God he has heaven as his throne!

**Fulfillment in Roman conquest.** He connects the prophecy to the Roman siege of Jerusalem, saying it came to pass that they suffered these things after the crucifixion of the Savior.

**The disciples' misunderstanding.** Cyril observes that the hearers did not understand the meaning of Jesus' teachings. They supposed his teachings concerned the consummation of the age. In other words, Cyril takes this prediction to refer to a historical event rather than the end of the world.

## 3. Hilary of Poitiers (*Commentary on Matthew* 25.1)

Hilary stresses the timing and the replacement of the physical temple.

**An attempt to move Jesus.** The temple's splendor was shown to Christ immediately after he had warned of Jerusalem's desolation, as though to move him.

**The eternal temple.** Jesus nonetheless affirmed its total destruction, for an eternal temple was being consecrated as a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. Like Origen, Hilary locates this temple in the believer: This eternal temple is the man who is made worthy of becoming God's habitation through knowledge of the Son, confession of the Father and obedience to the commandments.

---

## Common Threads

- **From stone to spirit:** Origen and Hilary both hold that the physical temple gives way to a spiritual one, located in the faithful believer (and, for Origen, also in Scripture rightly understood).
- **Historical fulfillment:** Cyril and Origen both see the prophecy fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall after the crucifixion.
- **Correcting misplaced focus:** All three present the disciples' admiration of the building as a misunderstanding of what Jesus valued.

**A note for modern readers:** Both Cyril and Origen describe Jerusalem's destruction as collective punishment of the Jewish people for Christ's death (e.g., Origen's reference to the crime they committed against Christ). This collective-guilt reading was common in the early church, but it has been widely repudiated by Christian churches and scholars today. It is best understood as part of these writers' historical context rather than as a necessary part of their spiritual insights about the temple.

# Bede's Commentary on Revelation 18: Key Theological Insights

All four excerpts come from one commentator, **the Venerable Bede**, so this is a summary of his reading rather than a comparison of several voices. Each excerpt opens with a phrase from Revelation 18 and then comments on it. Together they follow the chapter's opening movement: the angel's announcement, the fall of Babylon, the merchants, and the call to come out.

## 1. The Angel from Heaven: Christ and the Church's Teachers

Bede comments on the passage where John says, "After these things, I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority". He reads the angel in two ways: "This strong angel illuminating the earth can also be understood as the Lord incarnate and the doctors of the Church; who, endowed with heavenly light, proclaim the fall of the world, saying: The kingdom of heaven is at hand".

**Insight:** Bede treats the departure of God's people as closely tied to Babylon's ruin. The departure is itself described as "the ruin of Babylon." As Sodom was destroyed once Lot left, the withdrawal of the faithful signals and accompanies judgment on the wicked city. The excerpt does not say who "he" is. It most likely refers to the author of Revelation, but the text does not state this.

1. **Spiritual interpretation:** Bede reads Babylon mainly as a spiritual reality, the devil's city, rather than only a historical one.
2. **Comfort for the faithful:** He reassures God's people ("Jerusalem") that the earthly city's apparent power is in fact its fall.
3. **Warning against worldliness:** The merchants show how temporal wealth gained through sin leads to spiritual poverty.

# Augustine of Hippo on the Opening of Genesis 1

All four excerpts come from **Augustine of Hippo**, drawn from three of his works. They focus on the opening verses of Genesis 1, especially the description of the earth as formless and the phrase "darkness was over the abyss." The rest of the chapter, such as the days of creation and the making of humanity, is not addressed in these excerpts.

## 1. "Heaven and Earth" as Unformed Raw Material
*(On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis 3.10 and 4.12)*

Augustine reads the first mention of "heaven and earth" not as the finished world but as the raw material from which it would be shaped. He writes that Scripture called heaven and earth that formless matter of the universe, which was changed into formed and beautiful natures by God's ineffable command. This material was confused and mixed up but suited to receive forms from God their maker.

He offers a memorable image for this. The unformed matter is like the seed of heaven and earth. In his reading, creation unfolds in stages: this matter that is ordered and distinguished by the next work of God is called the invisible and unformed earth and the deep that is lacking light.

**Theological insight:** God is the source of both the material of creation and its form and beauty. Creation is pictured as an orderly process of God shaping what he first brought into being.

## 2. Why Scripture Speaks This Way
*(Confessions 12.15)*

In the *Confessions*, Augustine explains why Scripture describes formlessness in concrete terms like "invisible" and "unorganized." Commenting on the words "The earth was invisible and unorganized, and darkness was over the abyss," he says that formlessness is suggested by these words, so that we might grasp the meaning by degrees, for we are unable to think cognitively about an absolute privation of form that still does not go as far as nothing. From this formless state, another visible and organized heaven and earth were to be made.

**Theological insight:** Scripture adapts its language to human limitations. Unformed matter is hard to imagine because it is something, yet not yet anything definite. The text therefore leads readers toward understanding step by step.

## 3. Darkness as the Absence of Light
*(On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis 4.12)*

Augustine argues that darkness is not a thing in its own right: One who diligently considers what darkness is really finds only the absence of light. So when Scripture says "darkness was over the abyss," as if to say, "There was no light over the abyss."

**Theological insight:** The darkness of Genesis 1 is not a rival power or substance alongside God. It is simply a lack of light, a condition waiting for God's next creative act.

## 4. Answering the Manichaeans: The Light in Which God Dwells
*(Two Books on Genesis Against the Manichaeans 1.3.6)*

Here Augustine defends the text against critics. The Manichaeans find fault with this and say, "Was God then in darkness, before he made the light?" Augustine replies that they themselves are truly in the darkness of ignorance, and for that reason they do not understand the light in which God was before he made this light. He diagnoses their error: they know only the light they see with the eyes of the flesh. Consequently, they worship this sun that every creature sees. Against this, he urges: let us understand that there is a different light in which God dwells.

**Theological insight:** Augustine distinguishes created, physical light from the uncreated light of God. Created light came into being through God's act, while God himself was never in darkness. Confusing the two leads to worshiping creation instead of the Creator.

## Summary of Key Themes

| Theme | Augustine's Insight |
|---|---|
| Creation's origins | "Heaven and earth" first names formless matter, the "seed" later shaped by God |
| Scripture's language | Concrete words help us grasp formlessness gradually |
| Nature of darkness | Darkness is only the absence of light, not a substance |
| God and light | God dwells in a light different from the physical light he created |

Together, these excerpts show Augustine reading Genesis 1 with close attention to its philosophical implications. He emphasizes God's sovereignty over creation, the ordered stages of God's work, and the vital distinction between the Creator and what he has made.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 24: A Summary

## John Chrysostom: Why the Text Mentions Abraham's Age

Chrysostom focuses on the chapter's opening. He quotes the verse: "Abraham was old, advanced in years. The Lord had blessed Abraham in every respect." He then asks why it mentioned this to us. His answer is that the detail prepares for what follows: since he was about to give good care and attention to Isaac, to the point of bringing him a bride, accordingly it mentioned to us the patriarch's age.

**Key insight:** Chrysostom reads the narrative details as purposeful. Abraham's old age frames the search for Isaac's bride as an act of fatherly care in the last stage of his life.

## Augustine of Hippo: The Oath "Under the Thigh" as a Prophecy of the Incarnation

Augustine discusses the oath Abraham requires of his servant in two works, and he interprets it the same way in both.

**From the *Tractate on the Gospel of John*:**
- He stresses the significance of the moment: an important thing was being done when a spouse was being sought for the seed of Abraham.
- In his view, the oath was meant to teach the servant that he did not desire grandchildren carnally and that he did not have any carnal conception about his progeny.
- He explains the symbol directly: by the thigh, his progeny.
- He concludes by asking, what was that swearing but a signifying that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from the progeny of Abraham?

**From *On the Good of Marriage*:**
- He repeats the reading. Swearing with a hand under the thigh signified that in that flesh, which took its origin from that thigh, the God of heaven would come.
- He applies the passage to Christian marriage. He calls marriage a good in which the married are better in proportion as they fear God more chastely and more faithfully, especially if they also nourish spiritually the children whom they desire carnally.

**Key insight:** For Augustine, the oath is a prophetic sign of Christ, who would come in the flesh from Abraham's line. Abraham's concern for descendants is therefore spiritual rather than merely biological. Augustine draws a pastoral lesson from this: married couples should desire children and also raise them spiritually in the fear of God.

## Origen of Alexandria: A Note on Relevance

This excerpt does not clearly address Genesis 24. It discusses the descendants of **Keturah**, Abraham's later wife, who appears in the following chapter. Origen's main point is that knowing these genealogies helps readers recognize more easily those things that are said about the diverse nations in the Scriptures. His example is Moses' marriage: because Midian is found to be a son of Keturah and Abraham, Origen concludes that Moses' wife is from the seed of Abraham and was not a foreigner.

Origen's closing remark appears garbled in this translation. It says Kedar descends from the very stock of Kedar and Abraham, which is circular as written. Without the original text, the intended meaning cannot be confirmed.

**Key insight:** Origen values the literal genealogies as a key to understanding how the nations in later Scripture relate to Abraham. This bears only indirectly on Genesis 24.

## Summary

| Commentator | Focus | Main Theological Point |
|---|---|---|
| Chrysostom | Abraham's age and blessing | Narrative details show Abraham's care in securing Isaac's bride |
| Augustine | The oath under the thigh | It is a prophetic sign that God would come in the flesh from Abraham's line, and it teaches that marriage and children should be valued spiritually |
| Origen | Keturah's descendants | Genealogies explain kinship among nations, but the excerpt concerns Genesis 25 more than Genesis 24 |

Augustine offers the most developed theological reading in these excerpts. He turns a puzzling ancient custom into a Christ-centered prophecy and draws from it a practical teaching on marriage.

# Romans 7 in Patristic and Medieval Commentary: A Summary

These excerpts focus mainly on the opening of Romans 7 (vv. 1–6), where Paul uses the analogy of marriage to explain how believers are released from the Law.

---

## Thomas Aquinas

Aquinas gives the most detailed treatment.

**The main point of the passage.** He reads the chapter as continuing Paul's argument about grace. After showing that we are set free from sin through the grace of Christ, the Apostle now shows that through the same grace we are freed from slavery to the Law.

**Which "law" Paul means.** Aquinas asks how Paul could address Roman Gentiles as people "who know the law." He mentions that some explained this as referring to the natural law, of which the Gentiles were not ignorant, but he rejects this view because it does not seem to agree with the intention of the Apostle who always has in mind the Law of Moses, when he speaks of the Law with no modifying qualifications. Instead, he concludes that the Roman believers were not only Gentiles; there were many Jews among them.

**The marriage analogy.** Aquinas explains that the Law was given to direct man in the way of this life... Therefore, the obligation of the Law is dissolved by death. Citing Augustine, he notes that since... marriage is a good of mortal man, its obligation does not extend beyond mortal life. He also sees a deeper meaning in the permanence of marriage: it is the sacrament of the indissoluble union of Christ and the Church.

**An apparent problem with the analogy.** Aquinas admits that Paul's application seems awkward, because in the preceding example the man, died and the woman remarried without obligation of the law. But here the one released from obligation is said to die. His answer is that since marriage is between two, it makes no difference which one dies. In either case the law is taken away by death. Believers die to the Law in becoming members of the body of Christ, dying and being buried with him, so that they may belong to Christ, in whom through rising with him you have received a new life.

**The purpose of this freedom.** The point is fruitfulness. If we have been made members of Christ and abide in Christ, we can bear fruit, i.e., good works, for the honor of God. Aquinas suggests the Law is called a "law of death" chiefly because if offered the occasion for spiritual death, and that believers now serve in the new life of the Spirit, i.e., renewed in the spirit through the grace of Christ.

**A practical side point.** From verse 3, Aquinas argues that second, third or fourth marriages are lawful of themselves, and not only by dispensation as Chrysostom seems to say. This view of Chrysostom comes from Aquinas's report; it does not appear in the Chrysostom excerpt provided.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 12)

**The link to Romans 6.** Chrysostom sees chapter 7 as building on Paul's earlier argument. Having said believers are "dead to sin," Paul here shows that not sin only, but also the Law, has no dominion over them. But if the Law has none, much less has sin.

**A "twofold freedom."** Where Aquinas treats the role reversal as a difficulty to resolve, Chrysostom sees it as strengthening the argument. Paul offers two arguments: One, that when a husband is dead, the woman is no longer subject to her husband... and the other, that in the present case it is not the husband only that is dead but the wife also. Therefore, if the one event frees her from his power, much more does the concurrence of both.

**Paul's choice of words.** Chrysostom notes that Paul does not say, husband or wife, but "man," which name is common to either creature, and concludes that the Law then is given for the living, but to the dead it ceases to be ordained (or to give commands).

---

## Origen of Alexandria

**Commentary on Romans.** This short excerpt does not say which verse it addresses. Its reference to "those who knew the law" suggests verse 1. Origen links it to verse 14 ("We know that the law is spiritual.") and argues that this knowledge was not Paul's alone. Before Christ, there were many Jews who grew in spiritual knowledge and saw God's glory, e.g., Isaiah. This offers a positive view of faithful Jews under the Law, in contrast to Aquinas's emphasis on the Law's slavery.

**Homilies on Genesis 6.3.** This excerpt comes from a sermon on Genesis, not a commentary on Romans, and does not cite Romans 7 directly. It does closely echo Paul's marriage imagery: The law of the letter must die so that, free at last, the soul may marry the spirit and receive the marriage of the New Testament. This reflects Origen's characteristic contrast between "letter" and "spirit."

---

## Key Themes Across the Commentaries

- **Freedom through death:** All three commentators read Paul's marriage analogy as teaching that death, specifically the believer's death with Christ, ends the Law's binding claim.
- **The analogy's "awkwardness":** Aquinas and Chrysostom both notice that Paul's application shifts who dies. Aquinas explains it away, while Chrysostom treats it as a double basis for freedom.
- **A new union:** Aquinas (belonging to Christ) and Origen (the soul marrying the spirit) both stress that release from the Law leads to a new, fruitful relationship.

# Patristic Commentary on Philippians 3:1–3: A Summary

These excerpts come from two early church writers, John Chrysostom and Didymus the Blind. Together they cover the opening verses of Philippians 3: Paul's encouragement to the church, his warning against those who insisted on circumcision, and his statement about true worship in the Spirit.

---

## John Chrysostom (*Homily on Philippians* 11)

### 1. Paul as a pastor to anxious believers
Chrysostom first looks at the emotional situation behind Paul's words. He observes that despondency and worry deprive the soul of its vitality. They put an immoderate strain upon the soul. For this reason, Paul comforts the Philippians, who were in great despondency because they did not know how things stood with Paul. In fact, they thought him already dead.

He also notes how Paul goes about it: he does not introduce his exhortation immediately, but after having heaped praises on them and expressed his wonder he praises them once again. For Chrysostom, Paul shows a pastoral wisdom that encourages people before correcting them.

*Note:* This excerpt does not quote or name a specific verse. It is filed under Philippians 3:1–3, but its exact link to the text has to be inferred.

### 2. The reversal of the term "dogs"
Chrysostom sees a sharp reversal in Paul's language. He writes that the Jews are no longer children. The Gentiles were once called dogs but now these [Judaizing Christians] are. His reason: just as the Gentiles were once strangers to Christ and God, so these have now become. The label also says something about their behavior, since Paul alludes to their stubborn shamelessness and their great tenacity against the faithful.

The theological point is that belonging to God depends on one's relationship to Christ, not on ethnic or ritual status.

### 3. Paul's wordplay: "concision" instead of "circumcision"
Chrysostom's most detailed comments concern Paul's wording. Because the Jews attached great solemnity to circumcision… Paul mutilates its name and says, "Beware of the concision."

He praises Paul's tact: He refrains from saying that circumcision is evil, that circumcision is superfluous, so as not to alarm these people, but he conveys his point more wisely, turning them away from the act indeed but being gracious in his words. Paul does not even give it the name circumcision. The reasoning is that when this happens unlawfully, it is nothing but a curtailment of the flesh, a "concision."

Chrysostom offers a second possible meaning as well: either this was the reason or else it was because they were trying to cut up the church in pieces. On this reading, the "cutting" refers both to the physical rite and to the division these teachers were causing in the community.

---

## Didymus the Blind (*On the Holy Spirit* 249)

### Reading Scripture "according to the Spirit"
Didymus uses Philippians 3 for a different purpose. He is not writing a running commentary on the chapter but explaining how to interpret Scripture. He argues that the word spirit signifies above all a deeper and mystic meaning in the holy Scriptures. He cites Paul's words as support: "We are the circumcision, who serve the Spirit of God and do not trust in the flesh."

He seems to take the contrast between "Spirit" and "flesh" in this verse as a contrast between the deeper, spiritual sense of Scripture and a merely literal one. However, the excerpt is short and partly omitted, so his full reasoning cannot be reconstructed from what is provided.

---

## Common Threads

# Summary of Patristic Commentary on James 2: Partiality and the Rich and Poor

These excerpts center on James 2:1 and its warning against favoritism. Only Bede comments directly on the verse. The others address the same theme, but their connection to James is thematic rather than explicit.

## Bede: Faith Without Matching Works

Bede gives the most direct and developed commentary, quoting the verse itself: "My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with partiality."

- **Diagnosis of the readers:** In Bede's reading, James showed that those to whom he wrote were indeed imbued with evangelical faith, but were empty in works.
- **The specific fault:** Christ taught that his commandments should be fulfilled through giving to the poor. James saw that his readers, contrary to what should be done for the poor for the sake of eternal rewards, were rather doing it for the rich for the sake of earthly advantages, and therefore he reproved them as they deserved.
- **The title "of glory":** Bede draws a theological point from the way James describes Christ. Calling the Lord "of glory" reminds readers that they should obey Christ, who, being the splendor of glory (Hebrews 1), rewards eternally whatever is given to the poor out of love for him. That eternal glory contrasts with the passing nature of human honor, which, citing Isaiah 40, is like grass whose glory like the flower of grass fades.

**Key insight:** Favoritism toward the rich exchanges Christ's eternal glory for fleeting human glory. It shows that faith has not yet produced the works it should.

## John Chrysostom: Unity in the Body and Inner Faith

Chrysostom's two excerpts come from a catena, a collection of patristic comments arranged by verse. They do not mention James 2 directly, but both bear on its theme.

- **Mutual belonging:** Chrysostom grounds the rejection of partiality in the unity of believers: "Are we not all one body, both great and small?" Because believers are members of one another, self-exaltation is senseless: why do you mindlessly exalt yourself? To shame a fellow believer is to wound oneself, for just as he is a part of you, so you too are a part of him.
- **Equality in Christ:** He states plainly that there is no difference between rich and poor in Christ. His practical counsel closely parallels James's concern: "Pay no attention to the outward appearance, but look for the inner faith instead."

**Key insight:** Partiality violates the organic unity of the church and judges by appearance rather than faith.

## Augustine of Hippo: God's Choice of the Lowly

This excerpt comes from Augustine's *Confessions* (8.4.9), not from a commentary on James, so its link to James 2 is thematic only.

- Augustine rejects any idea that in your tabernacle, Lord, the rich should be more highly regarded than the poor, or the noble than the less well-born.
- He grounds this in God's own way of acting: You have chosen the weak things of this world to put the strong to shame, and you have chosen things which are dishonorable, despised and of no account, in order to bring to nothing the things which are.

**Key insight:** Favoring the rich and noble in God's house runs against God's own pattern of choosing the lowly.

## Common Thread

The three writers approach the issue differently but agree that favoritism based on wealth or status has no place in the church.
- **Bede** frames it as a failure of faith to produce works, and as a choice of earthly over eternal reward.
- **Chrysostom** frames it as an offense against the unity of the body.
- **Augustine** frames it as contrary to God's own choice of the weak and despised.

# Bede on Revelation 8: Summary of Key Insights

**A note on sources:** All four excerpts come from one commentator, the Venerable Bede, so this summary covers his views only. Bede quotes Jerome once, and that is marked below as Bede citing Jerome. All the excerpts clearly address Revelation 8.

## 1. The Silence of the Seventh Seal (8:1): Rest After Trial

Bede reads the "silence in heaven" as a time of peace for the Church at the end of history. After the destruction of the Antichrist, a brief rest is believed to come in the Church, which he links to Daniel 12.

- **Bede citing Jerome:** Bede draws on Jerome, who explains that "Blessed... is he who, after the Antichrist is killed, awaits beyond the one thousand two hundred and ninety days, that is, three and a half years, forty-five days, during which the Lord and Savior is to come in his majesty."
- **Humility about the mystery:** Bede does not overreach. He says that why there is a silence of forty-five days after the killing of the Antichrist is known to divine knowledge. He offers only a tentative suggestion: the delay of the kingdom of the saints is a test of patience.
- **A link to Christ's Passion:** Bede notes that in the sixth seal he sees the greatest pressures on the Church, in the seventh he sees rest, because the Lord, crucified on the sixth day, rested on the Sabbath, waiting for the time of resurrection. The Church's history follows the pattern of Christ's own suffering and Sabbath rest.

## 2. Recapitulation: Revelation Retells the Same Story

Bede holds that Revelation does not move in strict chronological order. Having finished the seals, John recapitulates from the beginning, intending to speak the same things differently. On this reading, the trumpets cover the same span of Church history as the seals, seen from a new angle.

## 3. The Seven Trumpets as the Church's Preaching (8:2)

Bede reads the seven angels as the Church itself. The Church, often commended by the number seven, is devoted to the duty of preaching. He then gives a symbolic meaning for each trumpet:

1. the common destruction of the impious by fire and hail
2. the devil expelled from the Church, more fervently inflaming the sea of the world
3. heretics falling away from the Church, corrupting the rivers of the Holy Scripture
4. the downfall of false brethren in the obscuration of the stars
5. the greater infestation of heretics preceding the time of the Antichrist
6. the open war of the Antichrist and his followers against the Church
7. the day of judgment, when the Lord will render the reward to His own and will destroy those who have corrupted the earth.

Several trumpets concern threats from inside the Church, such as heretics, false brethren, and corrupted Scripture. Bede sees internal corruption as a major danger alongside outward persecution.

## 4. The "Other Angel" as Christ (8:3)

Bede pays attention to the text's structure. John did not say, "Then he came," but proposing that the angels had received the trumpets, he goes back to explain how they had received them. In other words, the passage looks back to how the Church's preaching mission began: although the Church preached before the coming of the Lord, it was not everywhere, until it was confirmed by His Spirit.

Bede identifies this angel with Christ, who appeared in the sight of the Church, having become the censer, from which God received the odor of sweetness, and was propitiated towards the world. Drawing on a variant reading ("upon the altar"), he sees here the cross: Christ offered His golden censer, that is, His immaculate body conceived by the Holy Spirit, upon the altar of the cross to the Father for us.

## 5. Incense and the Prayers of the Saints (8:3–4)

- **Christ as mediator of prayer:** From the prayers of the saints he offered the incense. Bede explains that he received from the prayers of the saints and offered it, because through him the prayers of all can sweetly reach God. He supports this with the Psalm: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight" (Psalm 140).
- **Sacrifice and repentance:** On the rising smoke, Bede writes that Christ the Lord offering Himself as a sacrifice of sweetness made the compunction of the hearts of the saints acceptable, which, being born from the inner fire, usually stirs up tears like smoke. Heartfelt sorrow and tears, like smoke from incense, rise to God and are made acceptable through Christ's sacrifice.

## Overall Takeaway

Bede reads Revelation 8 through Christ and the Church. The silence follows the pattern of Christ's Sabbath rest. The trumpets describe the Church's preaching mission and its struggles throughout history. The angel at the altar is Christ himself, whose sacrifice on the cross carries the prayers and repentant tears of believers to God.

# Summary of Commentaries on Hebrews 2

**Scope:** The excerpts cover only the first part of Hebrews 2. Chrysostom's material addresses verses 1–4, and much of it is moral exhortation rather than line-by-line exposition. Aquinas's material runs through verse 8. Neither excerpt treats verses 9–18 (Christ's suffering, His sharing in flesh and blood, and His high priesthood), so those themes cannot be summarized here.

---

## John Chrysostom (Homily 3 on Hebrews)

**1. "More earnest heed," meaning more than to the Law (v. 1)**
Chrysostom notes the comparison is implied rather than stated. The author meant "more earnest" than to the Law: but he suppressed the actual expression of it, and yet makes it plain in the course of reasoning, not in the way of counsel, nor of exhortation. He judges this tactful approach the wiser one: For so it was better.

**2. God Himself confirms the message (vv. 3–4)**
Chrysostom raises an objection: What if those that heard were forgers? His answer is that if they had gone astray, God would not have borne witness to them. Faith therefore rests on God, not on human messengers: we did not believe them simply, but through signs and wonders: wherefore we believe not them, but God Himself. He takes "various miracles" as declaring the abundance of the gifts: which was not so in the former dispensation. He also contrasts these with the works of wizards, which were not miracles, [or powers, ] but weakness and fancy, and things altogether vain.

**3. Gifts "according to His will": a pastoral insight**
Chrysostom reads this phrase as a comfort to readers whose spiritual gifts had faded. It is not likely there were many there who had gifts, but that these had failed, upon their becoming more slothful. Rather than leave them discouraged, he referred all to the will of God. God sometimes withholds gifts even from the virtuous, lest they might be made haughty, that they might not be puffed up.

**4. Application: love is the greatest gift**
From verse 4 Chrysostom moves into broader exhortation:
- **Be faithful in small things.** He urges hearers to show in the little, what you would have been, if you had had the other. Even those who cannot preach publicly can encourage family and friends in private.
- **Charity surpasses miracles.** Asked what the greatest gift is, he answers charity. He calls it greater than raising the dead.
- **Love is open to everyone.** This gift not one or two, but all may have. He explains why it ranks above miracles: that indeed is wholly of God's grace, but this, of your own earnestness also.
- **Love makes us like God.** Herein we shall be like God if we love all men, even our enemies; not, if we work miracles.

---

## Thomas Aquinas (Commentary on Hebrews)

**1. Why Christ's teaching demands greater obedience (vv. 1–4)**
Aquinas reads the passage as a conclusion drawn from chapter 1: after showing in a number of ways Christ's superiority over the angels, the Apostle here concludes that Christ's doctrine, namely, the New Testament, deserves more obedience than the Old Testament. He gives three reasons:
- **Authority:** the speaker is the Creator and the Son of God and not a creature of God's minister.
- **Usefulness:** they are the words of eternal life.
- **Sweetness:** they are sweet.

**2. Degrees of "drifting away"**
Aquinas sees escalating danger: someone drifts away by bodily punishments, he drifts away worse through guilt; but he drifts away worst by eternal damnation, because not a shard remains.

**3. The Law's authority and just penalties (v. 2)**
The Law was not delivered by human authority but by angels, and it was "valid" because everything foretold in the Old Law has been fulfilled.

He reads "transgression or disobedience" as covering two kinds of sin, the sin of omission and of transgression. The penalty was "just" because according to the amount of sin there is a certain amount of punishment.

**4. What makes salvation "so great" (v. 3)**
The key contrast is that the Law gave knowledge, notably knowledge of sin, but it did not confer grace, for grace is conferred in the New Testament. Salvation is great for three reasons:
- **Its depth:** it frees us not only from the dangers of bodily death but of spiritual.
- **Its reach:** it is for all men and from all enemies.
- **Its duration:** it is eternal.

The message also has a twofold origin. It came not by angels but by Christ, and secondly through the apostles, who head from Christ.

**5. Signs, wonders, and the Spirit's gifts (v. 4)**
Aquinas distinguishes the two: a sign would be something beyond and above nature, though not contrary to it; while a wonder is something contrary to nature, as the raising of the dead. He adds that the greatest wonder was that God became man.

How can the one Spirit be "distributed"? Aquinas explains that He is not distributed as to His essence, but as to His gifts.

**6. The world to come belongs to Christ, not angels (v. 5)**
Those who disobey Christ face severer punishment because Christ is Lord, and a person who offends his Lord is punished more than one who sins against a servant. Angels do have roles over nations, but people are not subject to them as to a lord, but as to a vicegerent.

**7. Psalm 8 as a portrait of Christ (vv. 6–8)**
Aquinas reads the quoted psalm as unfolding the mystery of the Incarnation; secondly, of the Passion (v. 7); thirdly, the mystery of the exaltation.
- **Incarnation:** The cause of the Incarnation is God's care of man. After the Fall God seemed to have forgotten humanity, but later he seems to have become mindful of him, when He sends a Redeemer.
- **"A little lower than the angels":** By suffering and death, Christ was made a little less than they: not that He had lost His fullness or was diminished in any way, but because He joined our smallness to Him self. This lowering was not in regard to his divinity nor in regard to His soul, but in regard to His body. It was also brief, because He lasted a short time.
- **Crowned:** The crown signifies victory, and Christ won this crown by the struggle of His Passion. What is natural to Christ as God becomes, inasmuch as He is man, they are the reward for the victory of his Passion.
- **A second reading:** Aquinas also applies the psalm to humanity in general. Man is crowned with glory through intellect, with honor through free will, and with power through dominion over creation.

**8. Answering Arius, and the "not yet" (v. 8)**
Against the claim that subjection makes the Son inferior, Aquinas answers that the Father subjected all things to the Son according to His human nature, in which He is inferior to the Father, but according to the divine nature Christ Himself subjected all things to Himself.

As for why we do not yet see all things subject to Him, it is because unbelievers, sinners and devils are not yet subject to Him. Yet in regard to his power all are subject to Him: now in regard to its authority, but later in regard to obedience.

---

## Points of Convergence

Both commentators stress that God Himself guarantees the gospel through miracles and the gifts of the Spirit. Both also read "according to His will" as showing that God distributes gifts as He sees fit. The main difference is approach:
- **Chrysostom** turns pastoral, pressing toward humility and love.
- **Aquinas** stays systematic, unpacking the Law/gospel contrast and the Christology of Psalm 8.

*Note on the text:* Some Scripture references in the Aquinas excerpt appear garbled in transmission. For example, "Heb. 3:1" is given for a line that does not come from Hebrews, and "Gal. 2:19" for a phrase about the Law "ordained by angels." Readers checking the references should verify them independently.

# Patristic Insights on Genesis 49: Jacob's Final Words to His Sons

All four excerpts deal directly with Genesis 49, where the dying Jacob gathers his sons. The commentators focus on three themes: the prophetic and end-times character of Jacob's words, the order in which he addresses his sons, and the moral lesson of Reuben's fall.

---

## 1. Origen of Alexandria: Jacob's Words and the End of the World

Origen reads Jacob's opening summons as a statement about the end of history. He says that on the consummation of the world, Jacob is the first to refer to this when, in giving his testament to his sons he says, "Gather to me, you sons of Jacob, that I may tell you what shall be in the last days," or, "after the last days."

From this he draws a theological conclusion about time itself: If then there are "last days," or a time "after the last days," it follows of necessity that the days that had a beginning also come to an end.

**Key insight:** Genesis 49 is not only family prophecy. For Origen it is the first biblical witness that created time has a set end.

---

## 2. Ambrose of Milan: Why Jacob Speaks of Things to Come Rather Than Blessing

Ambrose looks at how Jacob's words to his sons relate to the blessing he had just given. He notes a shift in approach: Whereas before he had preferred the younger to the elder, he begins with the eldest. He explains the difference this way: In the former case he preferred the symbolic gift; in this one he maintains the order of age.

He also explains why Genesis 49 is framed as prophecy rather than another blessing. Jacob had blessed all men with all their posterity and offspring of times to come in the persons of the two brothers; a repetition of that blessing of the people might seem superfluous, or the earlier blessing might be considered invalid. Therefore, it is with reason that Jacob says he is presenting anew his announcement of events that were to come in later ages, rather than a blessing.

**Key insight:** Ambrose reads Genesis 49 together with the preceding blessing. Because the earlier blessing had already covered all future generations, Jacob's final words serve as a prophetic announcement that keeps that blessing valid instead of repeating or replacing it. (The excerpt refers to "the two brothers" but does not name them.)

---

## 3. John Chrysostom: Inspired Prophecy and Moral Responsibility

### a. The Spirit-inspired character of Jacob's words
Chrysostom stresses Jacob's wisdom in using his final moments well: Since he foresaw the moment of his death, he summoned his sons. In his paraphrase, Jacob says his words concern not the immediate future but what will happen in the last days. Above all, Chrysostom gives the source of the prophecy: This I foretell to you not of myself but under the inspiration of the Spirit; hence I predict ahead of time what will occur after many generations.

He also sees fairness in how Jacob proceeds: with his sons gathered together the good man follows the order of their birth and in this way bestows curse or blessing appropriate to each, showing by this procedure the extraordinary degree of his own virtue.

### b. Reuben: birthright is not enough without virtue
Chrysostom's most pointed teaching concerns Reuben. Jacob first acknowledges the privileges conceded him by nature and the precedence he enjoyed in being the beginning of his line and enjoying the dignity of firstborn. Then he records his sins of free will as if on a bronze pillar to show that no advantage comes to us from natural advantage unless accompanied by good deeds of free will—these, you see, are what bring us commendation or lend us the stigma of blame.

He sums up the lesson of Reuben's fall: the pride of place accorded you by nature you have forfeited by your own headstrong behavior.

**Key insight:** Privileges of birth count for nothing without virtuous choices. Human beings are judged by what they freely do, not by the status they inherit.

---

## Common Threads

- **Prophetic and end-times focus:** Origen and Chrysostom both stress Jacob's reference to "the last days." Origen draws a lesson about the end of time, and Chrysostom emphasizes the Spirit's inspiration of the prophecy.
- **Order of birth:** Ambrose and Chrysostom both note that Jacob addresses his sons from eldest to youngest. Ambrose contrasts this with the earlier blessing, while Chrysostom sees it as evidence of Jacob's fairness and virtue.
- **Moral seriousness:** Chrysostom's treatment of Reuben turns the chapter into a lesson on free will and personal responsibility, which complements the more prophetic readings of Origen and Ambrose.

# Patristic and Medieval Commentary on Romans 3: A Summary

**A note on scope:** All the excerpts deal with the *opening* of Romans 3 (roughly verses 1–8), where Paul asks what advantage the Jew has. Aquinas covers the whole of verses 1–8. Chrysostom and Origen deal only with verses 1–2. None of the excerpts addresses the later parts of the chapter, such as the universal indictment of sin or the teaching on righteousness through faith, so this summary does not cover them. The two Chrysostom documents come from the same homily (Homily 6), so they are treated together.

---

## 1. Thomas Aquinas

Aquinas offers the most detailed treatment, following Paul's argument step by step.

**The objection Paul raises against himself.** Aquinas presents verse 1 as an objection that follows from Paul's own teaching in chapter 2: If what I say is so, i.e., that the true Jew and true circumcision are not something outward but inward in the heart, then what advantage has the Jew, i.e., what has been given to him more than to others? Denying any advantage seems wrong, since the Lord had said: "The Lord, your God, has chosen you to be a people for his own possession" (Dt 7:6).

**"Much in every way."** Aquinas reads Paul's answer as claiming an advantage that is both quantitative, which is indicated when he says, much, and numerical, which is indicated when he says, in every way. He grounds its greatness in the principle that man's greatest good lies in knowing God, in clinging to God and in being instructed by God. The chief advantage is that to them are entrusted the oracles of God, being His friends.

**Human unbelief does not cancel God's faithfulness (v. 3).** Aquinas argues that if the Jews' prerogative were taken away on account of the unbelief of some, it would follow that man's unbelief would nullify God's faithfulness -- which is an unacceptable conclusion. He reads "the faithfulness of God" in two ways:
- As the faith of believers, which is not undone by others' unbelief, because the evil in some members of society does not nullify the good in other members.
- As the faith with which God is faithful in keeping His promises.

**"Let God be true, though every man be false" (v. 4).** This is Aquinas's most philosophical point. Truth implies agreement between a thing and an understanding, but the relationship runs differently for humans and for God. Our intellect derives its knowledge from things; consequently, the cause and measure of our truth stems from the thing's being. Therefore, of himself every man is false in his intellect and is true only in virtue of participating in the divine truth. By contrast, the divine intellect, on the other hand, is the cause and measure of things. For this reason it is of itself unfailingly true, and everything else is true inasmuch as it conforms to that intellect.

**David and Psalm 51.** Aquinas explains why Paul cites Psalm 51. God through the prophet Nathan had promised David that He would establish his kingdom forever in his seed. After David's adultery and murder, some said that on account of these sins God would not keep the promises made to him. The psalm shows that God's justice, which involves keeping His promises, is not changed on account of sin.

**Two kinds of prophecy.** Aquinas distinguishes between them. God's promise to David was a predestinative prophecy, in which something is promised as destined to be fulfilled in every way; whereas something promised or foretold by a prophecy of warning is not predicted as destined to be fulfilled in every way but according to men's merits, which can change. If a warning goes unfulfilled, this is not prejudicial to God's justice, but indicates a change in deserts.

**Sin does not *cause* God's glory (vv. 5–8).** Aquinas guards against a dangerous misreading. Someone might take the word "that" causally, so that man's sin would be directly ordained to commend God's justice. Paul instead uses "that" consecutively, on the ground that David sinned and then the manifestation of divine justice followed, but not causally, as if a man's sin commended God's justice. If sin really served God's justice, it would not be deserving of punishment but of reward. Consequently, God would be unjust in punishing men for sin. Aquinas also adds that it is necessary that the first and highest item in every class be unerring, just as the first mover is unchangeable.

**"Do evil that good may come" (v. 8).** Aquinas notes that this slander arose because the apostles preached that through the abounding grace of Christ the debt for an abundance of sins was paid. He rejects the slogan on moral grounds: just as it is not correct to deduce truth from falsity, so it is wrong to reach a good end through evil means.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom (Homily 6)

Chrysostom's excerpt is shorter and attends more to Paul's *pastoral tone* than to his logic.

**The objection.** Chrysostom states it plainly: If, he means, these things are no use, what reason was there for that nation being called, and the circumcision too being given?

**God's gifts, not human merit.** Paul answers by speaking not of their praises but of the benefits of God. Chrysostom stresses that Israel's privileges were gifts: to be called a Jew and to know His Will and to approve the things which are more excellent, was no well doing of their own, but came of the grace of God.

**Gentleness toward the Law, firmness toward the people.** Chrysostom observes that Paul phrases things carefully. He did not say, Circumcision is valueless without a good life, but, Circumcision is of value with a good life, pointing out the same thing but in a more subdued tone. In this way Paul is sparing the things of the Law, and smiting the persons.

**Privilege brings accountability.** On "what advantage then has the Jew?", Chrysostom notes that Paul says not, None, but he concurs with the statement, and confutes it again by the sequel, and shows that they were even punished owing to this preëminence. The excerpt ends before Chrysostom explains *how* Paul shows this, so his full argument on this point is not available here.

---

## 3. Origen of Alexandria

Origen focuses on what it really means to be "entrusted with the oracles of God" (v. 2).

**First, but not only.** Origen notes that even though the oracles of God are now entrusted to the Gentiles as well, they were first entrusted to the Jews, as Paul says.

**The problem of study without understanding.** Origen raises a hard question: For we see many Jews who from infancy to old age never stop studying, yet they never come to a knowledge of the truth. He answers that Paul's statement applies especially to Moses, the prophets and others like them, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted. He adds that even the apostles of Christ and Paul himself, the vessel of election, came from the Jews and from the circumcision.

**The letter versus the oracles.** This is Origen's distinctive insight. He points out that Paul says that the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews, not merely the letter of the text. # Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 7: A Summary

## Overview
All of these excerpts focus on the chapter's opening verse, Paul's call to cleanse ourselves "from all defilement of flesh and spirit" and to perfect holiness "in the fear of God." None addresses the rest of the chapter. Three Church Fathers are represented, and John Chrysostom's material is by far the most substantial.

---

## Theodoret of Cyrus: Clarifying a Key Term
Theodoret makes a brief vocabulary point: Paul uses the word spirit in this verse to mean "soul." So Paul's "defilement of flesh and spirit" refers to impurity of both body and inner self, not to the Holy Spirit. The excerpt does not name the verse, but the context fits the "flesh and spirit" language of the chapter's opening.

---

## Basil of Caesarea: Gratitude That Leads to Reverent Purity
Basil links the call to purity with wonder at God's goodness. In his reading, we are instructed to marvel at the unspeakable benevolence of God in Christ Jesus and with the greater fear to cleanse ourselves of every defilement of the flesh and the spirit. The more we grasp God's kindness, the more reverently we should pursue holiness.

---

## John Chrysostom: Holiness as Active, Whole-Life Purity

**1. The promises that motivate holiness.** Paul says "having therefore these promises," and Chrysostom explains which promises he means: that we should be temples of God, sons and daughters, have Him indwelling, and walking in us, be His people, have Him for our God and Father. Holiness is a response to God's promises of relationship.

**2. Two dimensions of cleansing.** Chrysostom interprets "flesh and spirit" this way: Let us neither touch unclean things, for this is cleansing of the flesh; nor things which defile the soul, for this is cleansing of the spirit.

**3. Avoiding sin is not enough.** This is perhaps his most important insight: not to touch the unclean thing does not make clean, but there needs something else besides to our becoming holy; earnestness, heedfulness, piety. Holiness requires positive devotion, not just abstaining from evil.

**4. Why "in the fear of God" matters.** Motive matters to Chrysostom, because it is possible to perfect chasteness, not in the fear of God but for vainglory. The fear of God is also a practical remedy against temptation: if lust be even an imperious thing, still if you occupy its territory with the fear of God, you have stayed its frenzy.

**5. Holiness means freedom from every sin.** Chrysostom widens the meaning of holiness beyond sexual purity: by holiness here he means not chastity alone, but the freedom from every kind of sin, for he is holy that is pure. A person becomes pure not if he be free from fornication only, but if from covetousness also, and envy, and pride, and vainglory.

**6. Vainglory corrupts almsgiving.** Building on that last point, Chrysostom warns that showy charity is not true charity: Not then the giving money, but the giving it out of mercy, is almsgiving. Public display shames the poor and can harm them further: when you parade your giving, you have both lowered the reputation of the receiver, and hast pulled back him that was about to give.

### A Note on the Rest of the Homily
In the remainder of the homily, Chrysostom moves away from the text of 2 Corinthians 7. He says he is returning to a certain necessary point left unfinished from his previous sermon: that the poor have spiritual advantages over the rich. He argues, for example, that pride, love of money, and vainglory lie especially near the rich, and he warns: Since then he is near both vainglory and arrogance, and the love of money, the root of all evils, what hope of salvation shall he have except he display much wisdom? He closes by urging his hearers to disregard what this man and that man thinks about these things, and inquire from the Scriptures all these things. This section is valuable moral teaching, but it is Chrysostom's own continuation of an earlier theme rather than an interpretation of the chapter.

---

## Key Takeaways
- **Holiness involves the whole person.** "Flesh and spirit" covers both body and soul (Theodoret, Chrysostom).
- **Holiness grows out of gratitude.** Wonder at God's kindness and promises motivates purity (Basil, Chrysostom).
- **Holiness is active.** Avoiding impurity is necessary but not sufficient; earnestness and piety are also required (Chrysostom).
- **Motive matters.** The "fear of God" separates true holiness from virtue performed for display (Chrysostom).

# Patristic Insights on Mark 3: The Healing of the Withered Hand

All four excerpts focus on one episode: Jesus healing a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath. Two of them (Chrysostom and Augustine) come from works that are not commentaries on Mark itself, as noted below.

---

## 1. Bede: *On the Gospel of Mark*

Bede gives the most extensive treatment. He reads the passage both literally and symbolically.

**The withered hand as a picture of fallen humanity**
- The man who had a withered hand indicates the human race withered in the fertility of good works, but cured by the Lord's compassion.
- He contrasts two trees: His right hand, which had withered in the first parent when plucking the forbidden tree's fruit, was restored to the health of good works' juices by the Redeemer's grace when He stretched out innocent hands on the tree of the cross.
- The setting matters: the hand was withered in the synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the danger of inexcusable guilt is more severe.

**The trap set by the opponents**
- Bede notes that Jesus was in a no-win position: if He heals on the Sabbath, they may charge Him with transgression; if He does not heal, they may accuse Him of cruelty or impotence.

**The true meaning of Sabbath rest**
- Bede argues they misread the law, thinking even from good works to rest on the Sabbath, while the law commands abstention from evil.
- He gives this a forward-looking dimension: those who have done good through the six ages of this world, will have rest in the seventh age, not from good works, but only from evil.

**"To save a life or to kill?"**
- Bede explains that this does not make God a source of harm. Rather, Scripture customarily speaks of not saving as killing. He compares this to Pharaoh's hardened heart: not that He made a soft heart hard, but that He did not mercifully soften it, hardened by preceding merits.

**Stretching out the hand as almsgiving**
- The command "Stretch forth your hand" becomes a moral lesson: in no better order is the fruitless weakness of the soul cured than by the largesse of alms.
- He closes pointedly: in vain does he stretch out his hands to God in prayer for sins, who does not extend them to a begging widow to confer a benefit.

---

## 2. Athanasius of Alexandria: *Homilies*

Athanasius focuses on the spiritual condition of the onlookers and on Jesus' method of teaching.

- **A double withering:** If he was withered in his hand, the ones who stood by were withered in their minds.
- **Preparing hearts before acting:** before doing the work, the Savior ploughed up their minds with words. Knowing their hostility, he first softened them up in advance with words so as to tame the wildness of their understanding.
- **Wise framing of the question:** Athanasius observes that if he had said to them, "Is it permitted to work?" immediately they would have said, "You are speaking contrary to the law." Jesus spoke as the One who established the laws concerning the sabbath.
- **The law itself permits preserving life:** He points to rescuing a person or animal from a hole, concluding that the law agrees that things relating to preservation may be done.
- **Hardened silence:** Even on an obvious question, they did not even so much as say, "Yes," because by then they were not in a good temper.

---

## 3. John Chrysostom: *Homily 40 on Matthew*

*Note:* This excerpt comes from Chrysostom's homilies on **Matthew**, not Mark. It addresses the same healing as told in Matthew's Gospel, so it is relevant to Mark 3 as a parallel account rather than a direct commentary on Mark's text.

- **Compassion as strategy:** Chrysostom asks readers to note the tender compassion of the Lord when he deliberately brought the man with the withered hand right into their presence. Jesus hoped that the mere sight of the misfortune might soften them.
- **The tragedy of hardness:** Instead, they remained callous and unfeeling. They preferred to do harm to the name of Christ than to see this poor man made whole.
- **Hostility that despises mercy:** Their wickedness showed in that they treated with disdain his mercies to others.

---

## 4. Augustine of Hippo: *The City of God*, Book 14

*Note:* This excerpt is not a commentary on Mark. It comes from a broader discussion of human emotions. It does, however, refer to the moment in this episode when Jesus looks on his opponents with anger and grief.

- **Righteous anger is not sin:** When such affections as anger are directed to their proper objects, they are following good reasoning, and no one should dare to describe them as maladies or vicious passions.
- **Christ's genuine humanity:** Surely the One who assumed a true human body and soul would not counterfeit his human affections.
- **Application to this episode:** the Gospel does not falsely attribute emotions to Christ when it speaks of him being saddened and angered by the lawyers because of their blindness of heart.

---

## Common Threads

- **The real "withering" is spiritual.** Bede, Athanasius, and Chrysostom all suggest that the onlookers' hardness of heart was a deeper problem than the man's physical condition.
- **The Sabbath is for doing good.** Bede and Athanasius both argue that the law, rightly understood, never forbade acts of mercy or the preservation of life.
- **Christ's compassion and anger go together.** Chrysostom highlights Jesus' tender effort to soften his opponents, while Augustine defends his anger and grief at their blindness as fully holy and fully human.

But they remained callous and unfeeling. They preferred to do harm to the name of Christ than to see this poor man made whole.
They betrayed their wickedness not only by their hostility to Christ, but also by their doing so with such contentiousness that they treated with disdain his mercies to others.

# Patristic Commentary on John 10: A Summary

## 1. Augustine of Hippo

Augustine's commentary is the longest and most developed of the excerpts. (Document 2, labeled *Tractates on the Gospel of John* 45.5, repeats a passage that also appears in Document 1, so the two are treated together here.)

**Context: the blindness of the Pharisees.** Augustine reads John 10 as a continuation of the healing of the man born blind. He notes that "Our Lord's discourse to the Jews began in connection with the man who was born blind and was restored to sight" and that the day's lesson "is interwoven with that one." The Pharisees declared that they were not blind; yet could they see only by being the sheep of Christ.

**Good living without Christ is not enough.** Augustine applies the parable to those who are morally upright but not Christian. Such people may keep the law's commands "yet are not Christians; and for the most part ask boastfully, like these men, Are we blind also?" His central claim is that no one has the true and certain hope of living always, unless he know the life, that it is Christ; and enter by the gate into the sheepfold.

**Heresy as climbing in "some other way."** Augustine names specific heresies as failing to enter by the door. Sabellius equated the Son with the Father. Of Arius he says "He would say rightly if he said, Another person; but not another thing." Against Photinus, who held that Christ was merely human, he answers that "He enters not in by the door, for Christ is both man and God." His summary: "Christ's sheepfold is the church. Whoever would enter the sheepfold, let him enter by the door; let him preach the true Christ. Not only let him preach the true Christ but also seek Christ's glory, not his own. For many, by seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ's sheep instead of gathering them."

**Christ, the low gateway.** One of Augustine's most memorable images concerns humility: "Christ the Lord is a low gateway: he who enters by this gateway must humble himself, that he may be able to enter with head unharmed. But he that humbles not, but exalts himself, wishes to climb over the wall; and he that climbs over the wall, is exalted only to fall."

**Thief versus robber.** He distinguishes the two terms: "he a thief, because what is another's he calls his own; a robber, because what he has stolen he also kills."

**The prophets were not "thieves and robbers."** Augustine addresses the apparent difficulty of the phrase "All that ever came." The prophets "did not come apart from Him, for they came with Him. When about to come, He sent heralds, but retained possession of the hearts of His messengers." He stresses the continuity of faith across the covenants: "Times vary, but not faith." Both Old Testament believers and Christians entered "by the one doorway of faith, that is, by Christ." He also says that "Under different signs there is the same faith."

**The puzzle of wandering sheep.** Augustine wrestles openly with a problem. If the sheep do not hear strangers, how can sheep go astray? He also observes that Judas "heard, and was a wolf", while some who crucified Christ were sheep. He resolves the problem through God's foreknowledge: "the Lord knows them that are His; they are the sheep." Hence his striking reflection: "how many sheep are outside, how many wolves within! And how many sheep are inside, how many wolves without!"

**The voice of perseverance.** The distinctive voice that only true sheep heed is the call to endure. Augustine writes: "it is easy to hear Christ, easy to praise the gospel, easy to applaud the preacher: but to endure unto the end, is peculiar to the sheep who hear the Shepherd's voice." He also offers pastoral encouragement: "A temptation befalls you, endure thou to the end, for the temptation will not endure to the end."

**"Go in and out, and find pasture."** Augustine interprets this phrase in terms of life now and life to come. Christ means "That they may have life in coming in, and have it more abundantly at their departure." Entering is the life of faith in the Church. Going out comes at the end of a faithful life, when believers "will have life more abundantly when they come whither the Shepherd has preceded them, where they shall die no more."

**Humility in interpretation.** Augustine models intellectual humility. He holds that the Lord "gives us what is plain, for food; what is obscure, for exercise." He also openly defers the question of the porter's identity to another time.

## 2. Theodore of Mopsuestia

Theodore's excerpt is very brief and offers only a general application of the image rather than detailed theology. He likens the present age to the sheepfold: "the thief comes from wherever it is possible for him to hide. His desire is to steal." By contrast, "the shepherd who has authority to use the entrance leads the sheep out to pasture, and they follow him, knowing their own shepherd, while they avoid the others whose voice they do not know." His emphasis falls on the shepherd's legitimate authority and the sheep's ability to recognize him.

## 3. Cyril of Alexandria

**The chapter's coherence.** Like Augustine, Cyril links John 10 to the preceding healing. He argues that careless readers may think the parable is out of place, but a thoughtful reader "will perceive here also that the argument proceeds so to speak straight forward, and swerves not at all from what is right and fitting."

**Christ answers hidden thoughts.** Cyril stresses that Christ customarily replied "not merely to the words which they expressed through their voice, but to speak with reference to their inward thoughts also". He sees the parable as a response to the Pharisees' crafty question.

**A parable about spiritual leadership.** Cyril's distinctive contribution is reading the passage as being about legitimate authority over God's people. Christ is "the Door introducing of His own will to the leadership of His rational flocks the man who is prudent and God-loving." The thief and robber is "him who thinks himself able to take by violence and tyranny the honour that is not given to him." True leadership was given to "the holy Apostles, and with the Teachers of the holy Churches after them."

**The porter.** Unlike Augustine, Cyril proposes identities for the porter: "either the Angel who is appointed to preside over the churches and to assist those whose lot is to minister in holy things for the good of the people, or else the Saviour Himself, Who is at the same time both the Door and the Lord of the Door."

**Sound teaching and discernment.** Cyril applies the sheep's recognition of the shepherd's voice to church teaching grounded in Scripture. Faithful believers "are obedient listeners to such teaching; but they turn away from the voices of falsifiers, and avoid them as a deadly evil."

**A warning to the Pharisees.** In summary, Cyril says Christ hints that "the Pharisees would never be leaders of those that should become believers in Him, but that His sheep would refuse their instruction and attach themselves to the shepherds appointed by Him."

## Brief Comparison

- **Shared ground:** Augustine and Cyril both read John 10 as directly connected to the Pharisees' spiritual blindness in John 9.
- **Augustine's focus:** salvation and the life of faith. His themes are Christ as the only door, humility, unity of faith across the ages, God's foreknowledge of His own, and perseverance.
- **Cyril's focus:** the legitimacy of spiritual leaders. Authority must be received through Christ rather than seized, and faithful believers discern true teachers from false ones.
- **Theodore:** too short to develop a full theology, but he highlights the shepherd's rightful authority and the sheep's recognition of his voice.

# Patristic Commentary on Titus: Summary of the Provided Excerpts

## A Note on Scope

Only **Jerome's** excerpts directly comment on Titus chapter 2, specifically verses 1–2. The **Chrysostom** excerpts are labeled as Titus 2 commentary, but their content addresses Titus 1:15 ("To the pure all things are pure…"), the verse just before chapter 2 begins. Chrysostom's homilies on Titus are traditionally numbered one through six, and this material corresponds to Homily 3, so the "Homily 83" label also appears to be incorrect. Document 2 is a shorter duplicate of the same passage. I include Chrysostom below, but his comments should not be read as exposition of chapter 2.

---

## Jerome: Commentary on Titus 2:1–2

### 1. Sound doctrine must be matched by sound living (Titus 2:1)

Jerome builds his comment on a careful reading of the phrase "speak what befits sound doctrine." He distinguishes two things: "The speaking of sound doctrine is one thing, the teaching of those things that are fitting for sound doctrine is another; in the one there is only the simplicity of instruction, while in the other there is also the correction of life in those who teach."

He supports this with Matthew 5:19, noting that "he who shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." He contrasts it with the scribes and Pharisees, who "preach but do not practice." His conclusion is that Paul teaches his disciple Titus, a son in Christ, to speak the things that are in accord with sound doctrine, for then there will be spiritual health when the teaching of the doctor and his life agree.

**Key insight:** For Jerome, "sound" (healthy) doctrine is not just correct content. It becomes healthy only when the teacher's life matches his words.

### 2. How Paul organizes the chapter's instructions

Jerome describes Paul's method in chapter 2: he explains in detail what is appropriate for each age group. He addresses older men first, then older women, then young people. Instructions for young women are given through the older women, who are to teach them. Finally, he fittingly established rules for servants, and for each age and condition, so that his speech becomes a guide to life and morals.

### 3. The virtues of older men (Titus 2:2)

Jerome comments on each quality Paul lists:

- **Sober:** He reads this as also meaning "watchful," since "νηφάλιοι" means both in Greek.
- **Honorable:** so that the gravity of age decorates the gravity of morals.
- **Chaste:** lest they luxuriate in someone else's youth, lest they be an example for young people to ruin in their lusts after their own blood has already cooled. In other words, older men's conduct sets an example the young will follow.

### 4. The threefold "health": faith, love, and patience

Jerome develops Paul's medical language of soundness into an extended meditation.

**Health in faith.** He gathers biblical examples of healthy faith, including Abraham, whose belief was counted to him for righteousness, and the roll call of faith in Hebrews 11. He notes particularly that so that Scripture might not seem to give no example of faith to women, it is written in the same Epistle that Sarah also received strength to conceive seed.

**Health in love.** Healthy love starts with God. Jerome asks, "who possesses the health of charity except the one who loves God first with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength?" It then extends to neighbor, because all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments. Drawing on 1 Corinthians 13 and Romans 8, he teaches that because love never fails, whoever is in the health of love, he never fails.

He also describes how love becomes sick. Love is warm in those who are fervent in spirit, but cooling, freezing, and cold in those who have received the hardest blasts of the North Wind. He offers a pastoral warning that a love which begins as holy can decay into disordered attachment: when our mind has been softened by affection, the healthy state of charity gradually fades away and begins to grow weak. For this reason he insists that all chastity is in flesh and spirit and soul.

**Health in patience.** Patience completes the other two and is especially tested in temptations. Jerome uses a memorable image: spiritual wealth is of no benefit unless all the goods and merchandise with which the ship is laden are preserved in the storm. He ends with Christ's words: "For he who shall have persevered even to the end, he shall be saved".

**Key insight:** Faith, love, and patience together make up the soul's spiritual health. Patience is what preserves the other two through trials until the end.

---

## John Chrysostom: On Purity and Impurity (Titus 1:15, not chapter 2)

### 1. Impurity begins in the perceiver

Chrysostom compares the false teachers' scruples to dizziness. Because they are unsteady and giddy, they think that the earth turns round with them, which yet turns not, but stands firm. Likewise, when the soul is unclean, it thinks all things unclean. He concludes that scrupulous observances are no mark of purity, but it is the part of purity to be bold in all things.

He applies this even to the Incarnation, arguing against Marcion: That He assumed flesh is a proof of purity; if through fear He had not taken it, there would have been defilement.

### 2. True uncleanness is moral

Asked what is truly unclean, Chrysostom answers: Sin, malice, covetousness, wickedness. He reads the Old Testament purity laws as signs pointing to spiritual realities. For example, the prohibition on touching a corpse teaches that sin is such, it is dead and offensive. Circumcision likewise points inward, for he who does not cut off the wickedness of his heart is the unclean person. Now, all is transferred to the soul. Christians ought not to be confined to figures, and shadows, but to adhere to the truth, and to uphold it: sin is the unclean thing.

### 3. Wickedness as injustice and excess

Chrysostom singles out greed: Nothing is more unclean than covetousness. It defiles the hands, the soul, the very house where the ill-gotten treasure is laid up.

He argues that sexual sin is unclean not on account of the intercourse, (for according to that reasoning a man cohabiting with his own wife would be unclean,) but because of the wickedness of the act, and the injury done to his neighbor. In the same way, anger defiles not in itself, but because of its excess. He closes with an appeal to be pure, in that which is real purity, that we may be thought worthy to see God.

**Key insight:** Purity is not a matter of avoiding external objects. It is freedom from sin, especially from injustice toward one's neighbor and from disordered desire.

---

## Observations

- **Jerome** offers the only true exposition of Titus 2 here. His central themes are the unity of teaching and life, and the "health" of faith, love, and patience.
- **Chrysostom's** material belongs to Titus 1, though his focus on inner moral purity fits well with the practical, character-centered instructions of chapter 2.
