# Patristic Insights on Genesis 47

## John Chrysostom: Life as a Pilgrimage, and God's Provision

**Jacob's answer to Pharaoh (Gen 47:8–9)**
Chrysostom finds a model of the believer's outlook in Jacob's description of his life as a "sojourn." He writes, "See how all good people have the same attitude to this life as if living in a foreign land." He links this to David, who says "I am a sojourner upon earth, sojourning in a strange place", and to Paul's remark that the patriarchs "recognized they were strangers and sojourners on earth."

He also reads Jacob's lament that his years were "few and harsh" against the hardships of his life. Jacob is referring to the years of servitude he endured under Laban in consequence of the flight made on account of his brother, and as well, following his return from there, the grief he suffered for so long on account of Joseph's death and all the misfortunes in the meantime. Chrysostom also points to the fear Jacob felt after Simeon and Levi's violence at Shechem, when Jacob said he could be exterminated along with my house. In Chrysostom's reading, Jacob's words are honest testimony to a life of real suffering, not mere complaint.

**Joseph's provision for his family (Gen 47:12)**
Commenting on the phrase "everybody individually," Chrysostom explains that it means enough for everyone. He notes that it is customary with Scripture to refer to every person sometimes as a soul and sometimes as a body. His theological point is the contrast between the surrounding devastation and the security of Jacob's household: Even though the whole of Egypt and Canaan was laid waste with famine, these people were comfortable through having a supply of grain flowing as if from a spring.

## Origen: Famine Does Not "Prevail" over the Righteous

Origen pays close attention to the wording of the famine narrative and sees in it censure of the Egyptians. He observes that although it is written that "the famine prevailed over the land," nevertheless it is not written that famine prevailed over Jacob or his sons, as it is said of the Egyptians, that "the famine prevailed over them."

His key distinction is that although famine should come also to the just, nevertheless it does not prevail over them. Hardship therefore has different meanings for different people: What therefore is an exercise of virtue for the just is a penalty of sin for the unjust. He finds the same pattern in the stories of Abraham and Isaac, concluding that famine therefore prevailed over neither Abraham nor Jacob nor their sons.

Origen then turns the point toward spiritual nourishment. Those who "mind earthly things" can suffer famine, but they can never be oppressed by the fasting of famine whose is that bread that "they should do the will of the Father who is in heaven" and whose soul that "bread which comes down from heaven" nourishes. He also defends the care of Scripture's wording against those who think the text of the divine Scripture was composed carelessly and awkwardly.

## Cyril of Alexandria: Joseph as a Figure of Christ

Only part of Cyril's excerpt directly concerns Genesis 47. Much of it summarizes earlier events, such as the brothers' recognition of Joseph and the meal at his table, which belong to the preceding chapters. The part that touches chapter 47 is his note that after Jacob arrived, Joseph gave them the best parts of his land.

Cyril reads this typologically, seeing Joseph as a figure of Christ. For him, the narrative is a clear sign that the Israelites themselves, by coming back in the latter times of the world, will be received by Christ, that is, when they will be in accord with the new people, that is symbolized, as I have said, by Benjamin. He connects the gift of land to the believer's hope of a heavenly inheritance. Drawing on Paul, he stresses that believers will not be perfected apart from the faithful who came before, and that together with the holy fathers of the first, the second and the last people we will receive the very good inheritance of the heavenly kingdom that is not made by human hands in Christ.

## Common Threads

- **Earthly life is temporary.** Chrysostom presents believers as sojourners, and Cyril points them toward a heavenly inheritance.
- **God provides for his people in crisis.** Chrysostom emphasizes the abundant grain, while Origen stresses that famine cannot overcome the righteous and that true nourishment is spiritual.
- **The details of Scripture matter.** Origen reads its precise wording closely, Chrysostom explains its idioms, and Cyril finds Christ foreshadowed in the narrative.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 9: The Healing of the Paralytic

All four excerpts address the opening of Matthew 9: Jesus' return to "his own city" and the healing of the paralytic. Jerome's contribution is very brief, while Chrysostom's is the most developed.

---

## 1. Which city was Jesus' "own city"?

Chrysostom and Jerome disagree on this.

**John Chrysostom** identifies it as Capernaum. He explains that that which gave Him birth was Bethlehem; that which brought Him up, Nazareth; that which had Him continually inhabiting it, Capernaum. For him, "his own city" means the place where Jesus actually lived during his ministry.

**Jerome** reads it differently: We should understand his town as none other than Nazareth, for he was called a Nazarean. He links the phrase to Jesus' identity as a Nazarene.

---

## 2. John Chrysostom: Christ's Authority and Equality with the Father

**A different paralytic from John 5.** Chrysostom first separates this miracle from the healing at the pool. He notes that the man in John was in a state destitute of protectors, but this had some to take care of him, who also took him up, and carried him. He makes this distinction lest any one should think there is a discrepancy from suspecting it to be one and the same paralytic.

**The Lord's humility.** Chrysostom asks readers to mark the humility and meekness of our Lord. Even Jesus' choice to cross by boat is meaningful: it was His will not to be always doing miracles, that He might not injure the doctrine of His humanity.

**Faith on behalf of others.** The friends put the sick man before Christ, saying nothing, but committing the whole to Him. Chrysostom observes that Christ does not on all occasions require faith on the part of the sick only. Still, he adds that the sick man too had part in the faith; for he would not have suffered himself to be let down, unless he had believed.

**Healing the soul first.** In response to their faith, Christ shows His power, with all authority absolving his sins, and signifying in all ways that He is equal in honor with Him that begot Him. Rather than seeking glory, He healed first that which is invisible, the soul, by forgiving his sins; which indeed saved the other, but brought no great glory to Himself.

**Turning His enemies' objection into testimony.** This is Chrysostom's most striking point. When the scribes murmur, This man blasphemes; who can forgive sins but God only?, Jesus does not deny the implication. Chrysostom reasons that if He were not equal, He should have said, Why fix upon me a notion which is not convenient? Instead, Jesus has both affirmed and ratified, as well by His own voice, as by the performance of the miracle. In this way, He, in fact, in His abundance of counsel, made use of their envy for the manifestation of the miracle. Chrysostom sees the same pattern in John 10, where Jesus again neither in that instance did He put down this opinion, but again confirmed it.

---

## 3. Hilary of Poitiers: The Paralytic as a Figure of Fallen Humanity

**Forgiveness before healing.** Hilary draws attention to Jesus' unexpected words: The paralytic is not told, "Be healed." He is not told, "Rise and walk." But he is told, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven you."

**An allegory of Adam.** Hilary reads the man as representing humanity. The paralytic is a descendent of the original man, Adam. In one person, Christ, all the sins of Adam are forgiven. The title "son" fits because he is God's first work. In this reading, pardon of the first transgression is granted. He also gives the bearers a symbolic meaning: the person to be healed is brought forward by ministering angels.

**Illness is not necessarily punishment for personal sin.** Hilary cautions against assuming the man's condition was caused by his own wrongdoing: We do not believe the paralytic committed any sin [that resulted in his illness], especially since the Lord said elsewhere that blindness from birth had not been contracted from someone's sin or that of his parents.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

| Commentator | Central Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Chrysostom** | Christ's divine authority and equality with the Father, shown through forgiveness and confirmed even by His opponents; His humility; the role of shared faith |
| **Jerome** | Identifies "his own city" as Nazareth (excerpt limited to this point) |
| **Hilary** | Symbolic reading: the paralytic represents Adam's descendants, and forgiveness addresses the first transgression rather than a personal sin behind the illness |

Chrysostom and Hilary share one thread: both see Jesus' choice to forgive sins *before* healing the body as theologically significant. They develop it differently. Chrysostom focuses on what it reveals about Christ's identity, while Hilary focuses on what it reveals about humanity's need for redemption.

# Augustine of Hippo on Matthew 10: Key Theological Insights

All three excerpts come from one commentator, **Augustine of Hippo**, drawn from three of his sermons. They are summarized below by sermon.

---

## 1. Sermon 64A.2: Christ's Presence with His Persecuted Followers

This excerpt clearly engages Matthew 10. Augustine cites Jesus' instruction about persecution: "But when they deliver you up, do not be anxious how or what you are to speak … for it is not you who are speaking but the Spirit of your Father who speaks through you."

**Key insights:**

- **Christ's promises reach beyond the original disciples.** Augustine pairs this passage with another saying of Jesus: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." He argues that the Lord was referring not only to those about to depart from this life but also to the others, including us and those who would come after us in this life.
- **The Church as one body.** Christ saw everyone in his single body. Later believers were included in His words because if we did not hear them then in our knowledge, we heard them in his foreknowledge.
- **Doves and snakes.** Taking up the image of sheep among wolves, Augustine urges believers to keep the commandments of him who directs us and to be "innocent as doves but cautious as snakes." His interpretation is practical: Innocent as doves that we may not harm anyone; cautious as snakes that we may be careful of letting anyone harm us.

---

## 2. Sermon 65.5–7: The True Death of the Soul

This excerpt is listed as commentary on Matthew 10, but it does not quote or name a specific verse from the chapter. It seems to reflect on Jesus' teaching about the body and the soul, but the connection is not stated in the text provided.

**Key insights:**

- **Spiritual death is the greater danger.** Augustine states that the gospel is life, while impiety and infidelity are the death of the soul.
- **How an immortal soul can "die."** The soul dies not in ceasing to be life but by losing its proper life.
- **An order of life.** The soul is the life of the body. God is the life of the soul. His conclusion: the body is dead without the soul, and the soul is dead without God.
- **The illustration of the house.** A corpse still has eyes and ears, but these are merely the windows of the house; its inhabitant is gone.
- **Pastoral challenge.** Augustine redirects his listeners' grief: You who bewail the dead rather should bewail sin. Bewail ungodliness. Bewail disbelief.

---

## 3. Sermon 65A.5: Loving Family Within, Not Above, Christ

This excerpt also does not quote a verse from Matthew 10 directly. Its theme, putting Christ before parents, appears related to the chapter's teaching on family loyalties, but the text does not make the link explicit.

**Key insights:**

- **Parents' claims are taken seriously.** Augustine does not dismiss parental love. He acknowledges their just claims: "I fathered you." The mother says, "I bore you."
- **Rightly ordered love.** His answer is: "I will love you in Christ, not instead of Christ. You will be with me in him, but I will not be with you without him."
- **Creator before family.** When parents reject Christ, the believer replies: "And I care for Christ more than I care for you. Should I obey the ones who raised me and lose the One who created me?"

---

## Common Threads

The same concern runs through all three excerpts: life must be ordered around God. Believers face hostility trusting Christ's lasting presence. They should fear spiritual death more than physical death, since God is the soul's true life. And they should love family deeply, but always within their love for Christ, never in place of it.

# Patristic Commentary on John 4: Summary of Key Insights

**A note on scope:** All of the provided excerpts address only the opening verses of John 4 (vv. 1–3), where Jesus learns that the Pharisees have heard he is baptizing more disciples than John, and he leaves Judea for Galilee. None of the excerpts discuss the rest of the chapter, such as the encounter with the Samaritan woman. Chrysostom briefly points ahead to the Samaritans, but the excerpt cuts off before he develops the point. Also, the two Chrysostom documents are largely two translations of the same passage, so they are treated together below.

---

## Augustine of Hippo (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 15.2–3)

### 1. Why Jesus left Judea: an example for persecuted believers
Augustine argues that Jesus's departure depended on how the Pharisees responded to his success. If their knowledge had led them wholeheartedly to follow him and desire baptism by him, he would not have left Judea; rather, he would have remained for their sake. But seeing that this knowledge was coupled with envy, making them persecutors instead of followers, he left.

Augustine insists this was not weakness. He also could have stayed among them, if he had wanted to, and escaped their hands. Instead, he wanted to provide himself as an example for believers in time to come, that it was no sin for a servant of God to seek refuge from the fury of persecutors.… He did it like a good teacher, not out of fear for himself but for our instruction.

**Insight:** Christ's withdrawal is a deliberate lesson that fleeing persecution is morally permissible for Christians.

### 2. Did Jesus baptize or not? Christ as the true baptizer
Augustine takes up the apparent tension in the text. It is said, "Jesus baptized more than John," and after this was added, "although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples did." Rather than treating the second statement as a correction of the first, he concludes that both are true: He did in fact baptize, because it was he who cleansed. And he also did not baptize, because it was not he who touched. The disciples supplied the ministry of the body; he afforded the aid of his majesty.

He then applies this to the ongoing life of the Church: Jesus, therefore, is still baptizing. And so long as we continue to be baptized, Jesus baptizes. His pastoral conclusion is: Let a person come without fear to the minister below, for he has a master above.

**Insight:** The power of baptism comes from Christ, not from the human minister. Believers can therefore trust the sacrament whatever the qualities of the person administering it.

---

## John Chrysostom (*Homilies on the Gospel of John* 31.1 and Commentary)

### 1. Who actually baptized
Chrysostom reads the report differently from Augustine. He holds that He indeed baptized not, but they who carried the news, desiring to excite their hearers to envy, so reported. In his view, the claim that Jesus was baptizing was exaggerated by people trying to stir up hostility.

### 2. Why Jesus departed: defusing envy, not fleeing in fear
Like Augustine, Chrysostom denies that fear was the motive. Jesus acted not from fear but to take away their malice and soften their envy.

### 3. Protecting belief in the real Incarnation
Chrysostom's most distinctive point is that Jesus deliberately avoided constant miraculous escapes. He was indeed able to restrain them when they came against him, but he did not want to be found doing this all the time. Otherwise people might not believe his incarnation in the flesh was real. For if he was always being seized, only to then escape, this would have raised a lot of suspicion. Therefore, for the most part, he did things in a human way instead.

He supports this with other Gospel passages. As He desired it to be believed that He was God, so also that, being God, He bore the flesh; therefore even after the Resurrection, He said to the disciple, Handle Me and see, for a spirit has not flesh and bones Luke 24:39; therefore also He rebuked Peter when he said, Be it far from You, this shall not be unto you.

### 4. Why the Incarnation matters so much
Chrysostom explains why Christ guarded this truth so carefully. It is the chief point of the salvation wrought for us; by which all has been brought to pass, and has had success, for it was thus that the bonds of death were loosed, sin taken away, and the curse abolished, and ten thousand blessings introduced into our life.

### 5. Balancing humanity and divinity
Even while acting in human ways, Jesus did not hide his divine identity. Yet while acting thus in regard of His Humanity, He did not allow His Divinity to be overcast. The journey also had a positive purpose: He went not away into Galilee simply, but in order to effect certain important matters, those among the Samaritans. The excerpt ends before Chrysostom explains this further.

---

## Comparing the Two Commentators

| Theme | Augustine | Chrysostom |
|---|---|---|
| **Motive for leaving** | To teach believers that fleeing persecution is not sinful | To soften envy and avoid suspicion about his true humanity |
| **Did Jesus baptize?** | Both yes and no: Christ cleanses inwardly while disciples administer outwardly | No: the report was spread by those trying to provoke envy |
| **Main theological emphasis** | Christ as the ongoing, true minister of baptism | The reality of the Incarnation as central to salvation |

**Common ground:** Both fathers firmly reject the idea that Jesus left out of fear. Both affirm that he could have resisted his opponents, so his departure was a deliberate choice that serves to teach the Church.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 43: A Summary

The four excerpts take three different approaches: **allegorical** (Ambrose), **textual** (Jerome), and **narrative and psychological** (Ephrem).

---

## 1. Ambrose of Milan: Benjamin as a Figure of Paul

Ambrose gives the richest theological reading. He treats the journey of Benjamin and the brothers' gifts as prefiguring the apostle Paul and the gospel.

**Benjamin held back by the law.** Benjamin's delay is read spiritually: "The bonds of the law held him back, and ancestral custom." Meanwhile, the famine was increasing because he was coming late.

**The two guarantors as law and gospel.** Ambrose assigns symbolic meanings to the brothers who vouch for Benjamin: "Two brothers, Reuben and Judah—that is, humility and confession—make intercession on his behalf." He adds that one of them is the firstborn, the other restored to life. The firstborn represents the law; the one restored to life, the gospel.

**The gifts as signs of apostolic ministry.** Each item carried to Egypt becomes a symbol:
- **Resin ("cement"):** Benjamin carries the cement with which stones of marble are fastened together; thus by his own preaching as by a spiritual cement he might fasten together living stones.
- **Honey:** It destroys the harmful effects of an internal wound, without the bitter pain of any cutting. Ambrose links this to Paul's preaching, which sought rather to cauterize the sick vitals of the heart than to cut them.
- **Incense, cassia, and aloes:** Drawing on the Psalms, Ambrose says the incense is a sign of prayer and the cassia and aloes are signs of burial. He connects these to the fact that Paul came to preach the cross of the Lord, an oak that is always verdant.
- **Almonds:** They are rather hard in the shell but more tender in the meat. Ambrose notes that Aaron's priestly rod was of the almond tree, and Jeremiah's staff as well.
- **Double money:** In it there is prefigured the coming of Paul, who presented presbyters who labor in the word and in the teaching with a double honor.

**Key insight:** For Ambrose, the patriarchal story and apostolic preaching share an enduring vitality: the life of the patriarch and the preaching of the apostle are always verdant in the heart of each person.

---

## 2. Jerome: Clarifying the Text

Jerome's contribution is philological rather than theological. He focuses on how the gifts in verse 11 should be translated.

- He gives the list of gifts as some resin, and honey, incense, and resin, and turpentine, and nuts, noting that "nuts" may instead be rendered as Aquila and Symmachus translated, almonds.
- He explains that the word rendered "incense" in Hebrew it is 'Necotha' (), which Aquila translated as storax.
- He connects this term to Isaiah's "house of nechota," understood as the most obvious cell for incense, or storax, as different fragrances are stored in it.

**Note:** Jerome offers no spiritual interpretation here. His value lies in helping readers understand what the gifts actually were. The Isaiah reference appears as "39:21" in the excerpt, which may be a transcription issue, since Isaiah 39 is a short chapter.

---

## 3. Ephrem the Syrian: The Human Drama of the Story

Although Ephrem's excerpts are labeled "37:3" and "37:4," which appear to be section numbers within his commentary, their content clearly concerns the events of Genesis 43. Ephrem stays close to the narrative and focuses on the characters' emotions and motives.

**Jacob's reluctant surrender.** Ephrem stresses the pressure of circumstances: Jacob was constrained by the famine, whether he was willing or not, to send Benjamin with them. He gives Jacob a moving lament: "Just as I was bereaved of Rachel, so am I now bereaved of Rachel's children."

**Judah's pledge.** Ephrem presents Judah alone as the guarantor. In contrast, Ambrose pairs Judah with Reuben. Ephrem writes: Judah comforted his father and said, "If I do not bring back Benjamin and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever."

**The brothers' fear and choice to confess.** When Joseph's servants take their baggage, the brothers fear a trap. They suspect it was with treachery that our money was put into the openings of our packs, so that if we escape [the charge of] spying they might seize us and make us slaves [on the charge] of theft. Their response is to be honest first: "Let us confess to the steward about the money before he begins to accuse us so that our brother Benjamin might free us from [the charge of] spying and the confession of our lips from [the charge of] theft."

**Key insight:** Ephrem portrays the brothers as men burdened by guilt who choose open confession. This quietly echoes the theme of confession that Ambrose develops allegorically.

---

## Summary Comparison

| Commentator | Approach | Central Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Ambrose** | Allegorical | Benjamin and the gifts prefigure Paul, the gospel, and Christian ministry |
| **Jerome** | Textual and linguistic | Clarifies the Hebrew terms behind the gifts, such as storax and almonds |
| **Ephrem** | Narrative and psychological | Highlights Jacob's grief, Judah's pledge, and the brothers' turn to confession |

Together, these readings show the range of early Christian interpretation: careful attention to the text, sensitivity to the human story, and a search for Christ and the Church within the patriarchal narratives.

# Patristic Commentary on 2 Corinthians 6: A Summary

The excerpts focus on the opening verses of 2 Corinthians 6, where Paul urges believers not to waste God's grace and declares that "now" is the time of salvation. One theme runs through them: **God's grace is a gift that calls for an urgent, active response.**

## Basil of Caesarea (*The Long Rules*)

Basil comments on two verses.

**1. Receiving grace "in vain" (6:1)**
Basil links Paul's warning to how a believer lives day to day. He describes the person in danger as one who does not throughout his whole life place before himself the will of God as his goal, so that in health he shows forth the labor of love by his zeal for the works of the Lord and in sickness displays endurance and cheerful patience.

He names two consequences of neglecting God's will:
- The first and greatest peril is that by not doing the will of God, he separates himself from the Lord and cuts himself off from fellowship with his own brothers
- secondly, that he ventures, although undeserving, to claim a share in the blessings prepared for those who are worthy.

He connects this directly to the words of the apostle: "And we helping do exhort you that you receive not the grace of God in vain." Because believers have been raised to a high calling, they who are called to be brothers of the Lord should not receive in a wanton spirit so great a divine grace nor fall from so high a dignity through negligence in doing the will of God.

**Key insight:** Wasting grace is not a passing failure. It damages a person's relationship with God and with fellow believers.

**2. "Now is the day of salvation" (6:2)**
Basil reads Paul's "now" as a contrast between this life and the next. He quotes Paul, "Now is the acceptable time," says the apostle, "now is the day of salvation." and then sets out the contrasts:
- This is the time for repentance; the next life, for reward.
- Now is the time to endure; then will be the day of consolation.
- Now God is the helper of such as turn aside from the evil way; then he will be the dread and unerring inquisitor of the thoughts and words and deeds of humankind.
- Now we enjoy his longanimity; then we shall know his just judgment

**Key insight:** The present is a limited window of God's patience and mercy. It calls for repentance now, before judgment comes.

## John Chrysostom (*Homilies on the Epistles of Paul to the Corinthians* 12.1)

Chrysostom stresses that being chosen by God is no reason to become complacent. In his reading, Paul is telling his hearers that they must not relax just because God has sought them out and sent them as ambassadors. In fact, for that very reason we should hasten to please him and reap our spiritual blessings.

**Key insight:** God's initiative in seeking us out should make us more eager to serve him, not less.

## Theodoret of Cyrus (*Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians* 318)

The excerpt from Theodoret is a single sentence: Paul backs his exhortation up with this prophetic testimony. He sees Paul's appeal as grounded in the authority of the prophets. However, the excerpt does not say which prophetic text he means or explain it further, so there is little more to draw from it.

## Common Thread

Basil and Chrysostom agree that grace brings responsibility. Being called by God, whether as "brothers of the Lord" (Basil) or as "ambassadors" (Chrysostom), requires diligence and faithful obedience. Basil adds a strong sense of timing: the "now" of salvation is the time to repent and endure, before the coming day of judgment.

# Patristic Insights on 1 Peter 5

## Bede: Peter's Credentials and the Shepherd's Motives

**Peter as witness and partaker of glory.** Bede explains why Peter can appeal to the elders with authority. Peter is a witness to Christ's sufferings in two senses. First, he is indeed a witness, who stood by him suffering, and saw all things as they happened. Second, he may be a witness because he himself, for the name of Christ, suffered imprisonment, chains, and scourging, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. Peter's claim to share in future glory also rests on experience. Bede says this was fulfilled when on the holy mountain he beheld the heavenly glory of His face with James and John, or when he saw the power of His resurrection and ascension with the other disciples who were present.

**Continuity of pastoral care.** Bede links Peter's charge to his own commission from Christ: Just as the Lord commanded Blessed Peter to have care for His entire flock, that is, the Church, so Peter rightly commands the subsequent pastors of the Church to protect with diligent governance the flock of God that is among them. Peter passes on to later leaders the responsibility he himself received.

**Serving willingly versus out of necessity.** Bede contrasts two kinds of ministers:
- The one who serves out of need: One who feeds the flock of God and provides out of necessity for material things, having nothing to live on, therefore preaches the Gospel so that he may live from the Gospel.
- The one who serves willingly: willingly and according to God is one who, looking not for any earthly reward, but only for the heavenly reward, preaches the word of God.

He supports this distinction with the Apostle Paul, who wrote, "For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if against my will, I have been entrusted with a stewardship." Bede likens the reluctant preacher to a servant carrying out a temporary assignment, such as one who is commanded to distribute his master's wheat to his fellow servants in due time.

**Against shameful gain.** Bede warns that a person serves for shameful profit, who preaches for gain and earthly benefits, while all works of religion ought to be done willingly. His model is the building of the tabernacle, which he reads as a picture of the Church. There all the multitude of the children of Israel offered the first-fruits to the Lord with prompt and devoted minds for the construction of the tabernacle, giving all things freely, and the craftsmen offered themselves willingly to do the work.

## Augustine: The Weight of Pastoral Responsibility

This excerpt comes from one of Augustine's letters, not a formal commentary, and it does not quote 1 Peter 5 directly. Still, its language closely echoes the chapter's themes of the "flock of God" and the "chief shepherd." Augustine tells his people, We are your guardians, and you are the flock of God. He stresses that leadership brings greater danger than privilege: Reflect and see that our perils are greater than yours, and pray for us. Pastors and people therefore owe each other prayer, that we may be able to give a good account of you to the prince of pastors and our universal head.

## John Chrysostom: The Paradox of Humility

Chrysostom's excerpt does not explicitly mention 1 Peter. It fits the chapter's call to humility, but that connection is thematic rather than stated. He starts from Christ's teaching, which he renders as "He who would be first among you, let him serve, for he who humbles himself will be exalted above all." He then voices the listener's doubt (If I humble myself, will I then be exalted?) and answers in Christ's voice: For such is my power that I can turn something into its exact opposite. In his reading, the reversal of humility into exaltation rests on divine power, since The nature of things obeys my will, not the other way round.

## Common Threads

- **Shepherding is a trust, not a possession.** Bede and Augustine both see Church leaders as caretakers of a flock that belongs to God, answerable to Christ as chief shepherd.
- **Motive matters.** Bede insists ministry be done freely, for heavenly rather than earthly reward.
- **Leadership means burden and humility.** Augustine stresses the leader's greater peril, and Chrysostom grounds the hope of exaltation in God's power to reverse the order of things.

# Patristic Insights on 1 Corinthians 7

These four excerpts from three early Church writers address marriage, sexual relations, and chastity, which are the central concerns of 1 Corinthians 7. Each brings a distinct emphasis.

## Theodoret of Cyrus

**The Corinthians' question and Paul's balanced answer.** Theodoret explains what prompted the chapter: the Corinthians were asking Paul whether it was right for lawfully married Christians, once they were baptized, to enjoy sexual relations with each other. He sums up Paul's reply as a three-part balance: Paul answered by praising chastity, condemning fornication and allowing conjugal relations.

**Equal moral standards for men and women.** Theodoret's most striking insight is a critique of the double standard in ancient society. He observes that human laws demand that women be chaste and if they are not they are punished for it, but they do not demand the same from men. He attributes this to self-interest: since it was men who made the laws, they did not make themselves equal with woman but allowed themselves extra indulgence. In contrast, he presents Paul as a moral innovator: the holy apostle, however, inspired by divine grace, was the first one who made the law of chastity apply to men as well.

## Origen of Alexandria

**Abstinence that harms a spouse is not true holiness.** Origen addresses a husband who has withdrawn from marital relations for the sake of greater purity. He acknowledges the man's intentions. The man claims he is not abusing her and that he can be chaste and live more purely. Origen then turns the focus to the wife's well-being: But look how your poor wife is being destroyed as a result, because she is unable to endure your purity!

His conclusion reframes marital intimacy as an act of love toward the other person: You should sleep with your wife, not for your sake but for hers. The theological point is that personal spiritual ambition must not come at the expense of the obligations and welfare of one's spouse.

## John Chrysostom

**Paul's words apply to everyone, not just clergy.** Chrysostom rejects a narrow reading of the passage: Some people think that this was written primarily for priests, but judging from what follows, this cannot be right. His reasoning is that if he had meant it only for priests, he would have said so, but throughout this [chapter] he speaks of persons in general.

*A note on context:* the excerpt does not say which verse "this" refers to, so the precise passage Chrysostom is discussing cannot be identified from the text provided.

**Marriage as concession, virginity as ideal.** Chrysostom reads Paul's underlying aim as favoring celibacy: Paul permits marriage as a concession, but the very fact that it is designed to avoid fornication shows that he is really trying to encourage virginity.

## Common Threads and Differing Emphases

- **Shared ground:** All three commentators see Paul as upholding chastity and rejecting sexual immorality while still permitting marriage.
- **Different accents:**
  - Chrysostom leans toward virginity as the higher calling and treats marriage mainly as a safeguard.
  - Origen warns against pursuing that ideal in ways that wound one's spouse.
  - Theodoret highlights the chapter's ethical fairness by stressing that Paul held men to the same standard of chastity as women.

Taken together, the excerpts show the early Church valuing celibacy while also insisting on mutual obligation and equal moral accountability within marriage.

# Patristic Insights on Matthew 28

These four excerpts fall into two groups. Augustine and Jerome address the **timing of the women's visit** to the tomb (Matthew 28:1). Cyril and Chrysostom focus on the **angel's announcement of the resurrection** (Matthew 28:5–6).

---

## Augustine of Hippo: Harmonizing the Gospel Accounts

Augustine takes up an apparent discrepancy among the Gospels. He insists that one must not dismiss lightly the question concerning the exact hour at which the women came to the tomb.

**The problem:** Matthew places the visit "in the evening of the sabbath, at the dawn of the first day of the week," while Mark says, "And early in the morning on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb at the rising of the sun".

**His resolution:**
- **Mark, Luke, and John agree.** Mark's phrase refers to the time when the heavens in the east were brightening, which is what customarily is called the dawn. This fits John's "still dark," for as day is breaking the remaining shadows of darkness diminish only in proportion to the sun's rising.
- **"Evening" in Matthew means the whole night.** Augustine argues that Matthew's own wording settles the matter. It would be impossible if we understood "in the evening" to signify only the first part of the night. He explains that it is divine Scripture's customary way of distinguishing the whole from the part. So by saying "evening" it signifies the whole night, the end of which is the dawn.
- **Conclusion:** Even if they came at the very end of the night, the fact remains without a doubt that they came at night.

**Key insight:** Augustine treats seeming contradictions as invitations to read carefully. He pays close attention to how Scripture uses language rather than assuming error.

---

## Jerome: Devotion Explains the Differing Times

Jerome addresses the same issue from a different angle. He argues that the fact that different times of these women are described in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood, as the wicked claim, but rather the diligent duty of visitation, as they frequently go and come back, and do not allow themselves to be away from the Lord's tomb for a long time or further.

**Key insight:** Augustine solves the problem through word meanings. Jerome solves it pastorally: the varied times reflect the women's repeated visits to the tomb, a sign of their love and devotion to Christ.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria: Christ as the "Death of Death"

Cyril emphasizes the angel's role: the angel became an evangelist and herald of the resurrection to the women.

*A note on the source:* The angel's words "Do not seek the one who lives among the dead" do not appear in Matthew's account. They match Luke's version of the scene. Only the phrase "He is not here... but he has been raised" directly parallels Matthew 28:6. The fragment therefore seems to draw on the resurrection narratives more broadly rather than on Matthew alone.

**Theological points:**
- **Christ is life itself.** He is the one who in his own nature is life.
- **The resurrection is for us.** He has become a way of ascent to immortality not only for himself but also for us.
- **The incarnation served this purpose.** He made himself nothing and put on our likeness, that "by the grace of God," just as the blessed Paul says, "he might taste death on behalf of all."
- **The result:** He has become the death of death.

**Key insight:** Cyril moves from the empty tomb to its saving meaning. He connects Christ's resurrection to his incarnation and to the believer's hope of immortality.

---

## John Chrysostom: The Evidence for the Resurrection

Chrysostom comments on Matthew 28:6. He asks how the angel's claim "He is risen" can be known. He identifies two proofs in the angel's words:

1. **Christ's own prediction.** The angel says "As He said," as if to say, if you refuse to believe me, he would say, remember His words, and neither will you disbelieve me.
2. **The empty tomb itself.** Come and see the place where He lay. Chrysostom adds that the angel had lifted up the stone, in order that from this too they might receive the proof.

**Key insight:** Chrysostom presents the resurrection as grounded in both Jesus' promise and visible evidence. He suggests the stone was rolled away to show the women that the tomb was empty, not to let Jesus out.

---

## Summary of Common Threads

- **Trustworthiness of the Gospels:** Augustine and Jerome both defend the accounts against charges of contradiction, by different methods.
- **The meaning of the resurrection:** Cyril focuses on its saving significance, Christ as "the death of death," while Chrysostom focuses on its evidential basis.
- **The angel's role:** Cyril and Chrysostom both treat the angel's message as central, as proclamation for Cyril and as reasoned proof for Chrysostom.

# Patristic Commentary on Luke 3: A Summary

## Cyril of Alexandria: John as Forerunner

Cyril's excerpt focuses on **how John the Baptist relates to Christ**. He sees John's ministry as foretold by Isaiah, who called Christ Lord and God: but John he styled His minister and servant.

Cyril uses three images to show that John's role was to prepare, not to be the center:
- **Lamp and light:** John was a lamp advancing before the true light.
- **Morning star and sun:** He was the morning star heralding the sun, foreshowing the coming of the day that was about to shed its rays upon us.
- **Voice and Word:** he was a voice, not a word, forerunning Jesus.

**Key insight:** Each pair contrasts something that announces with the reality it announces. The voice-and-word image is especially rich, since it subtly points to Christ as the Word. John is honored, but always in service to the One who comes after him.

## Bede: The Historical Setting and Its Meaning

Bede's commentary has two parts: historical background, and theological reflection on why Luke dates John's ministry so carefully.

### Historical Background
Bede explains that Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, who governed Judea with the Roman prefect Pilate, were the sons of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. He notes that Augustus took care to divide the kingdom of Judea into tetrarchies so that it would become less powerful.

On the high priests, Bede explains that Annas and Caiaphas are named together because Annas held the office for that year, while Caiaphas administered it in the year when the Lord ascended the cross, with others serving in between. He sees this as a sign of decline: legal precepts having ceased through force and ambition, the honor of the pontificate was conferred neither on account of life nor lineage, but by Roman authority. Drawing on Josephus, he concludes that the whole time in which our Lord is described as teaching on earth is confined within a span of four years.

### Theological Insights
Bede finds meaning in Luke's list of rulers:

1. **Jews and Gentiles:** Because John was coming to preach about Him who would redeem some from Judea and many from the Gentiles, the times of his preaching are designated by the king of the nations and the princes of the Jews.

2. **A united empire and a divided kingdom:** He contrasts Rome, where one is described as presiding, with Judea, where many ruled by quarters. He links this to Christ's saying that "Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolate", and concludes that the kingdom of Judea had come to an end since it was subjected to division under so many kings.

3. **King and priest:** Bede sees significance in Luke naming both rulers and priests: because John the Baptist was to preach about Him who would also be king and priest at the same time, Luke the evangelist designated the times of his preaching by the kingdom and the priesthood.

**Key insight:** For Bede, Luke's dates are not just historical markers. They point to Christ's dual office as King and Priest and to the gospel reaching the Gentiles.

## Clement of Alexandria: A Chronological Witness

Clement's excerpt contains **little direct commentary**. He quotes Luke's dating of John's call, "And in the fifteenth year, in the reign of Tiberius Caesar, the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zacharias., and Jesus "being about thirty years old" at His baptism.

He introduces these verses with to prove that this is true, so he is using Luke as evidence for an argument, apparently about chronology. However, the excerpt does not say what claim he is proving, so no clear theological insight can be drawn from it alone.

## Summary of Common Themes

- **John's subordinate yet vital role:** Cyril shows John as the herald who points beyond himself to Christ.
- **History with meaning:** Bede treats Luke's historical details as carrying theological significance.
- **Christ as King and Priest:** Bede reads the pairing of political and religious rulers as pointing to Christ's two offices.
- **Luke's historical reliability:** Both Bede and Clement treat Luke's dating as a firm foundation, Bede for interpretation and Clement for evidence.

# Augustine of Hippo on the Wedding Garment (Matthew 22)

**Note on scope:** All four excerpts come from a single commentator, Augustine of Hippo (Sermon 90, sections 4 and 6). They focus entirely on the parable of the wedding feast, and specifically on the guest without a wedding garment. The excerpts do not address other parts of Matthew 22, so this summary does not cover them.

---

## 1. The One Guest Represents Many

Augustine starts with an objection a listener might raise: What great matter is it that one man among this large crowd does not have a wedding garment? Why rivet attention on this one man? His answer is that the figure is representative: This man represents a whole class of persons of whom there are many. The lone guest is therefore a warning that applies broadly within the community of those invited, not a minor detail of the story.

## 2. Judgment Belongs to the King, Not the Servants

Augustine draws a careful distinction between the roles in the parable. The servants' business was only to invite and bring in the good and bad. He stresses that the text does not say the servants took notice of the guests, found among them a man who had no wedding garment and spoke to him. Instead, the master of the house came in, the master saw him, the master of the house inspected, the master of the house hauled him off and threw him out.

The implication is that those who serve God are called to invite, while the final examination of hearts belongs to God alone. The guest's silence fits this: the one who questioned him was one to whom he could give no deceptive reply.

## 3. The Garment Is Inward, Not Outward

This is one of Augustine's central insights: The garment that is required is in the heart, not on the body, for if it had been put on externally, it could not have been concealed even from the servants. This explains why the servants missed it and only the King could see it. What is lacking is something no human observer can detect.

## 4. The Garment Is Righteousness and Charity

Augustine identifies the garment in two connected ways:

- **Righteousness:** He appeals to the words "May your priests be clothed with righteousness," and links this to the apostle's statement, "Because when we are clothed, we are not found naked."
- **Charity (love):** In section 6 he defines it more specifically: "The goal of this command is charity," says the apostle, "which comes from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith." This is the wedding garment.

## 5. Not Just Any Kind of Love

Augustine warns against a loose understanding of "love." The garment is not charity of any kind whatever—for very often they who are partakers together of an evil conscience seem to love one another. He gives examples: those who rob together, practice witchcraft, or cheer together at the coliseum may be said to love one another.But in these is no charity from a pure heart, a good conscience and a faith unfeigned. Shared enthusiasm or loyalty is not the same as the charity that clothes a guest for the King's feast.

## 6. Spiritual Gifts Cannot Replace Charity

Augustine imagines the guest defending himself by pointing to impressive gifts: "But I have the gift of prophecy and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains." His verdict: if he has no charity, he has nothing. Such may be the clothing of those who in fact lack the wedding garment.

He is careful, however, not to belittle these gifts: It is not that these are nothing. But "I, if I have them, and have not charity, am nothing." The problem is not the gifts themselves but trusting in them while lacking the love that gives them their worth.

---

## Key Takeaway

For Augustine, the wedding garment parable is a sobering reminder that being invited and present at the feast is not enough. The garment God looks for is an inward reality: righteousness expressed as genuine charity flowing from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. Only the King can see it, and no outward gift or appearance can substitute for it.

# Bede on Luke 14: Summary of Key Insights

All four excerpts come from **one commentator, the Venerable Bede** (*On the Gospel of Luke*). They focus on a single episode at the start of Luke 14: Jesus healing a man with dropsy at a Pharisee's house on the Sabbath. The rest of the chapter is not addressed here.

---

## 1. Dropsy as a Picture of Spiritual Disease

Bede begins with the illness itself. He notes that the disease of dropsy takes its name from a watery humor. For in Greek, ὕδωρ means water. The symptom he emphasizes is that for the dropsical person, the more the disordered humor abounds, the more they thirst.

He uses this paradox as a spiritual image. The condition is rightly compared to him whom the flowing excess of carnal pleasures oppresses, and also to the avaricious rich man, who, the more abundant his riches are, which he does not use well, the more ardently he covets such things.

**Insight:** Sin, especially greed, is self-intensifying. Indulging it does not satisfy it. It only deepens the craving.

## 2. The Pharisees' Silence and the Sabbath Dilemma

Bede observes that Jesus is said to be "answering" even though no one had spoken aloud. This answer refers to what has been mentioned earlier: And they watched him closely. For the Lord knows the thoughts of men.

He explains why the Pharisees stay silent: whatever they say is said against them. Their position traps them either way: For if it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, why do they watch the Savior to see if he heals? If it is not lawful, why do they themselves provide care for animals on the Sabbath?

**Insight:** Christ answers unspoken hostility, and his question exposes the inconsistency of those looking to accuse him.

## 3. The Healing as an Enacted Rebuke of Greed

For Bede, the miracle is deliberately placed. By provident dispensation the Lord heals the dropsical man before the lawyers and Pharisees, and soon disputes against avarice, so that through the sickness of this body, the sickness of their heart might be expressed.

He supports this with a later remark in Luke's narrative: "But the Pharisees who were lovers of money heard all these things, and they derided him." He then restates the parallel: the dropsical man, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. And every greedy person multiplies his thirst, who, when he has obtained the things he desires, pants for others even more.

**Insight:** The physical healing works as a living parable. The swollen, thirsting body mirrors the condition of the Pharisees' own hearts.

## 4. The Ox and Donkey in the Pit: Mercy and Motive

Bede reads Jesus' question about rescuing an animal from a pit as a further charge of avarice. He paraphrases Christ's point this way: "If you on the Sabbath hasten to rescue a donkey or an ox or any other animal that has fallen into a pit, not for the sake of the animal, but consulting your avarice, how much more ought I to free a man, who is much better than an animal?" In other words, the Pharisees' Sabbath exceptions protect their property, while Christ's protect a person.

He finds the image fitting, since Jesus compared the dropsical man to an animal that had fallen into a pit, for he was oppressed by fluid. He links it to an earlier healing, just as he had compared the woman who had been bound for eighteen years and was freed from that bondage to an animal that is loosed to be led to water.

## 5. Universal Need for Redemption

Bede gives the ox and donkey an allegorical reading. Whether they signify the wise and the dull, or "both peoples," the point is the same: the Savior, coming, found all bound in the chains of Satan, all sunk in the deep pit of desire. He grounds this in Paul: For there is no distinction. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom. III).

**Insight:** The man in the pit represents all of humanity. Everyone is trapped by desire, and everyone is rescued only by Christ's grace.

---

## Key Takeaway

Bede turns a brief Sabbath healing into a meditation on the nature of sin and salvation. Dropsy becomes an image of insatiable greed. The Pharisees' silence exposes their self-interest. The animal in the pit points to a humanity that cannot rescue itself and is freed only through Christ.

# Bede on Luke 22:1–6: Summary of Key Insights

**Note on sources:** All four excerpts come from a single commentator, the Venerable Bede, in his commentary *On the Gospel of Luke*. Every insight below is therefore Bede's. The excerpts cover only the opening verses of Luke 22: the approaching Passover, the leaders' plot, Satan entering Judas, and Judas's agreement with the chief priests. They do not reach the Last Supper or later events in the chapter.

---

## 1. The Meaning of "Passover": Transition, Not Suffering

Bede begins by explaining the word itself. The Passover, which in Hebrew is called phase, is named not from suffering, as many suppose, but from the transition, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not strike them, or the Lord Himself, providing help to His people, walked above.

He then connects this to Christ, drawing on John's Gospel. He says John clearly declares that by the law the day of this festival is mystically called transition because the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, would either himself be passing from this world on that day or would lead us in a healthful transition as if out of Egyptian bondage.

**Key insight:** The Passover is about a *crossing over*. Christ passes from this world to the Father, and he leads believers out of bondage, just as Israel was led out of Egypt.

## 2. Passover and Unleavened Bread: A Pattern for the Christian Life

Bede notes the technical distinction in the Old Testament: the Passover is called the day alone on which the lamb was slain in the evening, that is, the fourteenth moon of the first month. On the fifteenth moon, when they went out of Egypt, the feast of unleavened bread followed. He also observes that the Scripture of the Gospel often uses the day of unleavened bread for the Passover and the days of unleavened bread in place of the Passover.

He finds a spiritual lesson in this sequence. For having slain the lamb in the evening on one particular day, seven consecutive days of unleavened bread follow. In the same way, Christ Jesus, having once suffered in the flesh for us in the fullness of times, orders us to live through all the time of this age, which is done in seven days, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth: always fleeing with earnest effort the desires of the world, as if the snares of Egypt.

**Key insight:** Christ's sacrifice happened once, but the believer's response lasts a lifetime. Bede describes Christians as if making a perpetual Passover, always called to leave the world behind.

## 3. Why the Leaders "Feared the People"

On the chief priests and scribes seeking to kill Jesus, Bede links Luke's account to Matthew's. Matthew places this plotting two days before the Passover, in the court of Caiaphas. Bede also clarifies the nature of their fear: they feared the people, not dreading an uprising, but taking caution lest he be taken from their hands by the aid of the people.

**Key insight:** The leaders were not worried about public disorder in general. They feared that the crowds would rescue Jesus from them.

## 4. Satan's Two "Entrances" into Judas

Bede addresses an apparent tension between the Gospels. Luke says Satan entered Judas before the Supper, while John places it after Jesus gives him the morsel. Bede argues that this does not contradict Luke, who recounts that Satan had already invaded him before the morsel, because the one whom he now entered to deceive, he later entered to possess more fully as one already handed over. In his words, Satan now entered to tempt as though he were still a stranger, then to drag him, as though already his own, to accomplish any harmful deeds he wished.

**Key insight:** Satan's hold on Judas grew in stages, from temptation to full possession. This harmonizes the two Gospel accounts and shows how evil gains ground step by step in a person who yields to it.

## 5. Judas Acted Freely

Bede stresses Judas's personal responsibility. Luke's phrase "he went and spoke" shows that he was invited by the chiefs, not constrained by any necessity, but of his own accord he entered into the plan with a wicked mind.

**Key insight:** Although Satan was at work, Judas was not a helpless puppet. He chose the betrayal willingly, so the guilt is his own.

---

## Overall Themes in Bede's Reading

- **Typology:** The Old Testament Passover foreshadows Christ, the true Lamb.
- **Moral application:** The feast becomes a lifelong call to sincerity, truth, and separation from worldly desires.
- **Harmonizing the Gospels:** Bede draws on Matthew and John to explain Luke and resolves apparent differences between the accounts.
- **Human responsibility:** Even under satanic influence, Judas's betrayal was his own free choice.

# Patristic Commentary on Genesis 33: A Summary

The excerpts come from two Church Fathers who read the chapter in very different ways. Cyril of Alexandria offers a **spiritual (typological) reading** of Jacob and Esau's reconciliation. Jerome focuses on **language and geography**, looking at place names in verses 17–18.

---

## Cyril of Alexandria — *Glaphyra on Genesis* 5.3

**1. The reunion of Jacob and Esau as a figure of Christ and Israel**
Cyril reads the brothers' embrace as a prophetic picture of the end of history: at the end of time our Lord Jesus Christ will be reconciled with Israel, his ancient persecutor, just as Jacob kissed Esau after his return from Haran. Jacob represents Christ, and Esau represents Israel.

**2. Israel's eventual restoration is certain**
Cyril is confident about this hope, insisting that no one who listens to the words of holy Scripture can actually doubt that with the passing of time Israel also will have to be received again into the love of Christ through faith. He supports this with a prophetic text, which he attributes only to one of the holy prophets. It foretells a period without king, sacrifice, or priesthood, after which the children of Israel shall return and shall seek the Lord, their God, and David, their king.

**3. The present age: the nations first, then Israel**
Cyril describes the current situation this way: while Christ, the Savior of us all, gathers believers from the nations, Israel is deserted, since it has no law to elect its leaders, and it cannot offer to the divine altar the sacrifices prescribed by the laws. Israel therefore awaits Christ's return from his action of converting the nations, so that he may receive it as well and unite it with the law of his love to the others.

**4. Jacob's wealth as a symbol of the Church**
Cyril also finds meaning in the details. He points to how Jacob, who rejoiced in the generation of his children and in his numerous herds of sheep, came back from Haran and received again Esau into his friendship. Jacob's large family and flocks stand for the gathered nations, and in time Israel itself will be converted after the calling of the nations and will admire these riches in Christ.

**Key insight:** For Cyril, Genesis 33 points to a final reconciliation within God's plan. The estranged brother is not abandoned but awaited.

---

## Jerome — *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*

Jerome's comments are mostly about language and geography rather than theology. They are useful for understanding names and places in the chapter.

**1. Succoth, the place of "Tabernacles" (Verse 17)**
On the verse where Jacob built a house there for himself, and he built shelters for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Tabernacles, Jerome notes the Hebrew: where we have tents, it is read in Hebrew as Sochoth. He adds that in his own day there is a city beyond the Jordan with this name in the region of Scythopolis.

**2. Shechem and the puzzle of "Salem" (Verse 18)**
Jerome addresses a difficulty: how Shechem is called the city of Salem, when Jerusalem, where Melchizedek reigned, was previously called Salem. The verse as quoted in the excerpt does not itself mention "Salem," so the wording of the text Jerome was working from is not fully shown here. He offers two solutions:
- **Two cities could share a name.** This happens elsewhere, since the same name of the city and place is in different tribes.
- **The word has two meanings.** Applied to Shechem, it translates to "consummated" or "perfect" in our language, and that the one which was later called Jerusalem is transferred to "peaceful", with the two senses distinguished by a slight difference in accent.

**3. A Jewish tradition about Jacob's healing**
Jerome also reports an interpretation from Jewish teachers: The Hebrews say that it refers to the limp of Jacob's thigh, where he became weakened and was healed. On this reading, the city is the same as the one that received the name of the cured and perfected. Jerome simply passes on this tradition. The excerpt does not show him developing it theologically, though it does suggest that Jacob arrives at Shechem "whole" after his earlier weakness.

**Key insight:** Jerome grounds the chapter in its Hebrew wording and real locations. The tradition he reports hints that Jacob's arrival in the land carries a sense of healing and completeness.

---

## Comparing the Two Approaches

| | **Cyril** | **Jerome** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | The Jacob–Esau reconciliation (spiritual meaning) | Place names in vv. 17–18 (literal and linguistic meaning) |
| **Method** | Typology and prophecy | Hebrew language, geography, Jewish tradition |
| **Main theme** | Christ's future reconciliation with Israel | Succoth as "tents"; Shechem/Salem as "perfect" or "healed" |

Together they show two complementary ways the early Church read Scripture: Cyril looks for how the story points to Christ and the end of history, while Jerome works to clarify the text's language and setting.

# Patristic Commentary on Acts 26: Summary

## Clement of Alexandria

Clement's excerpt is a **quotation of Paul's commission** rather than an interpretation of it. He cites the passage in which Paul is sent "to the Gentiles... to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God; that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them that are sanctified by faith which is in Me."

**Note:** The excerpt contains no explanation of how Clement understands or applies the verse. It shows that he considered this commission worth citing, but it offers no distinct theological insight we can attribute to him.

## John Chrysostom

Chrysostom's excerpts give more interpretation. They focus on Paul's character and manner as a witness.

### 1. Paul's mildness and the persuasive power of the vision
Chrysostom points out the gentle tone of Paul's defense: "observe how mildly he discourses— God, he says, said (this) to me". He reads Paul's conversion as being won over by God rather than forced: "By these things, says he, I was persuaded, by this vision He drew me to Himself, and so persuaded me, that I made no delay."

**Insight:** Paul presents his mission as God's initiative, not his own. Chrysostom sees his immediate obedience as the fruit of God drawing him.

### 2. Obedience expressed in preaching repentance
Chrysostom follows Paul's account of what that obedience looked like. Paul "showed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance."

**Insight:** True conversion leads to action. Paul's response was outward-facing ministry, and his message called for repentance shown in deeds.

### 3. Calm reply to Festus's accusation
Chrysostom notes the contrast in tone. Festus spoke "in such anger and displeasure... Paul, you are beside yourself." Paul answers calmly, "I am not mad", and appeals to public evidence: "For this thing, he says, was not done in a corner."

**Insight:** The gospel rests on publicly known events, not private delusion. Paul answers hostility with composure.

### 4. Paul's reply to Agrippa: a distinctive reading
Chrysostom offers an unusual interpretation. He suggests Paul did not understand what the phrase ἐν ὀλίγῳ meant: he thought it meant ἐξ ὀλιγου (i.e. with little cost or trouble), wherefore also he answers (as) to this: so unlearned was he. In other words, Chrysostom thinks Paul took Agrippa's words in a different sense than Agrippa meant them, and attributes this to Paul's lack of learning.

He also praises Paul's sincerity: "And he said not, I do not wish (that), but, I pray that not only thou, but also all that hear. Mark how free from flattery his speech is.— I pray that this day they may be all such as I am, except these bonds."

**Insight:** Paul speaks to a king without flattery. His wish is for the salvation of *all* his hearers, while he sets aside the chains he wears. This shows both his honesty and his goodwill toward those who sit in judgment over him.

## Key Takeaways

- **Clement** preserves the core statement of Paul's mission (turning people from darkness to light and toward forgiveness) but adds no commentary of his own in this excerpt.
- **Chrysostom** focuses on **Paul's character as a witness**: gentle in speech, quick to obey, calm under accusation, grounded in public events, and free of flattery, with a sincere desire that everyone hearing him would come to share his faith.

# Patristic Insights on Hebrews 8: Christ as Priest and Offering

All four excerpts focus on one theme: Christ's role as high priest, and in particular what he offered. Two commentators address Hebrews 8:3 directly. The other two are thematically related but do not explicitly reference the chapter.

## John Chrysostom: Why the Exalted Christ Is Still Called "Priest"

Chrysostom quotes the verse directly: "every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer." He sees a tension the author of Hebrews is resolving. Christ is described as seated in heaven, but readers should not, because you hear that he sits, suppose that his being called high priest is mere idle talk.

He distinguishes two truths about Christ. The former—his sitting—belongs to the dignity of the Godhead, but this [his being a priest] to his great lovingkindness and his tender care for us. In his view, the author emphasizes Christ's priesthood for he feared lest the other truth should overthrow it.

Chrysostom also says this reasoning answers a practical question, since some were inquiring why he died. His logic is simple: He was a priest. But there is no priest without a sacrifice. It is necessary then that he also should have a sacrifice.

**Key insight:** Christ's priesthood expresses his compassion, and it explains why his death was necessary.

## Theodoret of Cyrus: The Incarnation as Priestly Offering

Theodoret also comments directly on 8:3, but very briefly. He affirms that it is proper for a high priest to offer gifts to the God of all. He then identifies what Christ offered: the only begotten, when he was made man and assumed our nature, offered it for us.

**Key insight:** The "something to offer" of 8:3 is the human nature Christ took on in the Incarnation.

## Augustine of Hippo: Christ Unites Every Element of Sacrifice

This excerpt comes from *On the Trinity*. It does not quote or name Hebrews 8, but it develops the same priest-and-sacrifice theme in depth.

Augustine describes what a true sacrifice requires. It must be offered by a holy and righteous priest, and it has to be without fault, so that it may be offered for cleansing those with faults. He argues that Christ meets every requirement:

- **A sinless priest:** Christ had no need to purge his own sins by sacrifice, neither original sins nor those that are added by human life.
- **A pure offering:** he points to the flesh born in and from the womb of a virgin without any infection of carnal desires.
- **Priest and sacrifice in one:** he asks what could be more acceptably offered and taken than that the flesh of our sacrifice be the body of our priest?

His most notable contribution is a four-part framework. Every sacrifice involves (1) to whom it is offered, (2) by whom it is offered, (3) what is offered, (4) for whom it is offered. In Christ, the one mediator might remain one with him [the Father] to whom he offered, might make those one in himself for whom he offered, and he himself might be in one both the offerer and the offering.

**Key insight:** Christ fulfills all four aspects of sacrifice in himself.

## Athanasius of Alexandria: Why Only the Word Could Make the Offering

This excerpt is from a letter and does not explicitly address Hebrews 8. Its language does echo the chapter's theme, however. Athanasius writes that the Word became man in the body for our salvation in order that, having something to offer for us he might save us all.

His distinctive point is about who could make the offering. It was not some man that gave himself up for us; since every man is under sentence of death. Nor yet was it any other of the creatures, since every creature is liable to change. Instead, the Word himself offered his own body on our behalf that our faith and hope might not be in man, but that we might have our faith in God the Word himself.

He also stresses that the Incarnation was a free act. It happened by the good pleasure of the Father, not because the Word became man in consequence of his nature.

**Key insight:** Only God the Word, not any human or creature, could offer a saving sacrifice. As a result, believers' faith rests in God himself.

## Summary

Together, these Fathers interpret the principle that a priest must "have something to offer" through the Incarnation:

- **Chrysostom** explains why Hebrews insists on Christ's priesthood and links it to his death.
- **Theodoret** identifies the offering as Christ's assumed human nature.
- **Augustine** shows Christ as both offerer and offering.
- **Athanasius** stresses that only the divine Word could make this offering effective.

# Patristic Insights on John 13: A Summary

## Origen of Alexandria (*On Prayer* 23.2)

**A note on relevance:** This excerpt does not quote John 13 directly. Its reference to "the one who loves Jesus' word" suggests its main focus may be elsewhere in John's Gospel. However, its language of Christ moving "from this world to the Father" closely echoes the opening of John 13, so it offers a useful perspective.

**Key insight: Christ's "departure" is not physical but a return to glory.**
- Origen insists that such language does not refer to the idea of a change of place with respect to the Father and the Son toward the one who loves Jesus' word, nor can it be understood in a spatial sense.
- Instead, the Word of God, by condescending to us and by being humbled, as it were, in regard to his own worth, when he is present with human beings, is said to change places from this world to the Father.
- The outcome is that we also see him in his perfection, returning from the emptying with which he emptied himself alongside us, to his own fullness.

In Origen's reading, "departing" describes the movement from humility back to divine fullness, not a journey through space.

---

## Augustine of Hippo (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 55 and related commentary)

*Note: Documents 2, 3, and 4 contain largely overlapping material from Augustine. The longer commentary (Document 2) goes further, covering the foot washing.*

### 1. The Meaning of "Passover": Christ's Passage and Ours
Augustine draws theological meaning from the word *Pascha*. He notes that it is not, as some think, a Greek noun, but it is Hebrew. In Hebrew it means "Passover," because the Pascha was then celebrated for the first time by God's people when, in their flight from Egypt, they passed over the Red Sea.

He sees the Exodus fulfilled in Christ. By his blood, that is, by the sign of his cross marked on our foreheads, we may be delivered from the perdition awaiting this world, just as Israel was delivered from the bondage and destruction of the Egyptians. For believers, We perform a most salutary journey when we pass over from the devil to Christ and from this unstable world to his well-established kingdom.

Christ's passing to the Father gives hope to his followers: The hope was thus given to the members in their Head, that they doubtless would yet follow Him who was passing before. Augustine also draws a sharp contrast: it is one thing to pass from the world, and another to pass away with it; one thing to pass to the Father, another to pass to the enemy. He illustrates this with the Egyptians, who did not pass through the sea to the kingdom, but in the sea to destruction.

### 2. "He Loved Them to the End": Love That Reaches Its Goal in Christ
Augustine reinterprets "to the end" as pointing to Christ himself: For what do these words "to the end" mean but "to Christ"? Christ is the end that consummates, not that consumes. He is our end. We pass into him.

He rejects reading the phrase as meaning Christ loved only until death. That reading is human, not divine, for it was not merely up to this point that we were loved by him who loves us always and endlessly. As he puts it, God forbid that he whose death could not end should have ended his love at death.

He does accept one related meaning: that he so loved them as to die for them. In other words, it was His very love that carried Him on to death.

### 3. The Timing of the Supper
Augustine clarifies a detail in the narrative. "Supper having taken place" does not mean the meal was finished, for it was still going on when the Lord rose and washed His disciples' feet. Rather, it means that it was now ready, and laid out on the table for the use of the guests.

### 4. Judas and the Nature of Temptation
On the devil putting betrayal into Judas's heart, Augustine explains that Such a putting [into the heart] is a spiritual suggestion: and enters not by the ear, but through the thoughts. He observes how subtly such suggestions mingle with human thoughts that a man accounts them his own. He adds that good suggestions also come from a good spirit, and what matters is to which of these the human mind yields assent.

He describes Judas at the meal as a spy on the Shepherd, a plotter against the Redeemer, a seller of the Saviour, who thought himself undiscovered: for he was deceived about Him whom he wished to deceive.

### 5. Christ's Sovereignty, Even Over Betrayal
Because the Father had given "all things" into Christ's hands, this included the traitor himself: for if He had him not in His hands, He certainly could not use him as He wished. Thus the Lord knew what He was doing for His friends, and patiently made use of His enemies. Christ came from God and returned to God, neither quitting God when He came from Him, nor us when He returned.

### 6. Majesty and Humility in the Foot Washing
Augustine notes that John deliberately highlights Christ's majesty before describing his humility: when about to speak of the pre-eminent humility of the Lord, it was his desire first to commend His majesty. The one who held all things discharged the office of a servant, not of God the Lord, but of man. That humility is magnified because He did not esteem it beneath His dignity to wash also the feet of one whose hands He already foresaw to be steeped in wickedness.

### 7. The Foot Washing as a Picture of the Incarnation and the Cross
Augustine reads each action as a symbol of Christ's saving work, drawing on Philippians 2:
- Laying aside his garments recalls the one who, being in the form of God, made Himself of no reputation.
- The basin of water recalls the one who poured His blood upon the earth to wash away the filth of their sins.

He adds an important distinction. Christ removed his garments to serve, but in becoming human He laid not down what He had, but assumed that which He had not before.

### 8. The Call to Imitate Christ's Humility
Augustine closes with a moral appeal: proud man would have perished eternally, had he not been found by the lowly God. Therefore, as he was lost by imitating the pride of the deceiver, let him now, when found, imitate the Redeemer's humility.

---

## Common Thread

Both commentators read Christ's "departure to the Father" theologically rather than literally:
- **Origen** sees it as the Word's return from self-emptying to divine fullness.
- **Augustine** sees it as the true Passover, a passage that believers are invited to share.

Both also emphasize Christ's voluntary self-emptying. Augustine develops this most fully through the foot washing, which he presents as a living picture of the Incarnation and the Cross, and as a model for Christian humility.
